title: MonaVec: A Training-Free Embedded Vector Search Kernel for Edge and Offline AI Systems
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/mona-hq/monavec (PyPI: monavec; crates.io: monavec-core). Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20559587
summary:
We present MonaVec, a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel for edge and offline AI -- settings where server infrastructure, network connectivity, and training data are all unavailable. Existing vector-search systems assume a persistent server, gigabytes of RAM, or a training pass over the corpus; MonaVec instead targets the deployment profile of SQLite: one file, one function call, runs anywhere. Its quantization core is training-free by default and data-oblivious: a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1), so precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8x smaller) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file whose embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed makes results reproducible across architectures and byte-identical within a build -- a determinism guarantee that parallel-build graph libraries cannot offer.
  On semantic embeddings (AG News, 45K x 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce reaches 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB -- leading float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall -- while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism. A single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the same data-oblivious pipeline to magnitude-sensitive L2 data, and optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends carry it to million-vector corpora.
  MonaVec is implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar). It targets on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval -- the niche SQLite occupies for relational data: one file, one call, runs anywhere.

AI.tldr: MonaVec is a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel targeting edge/offline AI, analogous to SQLite for vector retrieval. It uses a training-free, data-oblivious quantization pipeline (Randomized Hadamard Transform + precomputed Lloyd-Max tables) to achieve 4-bit compression without learning codebooks. Results show 0.960 Recall@10 on AG News with BGE-M3 embeddings in 27 MB, outperforming float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall while guaranteeing byte-identical determinism.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-search systems assume server infrastructure, ample RAM, or require a training pass over the corpus. The authors identify a gap for embedded/offline deployment scenarios — analogous to SQLite's role for relational data — where no server, no network, and no training data are available. They seek a single-file, single-function-call, runs-anywhere solution with deterministic, reproducible results.
AI.method: The core innovation is a training-free, data-oblivious quantization pipeline: (1) a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions arbitrary input distributions toward N(0,1); (2) precomputed Lloyd-Max tables then quantize to 4 bits (8× compression) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file with an embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed ensuring byte-identical reproducibility across architectures. An optional single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the pipeline to L2 data. Backends include BruteForce, IvfFlat, and HNSW for scaling to million-vector corpora. Implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar).
AI.result: On AG News (45K × 1024-dim BGE-M3 embeddings, cosine similarity), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce achieves 0.960 Recall@10 using only 27 MB, surpassing float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall. The system trades peak throughput for byte-identical determinism across architectures. The pipeline also generalizes to magnitude-sensitive L2 data via a single-pass fit() standardization step.
AI.conclusion: MonaVec successfully fills the niche of embedded vector search — the "SQLite for vector data" — providing a deterministic, training-free, single-file solution that runs anywhere. It achieves competitive or superior recall with significant memory savings (4-bit quantization) while guaranteeing cross-architecture reproducibility, making it suitable for on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval applications.

title: Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center
summary: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

AI.tldr: A formal model for decentralized inference across independent agents who share only typed observations (not weights, gradients, or hidden states), proving convergence to a unique answer, identification-completeness under carrier-connected views, and confidentiality through an observation-only policy—all governed by a single admission/emission framework grounded in coupled free energy minimization.
AI.motivation: Current distributed or federated learning paradigms require sharing of weights, gradients, or hidden states, which exposes internal agent information and requires central coordination. The authors seek a truly decentralized inference mechanism where agents retain complete privacy of their internals while collectively arriving at conclusions no single agent could reach alone, motivated by the principle that model querying is fundamentally energy-minimizing inference.
AI.method: The authors formalize mesh inference as a coupled free energy system where each agent performs local relaxation. They prove that the coupling matrix is always an M-matrix, guaranteeing unique convergence regardless of admission symmetry. Three properties are derived from a unified admission/emission policy: (1) convergence to a unique fixed point, (2) identification-completeness (exact centralized optimum recovery when views are carrier-connected), and (3) observation-only confidentiality as the dual of identification. In the linear-Gaussian regime, they characterize O(diam²) latency as the price of decentralization, and frame the process as one turn of a center-free learning loop.
AI.result: Mesh inference converges uniquely for any admission policy; it exactly recovers the centralized optimum under carrier-connected views; confidentiality is formally established as the dual of identification, with content-addressed lineage as the sole side-channel; and in the linear-Gaussian case, every derived answer equals the centralized optimum with O(diam²) latency.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the first formal model of mesh inference, establishing a principled foundation for fully decentralized, privacy-preserving collective inference. An open problem remains: determining under what conditions non-linear closure improves collective knowledge versus producing confident errors.

title: Supporting Design Decisions in Rule-Based Model Transformations
summary: Model Driven Engineering relies on model transformations to automate the derivation of target models or source code from source models. However, the design decisions that govern how source elements are mapped to target artifacts typically remain embedded in the transformation source code, limiting flexibility, reusability, and traceability. This paper proposes an approach to explicitly model and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations. Design decisions are separated from transformation implementation through three mechanisms. First, a decision model captures design decisions and their options independently of any source modeling language for a given transformation domain. Second, a binding model connects these decisions to specific metamodel concepts in a given source modeling language, enabling reuse of the same design knowledge across transformations from similar languages. Third, a configuration model records the specific option chosen for each applicable source model element, with defaults pre-selected automatically. During execution, variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically according to configured choices. A trace model records which rules and options were applied to produce each target element. We establish a formal mathematical framework that defines the core concepts of variability-based transformations and proves key properties of the resulting transformations. The formal concepts are realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models. We demonstrate practical feasibility by extending an existing embedded domain-specific language for model-driven engineering with variability support and illustrate the approach with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

AI.tldr: Proposes an approach to externalize design decisions from model transformation code using decision, binding, and configuration models, supported by a formal framework and demonstrated with an ER-to-Relational transformation example.
AI.motivation: In model-driven engineering, transformation design decisions are typically hard-coded within transformation source code, which limits flexibility (difficult to switch mapping strategies), reusability (decisions tied to specific languages), and traceability (unclear which decisions produced which target artifacts).
AI.method: The approach introduces three separation mechanisms: (1) a decision model capturing design options independently of any source metamodel; (2) a binding model linking generic decisions to specific metamodel concepts, enabling cross-language reuse; (3) a configuration model recording per-element option choices with automatic defaults. Variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically at execution. A trace model records rule-option-to-target-element provenance. A formal mathematical framework defines variability-based transformations and proves key properties, realized in a four-artifact architecture. Feasibility is shown by extending an embedded DSL for MDE and applying it to ER-to-Relational mapping.
AI.result: A formal framework with proven properties for variability-based transformations; a practical architecture of four interconnected models (decision, binding, configuration, trace); a working extension of an embedded DSL demonstrating the approach on a complete ER-to-Relational transformation.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling transformation design decisions as first-class artifacts improves flexibility, reusability, and traceability in rule-based model transformations, with formal guarantees and practical feasibility demonstrated.

title: Exposing the Unsaid: Visualizing Hidden LLM Bias through Stochastic Path Aggregation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit representational and syntactic biases that are difficult to evaluate due to the stochastic nature of text generation. Standard auditing methods rely on a single output inspection or static automated metrics. These approaches obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. This paper introduces TreeTracer, a visual analytics tool designed to evaluate LLM bias through aggregated comparison. Using a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline, the tool replaces ontology-defined terms in each input prompt, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure, and then performs classification-aware node merging with an auxiliary language model. The resulting structure is visualized through a custom Sankey diagram. By juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, the workspace enables direct comparison between semantic contexts and supports systematic bias detection. Because any visualization reflects only a subset of the model's learned behavior, the system further applies contrastive inference to compute and directly display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts, reducing the risk of misinterpreting the presence of bias. We validate the workspace through case studies comparing an unaligned baseline model GPT-2 XL against the constitutionally aligned Apertus models. The visual aggregation successfully exposes hidden representational harms, such as counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.

AI.tldr: TreeTracer is a visual analytics tool that aggregates hundreds of stochastic LLM generations into hierarchical Sankey diagrams, enabling systematic comparison of biases across semantic contexts. It uses perturbation analysis, syntax-aligned tree structures, and contrastive inference to expose hidden representational harms like pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM bias auditing methods (single-output inspection, static metrics) obscure underlying probability distributions and miss biases in lower-probability generation branches. There is a need for aggregated, comparative, visually interpretable methods that capture the stochastic nature of text generation and reveal latent representational harms.
AI.method: TreeTracer employs: (1) a perturbation analysis pipeline that replaces ontology-defined terms in prompts; (2) aggregation of hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure; (3) classification-aware node merging using an auxiliary language model; (4) visualization via custom Sankey diagrams juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees; and (5) contrastive inference to compute and display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts.
AI.result: Case studies comparing GPT-2 XL against Apertus models successfully exposed hidden representational harms, including counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization. A preliminary user study confirmed that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports bias detection.
AI.conclusion: TreeTracer demonstrates that aggregated, comparative visualization combined with contrastive inference provides a rigorous and interpretable framework for auditing LLM biases. The approach mitigates misinterpretation risks inherent in single-output or static-metric methods and proves effective for human analysts detecting systemic representational harms.

title: Secure Coding Drift in LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix
comment: Accepted for 2026 SIGIR Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information Retrieval track
summary: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Secure Coding Drift in PQC," a socio-technical vulnerability model describing how sustained LLM reliance degrades secure coding practices over time in Post-Quantum Cryptography implementation, and proposes a gamified, LLM-augmented framework with adversarial evaluation and behavioural feedback to mitigate this drift.
AI.motivation: PQC implementation demands rigorous constant-time execution, side-channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. While LLMs are increasingly embedded in cryptographic engineering workflows, they frequently produce insecure or suboptimal code. Existing research focuses on static vulnerabilities, failing to capture the longitudinal, behavioural degradation of secure coding practices that emerges from sustained human-AI interaction.
AI.method: The authors conceptualise "Secure Coding Drift" as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon and propose a gamified, LLM-augmented secure coding framework. This framework integrates three components into development workflows: (1) adversarial evaluation to probe code security, (2) behavioural feedback mechanisms to alert developers, and (3) security scoring to incentivise adherence. The approach reframes LLMs from passive code generators into active security co-pilots.
AI.result: The paper is conceptual and does not present empirical results. It contributes the Secure Coding Drift model and the architectural design of the proposed mitigation framework as theoretical and methodological contributions toward safer PQC implementation.
AI.conclusion: Sustained LLM reliance in PQC engineering creates a gradual erosion of secure coding practices — Secure Coding Drift — which static vulnerability analysis cannot capture. Embedding adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into LLM-augmented workflows can transform LLMs into active security co-pilots, contributing to safer PQC adoption in AI-mediated development environments.

title: Computational Identifiability
summary: Identification conditions describe the computability of a target query or parameter of interest as a function of the type and amount of information available. In causal identification, this information is often expressed in the form of a causal graph, and data are observed or collected for some subset of variables in the graph. Target queries may be for a single effect alone or for a class of effects in a given model. The derivation of an identification algorithm then defines mathematically the process by which the desired causal effect(s) can be uniquely determined, theoretically, in expectation. Identifiability in expectation, or 'theoretical identifiability,' generally assumes asymptotic properties, infinite data, or other mathematically idealized conditions. In this paper, we explore a fundamental distinction between this theoretical, idealized notion of identifiability and a proposed alternative that is computation-bound. The framework we propose - 'computational identifiability' - is to instead define a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If this process finds an estimator empirically, within a desired error tolerance, then identifiability is satisfied, conditional on the specified assumptions of the search (i.e., a prior distribution over the parameters) and conditional on the search procedure itself. Through several experiments, we demonstrate how this framework allows us to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions, such as identification with small finite samples, with ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands. Code is available at https://github.com/lbynum/metadentify.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "computational identifiability," a practical alternative to traditional theoretical identifiability. Instead of relying on asymptotic assumptions and idealized conditions, it defines identifiability through a finite computational search procedure that empirically finds an estimator within a specified error tolerance, conditional on the search's priors and procedure.
AI.motivation: Traditional causal identifiability relies on asymptotic properties and infinite data assumptions, which fail to address practical challenges like small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and counterfactual estimands. There is a need for a more practical, computation-bound notion of identifiability that can handle these real-world constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework called "computational identifiability" that defines a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. Identifiability is satisfied if the search finds an estimator empirically within a desired error tolerance, conditional on assumptions of the search (a prior distribution over parameters) and the search procedure itself. The framework is demonstrated through multiple experiments on the Metadentify platform.
AI.result: The framework successfully addresses fine-grained practical identification questions involving small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and counterfactual data and estimands — scenarios where traditional theoretical identifiability falls short.
AI.conclusion: Computational identifiability offers a meaningful departure from idealized identifiability by grounding identification in finite, empirical computation. It provides a pragmatic lens for answering practical causal identification questions that theoretical approaches cannot adequately handle. Code is publicly available.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. To be published in the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Agentic Services which is part of the IEEE Conference on Web Services
summary: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AgenticRei, a governance framework for LLM-driven autonomous agents that extends beyond permit/prohibit access control to include deontic concepts (obligations, dispensations, meta-policy conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning), implemented via OWL-based Rei policies evaluated outside the LLM by a logic engine.
AI.motivation: Current policy engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar) only address permit/prohibit decisions. LLM-based autonomous agents present a broader governance challenge: they invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate across organizational boundaries. This requires specifying obligations (e.g., notify CISO after certain actions), dispensations (waiving obligations under conditions), meta-policy conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning over domain hierarchies — all absent from existing production systems.
AI.method: The authors propose AgenticRei, which extends the Rei deontic policy framework using OWL (Web Ontology Language) for policy expression. Governance policies are evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine operating entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages. The system composes with industry frameworks like A2AS.
AI.result: Through examples, the paper demonstrates that deontic policies can capture security and privacy governance constraints that are largely inexpressible in current production policy engines, covering obligations, dispensations, and conflict resolution alongside standard permit/prohibit rules.
AI.conclusion: AgenticRei fills a critical gap in enterprise governance for autonomous AI agents by providing a complete deontic policy framework. It enables expression of obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning — capabilities beyond current engines — while integrating with existing standards like A2AS.

title: SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design
summary: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational. Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD, the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline, by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points, respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points. These results suggest that compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SIGMA-2338/.

AI.tldr: SIGMA proposes a skill-incidence graph framework for multi-agent systems where agents are dynamically composed from reusable skills based on task requirements, rather than being fixed entities. It predicts which skills to activate, composes agent embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology — achieving superior performance and robustness across reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based multi-agent systems optimize communication topologies but treat agents as fixed, closed-set entities. This limits generalization to tasks requiring unseen combinations of capabilities. The authors identify compositional node construction — dynamically assembling agents from skills — as a neglected complementary axis to topology optimization.
AI.method: SIGMA operates in three stages: (1) given a task and a skill library, it predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix determining which skills compose each agent; (2) it generates agent node embeddings by aggregating embeddings of selected skills; (3) it decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. At execution time, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to relevant capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational.
AI.result: Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance, outperforming the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline (CARD) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points on the three LLMs. It demonstrates stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points.
AI.conclusion: Compositional node construction — dynamically assembling agents from reusable skills — is a complementary and important design axis for multi-agent systems beyond communication topology optimization. SIGMA's strong generalization to unseen skill combinations validates this approach.

title: ClayBuddy: A Framework, Evaluation, & Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures
summary: Software engineering and deployment are increasingly delegated to AI coding agents. The scale of their adoption is surfacing rare, but highly destructive, failure modes. In this paper, we study these failure modes as stemming from three distinct mechanisms: underspecification, where default model behavior is unsafe; capability errors, where the safe action is available but the model does not adhere to it due to bias or capability limitations; and agent harness errors, where the model fails to execute the safe action through the harness. We assess these across 8 different evaluations, each inspired by real-life deployment failures, totaling 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. Based on this evaluation, we propose ClayBuddy, a harness that molds to user preferences and can be modified by the model in-session, to mitigate these errors. By adding tools for the agent to edit its own context, an extended system prompt, a customizable command classifier, and deterministic guardrails, we show that ClayBuddy is safer across a statistically significant number of samples. Thus, we suggest concrete mitigations for current coding agents and a design philosophy for future agent harness features.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three failure modes in AI coding agents—underspecification, capability errors, and agent harness errors—evaluates them across 8 assessments based on real deployment failures, and proposes ClayBuddy, a customizable harness that mitigates these errors through in-session editing tools, extended prompts, a command classifier, and deterministic guardrails.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents are increasingly used for software engineering and deployment, rare but highly destructive failure modes are emerging. These failures stem not from a single source but from a combination of specification gaps, model limitations, and harness-level execution issues. The authors aim to systematically categorize and evaluate these failure mechanisms and propose actionable mitigations.
AI.method: The authors taxonomize failures into three mechanisms: underspecification (unsafe default behaviors), capability errors (model fails to select a safe action despite its availability, due to bias or capability limits), and agent harness errors (model correctly identifies the safe action but the harness fails to execute it). They evaluate these across 8 assessments inspired by real deployment incidents, using 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. They then develop ClayBuddy, a harness featuring in-session context-editing tools, an extended system prompt, a customizable command classifier, and deterministic guardrails, and test its safety improvements statistically.
AI.result: ClayBuddy demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements over baseline harnesses across the evaluated samples, effectively mitigating all three failure mechanisms through its combination of user-preference molding, model-modifiable context, and deterministic safeguards.
AI.conclusion: The three-mechanism taxonomy provides a useful lens for diagnosing AI coding agent failures. ClayBuddy offers concrete, implementable mitigations and embodies a design philosophy where agent harnesses should be mutable by the model in-session while respecting user preferences and retaining deterministic guardrails—pointing toward safer future coding agent architectures.

title: Ensembles of Large Language Models for Identifying EQ-5D Studies in PubMed Based on Their Abstracts
summary: The rapid increase in scientific publications leads to the fact that manual study screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource consuming, inefficient, and inconsistent. Classifying studies that clearly report health-related quality-of-life results, such as EQ-5D data, requires a high level of clinical interpretation and poses challenges for human reviewers. This study investigates the use of Google's Gemini and Gemma large language models (LLMs) in automating EQ-5D detection in the PubMed biomedical database based only on published abstracts. A multi-phase framework is proposed that integrates few-shot prompting, weight ensembling aggregation, and a soft stacking meta-classifier. Nine LLMs are evaluated on a dataset of PubMed studies manually labeled by two experts regarding EQ-5D reporting. The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b obtained a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding individually attained results. The ensembling of top-performing models improved the balance between precision and recall compared to individual models, while the soft stacking approach provided greater reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis shows that the probability results from the models are important in guiding the final predictions. The findings suggest that an ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating screening in biomedical research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-phase ensemble framework using Google's Gemini and Gemma LLMs (few-shot prompting, weight ensembling, soft stacking) to automate detection of EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life results in PubMed abstracts, achieving 0.74 weighted F1-score and accuracy, outperforming individual models.
AI.motivation: Manual study screening for systematic literature reviews is increasingly resource-intensive, inefficient, and inconsistent due to the rapid growth of scientific publications. Detecting studies reporting EQ-5D data requires high-level clinical interpretation, posing particular challenges for human reviewers.
AI.method: A multi-phase framework integrating: (1) few-shot prompting of nine LLMs (Gemini and Gemma variants); (2) weight ensembling aggregation combining top-performing models; and (3) a soft stacking meta-classifier. Models are evaluated on a PubMed dataset manually labeled by two experts for EQ-5D reporting. Feature analysis examines model probability outputs as predictors.
AI.result: The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b achieved 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding all individual model performances. Ensembling improved precision-recall balance, while soft stacking provided greater reliability and interpretability. Model probability outputs were key features guiding final predictions.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble-based LLM approach is a reliable, scalable solution for automating biomedical screening tasks, with the combination of multiple models improving both performance and interpretability over single-model baselines.

title: FloatDoor: Platform-Triggered Backdoors in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive settings such as software engineering, where their outputs directly shape downstream artifacts. Recent work has shown that an identical model can produce measurably different outputs depending on the deployment platform, a consequence of non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. We study the security implications of this platform-dependent variability and uncover a novel attack surface on LLM deployments. We introduce FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against generative LLMs. The compromised model exhibits adversary-chosen behavior when served on a target platform and is otherwise benign. FloatDoor is realized through two lightweight LoRA adapters, one that amplifies inter-platform numerical divergence and one that binds the resulting platform signature to a malicious downstream task, while leaving aggregate model utility largely intact. FloatDoor exploits a pronounced time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving. We demonstrate FloatDoor on Qwen3-4B across a broad range of deployment targets, including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. As a final case study, we show that FloatDoor reliably induces exploitable code vulnerabilities on a chosen target platform. Our results establish a new class of attacks on LLM deployments and underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

AI.tldr: FloatDoor is the first input-independent backdoor attack on LLMs triggered solely by the deployment platform. It uses two lightweight LoRA adapters — one to amplify floating-point divergence across platforms and one to bind the resulting platform signature to malicious behavior — enabling a compromised model to behave normally during auditing but exhibit adversary-chosen behavior only on a specific target platform (e.g., NVIDIA GPU, Google TPU).
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in sensitive domains (e.g., software engineering) produce measurably different outputs on different hardware platforms due to non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. This phenomenon creates a time-of-check, time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap between model auditing and serving, which the authors exploit to mount a novel supply-chain attack where a model passes integrity checks but behaves maliciously only when served on a specific target platform.
AI.method: The attack, FloatDoor, uses two lightweight LoRA adapters: (1) a Divergence Amplification Adapter that magnifies inter-platform numerical differences to create a stable, detectable platform signature, and (2) a Trigger Binding Adapter that associates this platform signature with a malicious downstream task. Both adapters are trained jointly while preserving the base model's aggregate utility. The attack requires no specific input trigger — the platform itself serves as the backdoor key.
AI.result: FloatDoor was demonstrated on Qwen3-4B across multiple deployment targets including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. The attack reliably induced exploitable code vulnerabilities (e.g., in generated software) on the chosen target platform while maintaining benign behavior on all other platforms and during pre-deployment auditing.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new class of platform-triggered backdoor attacks on LLM deployments, exposing a critical vulnerability in model supply chains. It underscores the urgent need for trusted, verifiable model supply chains and platform-aware integrity guarantees in sensitive LLM-powered applications.

title: When to Trust, How to Distill: Multi-Foundation Model Guidance for Lightweight, Robust Scientific Time Series Forecasting
comment: KDD 2026, paper decision: Accepted, track: AI for Science. total 12 pages including references and appendix
summary: The deployment of Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in physical sciences is hindered by a critical trade-off: while these models encode rich, universal temporal dynamics, they suffer from severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and their computational cost prohibits deployment in edge-computing sensor networks. We address a fundamental challenge: How can we extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models (FM) to train lightweight, specialized forecasters? We propose Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation (Guard), a novel framework that reframes multiteacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality. We evaluate our proposed lightweight framework on four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids. Our method significantly reduces RMSE relative to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline, successfully distilling knowledge from pretrained FMs (teachers) even when they exhibit suboptimal zero-shot accuracy due to distribution shift between the original and target data domains. We demonstrate that these domain-misaligned teachers can still serve as critical correctives, outperforming the globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. Ultimately, this enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/RupasreeDey/GUARD-KDD2026.

AI.tldr: GUARD proposes a multi-teacher distillation framework with dynamic teacher routing and uncertainty-gated knowledge transfer, enabling lightweight forecasters for edge deployment by extracting useful structural knowledge even from domain-misaligned time-series foundation models.
AI.motivation: Time-Series Foundation Models suffer from distributional misalignment in specialized scientific domains and are too computationally expensive for edge deployment. The core question is how to salvage latent structural knowledge from these misaligned models to train efficient, domain-specialized forecasters.
AI.method: GUARD introduces two novel mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that performs instance-wise teacher selection based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that dynamically attenuates distillation strength when teacher predictions diverge from the target domain, acting as a circuit-breaker to prevent harmful knowledge transfer.
AI.result: GUARD significantly reduces RMSE compared to fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baselines across four climate-critical domains (meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, energy grids). Misaligned teachers still provide critical corrective signals, outperforming globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances.
AI.conclusion: Domain-misaligned foundation models retain valuable structural knowledge that can be effectively extracted via adaptive, uncertainty-aware distillation, enabling high-precision scientific forecasting on resource-constrained edge devices.

title: Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023
summary: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: A reproducible human-in-the-loop pipeline measures undergraduate CS program coverage against curricular guidelines (CS2013 and CS2023) using semantic retrieval and human validation, revealing near-constant coverage (~50%) across a decade, persistent structural gaps, and a drop in cognitive-depth alignment due to raised expectations in CS2023.
AI.motivation: Undergraduate CS programs lack a reliable, reproducible instrument to measure how completely they cover international curricular guidelines (like the ACM/IEEE CS Curricula) and how coverage shifts when those guidelines are restructured, hindering systematic curricular quality assurance.
AI.method: A retrieve-then-confirm pipeline: (1) the program syllabus and curricular guidelines are represented as structured corpora; (2) candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches are generated via semantic retrieval (seven retrievers benchmarked, with a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble proving strongest); (3) matches are confirmed by human judgment under an explicit coverage definition; (4) validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's κ). The pipeline is applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc program against CS2013 and CS2023, including competency articulation and cognitive depth analysis.
AI.result: Coverage was 49.7% (CS2023) and 50.9% (CS2013), near-constant across a decade. Inter-rater reliability: κ=0.64 (CS2023), κ=0.69 (CS2013). A small sentence model outperformed a long-context model in retrieval. Competency articulation covered ~88% of covered units under both guidelines; recommended cognitive depth was met for 76% (CS2023) vs. 95% (CS2013) of present units. Persistent structural gaps identified: parallel/distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a reusable, validated instrument for curricular coverage measurement. The near-constant coverage over a decade suggests program stability, while the cognitive-depth drop reflects CS2023's raised expectations rather than program decline. The approach cleanly separates persistent gaps from guideline-evolution effects, offering programs a practical tool for evidence-based curricular improvement.

title: Token Factory: Efficiently Integrating Diverse Signals into Large Recommendation Models
summary: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in industry-scale recommendation tasks. However, holistically integrating traditional signals into these transformer-based architectures effectively and efficiently remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches that "textualize" these signals directly or create discrete item representations often lead to excessively long prompts, substantial memory footprints, and high computational overhead. To overcome these limitations, we propose "Token Factory", a framework designed to transform traditional signals into "soft tokens" that can be directly processed by LRMs. This approach enables efficient integration and compression of heterogeneous input features, preventing prompt length explosion while enhancing model performance. We detail the architecture of Token Factory and present experimental results validating its effectiveness in a production-scale recommendation environment.

AI.tldr: Token Factory transforms traditional recommendation signals into compressed "soft tokens" for direct processing by Large Recommendation Models, preventing prompt length explosion while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Integrating traditional signals (categorical, numerical, sequential features) into transformer-based LRMs via textualization or discrete tokenization causes prohibitively long prompts, large memory footprints, and high computational costs, limiting practical deployment.
AI.method: Token Factory framework that converts heterogeneous input features into learnable, compressed "soft tokens." These soft tokens serve as continuous vector representations directly consumable by LRMs, enabling efficient feature integration and compression without explicit textualization.
AI.result: Experimental results in a production-scale recommendation environment validate the effectiveness of Token Factory, demonstrating improved model performance alongside reduced prompt length and computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Token Factory offers a practical solution for holistically and efficiently integrating traditional recommendation signals into transformer-based LRMs, addressing the core tension between feature richness and computational feasibility in industry-scale deployments.

title: Blame is easier than praise: Measuring off-ball defensive performance in football
summary: The defensive performance of football players is commonly measured through a limited number of actions like tackles and interceptions while their continuous impact through positional behaviour has hardly been studied before. We formulate this problem as an attribution over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth labels, where event-level changes of expected threat are distributed among individuals. We propose a framework that performs this attribution using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). By computing role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures, we can determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through arbitrary passes. The validity and robustness of this approach are evaluated on a uniquely extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data set, including positional and event data from 64 matches of the men's World Cup, 116 matches of the women's German Bundesliga and 336 matches of the men's German 3. Liga. In the absence of a ground truth, we propose an evaluation protocol that combines multiple relatively weak proxies into robust summary scores. We find a validity score that is improved by around 1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric and demonstrate that many popular measures show limited validity. The "blame" for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric in football to reliably measure positioning errors. All code underlying this work is publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for attributing defensive responsibility in football by analyzing continuous positional behavior through defensive pressure areas (DPAs), rather than relying solely on discrete actions like tackles. It introduces role-conditioned baselines within auto-detected team structures to quantify each defender's expected responsibility for conceded threat, and validates the approach on a large cross-gender, cross-competition dataset using a novel evaluation protocol that combines multiple weak proxies.
AI.motivation: Traditional defensive metrics in football rely on sparse, discrete actions (tackles, interceptions) and ignore the continuous positional impact of players. There is no established method to attribute responsibility for defensive errors from spatiotemporal tracking data, and no ground truth exists for evaluating such attributions. The authors aim to fill this gap with a principled, validated framework.
AI.method: The framework formulates defensive attribution as distributing event-level changes in expected threat among players based on player involvement scores derived from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). Role-conditioned baselines are computed within automatically detected team structures (using role clustering) to establish each defender's expected responsibility for threat conceded through passes. For evaluation, in the absence of ground truth, the authors combine multiple relatively weak proxies (external ratings, market values, etc.) into robust summary validity scores.
AI.result: The proposed validity score improves by approximately 1 standard deviation over the best action-based metric. The "blame" metric for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published football metric to reliably measure positioning errors. Many popular existing measures demonstrate limited validity under this evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: The DPA-based attribution framework provides the first reliable, validated method for measuring defensive positioning errors in football. It significantly outperforms action-based metrics and offers a reproducible, open-source approach applicable across genders and competitions, enabling deeper analysis of continuous defensive behavior beyond discrete actions.

title: DynAMO:Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration via Topological Multi-Agent Scheduling
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, 4 algorithms. Evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark. Code: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO
summary:
While LLM-powered agents offer end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, real-world Industry 4.0 deployment is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. We present DynAMO (Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration), a deployment-ready engine using a Plan-then-Execute architecture to generate verifiable workflow graphs. DynAMO supports both SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). By dynamically identifying independent tasks, DynAMO preserves structural correctness and safety while significantly improving efficiency through controlled reasoning overlap.
  Across six controlled experiments on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark, DynAMO demonstrates substantial performance and robustness gains. Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6x over sequential orchestration, rising to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows. After instrumenting external tool calls with realistic latencies, a latency decomposition shows that LLM reasoning and orchestration still account for more than 90% of execution time, identifying model inference as the primary system bottleneck. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by approximately 30%, and DynAMO maintains correct functional behaviour (task completion, agent sequencing, and output quality) while exhibiting graceful degradation under controlled fault injection. Reproducibility analysis further confirms stable execution under repeated runs, with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance. These findings establish DynAMO as a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO

AI.tldr: DynAMO is a deployment-ready agent orchestration engine for Industry 4.0 that uses a Plan-then-Execute architecture with verifiable workflow graphs, supporting both sequential and parallel execution. It achieves 1.6–1.8× latency reduction via parallelization, identifies LLM inference as the primary bottleneck (>90% of execution time), reduces inference latency by ~30% via context pruning, and maintains correctness under fault injection.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents promise end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, but real-world Industry 4.0 deployment faces three key barriers: high latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. Existing orchestration approaches lack a practical, verifiable, and latency-aware execution framework suitable for industrial pipelines.
AI.method: DynAMO employs a Plan-then-Execute architecture that generates verifiable workflow graphs. It supports two execution modes: SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). The system dynamically identifies independent tasks to enable controlled reasoning overlap while preserving structural correctness and safety. Structured context pruning is applied to reduce inference latency. The system is evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark across six controlled experiments, including fault injection and reproducibility analysis.
AI.result: Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6× over sequential orchestration (up to 1.8× on highly parallelizable workflows). Latency decomposition reveals LLM reasoning and orchestration account for >90% of execution time. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by ~30%. DynAMO maintains correct functional behavior (task completion, agent sequencing, output quality) with graceful degradation under fault injection. Reproducibility analysis confirms stable execution with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance.
AI.conclusion: DynAMO provides a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines, demonstrating that dependency-aware parallel orchestration combined with context pruning can substantially improve performance without sacrificing correctness or robustness.

title: Disentangling Linguistic Relatedness from Task Alignment in Cross-Lingual Transfer
summary: We study cross-lingual transfer by fine-tuning seven large language models (4B--671B parameters) on Arabic and evaluating zero-shot reading comprehension on Semitic languages and non-Semitic controls. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, we find no evidence of Semitic-specific transfer: models with weak baselines improve dramatically across all languages, while strong-baseline models show only marginal gains regardless of language family. A chain-of-thought ablation reinforces this finding -- the same models that benefit most from fine-tuning benefit equally from inference-time reasoning, suggesting both mechanisms address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic yields zero-shot reading comprehension gains that are uniform across languages — both Semitic and non-Semitic — challenging the hypothesis of language-family-specific cross-lingual transfer. Gains are driven by task-format alignment, not linguistic knowledge transfer.
AI.motivation: To test whether cross-lingual transfer from Arabic to other Semitic languages is stronger than to non-Semitic languages, and to determine whether observed improvements reflect genuine linguistic knowledge transfer or merely task-format adaptation.
AI.method: Seven LLMs (4B–671B parameters, spanning dense and MoE architectures) are fine-tuned on Arabic reading comprehension data, then evaluated zero-shot on Semitic languages (including Hebrew, Amharic) and non-Semitic controls (e.g., English, French). A chain-of-thought ablation compares inference-time reasoning against fine-tuning to disentangle task-format alignment from cross-lingual transfer.
AI.result: No Semitic-specific transfer was observed. Weak-baseline models improved dramatically on all languages regardless of family; strong-baseline models showed only marginal gains. The CoT ablation revealed that models benefiting most from fine-tuning also benefited equally from inference-time reasoning, indicating both address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
AI.conclusion: Apparent cross-lingual transfer from fine-tuning may be largely attributable to learning the task format rather than transferring linguistic knowledge across related languages. This has important implications for how multilingual LLM capabilities are evaluated and interpreted.

title: G-Lox: Group-Adaptive, Privacy-Preserving Bridge Distribution with Two-Party Computation
summary:
We present G-Lox (group-adaptive Lox), a bridge-distribution system that preserves Lox-style distributor blindness while enabling hidden, stateful group-level adaptation. G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall, so no single server learns group identifiers or group-to-bridge assignments. Private state access and state-dependent updates use two-server DPF/FSS protocols and secure two-party computation, supporting blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting.
  We evaluate G-Lox through system measurements and policy simulation. In our C++/EMP implementation over real TCP sockets, private state access has low client-visible overhead: across state sizes up to 2^16, communication remains in the low-KiB range per iteration. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in about 0.25 s. Simulations with group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration show that G-Lox improves robustness over Lox- and rBridge-like baselines among systems that maintain broad issuance.

AI.tldr: G-Lox extends the Lox bridge-distribution system with group-adaptive assignment while preserving distributor blindness. It uses a two-server privacy wall with DPF/FSS and secure two-party computation to enable stateful, group-level adaptation (blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, group splitting) without any single server learning group identities or assignments. Evaluations show low overhead (∼0.25s per iteration, low-KiB communication) and improved robustness against group-specific blocking and Sybil attacks compared to Lox and rBridge baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing bridge-distribution systems like Lox offer distributor blindness but lack group-level adaptation, making them vulnerable to group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration attacks. The authors aim to add stateful, group-adaptive assignment logic while maintaining the strong privacy guarantee that no single server learns group identifiers or group-to-bridge mappings.
AI.method: G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall. It uses distributed point function (DPF) / function secret sharing (FSS) protocols combined with secure two-party computation (2PC) to perform private state access and state-dependent updates. The two-server architecture ensures neither server individually learns group identifiers or assignments. The system supports three adaptive mechanisms: blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting. Implementation is in C++ using the EMP toolkit, evaluated over real TCP sockets.
AI.result: At M=1024, a client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in approximately 0.25 seconds. Communication stays in the low-KiB range across state sizes up to 2^16. Policy simulations demonstrate that G-Lox improves robustness against group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration compared to Lox-like and rBridge-like baselines, while maintaining broad issuance.
AI.conclusion: G-Lox successfully combines distributor blindness with hidden, stateful group-level adaptation, achieving meaningful robustness improvements over static alternatives with acceptable computational and communication overhead.

title: Closing the Social-Semantic Gap: SPSD for Edge-Based Prompt Compression in Cloud LLM Inference
summary: The prefill stage of Large Language Model (LLM) inference is a growing contributor to cloud-scale energy cost. Many consumer-support and conversational prompts contain social scaffolding: politeness markers, apologetic preamble, repetition, and rapport-building language that is important for human communication but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning. We call this discrepancy the Social-Semantic Gap. We present SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation), an edge-based pipeline that compresses user prompts using a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model before transmission to a cloud-deployed LLM. Evaluation on a 248-prompt corpus using Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) as the SLM and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud evaluation model yields a mean input token saving of 99.9 tokens per distilled call, with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. Response quality, assessed by blind LLM-as-judge scoring across 121 pairs, is non-inferior to the raw path within a pre-specified 1-point margin on a 15-point rubric; the judge awarded 43 percent ties, 28 percent distilled wins, and 29 percent raw wins. Cosine similarity is mixed: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1 percent of pairs above the 0.70 reference threshold. Safety-critical domains are conservatively routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Per-call net energy saving is estimated at 70-270 uWh under stated assumptions. SPSD shows that on-device prompt distillation can reduce cloud LLM input-token cost while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin.

AI.tldr: SPSD uses a 4-bit quantized small language model on edge devices to distill verbose, socially polite user prompts before sending them to cloud LLMs, saving ~100 input tokens per call with non-inferior response quality.
AI.motivation: LLM inference prefill is a growing cloud energy cost. Many user prompts contain "social scaffolding" — politeness, apologies, repetition, rapport-building — that is important for human interaction but semantically redundant for machine reasoning. This "Social-Semantic Gap" represents wasted compute and energy.
AI.method: SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation) is an edge-based pipeline: a 4-bit quantized Small Language Model (Gemma-2-2B-Instruct Q4_K_M) compresses prompts on-device, stripping social scaffolding while preserving core semantics and sentiment. Distilled prompts are transmitted to a cloud LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Safety-critical prompts are routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Evaluation uses blind LLM-as-judge scoring on a 15-point rubric across 121 response pairs from a 248-prompt corpus.
AI.result: Mean input token savings of 99.9 tokens per distilled call; all 146 distilled calls achieved positive savings. Blind judging: 43% ties, 28% distilled wins, 29% raw wins — non-inferior within a 1-point margin on a 15-point scale. Cosine similarity: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1% of pairs above 0.70 threshold. Estimated per-call net energy savings: 70–270 μWh.
AI.conclusion: On-device prompt distillation via quantized SLMs can meaningfully reduce cloud LLM input-token costs and energy consumption while maintaining response quality within acceptable non-inferiority margins, offering a practical deployment strategy for conversational AI systems.

title: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic experimental analysis of eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) across eight benchmarks, evaluating generation quality and computational efficiency while examining the impact of inference-time design choices such as denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies.
AI.motivation: Despite the emergence of numerous diffusion-based language architectures, the field lacks a standardized comparison framework. Variations in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters across prior work make it difficult to meaningfully compare DLM capabilities and understand their trade-offs relative to each other and to autoregressive LLMs.
AI.method: The authors evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs on eight benchmarks covering reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving. They systematically analyze inference-time factors (denoising steps, context length, block size, parallel unmasking strategies) through both large-scale experiments and controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions, explicitly measuring generation quality and computational efficiency.
AI.result: DLM behavior is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, creating distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. The study characterizes strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs, offering guidance for practitioners on the performance-efficiency trade-offs inherent in diffusion-based language generation.

title: SAFE-Cascade: Cost-Adaptive Vision-Language Routing for Chart Question Answering
comment: Demo paper submitted at CIKM 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful for chart question answering, but invoking a VLM for every query can be unnecessarily expensive when many questions are answerable from OCR text and lightweight language reasoning. We demonstrate SAFE-Cascade, an interactive system for cost-adaptive chart question answering. Given a chart image and a natural-language question, SAFE-Cascade first extracts chart text with OCR, obtains a provisional answer from a text-only language model, and then uses a learned router to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM. The demo exposes this decision process to users: OCR evidence, text-only answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and estimated latency are shown side by side. SAFE-Cascade is designed as a transparent interface for understanding when visual grounding is actually needed. Users can upload or select charts, ask questions, inspect the evidence used by each pathway, compare text-only and VLM answers, and adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost frontier. The system is implemented with Azure Document Intelligence for OCR, gpt-5-mini as the text-only model, gemini-2.5-flash-image as the VLM, and a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features. On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples from a 2,500-example experiment, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared with 67.7% accuracy and 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The observed +1.4 percentage-point difference is statistically uncertain, so we interpret SAFE-Cascade as matching full-VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%. The demonstration shows how selective modality routing can make multimodal knowledge systems more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware.

AI.tldr: SAFE-Cascade is a cost-adaptive chart QA system that uses a learned router to decide whether to answer with a cheap text-only LLM (using OCR-extracted text) or escalate to an expensive VLM. It matches full-VLM accuracy while reducing VLM calls by ~27% and cost by ~9%, with a transparent UI exposing routing decisions.
AI.motivation: Invoking a VLM for every chart question is computationally and financially expensive, yet many chart questions can be answered from OCR-extracted text alone using lightweight language reasoning. The authors aim to reduce this unnecessary cost while maintaining accuracy, and to make the routing decision process transparent to users.
AI.method: SAFE-Cascade employs a two-stage pipeline: (1) OCR text extraction from chart images via Azure Document Intelligence, followed by a provisional answer from a text-only LLM (gpt-5-mini); (2) a learned Random Forest router trained on inference-time features decides whether to accept the text-only answer or escalate to a VLM (gemini-2.5-flash-image). The system exposes all intermediate evidence — OCR output, text answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and latency — in an interactive UI where users can also adjust the escalation threshold.
AI.result: On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, versus 67.7% accuracy with 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The +1.4pp accuracy difference is not statistically significant, so performance is interpreted as matching the baseline while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%.
AI.conclusion: Selective modality routing via SAFE-Cascade demonstrates that multimodal QA systems can be made more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware without sacrificing accuracy, by invoking expensive visual reasoning only when necessary.

title: Human-like autonomy emerges from self-play and a pinch of human data
summary: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and full source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.

AI.tldr: A method that uses minimal human demonstrations (30 minutes) as a regularization objective atop a safe goal-reaching reward in self-play RL, producing driving policies that coordinate with human driving conventions while requiring 2500x less human data than imitation learning baselines.
AI.motivation: Pure self-play reinforcement learning for autonomous driving can produce effective but alien driving behaviors incompatible with human drivers. Prior mitigation attempts rely on brittle, labor-intensive reward engineering and domain randomization. The authors aim to bridge the behavioral alignment gap without discarding the sample efficiency benefits of self-play, using only a minimal amount of human data.
AI.method: The method uses self-play RL with a minimal safe goal-reaching reward (sparse reward for reaching goal without collisions), augmented by a regularization term derived from a small dataset of human driving demonstrations (30 minutes). Human data serves as an auxiliary objective that penalizes deviation from human-like behavior, rather than as the primary supervision signal. This "spice" approach preserves self-play's exploration benefits while softly constraining policy behavior toward human conventions.
AI.result: Policies trained with the method successfully coordinate with held-out human trajectories. Training completes in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. The approach requires only 30 minutes of human demonstrations — 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning methods.
AI.conclusion: A small amount of human data used as regularization is sufficient to align self-play RL driving policies with human conventions, dramatically reducing data requirements compared to imitation learning while preserving the efficiency and scalability of simulation-based self-play training.

title: Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Sequel to arXiv:2606.04296. Pre-registered; falsification clauses honored (H5 unsupported; H7 strict band 16/20) repo:https://github.com/2025eb1100268-tech/intervention-timing-saturation-trap
