summary: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. Real agent runs measure latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s); real coding cadence sits inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.

AI.tldr: A prior paper's reported "State Saturation Trap" (threshold-on-state triggers firing near-constantly) was caused by a bug where dt=0 disabled exponential decay. Correcting this reveals a fundamental property: wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors inevitably fail on agent streams with variable inter-action times, producing either constant alarms or silence depending on dt. Sample-time methods (CUSUM) and rising-edge triggers escape this trap.
AI.motivation: To correct a prior publication's erroneous finding (State Saturation Trap), investigate the underlying cause (dt=0 bug disabling decay), and determine whether threshold-on-state monitoring is fundamentally flawed on agent streams or merely misconfigured. The broader motivation is understanding how monitor calibration (wall-clock vs. sample-time) interacts with the variable inter-action timing characteristic of autonomous agent trajectories.
AI.method: The authors treat the original dt=0 bug as a natural experiment exposing a critical variable: calibration domain (sample-time vs. wall-clock time). They conduct a pre-registered parameter sweep over uniform dt intervals (0-600s) across 20 SWE-bench trajectories, comparing: (1) a wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator threshold-on-state trigger, (2) a sample-time CUSUM over the identical error stream, and (3) a rising-edge trigger with hysteresis. Real agent latency is measured (median 1.53s, p90 2.33s) to situate actual operating conditions within the parameter space.
AI.result: The wall-clock trigger exhibits a sharp cliff: at dt≤1s, constant alarms (20/20 trajectories, median 18 firings); at dt≥60s, complete silence; all critical dt values fall in (1,30]s. Real agent coding cadence falls squarely in the trap regime. A minimal wall-clock accumulator (no affect model) reproduces the identical cliff. The sample-time CUSUM is exactly dt-invariant (20/20 across all conditions). The rising-edge trigger fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition, escaping the trap.
AI.conclusion: Wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they function as moment detectors on agent streams — they either saturate or go silent. This is a structural property of the calibration class, not a specific engine flaw. Transition detection (rising-edge with hysteresis) escapes the trap at all cadences but cannot recover human intervention timing. Sample-time methods like CUSUM remain dt-invariant and thus suitable.

title: How LLMs Fail and Generalize in RTL Coding for Hardware Design?
summary: Translating sequential programming priors into the parallel temporal logic of hardware design remains a crucial bottleneck for large language models(LLM). To investigate this, we introduce a new error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability, inspired by cognitive theory. Our taxonomy categorizes failures into syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional types. Evaluations reveal a strict empirical ceiling on the VerilogEval benchmark, as frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate. These plateaus are defined by unsolvable functional errors, exposing persistent knowledge gaps immune to test time compute scaling. Furthermore, we expose a striking surface convergence gap: optimization readily eliminates syntax errors but concurrently exacerbates deeper functional failures. Our findings demonstrate that alignment techniques merely teach models to compile. While repeated sampling strategies can patch solvable errors, register-transfer level(RTL) coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge. Addressing challenges in the current LLM based hardware generation pipeline requires more studies in model reasoning rather than alignment interventions.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs plateau at ~90.8% on VerilogEval due to unsolvable functional errors rooted in pretraining knowledge gaps. Alignment helps models compile but fails to improve RTL reasoning; repeated sampling patches only solvable errors, exposing a fundamental ceiling that requires better reasoning rather than more alignment.
AI.motivation: Translating sequential programming knowledge into parallel hardware description logic (RTL) remains a critical bottleneck for LLMs in hardware design. The authors aim to systematically characterize why frontier models plateau and whether test-time compute or alignment can overcome these limits.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel error taxonomy grounded in cognitive theory and problem solvability, classifying failures into four categories: syntactic errors, semantic errors, solvable functional errors, and unsolvable functional errors. They evaluate frontier LLMs on the VerilogEval benchmark and analyze the effects of alignment techniques, repeated sampling, and test-time compute scaling on each error type.
AI.result: Frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate, constrained by unsolvable functional errors that are immune to test-time compute scaling. A "surface convergence gap" is identified: optimization readily eliminates syntax errors but concurrently exacerbates deeper functional failures. Repeated sampling can resolve solvable functional errors, but RTL coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Alignment techniques merely teach models to compile rather than reason about hardware design. Addressing the LLM-based hardware generation bottleneck requires advancing model reasoning capabilities, not further alignment interventions.

title: PUFFERDOS: Efficient and Effective Attack String Generation for Regular Expression Denial of Service Vulnerabilities
summary: ReDoS attacks constitute a critical class of resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities. In such attacks, adversaries exploit the pathological worst-case execution behavior of regular expression (regex) engines to induce highly asymmetric computational workloads, ultimately exhausting system resources and degrading service availability. To protect systems against ReDoS attacks, numerous detection techniques have been proposed that simulate the attack process by generating attack strings to proactively exploit ReDoS vulnerabilities at the early development stage and facilitate remediation. Existing techniques broadly fall into two classes: static analyses that search for pathological regex structures, and dynamic exploration methods that synthesize candidate attack strings. However, the generated attack strings are often impractical for real-world exploitation because they usually assume unrealistic input-length budgets and do not validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the attack at the program level. Therefore, many generated strings fail to trigger vulnerable regexes when applied to real-world programs, further limiting the practical utility. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an effective and efficient attack string generator, PUFFERDOS, designed to synthesize attack inputs that are both feasible within realistic length budgets and validated at the program level, enabling effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs. Specifically, we first define three vulnerable patterns based on our observation and formal verification. According to the patterns, PUFFERDOS conducts a synthesis technique to generate attack strings, and then refines and validates the strings with ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to guarantee real-world exploitability.

AI.tldr: PUFFERDOS is a practical ReDoS attack string generator that synthesizes feasible attack inputs under realistic length budgets and validates them at the program level using compositional concolic execution, addressing the key limitation of existing tools that generate impractical attack strings.
AI.motivation: Existing ReDoS detection techniques generate attack strings that are impractical for real-world exploitation because they assume unrealistic input-length budgets and fail to validate attack effectiveness/efficiency at the program level. Consequently, many generated strings cannot trigger vulnerable regexes in actual programs.
AI.method: PUFFERDOS defines three vulnerable regex patterns based on observation and formal verification. It then synthesizes attack strings guided by these patterns and refines them using ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution that validates real-world exploitability under realistic length constraints.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper claims PUFFERDOS enables effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs by generating feasible, program-level-validated attack strings.
AI.conclusion: By constraining attack string generation to realistic length budgets and incorporating program-level validation via compositional concolic execution, PUFFERDOS significantly improves the practical utility of ReDoS vulnerability detection and exploitation compared to prior approaches.

title: Performance Analysis and Optimization of 3D Generative Diffusion Models across GPU Architectures
summary: Diffusion models have become essential for high-fidelity 3D MRI synthesis, yet their deployment remains constrained by substantial GPU resource demands arising from hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and a highly heterogeneous kernel behavior. This paper performs a comprehensive performance analysis of the state-of-the-art medical diffusion model, Med-DDPM, across three generations of NVIDIA architectures to study kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. We show that training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies arising from memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. Guided by these insights, we evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations TF32 Tensor Core activation and a 3D channels-last layout and demonstrate that they reduce SM cycles by up to 100x, cut dynamic instructions by 100x, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45 to 9.98x, and increase IPC by 7% on A100, all without degrading synthesis quality.

AI.tldr: A performance analysis of Med-DDPM across three NVIDIA GPU generations reveals that training is bottlenecked by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels with poor Tensor Core utilization. Two architecture-aware optimizations — TF32 Tensor Core activation and 3D channels-last layout — reduce SM cycles by up to 100×, cut dynamic instructions by 100×, and boost Tensor Core utilization from 1.45× to 9.98× on A100 without degrading output quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models for 3D MRI synthesis are prohibitively expensive to deploy due to hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample combined with heterogeneous and inefficient kernel behavior on modern GPUs. Understanding precisely where and why performance is lost is a prerequisite for unlocking practical, cost-effective deployment.
AI.method: The authors conduct an exhaustive kernel-level profiling of Med-DDPM on three NVIDIA GPU generations (covering convolution, GEMM, memory, and warp-level metrics), then propose and evaluate two targeted architecture-aware optimizations: enabling TF32 Tensor Core acceleration for convolutions and adopting a 3D channels-last memory layout to improve data locality and Tensor Core throughput.
AI.result: Profiling shows training is dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies from poor memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and low Tensor Core usage. The two optimizations achieve up to 100× reduction in SM cycles and dynamic instructions, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45× to 9.98×, and improve IPC by 7% on A100 — all while preserving synthesis quality.
AI.conclusion: Architecture-aware, kernel-level optimization — specifically TF32 Tensor Core activation and channels-last layout — can dramatically improve the throughput and efficiency of medical diffusion models without any fidelity trade-off, making GPU-accelerated 3D MRI synthesis substantially more practical.

title: Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation, where agents exchange and revise answers over several rounds, is increasingly used to improve reasoning and accuracy, yet how and why it works is rarely modelled. Such deliberation mirrors how humans reach decisions. As social animals we are pulled both by the group, the herd effect that classical opinion-dynamics models such as DeGroot and Friedkin--Johnsen capture, and by our own internal belief, which they do not. We model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system in which each agent carries a hidden internal belief, its anchor, that continually pulls its opinion regardless of its neighbours. We show this anchor can be recovered from the deliberation alone, and that it explains a behaviour classical consensus rules forbid: an agent's confidence in the correct answer can climb past where any agent started, escaping the space (convexhull) formed by the initial beliefs. Checking whether the recovered anchor also predicts held-out runs (generalizes) gives a simple test for when a model is truly driven bysuch an anchor. Across three open-weight model families this is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing. All anchors' influence are about equally strongly, but they differ in where the anchor sits, and only when it sits far from the initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull and need the full closed-loop model.

AI.tldr: This paper models multi-agent LLM deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal belief ("anchor") that continually pulls its opinions. The anchor can be recovered from deliberation data, explains how confidence can exceed initial bounds (escaping the convex hull), and its generalizability provides a test for whether deliberation is truly anchor-driven.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM deliberation improves reasoning and accuracy, but the mechanisms behind it are poorly understood. Classical opinion-dynamics models (DeGroot, Friedkin-Johnsen) capture the herd effect but fail to model internal beliefs that anchor agents. A formal model is needed to explain emergent behaviors like confidence climbing beyond initial bounds.
AI.method: The authors formalize multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent maintains a hidden internal belief (anchor) exerting a constant pull on its opinion, alongside neighbor influence. They develop a method to recover this anchor from deliberation trajectories alone and test whether the recovered anchor generalizes to held-out runs. Experiments span three open-weight LLM families.
AI.result: The anchor can be reliably recovered from deliberation data. It explains a key phenomenon that classical models cannot: an agent's confidence can exceed the convex hull of initial beliefs. Anchor influence strength is similar across models, but anchor position varies; only when the anchor sits far from initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull. Generalization of the recovered anchor falls on a spectrum rather than being all-or-nothing.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM deliberation is well-characterized by the closed-loop anchor model. The anchor recovery and generalization test offer a principled diagnostic for when deliberation is truly driven by internal beliefs, and the spectrum of generalization across model families suggests nuanced architectural differences in how LLMs internalize beliefs during deliberation.

title: Closing the Calibration Gap in Semantic Caching
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures. Source code: https://github.com/aditeyabaral/calibration-gap-semantic-caching ; Models and Datasets: https://huggingface.co/redis
summary: Semantic caching cuts LLM inference costs by serving a cached response to semantically similar queries. Standard practice evaluates these systems using PR-AUC, a metric that only measures how well scores rank and ignores whether they are usable at a fixed threshold. We show this mismatch leads to systematically poor deployment choices, as models with the highest PR-AUC are often the worst in operation. We introduce Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, a cache-aware metric that measures precision across cache utilization levels, and Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which captures how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. We decompose the operational gap between offline and deployed quality into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component fixed by the dataset's positive rate. Our experiments show that the calibration gap is governed by the training objective rather than data scale, and post-hoc calibration only partially closes it. Ultimately, model selection for semantic caching is a calibration problem, not a ranking one, and measuring it is the first step to closing the gap.

AI.tldr: Semantic caching evaluation is broken: PR-AUC, the standard metric, ignores calibration and leads to poor model selection. The authors propose P-CHR AUC and CRR to measure cache-aware precision and calibration retention, showing that model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem, not a ranking one.
AI.motivation: Current semantic caching systems rely on PR-AUC for model evaluation, but this metric only assesses ranking quality without accounting for whether similarity scores are calibrated for fixed-threshold deployment. This mismatch causes systematically suboptimal model choices, where top PR-AUC models perform worst in production.
AI.method: The authors introduce two new metrics: (1) P-CHR AUC (Precision-Cache Hit Ratio AUC), which measures precision across varying cache utilization levels, and (2) CRR (Calibration Retention Rate), which quantifies how much offline ranking quality is preserved at deployment. They decompose the operational gap into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component determined by the dataset's positive rate. Experiments examine how training objectives versus data scale influence this gap and whether post-hoc calibration can close it.
AI.result: Models with the highest PR-AUC frequently perform worst under operational conditions. The calibration gap is primarily governed by the training objective rather than the scale of training data. Post-hoc calibration methods only partially close the gap, indicating recalibration cannot fully compensate for this mismatch.
AI.conclusion: Model selection for semantic caching is inherently a calibration problem, not a ranking problem. Properly measuring calibration via P-CHR AUC and CRR is the essential first step toward closing the deployment gap.

title: Interpretable and Verifiable Hardware Generation with LLM-Driven Stepwise Refinement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in software development. However, they are susceptible to hallucinations, meaning that they can introduce subtle semantic and logical errors. Due to the high stakes in chip design and manufacturing, hardware engineers are still reluctant to rely on LLMs for register-transfer level (RTL) generation. In this paper, we propose a hardware generation framework that combines the creativity and broad knowledge of LLMs with the explainability and mathematical rigor of formal methods. Specifically, we devise a set of transformation rules that cover various design decisions and hardware features. By iteratively applying these rules, an LLM agent can convert a design specification into an RTL program with guaranteed correctness. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the framework.

AI.tldr: A framework combining LLMs with formal methods for verified RTL generation, using iterative transformation rules to guarantee correctness and address LLM hallucination risks in hardware design.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel in software but suffer from hallucinations (subtle semantic/logical errors), making them unreliable for high-stakes chip design. Hardware engineers need guaranteed correctness for RTL generation.
AI.method: A hybrid framework pairing LLM creativity with formal methods. The core is a set of transformation rules covering design decisions and hardware features, applied iteratively by an LLM agent to convert specifications into provably correct RTL.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and efficiency in generating correct RTL programs.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with formal methods via transformation rules offers a viable path to trustworthy, automated RTL generation for hardware design.

title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
summary: We present a preview version of DeepSeek-V4 series, including two strong Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models -- DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated) -- both supporting a context length of one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4 series incorporate several key upgrades in architecture and optimization: (1) a hybrid attention architecture that combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) to improve long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) that enhance conventional residual connections; (3) and the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and greater training stability. We pre-train both models on more than 32T diverse and high-quality tokens, followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline that unlocks and further enhances their capabilities. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max, the maximum reasoning effort mode of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, redefines the state-of-the-art for open models, outperforming its predecessors in core tasks. Meanwhile, DeepSeek-V4 series are highly efficient in long-context scenarios. In the one-million-token context setting, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache compared with DeepSeek-V3.2. This enables us to routinely support one-million-token contexts, thereby making long-horizon tasks and further test-time scaling more feasible. The model checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.

AI.tldr: DeepSeek-V4 introduces two MoE models (Pro: 1.6T/49B activated; Flash: 284B/13B activated) with 1M-token context support, featuring hybrid attention (CSA+HCA), manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC), and the Muon optimizer, achieving state-of-the-art open-model performance with dramatic long-context efficiency gains over DeepSeek-V3.2.
AI.motivation: To advance open-source language models by simultaneously pushing the frontier of reasoning capability and long-context efficiency, addressing the computational bottlenecks (FLOPs, KV cache) that previously made million-token contexts impractical at scale.
AI.method: The DeepSeek-V4 series employs three architectural/optimization innovations: (1) a hybrid attention mechanism combining Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) for long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) to improve upon standard residual connections; (3) the Muon optimizer for accelerated convergence and training stability. Both models are pre-trained on >32T tokens with a comprehensive post-training pipeline. A "Pro-Max" mode leverages maximum test-time reasoning effort.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max achieves state-of-the-art results among open models on core tasks. In 1M-token contexts, DeepSeek-V4-Pro uses only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache compared to DeepSeek-V3.2, making routine long-context deployment and test-time scaling feasible.
AI.conclusion: DeepSeek-V4 represents a significant leap in open-source LLMs, with architectural innovations that dramatically improve long-context efficiency without sacrificing core capability, enabling practical deployment of million-token contexts and advancing test-time compute scaling.

title: A Layered Security Framework Against Prompt Injection in RAG-Based Chatbots
comment: Submitted in ICCK Transactions on Information Security and Cryptography
summary: Prompt injection is ranked as the most critical vulnerability in large language model (LLM) deployments by the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, yet existing defenses operate at isolated pipeline stages and remain incomplete. Input filters cannot inspect retrieved documents, while output monitors cannot prevent malicious payloads from reaching the model. Consequently, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbots remain vulnerable to indirect injection, where a poisoned knowledge-base document compromises every user whose query retrieves it. We present a three-layer framework that intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection throughout the inference pipeline. Layer 1 screens user input using a rule-based pattern library and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier. Layer 2 enforces a provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly, preventing retrieved content from overriding operator policy. Layer 3 audits model output using a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector before delivery. A continuous audit loop aggregates structured logs and supports retraining to adapt the classifier to emerging attack patterns. The framework is model-agnostic and deploys as middleware without modifying the underlying LLM. Evaluation on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B shows that the framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 71.4\% to 11.3\%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 percentage points and a published guardrail system by 23.8 percentage points, while maintaining a 4.8\% false positive rate and a median latency overhead of 61.2 ms. Ablation studies confirm that all three layers provide complementary protection and that their combined effect exceeds the sum of individual contributions.

AI.tldr: A three-layer defense framework for LLM deployments intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection across the entire inference pipeline. Combining input filtering, provenance-based context assembly, and output auditing, it reduces Attack Success Rate from 71.4% to 11.3% across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B, outperforming single-layer baselines by 27.3 points and published guardrails by 23.8 points, with only 4.8% false positives and 61.2 ms median latency overhead.
AI.motivation: Prompt injection is the #1 LLM vulnerability per OWASP Top 10, yet existing defenses are fragmented: input filters miss retrieved documents, output monitors cannot block payloads before they reach the model. This is especially dangerous in RAG systems where a single poisoned knowledge-base document compromises all users who retrieve it. No existing solution provides end-to-end protection across the full inference pipeline.
AI.method: A model-agnostic middleware framework with three layers: (1) input screening via rule-based pattern matching and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier; (2) provenance-based instruction hierarchy enforcement during context assembly to prevent retrieved content from overriding system policies; (3) output auditing via a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector. A continuous audit loop aggregates logs for classifier retraining against emerging attacks.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B: ASR reduced from 71.4% to 11.3%. Outperforms best single-layer baseline by 27.3 percentage points and a published guardrail system by 23.8 points. False positive rate: 4.8%. Median latency overhead: 61.2 ms. Ablation studies confirm all three layers are complementary, with combined effect exceeding the sum of individual contributions.
AI.conclusion: The three-layer, pipeline-spanning approach provides robust defense against both direct and indirect prompt injection in RAG chatbots. The complementary nature of the layers and the continuous audit loop for adaptive retraining make the framework practical for real-world deployment, achieving strong protection with minimal latency and false positive overhead.

title: Information Lattice Learning as Probabilistic Graphical Model Structure Learning
summary: Information lattice learning (ILL) learns interpretable rules of a signal by alternately projecting the signal onto a partition lattice that encodes a hierarchy of abstractions and lifting selected rules back to the signal domain. When the signal is a probability mass function, we show the probabilistic rules learned by ILL admit a natural probabilistic graphical model (PGM) interpretation and develop this interpretation in detail. A partition in ILL induces a deterministic quotient variable, and a rule is the marginal law of that quotient variable. A rule set is therefore a collection of marginal constraints over interpretable abstractions. General lifting is the feasible family of all joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting chooses a maximum-ignorance reconstruction, implemented in ILL by an L2 uniformity principle closely related to maximum entropy. Under a Shannon-entropy lifting, the same constraints yield a log-linear factor graph whose factors are indexed by learned abstractions. The information lattice itself, however, is not a Bayesian network: its edges encode refinement and coarsening of abstractions, not conditional dependence. Thus ILL is best viewed as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables. This view clarifies how ILL relates to graphical models and maximum entropy models, while suggesting new directions for inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

AI.tldr: Information Lattice Learning (ILL) learns interpretable rules by projecting signals onto partition lattices and lifting rules back. For probability mass functions, the resulting probabilistic rules correspond to marginal constraints over quotient variables. A Shannon-entropy lifting yields a log-linear factor graph, positioning ILL as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs rather than Bayesian networks.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous probabilistic graphical model interpretation for the rules learned by Information Lattice Learning (ILL), clarifying how ILL relates to established frameworks like graphical models, maximum entropy models, and structure learning.
AI.method: The authors develop a PGM interpretation of ILL by analyzing its two core operations: (1) projection onto a partition lattice, where each partition induces a deterministic quotient variable and a rule is the marginal law of that variable; (2) lifting, where general lifting defines the family of all joint distributions satisfying marginal constraints, and special lifting uses an L2 uniformity principle (closely related to maximum entropy) for maximum-ignorance reconstruction. Under Shannon-entropy lifting, constraints yield a log-linear factor graph with factors indexed by learned abstractions.
AI.result: ILL-learned rules form a collection of marginal constraints over interpretable quotient-variable abstractions. Under Shannon-entropy lifting, these constraints produce a log-linear factor graph. The information lattice's edges encode refinement/coarsening relations, not conditional dependence, so the lattice is not a Bayesian network. ILL is thus best characterized as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables.
AI.conclusion: ILL is best viewed as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs, not Bayesian networks. This framing clarifies ILL's relationship to graphical models and maximum entropy, while opening new directions for inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
summary: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

AI.tldr: DeXposure-Claw introduces an agentic supervision system for decentralized finance (DeFi) that uses a graph time-series foundation model (DeXposure-FM) to forecast credit exposure networks, then routes LLM decisions through structured evidence, deterministic monitors, and confidence gates to produce auditable supervisory tickets. A companion benchmark, DeXposure-Bench, evaluates performance using regulator-aligned absolute-loss and false-intervention rate metrics.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM agents perform poorly in DeFi supervision because they over-read weak evidence and recommend excessive high-stakes interventions. Existing evaluation frameworks lack regulator-aligned metrics to quantify false alarms. There is a need for a structured, forecast-grounded system tailored to fast-moving, networked credit risks in decentralized finance.
AI.method: DeXposure-Claw consists of three components: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model that forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios that convert forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; (3) data-health and confidence gates that constrain escalation before the system emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. DeXposure-Bench provides a six-axis evaluation harness with a decision axis scoring tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate.
AI.result: Experiments conducted on five years of weekly real data fully support the effectiveness of the DeXposure-Claw system, demonstrating improved supervisory decision-making compared to general-purpose LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Structured, forecast-grounded agentic supervision with deterministic guardrails significantly outperforms general-purpose LLM agents for DeFi credit risk oversight, and regulator-aligned benchmarking enables meaningful measurement of false-intervention trade-offs.

title: Stellar: Scalable Multimodal Document Retrieval for Natural Language Queries
summary: Multimodal document retrieval--selecting the most relevant multimodal document from a large corpus to answer a natural language query--plays an essential role in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. State-of-the-art methods represent each document and query with multiple token-level embeddings and use late interaction to achieve high effectiveness. However, such multi-vector representations incur substantial memory overhead during retrieval, leading to poor scalability and hindering real-world deployment. In this paper, we present Stellar, a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that stores token-level document embeddings on disk and loads only a small set of candidate embeddings into memory for late interaction. Stellar comprises two key components: (i) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a sparse encoder to produce high-quality lexical representations, enabling efficient and effective document filtering to significantly reduce the candidate set; (ii) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which designs an on-disk token embedding storage layout guided by a balanced clustering algorithm, and dynamically loads only the necessary token embeddings into memory using a simple yet effective cost model. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly presented large-scale dataset demonstrate that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods without compromising retrieval effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Stellar is a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that stores token-level embeddings on disk and selectively loads only necessary candidates into memory, achieving 1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in memory and latency without sacrificing retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal document retrieval methods use multi-vector (token-level) representations with late interaction for high effectiveness, but this incurs massive memory overhead during retrieval, limiting scalability and real-world deployment.
AI.method: Stellar has two components: (1) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes an MLLM as a sparse encoder to produce lexical representations for efficient candidate filtering; (2) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which uses a balanced clustering algorithm to organize token embeddings on disk and a cost model to dynamically load only necessary embeddings into memory.
AI.result: Experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly introduced large-scale dataset show Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods, while maintaining retrieval effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Stellar makes multi-vector late-interaction retrieval practically scalable for multimodal document RAG systems by shifting the memory bottleneck to disk without degrading accuracy.

title: Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. LNCS format. Code, dataset, and mining toolkit: https://github.com/neul-labs/grite
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open millions of pull requests, yet large-scale studies find their PRs are produced faster but accepted less often - a coordination and trust gap that pull-request-level telemetry cannot explain. We argue the missing signal lives before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. We study this process through grite, our open-source coordination substrate that needs no central server and stores its records inside git itself, so its append-only, signed event log captures the coordination process directly. We show that (i) this shared substrate reduces duplicate and conflicting work at bounded overhead - the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task falls from 78% to 0% while useful throughput more than triples; (ii) every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, where a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes; and (iii) the log is a mineable artefact from which concrete failure modes - conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close - are automatically recoverable with provenance, several invisible in pull-request history. We release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit.

AI.tldr: Autonomous coding agents face a coordination gap where pull requests are fast but frequently rejected. The authors present grite, a git-native, serverless coordination substrate that uses an append-only signed event log to prevent duplicate work, eliminate lost writes, and enable automatic recovery from failure modes invisible in PR history.
AI.motivation: Large-scale studies show that autonomous coding agents produce pull requests faster but suffer lower acceptance rates, pointing to a coordination and trust gap. Existing PR-level telemetry cannot explain this gap because the critical failures — duplicate work, conflicting edits, lock starvation — occur before the PR is created.
AI.method: The authors build grite, an open-source coordination substrate that requires no central server. It stores coordination records (task claims, divisions, collisions) directly inside git as an append-only, signed event log. This log converges to identical state across all agents without silent write drops. The system is evaluated by benchmarking against a file-based tracker across dimensions of duplicate work reduction, throughput, write convergence, and failure-mode detectability.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) grite reduces duplicate/redundant work from 78% to 0% while more than tripling useful throughput with bounded overhead; (ii) every agent's log copy converges to the same state with no silently dropped writes, unlike a file-based tracker that loses concurrent writes; (iii) the log enables automatic recovery from failure modes (conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close) with full provenance, many of which are invisible in pull-request history.
AI.conclusion: Coordination failures among autonomous coding agents stem from pre-PR contention over shared work. Embedding a verifiable, decentralized coordination log inside git itself — as grite does — eliminates redundant work, ensures write integrity, and surfaces previously invisible failure modes, offering a principled substrate for multi-agent software engineering.

title: Beyond the GUI Paradigm: Do Mobile Agents Need the Phone Screen?
summary: Recent advances in mobile agents are dominated by the GUI paradigm, in which agents perceive UI information and emit screen interactions. However, mobile platforms also expose a command-line interface (CLI) that provides direct access to device services and data. We argue CLI deserves first-class consideration alongside GUI. We evaluate three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld without any mobile-specific post-training, comparing against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Claude Code (Opus 4.7) reaches 71.8\% and 51.9\%, outperforming every reproducible GUI baseline (69.3/68.1/57.8\% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3\% on MobileWorld), while every other CLI configuration remains competitive. To establish the paradigm's ceiling, we provide oracle CLI solutions that reach 88.8\% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks CLI-solvable) and 86.3\% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks CLI-solvable), indicating substantial room for future improvement. To cover everyday user intents beyond the GUI scope, we introduce the \textbf{CLI-Advantage Task Suite}, comprising 45 templates across five categories: bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, and hidden device state. Every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline in all five categories, with substantially fewer steps per task (10.7 vs.\ 18.6). To support future research on mobile CLI agents, we will open-source agent implementations, oracle solutions, the CLI-Advantage suite, and evaluation infrastructure.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the command-line interface (CLI) on mobile devices deserves equal consideration to GUI-based approaches for mobile agents. Evaluating three coding agents across four models on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks, Claude Code with Opus 4.7 achieves state-of-the-art results (71.8%/51.9%), outperforming all GUI baselines. Oracle CLI solutions reveal a high ceiling (88.8%/86.3%), and a new CLI-Advantage Task Suite demonstrates CLI agents consistently beat GUI baselines across five task categories with fewer steps.
AI.motivation: Current mobile agent research is overwhelmingly dominated by GUI-based paradigms (perceiving screens and emitting touch interactions), while mobile platforms also expose a CLI (e.g., ADB shell) that provides direct, programmatic access to device services and data. The authors argue that CLI is an underexplored yet powerful modality that merits first-class status alongside GUI, potentially enabling more efficient, expressive, and generalizable mobile automation.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld without any mobile-specific fine-tuning. These CLI agents are compared against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). To establish an upper bound, oracle CLI solutions are manually constructed. Additionally, a new CLI-Advantage Task Suite is introduced with 45 templates spanning five categories (bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, hidden device state) to evaluate tasks where CLI has inherent structural advantages over GUI.
AI.result: Claude Code (Opus 4.7) achieves 71.8% on AndroidWorld and 51.9% on MobileWorld, surpassing all GUI baselines (69.3/68.1/57.8% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3% on MobileWorld). All other CLI configurations remain competitive. Oracle CLI solutions reach 88.8% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks solvable) and 86.3% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks solvable), indicating substantial headroom. On the CLI-Advantage Task Suite, every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline across all five categories while using substantially fewer steps (10.7 vs. 18.6 on average).
AI.conclusion: CLI is a viable and often superior paradigm for mobile device automation, achieving state-of-the-art results without mobile-specific training. The high oracle ceiling and systematic advantages on CLI-favorable tasks suggest significant potential for future research. The authors commit to open-sourcing all artifacts to support the community in advancing mobile CLI agents.

title: Where to Place the Query? Unveiling and Mitigating Positional Bias in In-Context Learning for Diffusion LLMs via Decoding Dynamics
summary: While In-Context Learning (ICL) is extensively studied in Autoregressive (AR) LLMs, its mechanism within Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) remains largely unexplored. Unlike AR models restricted by unidirectional causal masking, dLLMs intrinsically utilize bidirectional attention, offering extensive spatial flexibility for query placement. Unfortunately, current practices conventionally inherit AR-style trailing-query templates, often overlooking the structural paradigm shift. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis unveiling that query position is actually a first-order variable in dLLMs. Through empirical decoupling, we demonstrate that positional variance impacts generation quality on par with example semantic quality. Internally, this positional sensitivity stems from a spatial ``Recency Effect'' in attention flow and task-dependent shifts in decoding trajectories. To mitigate this instability without ground-truth labels, we reveal that traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$) fails in dLLMs. Instead, we propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), a novel metric tracking the iterative decoding process. By establishing the foundational spatial ICL baselines, we introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement, robustly approaching oracle performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that query position is a critical first-order variable in Diffusion LLMs for In-Context Learning, introduces a new metric called Average Confidence for evaluating generation quality without ground-truth labels, and proposes Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement to approach oracle-level performance.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) use bidirectional attention, unlike Autoregressive LLMs, yet current ICL practices blindly inherit AR-style trailing-query templates without considering the fundamental structural differences. The authors aim to systematically investigate how query positioning affects ICL performance in dLLMs and develop methods to optimize it.
AI.method: The authors conduct empirical decoupling experiments to isolate the effect of query position from example semantic quality. They analyze internal mechanisms, revealing a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention flow and task-dependent decoding trajectory shifts. They propose Average Confidence (C-bar), a metric that tracks the entire iterative decoding process, as traditional single-step confidence fails for dLLMs. Building on spatial ICL baselines, they develop Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy for dynamic query placement optimization.
AI.result: Query positional variance impacts generation quality comparably to example semantic quality. The proposed Average Confidence metric successfully captures decoding quality without ground-truth labels, where single-step confidence fails. Auto-ICL robustly approaches oracle performance across diverse reasoning and perception tasks.
AI.conclusion: Query position is a first-order variable in dLLMs that demands explicit optimization. The spatial "Recency Effect" and task-dependent trajectory shifts explain this sensitivity. Average Confidence provides reliable zero-label quality assessment, and Auto-ICL offers an effective training-free solution for optimal query placement in dLLM-based ICL.

title: When Global Gating Is Enough: Admission-Time Hubness Control in Anisotropic Vector Retrieval Systems
summary: Vector hubness, where a few points become nearest neighbors of many queries, creates a poisoning risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): one injected document can influence unrelated requests. Existing defenses use periodic reverse-kNN scans, leaving an exposure window and repeated corpus-wide work. We study admission-time control, scoring each candidate against sentinel queries and quarantining hub-like documents before insertion. Across two 100,000-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker and defender query sets, a global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (>=0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 +/- 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. A per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, with corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. On HNSW, admission adds about 3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, none involving attacks. Provenance complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses vector hubness as a poisoning vector in RAG systems, proposing admission-time gating that quarantines hub-like documents before insertion using sentinel queries, achieving high recall against attacks with minimal false positives and low ingestion overhead.
AI.motivation: Vector hubness—where a few points dominate nearest-neighbor results—enables poisoning attacks in RAG: a single malicious document can be retrieved for many unrelated queries. Existing defenses rely on periodic reverse-kNN scans, which leave an exposure window between scans and impose repeated corpus-wide computational cost. The authors seek an admission-time solution that prevents hub-like documents from entering the index at all, eliminating the exposure window and amortizing cost.
AI.method: The paper proposes a global admission gate: before insertion, each candidate document is scored against a fixed set of sentinel queries. Documents exhibiting hub-like behavior (high aggregate similarity to many sentinels) are quarantined. Thresholds are maintained incrementally. The method is evaluated across two 100K-document corpora and five encoders, with disjoint attacker and defender query sets. Both global and per-topic gating variants are tested, along with HotFlip adversarial attacks. Integration with HNSW approximate indexing is benchmarked for ingestion latency, scoring scalability, and decision stability.
AI.result: The global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (≥0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91±0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on benign documents. Per-topic gating provides no reliable benefit, attributed to anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Insertion cost is corpus-size-independent; amortized deletion cost is minimal. On HNSW, admission adds ~3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and only 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing (none involving attacks). Provenance analysis complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.
AI.conclusion: Admission-time gating with sentinel queries is an effective, low-overhead defense against hubness-based poisoning in RAG, eliminating the exposure window of periodic scans, scaling independently of corpus size, and maintaining high recall against both natural and adversarial hubs with few false positives.

title: Weibull Weight-Scale Parameter Evolution under AdamW Training Dynamics
summary: Building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, we study why the Weibull weight-scale parameter $λ$ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training. We derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update: an alignment force measuring the correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction, an injection force from adaptive step magnitude, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, contributing 88-94% of the absolute force budget across four random seeds and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from weight-scale growth to relaxation. These force dynamics directly govern the squared-norm component underlying $λ(t)$; the remaining RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is measurable and decomposes into bridge and integration components, totaling approximately 5-6% in densely sampled regions. To extend the analysis to real models where optimizer moments are unavailable, we introduce a spline displacement method that recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints with approximately 92-94% accuracy, about twice the naive two-point baseline. We further observe that the peak value of $λ(t)$ varies with training-data coherence in our experiments, suggesting a data-dependent component of weight-scale growth that we leave to a controlled follow-up study. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why the Weibull weight-scale parameter λ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training, decomposing the squared weight norm dynamics into three forces: alignment, injection, and decay. A spline displacement method is introduced to recover force signals from sparse checkpoints when optimizer states are unavailable.
AI.motivation: Understanding the empirical dynamics of the Weibull weight-scale parameter λ(t) during AdamW training — specifically why it exhibits growth, overshoot, and relaxation — and linking these macroscopic distributional changes to microscopic optimizer update mechanics.
AI.method: The authors derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update rule: (1) alignment force (correlation between weights and adaptive update direction), (2) injection force (adaptive step magnitude), and (3) decay force (from decoupled weight decay). Experiments are conducted on self-trained Pythia-70M models preserving ground-truth optimizer moments. A spline displacement method is introduced to recover alignment forces from sparse checkpoints when optimizer states are missing. The RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is decomposed into bridge and integration components.
AI.result: Alignment force dominates the rise phase (88-94% of absolute force budget across four seeds), remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the λ(t) peak and subsequent relaxation. The reconstruction offset totals ~5-6% in densely sampled regions. The spline displacement method recovers alignment force with ~92-94% accuracy from sparse checkpoints, roughly doubling the naive two-point baseline. Peak λ(t) varies with training-data coherence.
AI.conclusion: Weight-scale dynamics under AdamW are primarily governed by an alignment force between weights and the adaptive update direction, with decay providing a balancing counterforce near saturation. The Weibull parameter λ(t) can be reconstructed from these force dynamics plus a small, measurable offset. The framework extends to real models via spline-based recovery from sparse checkpoints, and data-coherence effects on λ peak height warrant further controlled study.

title: LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can recognize their own knowledge limits on structured clinical data. Findings reveal LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, an inverse difficulty effect exists, few-shot examples and SHAP evidence are super-additive, and a cross-model attribution divergence calibrator dramatically reduces calibration error — framing this as a cold start problem for LLM epistemic self-awareness on structured tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed on structured clinical data, but their ability to recognize the boundaries of their own knowledge (epistemic self-awareness) on such tasks is unexplored. Reliable uncertainty quantification is critical in clinical settings, and the authors aim to reduce epistemic uncertainty through cross-model attribution divergence analysis.
AI.method: The study compares Qwen 2.5 7B against XGBoost on a structured clinical prediction task using attribution divergence analysis. Key experimental manipulations include: (1) measuring LLM verbalized confidence across varying accuracy regimes, (2) analyzing performance conditional on XGBoost's correctness/difficulty, (3) testing few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence as interventions (both independently and jointly), and (4) building a cross-model calibrator that uses attribution divergence signals to estimate patient-specific LLM reliability without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. The Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) and expected calibration error (ECE) serve as primary metrics.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) LLM verbalized confidence is near-constant (0.856–0.937) regardless of actual accuracy (49%–75.3%), tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. (2) An inverse difficulty effect: LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) under moderate uncertainty. (3) Few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions, jointly reducing ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and boosting accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. (4) The cross-model calibrator reduces ECE from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates.
AI.conclusion: The results characterize a "cold start" problem: LLMs lack genuine epistemic self-awareness on structured data, but cross-model attribution divergence signals can serve as an effective external reliability proxy. This outlines a viable path toward calibrated, trustworthy LLM deployment on structured clinical tasks without requiring model internals access or costly repeated inference.

title: PACMS: Submodular Context Selection as a Pluggable Engine for LLM Agents
summary:
Conversational and tool-using LLM agents operate over a context window that fills from several directions simultaneously. As a session proceeds, the agent accumulates user and assistant turns, entries drawn from a persistent memory store, and often largest of all, the verbatim outputs of tool calls such as file reads, search results, and API responses. Once the cumulative context exceeds the model's token budget, the framework must decide what to keep.
  The prevailing mechanism is recency truncation, sometimes paired with periodic summarization. This is topic-blind: a fact established early in a session is discarded simply because it is old, even when the current user query is about exactly that fact; conversely, verbose but irrelevant recent material is retained. Agents that must recall information across many turns, the defining case for memory, are precisely where recency truncation fails.
  Existing alternatives sit outside the agent's assembly step. Retrieval augmented generation fetches external documents into the prompt but does not arbitrate the agent's \emph{already-present} pooled context. Context-compression methods reduce token count by rewriting or pruning text, but operate query-blind and lossily. Neither treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool to be selected from by relevance at the moment the prompt is assembled.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques recency-based context truncation in LLM agents, arguing it is topic-blind and fails when long-term recall is needed. It identifies a gap: existing alternatives (RAG, context compression) do not treat the agent's full accumulated context (conversation, memory, tool outputs) as a unified candidate pool for relevance-based selection at prompt assembly time.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that use conversation and tools accumulate heterogeneous context (user turns, assistant turns, memory store entries, tool call outputs). The prevailing "recency truncation" strategy is topic-blind — it discards old but potentially relevant facts while retaining recent but irrelevant material. This fundamentally fails in the very scenario that defines memory: recalling information across many turns. Existing alternatives (RAG fetches external docs; compression rewrites lossily) do not address the core problem of intelligently selecting from the agent's already-present pooled context based on relevance at prompt-construction time.
AI.method: This appears to be an abstract/introduction positioning piece. The paper identifies the problem and surveys existing approaches (recency truncation, summarization, RAG, context compression), then argues for a new paradigm: treating memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool and performing relevance-based selection at prompt assembly time. The full methodology is not yet described in this excerpt.
AI.result: The abstract does not present experimental results. It is a problem-statement and gap-analysis contribution.
AI.conclusion: A new mechanism is needed that unifies all context sources (memory, conversation, tool outputs) into a single pool and selects entries by relevance to the current query — not by recency — at the moment the prompt is assembled. This addresses a critical failure mode in agent architectures that require long-horizon recall.

title: Exit-and-Join Dynamics for Decentralized Coalition Formation
summary: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions. Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value, so payoffs are computed within the agent's current coalition rather than through a globally negotiated coalition structure. The resulting model links cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior: a terminal partition is precisely a coalition structure with no admissible, individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. We establish equilibrium characterizations, identify conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, and analyze how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a special convex-game benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper models coalition formation as a decentralized process where agents unilaterally decide to exit or join coalitions based on the Aumann-Drèze value. It connects cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative dynamics, characterizes equilibria, identifies conditions for Lyapunov/potential representations, and examines how switching/acceptance costs affect stability.
AI.motivation: Traditional coalition formation models often rely on global negotiation and centralized payoff allocation (e.g., the Shapley value across the grand coalition). The authors seek to model coalition formation as a realistic, decentralized process where agents make local, self-interested moves — bridging the gap between cooperative solution concepts and noncooperative, best-response dynamics.
AI.method: The authors formalize a dynamical system where agents iteratively evaluate unilateral exit-and-join moves. Payoffs are computed via the Aumann-Drèze value, which distributes coalitional surplus only among members of the agent's current coalition (not globally). A terminal state is defined as a partition where no agent has an individually profitable deviation. The analysis establishes equilibrium characterizations, derives conditions for the dynamics to admit scalar Lyapunov functions or exact-potential representations, and incorporates switching and acceptance costs to assess their impact on local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a convex-game benchmark.
AI.result: The paper establishes characterizations of terminal coalition structures as equilibria under the exit-and-join dynamics. It identifies structural conditions under which the process admits a Lyapunov function or an exact potential game representation, guaranteeing convergence. Switching and acceptance costs are shown to enhance local stability by creating frictions that deter excessive reconfiguration. Numerical experiments demonstrate finite-time convergence to stable partitions, quantify sensitivity to cost parameters, and validate the framework on a convex-game benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The decentralized exit-and-join model, combined with the Aumann-Drèze value, provides a coherent bridge between cooperative and noncooperative coalition formation. The dynamics converge under identifiable conditions, and costs can be tuned to ensure stability. The framework offers both theoretical insights and practical computational tools for analyzing self-organizing coalitional systems.

title: Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework
summary: A protocol driven framework is presented that binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed from declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay. Evaluation uses approximately 10000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads 50 to 5000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.

AI.tldr: A framework that links SBOM/AIBOM artifacts with deterministic environment capture and runtime telemetry to compute exploitability, generate signed CSAF VEX advisories, and validate through deterministic replay, evaluated on ~10,000 components in Agentic AI workloads.
AI.motivation: Current vulnerability management lacks a unified approach that connects static software and AI bills of materials (SBOM/AIBOM) with actual runtime conditions, leading to imprecise exploitability assessments and unverifiable advisory generation.
AI.method: A protocol-driven framework that: (1) deterministically captures environment state and runtime telemetry; (2) computes exploitability by correlating declared artifacts, activation conditions, and execution policies; (3) generates cryptographically signed CSAF VEX advisories; and (4) validates findings through deterministic replay.
AI.result: Evaluation across ~10,000 component entries using synthetic Agentic AI workloads (50–5000 components) integrated with OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets demonstrates the framework's capability for evidence-backed, replay-verifiable exploitability assessment and advisory generation.
AI.conclusion: Binding SBOM/AIBOM artifacts to deterministic runtime evidence enables cryptographically verifiable, replay-validated VEX advisories, significantly improving the precision and trustworthiness of vulnerability exploitability assessments in complex, component-rich environments.

title: Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on LLM Reasoning. 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

AI.tldr: CAP is a training-free pruning method that uses causal attribution at the attention-head level to identify which heads matter most for reasoning, then guides fine-grained weight pruning, outperforming correlation-based methods like Wanda especially on reasoning benchmarks at moderate sparsity.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at multi-step reasoning but suffer from high inference costs. Existing pruning methods rely on magnitude or activation-based (correlational) criteria, which fail to capture the functional causal contribution of attention heads, leading to degraded reasoning performance post-pruning.
AI.method: CAP operates in three steps: (1) For each attention head, mask it during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems and measure the expected performance degradation (causal score). (2) Convert these head-level causal scores into weight-level importance values for the corresponding Q/K/V/O projection matrices. (3) Prune weights globally based on these importance values to reach a target sparsity level, without any retraining.
AI.result: On ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity, CAP achieves relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda. Across GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10-20% sparsity, CAP outperforms Wanda in most configurations, with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. At 50% sparsity, performance is limited by coarse MLP attribution.
AI.conclusion: Attention-head-level causal attribution better preserves reasoning performance than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, though the approach remains limited by coarse MLP attribution at high sparsity levels (50%).

title: SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling
summary: Speculative inference accelerates large language model (LLM) decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees. Existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference: they either introduce additional computation or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating acceleration benefits. This reveals a fundamental incompatibility between current safety methods and speculative decoding. We propose SafeSpec, a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation. We model jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase the probability of harmful continuations without eliminating safe ones. Under this model, SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process. Across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks, SafeSpec achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads, demonstrating that speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized.

AI.tldr: SafeSpec integrates safety evaluation into speculative inference by attaching a latent safety head to the target model, enabling joint verification of semantic validity and safety in one forward pass, with rollback and reflective multi-sampling for safe recovery when unsafe content is detected.
AI.motivation: Current safety defenses are incompatible with speculative inference—they add computation or break the draft-verify pipeline, negating speedup. There is a fundamental tension between inference-time safety and speculative decoding that needs resolution.
AI.method: SafeSpec adds a lightweight latent safety head to the target model for joint validity-safety verification in a single forward pass. Upon detecting unsafe generations, it employs rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations. Jailbreak attacks are modeled as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, and SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while maintaining a 2.06× inference speedup on benign workloads, achieving a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized. SafeSpec demonstrates that safety need not come at the cost of efficiency in speculative decoding.

title: Zero-Inflated Gaussian Distributions Enable Parameter-Space Sparsity in Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
summary: Estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) are a powerful class of evolutionary methods for black-box optimization, especially when little is known about the structure of the objective. Whereas classical evolutionary algorithms rely on hand-designed mutation and crossover operators, hard to devise for unknown problem structures, and a source of bias, EDAs sidestep operator design entirely: they fit a probability distribution to the best individuals and sample the next generation from it. EDAs are well established on continuous parameter spaces, but they have not previously been generalized to sparse ones, in which most coefficients of a good solution are exactly zero.
