Existing sparse black-box optimizers therefore reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes alternating between support set and active values, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. We close this gap by proposing multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and the interactions between the two, so sparsity patterns and active values are optimized jointly, hierarchy-free. We show that the latent parameters of this model are identifiable from observed samples, unlike in the missing-data settings where related constructions originate, and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators for them. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures, and on the Lunar Lander benchmark the resulting ZIG-EDA converges faster and reaches higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithm (EDA) for sparse black-box optimization using multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions, eliminating the need for hand-crafted sparsity operators. The ZIG-EDA jointly optimizes sparsity patterns and active parameter values, with identifiable latent parameters and amortized inversion-based estimators, outperforming dense and ad-hoc sparse baselines on the Lunar Lander benchmark.
AI.motivation: EDAs avoid hand-designed operators by learning a probabilistic model from elite individuals, but they have never been generalized to sparse optimization domains where most optimal coefficients are zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers reintroduce precisely what EDAs were designed to avoid—hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes, and zeroing thresholds—creating unwanted bias. The gap is a principled, probabilistic EDA that natively handles sparsity without baked-in structural assumptions.
AI.method: The authors propose using multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as the sampling distribution within an EDA framework. The ZIG model employs a latent Gaussian with separate indicator and value dimensions, capturing sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and interactions between the two. This enables joint, hierarchy-free optimization of sparsity and active values. They prove identifiability of the latent ZIG parameters (unlike related missing-data settings) and develop practical amortized inversion-based estimators. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures from observed samples.
AI.result: The proposed ZIG-EDA converges faster and achieves higher final returns than three baselines—a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA—on the Lunar Lander benchmark while producing controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active. The amortized estimators also accurately recover latent correlation structures in synthetic experiments.
AI.conclusion: The ZIG-EDA successfully extends EDAs to sparse optimization domains without reintroducing hand-crafted sparsity mechanisms. The identifiability and estimation results provide theoretical grounding, and the empirical gains on Lunar Lander demonstrate practical effectiveness for learning compact, high-performing sparse controllers.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk
summary: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a continuous, learnable formulation of phenotypic similarity for contrastive vision-language alignment, replacing rigid discrete grouping with soft, differentiable weighting derived from intra-modality embeddings. Applied to retinal imaging and clinical risk narratives from UK Biobank, the method improves incident Alzheimer's disease prediction over discrete group-based and standard baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing retinal-based AD prediction methods (e.g., REVEAL) use phenotypic grouping in contrastive learning but treat similarity as a discrete construct with hard group assignments. This rigid supervision decouples group formation from representation learning and fails to capture the continuous, spectrum-like nature of neurodegenerative risk.
AI.method: The authors introduce a continuous phenotypic structure model within contrastive learning: (1) inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function based on intra-modality embedding similarities from both retinal images and clinical risk profiles; (2) soft multi-positive relationships are defined via a continuous aggregation operator that provides graded supervision; (3) a soft-target contrastive objective jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end, rather than using fixed cluster assignments.
AI.result: Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms both discrete group-based contrastive learning approaches and standard vision-language baselines.
AI.conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a more principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling using multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

title: Organizing in the Digital Age: Understanding Community, Challenges, and Consequences in Digitally-facilitated Labor Organizing
summary: The contemporary American labor force is highly dispersed, necessitating the use of digital communication tools to bridge spatial and temporal gaps in union organizing. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how workers within various labor unions utilize digital, text-based communication platforms -- including Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack -- for labor organizing. Through 17 qualitative interviews, we examine the challenges and opportunities presented by digital organizing, identifying both technical and social obstacles. Our findings reveal that although digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, they also introduce new complexities, such as navigating technical security, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus. Based on these insights, we draw connections to broader understandings of digital organizing and the role of digital tools in unions.

AI.tldr: This study examines how U.S. labor unions use digital text-based platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing. Based on 17 qualitative interviews, it identifies both the benefits (bridging spatial/temporal gaps) and challenges (security, information overload, trust-building) of digital organizing tools.
AI.motivation: The contemporary American workforce is geographically dispersed, creating spatial and temporal barriers to traditional union organizing. Digital communication tools have become essential to bridge these gaps, yet there is limited in-depth understanding of how workers actually use these platforms and what challenges arise in digital labor organizing contexts.
AI.method: The researchers conducted 17 qualitative interviews with workers across various labor unions who use digital, text-based communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing purposes. The interview data was analyzed to identify technical and social obstacles as well as opportunities in digital labor organizing.
AI.result: Digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, but they introduce new complexities in three key areas: (1) navigating technical security concerns, (2) managing information overload, and (3) building trust and consensus among workers in text-based environments. These findings connect digital organizing practices to broader sociotechnical dynamics within unions.
AI.conclusion: While digital communication platforms are indispensable for modern union organizing given workforce dispersion, their adoption is not frictionless. Unions must contend with the dual-edged nature of these tools — they enable coordination across distance but simultaneously surface challenges around security, information management, and the social dynamics of trust-building that differ from face-to-face organizing.

title: Generative Engine Optimization at Scale: Measuring Brand Visibility Across AI Search Engines
summary:
People increasingly get answers straight from AI search engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini rather than scrolling search results. Brands that once focused on search engine optimization (SEO) must now optimize for how these engines represent, cite, and recommend them -- a shift variously called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), and AI Search Visibility. We treat AEO and AI Visibility as part of GEO, and study how to measure brand visibility across AI engines: what they value when they cite a brand, which sources they rely on, and what content large language models surface. The hard case is everyone outside the already-authoritative top brands -- SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and early-stage startups.
  We analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on Ranqo between March and May 2026. First visibility runs form a clear three-tier brand-stature ladder: global household names (e.g., Stripe, Nike) appear in 73% of relevant AI answers on their first run; established mid-market and regional brands (e.g., Olipop, Klaviyo) in 44%; niche and small brands in just 11% -- about 30 percentage points per step. When engines cite sources, about 78% go to corporate websites; among non-corporate sources YouTube leads, ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. The highest-leverage page is the ranked "best-of" listicle, the most-cited content format at about 21% of all citations. Sentiment is the unstable signal: whether a brand is framed positively or negatively flips about 6.7 times more often than whether it is mentioned at all.
  These findings provide a first large-scale baseline for measuring GEO: AI brand visibility can be measured, differs by platform, and varies strongly by brand maturity. We close by proposing seven v1.1 protocols to test whether specific recommendations can causally improve AI visibility.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first large-scale empirical baseline for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), analyzing 100K+ AI search responses across 100+ brands. It reveals a stark three-tier visibility hierarchy (73% vs. 44% vs. 11% mention rates), identifies key citation patterns (78% corporate sources; "best-of" listicles as the top format), quantifies sentiment instability (6.7× more volatile than mentions), and proposes seven testable protocols for improving AI brand visibility.
AI.motivation: The shift from traditional search engines to AI answer engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini) fundamentally changes how brands gain visibility. While SEO is well-understood, GEO/AEO lacks empirical measurement baselines. The authors identify a critical gap: existing knowledge applies mainly to already-authoritative global brands, leaving SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and startups without actionable data on how AI engines cite, represent, and recommend brands.
AI.method: The study analyzed over 100,000 prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on the Ranqo platform between March and May 2026. Brands were categorized into a three-tier maturity ladder: global household names, established mid-market/regional brands, and niche/small brands. For each tier, the authors measured visibility rates (appearance in relevant AI answers), citation source distribution (corporate vs. non-corporate), content format prevalence, and sentiment stability across AI engines.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) A clear three-tier visibility ladder with roughly 30-percentage-point gaps between each tier — global brands at 73%, mid-market at 44%, and niche brands at just 11% mention rates on first run. (2) Citation patterns show 78% of sources are corporate websites; among non-corporate sources, YouTube leads, followed by Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. "Best-of" listicles are the single highest-leverage content format at ~21% of all citations. (3) Sentiment is highly unstable — brand framing flips positive/negative ~6.7× more frequently than brand mention status changes.
AI.conclusion: AI brand visibility is measurable, varies significantly by platform and brand maturity, and follows predictable structural patterns. The authors propose seven v1.1 protocols as testable interventions to causally improve AI visibility, establishing a foundation for empirical GEO research and practice beyond the current reliance on authoritative incumbents.

title: Library-Aware Doubles and Iterative Repair for Large Language Model-Generated Unit Tests in OpenSIL Firmware
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 1 Table. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Validating changes in low-level C firmware is expensive because unit tests (UTs) are fragile under strict build constraints, where missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. This study introduces an automated UT authoring workflow for the Open-Source Silicon Initialization Library (openSIL) firmware codebase maintained by Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) that reduces manual effort through a large language model (LLM) guided multi-agent pipeline. The workflow combines automated generation of test scaffolds, library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. We evaluate the approach using compilation success, repair iterations, dispatch success, and line coverage, with time, cost, and token usage as secondary measures. Across 76 functions under test, the workflow generated compilable UTs for 73 functions. In a configuration without line coverage guidance or retrieval augmentation, mean line coverage reached 73.9%. On a 48-function subset evaluated under both configurations, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with line-coverage guidance alone and reached 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval. Results show that automated generation-and-repair pipelines can substantially improve UT creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-guided multi-agent pipeline for automatically generating and repairing unit tests for low-level C firmware (AMD's openSIL). Across 76 functions, 73 produced compilable tests. With line-coverage feedback, mean coverage reached 98.8% on a 48-function subset, demonstrating that iterative compile-dispatch-repair loops significantly improve test generation efficiency and coverage in constrained firmware environments.
AI.motivation: Validating low-level C firmware changes is expensive because unit tests are fragile under strict build constraints — missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. Manual effort to resolve these issues is substantial, motivating an automated approach.
AI.method: An automated UT authoring workflow using an LLM-guided multi-agent pipeline with three key components: (1) automated generation of test scaffolds, (2) library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and (3) an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. Two configurations are compared: line-coverage guidance alone versus line-coverage guidance combined with vector-database retrieval augmentation.
AI.result: Out of 76 functions under test, 73 produced compilable unit tests. Without coverage guidance or retrieval, mean line coverage was 73.9%. On a 48-function subset, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with line-coverage guidance alone and 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Automated generation-and-repair pipelines substantially improve UT creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort. Line-coverage feedback alone proved most effective; adding retrieval augmentation slightly reduced coverage, suggesting careful integration is needed.

title: DevOps and General Developers: Insights from Stack Overflow's 2023 Survey
comment: 17 pages, 11 tables, research paper based on the 2023 Stack Overflow Developer Survey data analysis
summary:
Purpose: To investigate the distinct roles of DevOps specialists and general software developers, examining their varying use of tools, technologies, methodologies, and demographics in the current software development environment. In addition, to differentiate these two professional groups regarding their unique contributions and challenges in the field.
  Design/Methodology/Approach: The research uses a quantitative approach to analyze data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey. It focuses on a comparative analysis of technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between DevOps specialists and general developers, highlighting key trends and differences. The data analysis was conducted using Python's Pandas library for data analysis.
  Findings: The research indicates no significant difference in the tool and technology preferences between DevOps specialists and general software developers, highlighting their complementary roles. DevOps specialists and general software developers use tools like Docker and Kubernetes, emphasizing efficiency and automation. While general developers employ diverse tools for various role demands, demographic trends show younger general developers and mid-career DevOps professionals. This age range reflects growing experience in DevOps, and both groups are adapting to remote and hybrid work models in the evolving tech industry.
  Practical Implications: This research offers perspectives on the dynamic roles within software development, emphasizing the growing importance of DevOps. It is a valuable resource for academic and industry professionals to understand the evolving dynamics in software development roles.
  Originality/Value: This research fills a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the evolving dynamics of software development roles.

AI.tldr: A quantitative comparative analysis of Stack Overflow 2023 survey data reveals that DevOps specialists and general software developers exhibit no significant differences in tool/technology preferences, with both groups adopting Docker and Kubernetes. Demographic distinctions include younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps professionals, with both adapting to remote/hybrid work models.
AI.motivation: To address a gap in the literature by systematically differentiating DevOps specialists from general software developers across multiple dimensions—tools, technologies, methodologies, demographics, and professional contributions—within the contemporary software development landscape.
AI.method: Quantitative comparative analysis using data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey, processed with Python's Pandas library. The study examines technological preferences, demographic profiles, and professional experiences to identify trends and distinctions between the two groups.
AI.result: No significant difference in tool/technology preferences was found; both groups commonly use Docker and Kubernetes. Demographic trends show younger individuals among general developers and mid-career professionals in DevOps. Both groups are increasingly adopting remote and hybrid work arrangements.
AI.conclusion: DevOps specialists and general developers occupy complementary rather than fundamentally distinct roles regarding tooling. The study highlights DevOps' growing importance and provides a resource for understanding evolving software development role dynamics, filling a notable literature gap.

title: Detecting Hallucinations for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning infers new knowledge from existing facts and is widely applied in question answering, recommendation, and decision support. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks have become increasingly popular by leveraging retrieved KG information. However, hallucinations in LLMs remain a critical issue. Even when relevant KG knowledge is incorporated, models may still generate incorrect outputs, leading to misinformation and unreliable decisions. Existing hallucination detection methods either focus on LLM internal states or verify consistency with retrieved contexts, but both overlook the structural information in KGs, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this gap, we propose LUCID, the first halLUcination deteCtIon method for LLM-based knowleDge graph reasoning frameworks. LUCID jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information. Specifically, it extracts node and edge features from attention scores and semantic similarities, and integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. We also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation. Experiments on nine datasets show that LUCID achieves state of the art performance compared to 15 baselines.

AI.tldr: LUCID proposes a hallucination detection method for LLM-based KG reasoning that combines LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information via graph neural networks, achieving SOTA on 9 benchmarks against 15 baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations even when relevant KG knowledge is provided, and existing detection methods overlook KG structural information, leading to suboptimal performance in KG reasoning contexts.
AI.method: LUCID extracts node and edge features from LLM attention scores and semantic similarities, then integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. Manually annotated benchmark datasets are constructed for evaluation.
AI.result: LUCID achieves state-of-the-art performance across nine datasets compared to 15 baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Jointly leveraging attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information via GNNs is highly effective for detecting hallucinations in LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks.

title: DISARM: Target Electronic Device Informed Mitigation of Software Runtime Side-Channel Vulnerabilities
summary: Program runtime or timing attacks exploit variations in a program's execution times to extract sensitive information from the program (e.g. encryption keys, sensitive variable data, intellectual property). State-of-the-art solutions to runtime side-channel attacks attempt to balance the execution time of the sensitive code for different control flow paths to eliminate the timing leakage. However, during the mitigation process, most techniques do not consider the underlying hardware or device on which the target program is supposed to run on. This can lead to over-fixing (unnecessary extra operations), under-fixing (not solving the imbalance properly), and even failures. We propose DISARM, a joint hardware-software methodology (unlike any existing solution) for mitigating runtime side-channel vulnerabilities that utilizes timing values from real embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes. We implement DISARM to support C, C++, and Java source codes and validate it across 22 standard benchmarks. DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions such as PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in terms of execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness on five different embedded or edge devices.

AI.tldr: DISARM is a joint hardware-software methodology that uses real-device timing measurements to generate targeted mitigations for runtime side-channel vulnerabilities, outperforming state-of-the-art solutions across multiple embedded devices.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime side-channel mitigation techniques (e.g., PENDULUM, DifFuzzAR) balance execution times without considering the underlying hardware, leading to over-fixing, under-fixing, or outright failures. A solution that accounts for real hardware timing characteristics is needed.
AI.method: DISARM uses timing values collected from real embedded/edge devices to inform targeted software fixes that balance execution time across control flow paths. It supports C, C++, and Java source code and employs a joint hardware-software approach.
AI.result: Validated on 22 standard benchmarks across five embedded/edge devices, DISARM outperforms PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating hardware-specific timing data into software-level mitigation yields more efficient and correct defenses against runtime side-channel attacks compared to hardware-agnostic approaches.

title: Emergent Alignment
summary: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "conscience step" where an LLM reviews its own outputs for ethical alignment, combined with DPO-based training loss, enabling online self-alignment without external judges. The key contribution is demonstrating "Emergent Alignment" — using a single introspective question to steer training toward ethical behavior, countering prior work on "Emergent Misalignment."
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that fine-tuning LLMs can produce emergent unethical behaviors (code hacking scenarios). The authors seek to determine whether LLMs can recognize their own ethical misalignments and self-correct, without relying on external judge models (weaker or stronger).
AI.method: The method consists of two components: (1) a "conscience step" where the model reviews its own reasoning and outputs via introspection, and (2) an extended training loss incorporating an alignment component via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using a frozen copy of the model as reference. This operates across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot settings.
AI.result: Under the same code-hacking scenario that previously produced Emergent Misalignment, the proposed method achieves "Emergent Alignment," where a single high-level introspective question successfully steers the model toward ethical behavior.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can discern and self-correct ethical misalignments through introspection combined with DPO, enabling online alignment without external judges. This transforms the Emergent Misalignment phenomenon into Emergent Alignment via a simple introspective mechanism.

title: DataMagic: Transforming Tabular Data into Data Insight Video
summary: Data videos integrate dynamic charts, voice narration, and synchronized animations to communicate data insights as temporal narratives, making them an effective medium for improving data consumption efficiency in the data management lifecycle. However, producing high-quality data videos requires expertise spanning data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches fall short: static visualization tools (e.g., BI dashboards) lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools require users to pre-prepare visualizations rather than working from raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. We demonstrate DataMagic, an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos. To ensure data fidelity, DataMagic introduces the declarative specification DVSpec, which binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields through data-driven semantic references. To address the combinatorial explosion of the design space, DataMagic adopts a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then optimizes narrative coherence through global orchestration. Leveraging DVSpec's decoupling of logic and rendering, the system further supports three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A, transforming one-way videos into explorable interactive data interfaces. Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of the DataMagic. Homepage: https://datamagic-home.github.io/

AI.tldr: DataMagic is an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos using a declarative specification (DVSpec) and a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture, while supporting interactive exploration and provenance-based Q&A.
AI.motivation: Producing high-quality data videos requires expertise in data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches are insufficient: static visualization tools lack narrative and animation; authoring tools require pre-prepared visualizations rather than raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance.
AI.method: The system introduces DVSpec, a declarative specification that binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields via data-driven semantic references. It employs a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then globally orchestrates them for narrative coherence. The system also leverages DVSpec's logic-rendering decoupling to support three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A.
AI.result: Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of DataMagic.
AI.conclusion: DataMagic offers a novel approach to automated data video generation that ensures data fidelity through declarative binding, manages design-space complexity via parallel generation with global orchestration, and transforms passive videos into explorable interactive data interfaces.

title: ScholarQuest: A Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark for Agentic Academic Paper Search in Open Literature Environments
summary: Academic paper search is a core step in scientific research, and LLM-based search agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for iterative, intent-driven literature exploration. However, existing benchmarks are insufficient for systematically evaluating agentic academic search under realistic open literature environments. We propose ScholarQuest, a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for agentic academic paper search. ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics and four representative research intents, including method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It further provides scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. Benchmarking results show that agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent only achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial room for improvement. In addition, analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases further highlight the benchmark's ability to provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals for academic paper search agents.

AI.tldr: ScholarQuest is a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for evaluating LLM-based search agents in academic paper search, revealing that the best agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100, leaving significant room for improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate agentic academic search in realistic open literature environments. There is a need for a systematic, reproducible benchmark that captures diverse research intents and provides multi-dimensional evaluation signals.
AI.method: ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 CS topics across four research intent types (method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, scope-controlled). It features scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend (ScholarBase) for reproducible evaluation. Both agentic methods and single-shot retrieval baselines are benchmarked.
AI.result: Agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines overall. However, the best-performing agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All. Analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases reveal multi-dimensional performance gaps.
AI.conclusion: ScholarQuest provides a robust, multi-dimensional evaluation framework for academic paper search agents, highlighting that current agents still underperform significantly, and substantial research is needed to bridge the gap between agentic and ideal retrieval performance.

title: Heterogeneous LLM Debate Under Adversarial Peers: Honest Gains, Replacement Costs, and Resilience
summary: Heterogeneous LLM debate is motivated by the promise that diverse peers correct one another, but the same exchange that carries correction also carries adversarial influence. We measure which dominates by tracking how a heterogeneous peer changes the honest agents' revision behavior: how often they change their answer, and whether the change is corrective or harmful. We compare matched panels (homogeneous baseline, honest-mixed, and adversarial-mixed) and contaminated panels in which a malicious same-family peer is already present, spanning four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. An honest heterogeneous peer sharply lowers harmful revision, and an adversarial one reverses it. For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the honest-slot harmful-revision rate falls from 89% in the homogeneous panel to 35% with an honest peer, and an adversarial peer returns it to 90%. The conditional rate hides this damage on weak defenders, but the end-of-debate flip rate exposes it. The pattern keeps its sign across families and benchmarks while its magnitude varies with the defender-benchmark regime. We also measure the effects when an adversarial same-family peer is already present: an honest heterogeneous peer lowers both harmful revision and the rate at which initially-correct answers are lost. On the same Llama-3.1-70B setting, the added honest peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% under a same-family adversary to 6%. Heterogeneity is therefore not only an attack surface but, when an adversary is already present, also a defense.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether heterogeneous LLM debate helps (through diverse corrective feedback) or hurts (through adversarial influence). By tracking revision behavior of honest agents when paired with honest vs. adversarial heterogeneous peers, the authors find that honest heterogeneity sharply reduces harmful revisions, while adversarial heterogeneity reverses this benefit. Notably, when a same-family adversary is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer serves as a defense, substantially reducing the loss of initially-correct answers.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous LLM debate (mixing models from different families) is motivated by the idea that diverse perspectives correct each other's errors. However, the same communication channel that enables correction also opens the door to adversarial influence. The authors aim to empirically measure which effect dominates in practice.
AI.method: The authors design controlled experiments comparing matched panels: (1) homogeneous baselines (same-family models), (2) honest-mixed panels (heterogeneous honest peer added), (3) adversarial-mixed panels (heterogeneous adversarial peer added), and (4) contaminated panels where a malicious same-family peer is already present. They track two key metrics: how often honest agents change their answers (revision rate) and whether those changes are corrective or harmful. Experiments span four model families and three reasoning benchmarks, using Llama-3.1-70B as the primary defender on MATH-hard.
AI.result: For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, harmful-revision rate drops from 89% (homogeneous) to 35% with an honest heterogeneous peer, but rises back to 90% with an adversarial one. The conditional rate masks this damage on weak defenders, but the end-of-debate flip rate reveals it. The sign of this pattern is consistent across model families and benchmarks, though magnitude varies by defender-benchmark regime. Crucially, when a same-family adversary is already present, an added honest heterogeneous peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct answers from 31% to 6%.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneity in LLM debate is a double-edged sword: it is an attack surface (adversarial peers can cause harm) but also a defense mechanism. When an adversary is already present in the debate, introducing an honest heterogeneous peer significantly mitigates damage, making heterogeneity a net positive in contaminated settings.

title: JustDiag!: A Diagnostic Justification Engine for Accountable Root Cause Analysis
summary: Large language models can produce fluent root cause analyses, but fluent final answers alone are insufficient evidence for accountability in high-stakes operations. In real incident response, engineers need to know what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remained, and whether the system resolved the case or preserved uncertainty. We address this gap with JustDiag, a diagnostic justification engine for RCA that maintains an explicit process state over evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. We evaluated the system on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality. Relative to a matched control without diagnostic justification, JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores, while accepting slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure. These results suggest that accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not only fluent final answers.

AI.tldr: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine for root cause analysis (RCA) that maintains explicit process state over evidence, hypotheses, and conflicts. Evaluated on 66 real-world incidents, it outperformed a baseline in outcome and process quality, while showing more calibrated non-closure, demonstrating that accountable RCA requires justification artifacts, not just fluent final answers.
AI.motivation: Fluent root cause analyses from LLMs are insufficient for high-stakes incident response because they lack transparency about supporting evidence, considered alternatives, unresolved contradictions, and whether uncertainty was preserved. Engineers need verifiable diagnostic reasoning for accountability, not merely plausible-sounding conclusions.
AI.method: JustDiag maintains an explicit process state tracking evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks throughout the diagnostic process. The system was evaluated on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer evaluation protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality, compared against a matched control without diagnostic justification capabilities.
AI.result: JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores relative to the control. It showed slightly lower terminal completion rates due to more calibrated non-closure — the system appropriately refrains from closing cases when evidence is insufficient rather than forcing a fluent but unsubstantiated answer.
AI.conclusion: Accountable RCA systems require explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not merely fluent final answers. Calibrated non-closure is a feature, not a bug, in high-stakes diagnostic settings.

title: Sign-Language Datasets at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey on Resources, Benchmarks, and Annotation Standards
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Sign languages are expressive visual languages used by Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) communities. Despite substantial progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, advances remain constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to reflect real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these limitations remain limited. In this survey, we present a comprehensive index of sign-language datasets, covering 120 resources across 35 sign languages. We analyze key challenges such as modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and outline considerations for future dataset design. We also introduce a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet and release a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Ginqwerty/Open-Sign-Language) to support standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation. Overall, our work provides a unified and practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey cataloging 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages, identifying key challenges (modality imbalance, annotation granularity, signer bias), proposing a standardized 24-field datasheet, and releasing a public repository to support reproducible and inclusive sign-language technology development.
AI.motivation: Existing sign-language datasets are fragmented, inconsistently annotated, and linguistically limited, failing to reflect real-world communication needs. No systematic analysis of these limitations exists, hindering progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale survey, compiling and systematically analyzing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages. They identified recurring challenges, proposed a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet for standardized documentation, and released a GitHub repository with an open index for reproducible evaluation.
AI.result: The survey reveals persistent issues: modality imbalance (over-reliance on RGB video, underuse of depth/pose data), coarse annotation granularity, and significant signer bias. The proposed datasheet and repository provide a structured framework for addressing these gaps.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified foundation for building more inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies by standardizing dataset documentation and enabling reproducible benchmarking across diverse sign languages.

title: ProMUSE: Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty-guided Staged Evidential Alzheimer Disease Classification
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a fatal disorder that destroys memory and cognitive skills in the elderly population. Most treatments for AD are effective in the early stage, leading to an increasing demand for early AD diagnosis. AD diagnosis increasingly relies on multimodal data such as clinical assessments, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MRI and PET acquisition remain costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality inference impractical in real-world clinical workflows. We propose ProMUSE, a Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty Guided Staged Evidential Network that adaptively determines when additional modalities are necessary, helping reduce the overall cost of data acquisition while maintaining accuracy. ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using low-cost clinical data and quantifies uncertainty via a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, ProMUSE progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty through Dempster-Shafer theory to obtain a calibrated multimodal prediction. This staged acquisition strategy enables accurate diagnosis while minimizing reliance on expensive imaging. Experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks demonstrate that ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%, yielding substantial cost savings. These results highlight ProMUSE as a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening.

AI.tldr: ProMUSE is a progressive multimodal network that uses uncertainty-guided staged acquisition—starting with cheap clinical data and only requesting costly MRI/PET when confidence is low—achieving competitive AD diagnosis accuracy while reducing imaging usage by 50–90%.
AI.motivation: MRI and PET imaging are expensive and not universally accessible, yet multimodal diagnosis using these modalities is increasingly demanded for early Alzheimer's detection. Full-modality inference is impractical in real-world workflows, motivating a cost-effective, adaptive acquisition strategy.
AI.method: ProMUSE performs evidential classification on clinical data with Dirichlet-based subjective logic to quantify uncertainty. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, it progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty via Dempster-Shafer theory for calibrated multimodal prediction.
AI.result: On ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS datasets across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks, ProMUSE matches or exceeds full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50–90%.
AI.conclusion: ProMUSE offers a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening by adaptively determining when costly imaging is necessary.

title: ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence
summary: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified neural architecture based on a learnable integral transform with a content- and position-dependent kernel (implemented as an MLP). It demonstrates that convolutions, self-attention, and various recurrent networks emerge as special cases, and a single ITNet matches or exceeds specialized baselines across diverse vision, language, and 3D recognition tasks.
AI.motivation: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers have remained mathematically distinct since their inception, each encoding different inductive biases (locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction). The authors argue this fragmentation reflects incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object — a learnable integral transform — rather than a fundamental diversity in signal processing.
AI.method: ITNet is built around a learnable kernel depending jointly on positions and features, implemented as a small MLP that models pairwise interactions. The framework unifies convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) as special cases under appropriate parameterizations. For practical scalability, the authors introduce tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization.
AI.result: A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K (vision), GLUE (language), ModelNet40 (3D), VQA v2, and NLVR2 (vision-language).
AI.conclusion: A single learned interaction mechanism — the integral transform kernel — can recover the behaviors of all three major architectural families (convolutional, recurrent, and attention-based) from data, demonstrating that their apparent diversity stems from parameterizations of a common mathematical framework rather than fundamentally different processing paradigms.

title: ELVA: Exploring Ranking-Driven Universal Multimodal Retrieval
summary:
Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via contrastive learning has become a mainstream paradigm for improving the performance of Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR). However, previous works have ignored the grain blindness when adapting the contrastive paradigm into retrieval tasks. Grain blindness refers to the tendency of the model to overlook grain-level information contained in the query, which is crucial for effectively handling complex queries. This stems from contrastive learning treating samples as a binary classification (positive/negative), while ignoring the different information carried by each negative sample. To address this, we argue that negatives should be treated differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, enabling the model to learn distinct grain information from each negative. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective framework, called ELVA, a novel rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness through ranking-driven MLLMs. 1) Instead of relying on reward models, we extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
  (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, allowing the model to explore new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. 2) By utilizing rule-based rewards, our approach jointly optimizes the ranking of negative samples while enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative. To more precisely measure grain blindness, we further introduce MRBench, a new benchmark specifically designed for multi-grain query scenarios. ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results across standard retrieval benchmarks, and its notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench further demonstrates its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

AI.tldr: ELVA is a rule-based RL framework that addresses "grain blindness" in multimodal retrieval by treating negative samples differently according to their similarity to positives, achieving a 13.1% improvement on the new MRBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive learning approaches for Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR) suffer from "grain blindness" — the model overlooks grain-level information in queries because contrastive learning treats all negatives uniformly as a binary classification problem, ignoring that different negatives carry varying degrees of information relevant to complex queries.
AI.method: The authors propose ELVA, which: (1) extends Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, enabling exploration of ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels; (2) uses rule-based rewards to jointly optimize negative sample ranking and enlarge the positive-negative similarity gap. They also introduce MRBench, a benchmark for multi-grain query scenarios.
AI.result: ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results on standard retrieval benchmarks and demonstrates a notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench, validating its effectiveness in mitigating grain blindness.
AI.conclusion: Treating negatives differently based on their similarity to positives, operationalized through a rule-based RL framework, effectively addresses grain blindness in multimodal retrieval and significantly boosts performance on complex, multi-grain queries.

title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
summary: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

AI.tldr: ScaffoldAgent introduces a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research (OEDR). It formalizes outline evolution as a structured decision process with Expansion, Contraction, and Revision operations, guided by a utility signal that estimates downstream value from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. Experiments show consistent improvements in long-form report quality and factual grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing OEDR methods either fix outlines before writing or refine them with local heuristics, causing scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. A principled mechanism for dynamically optimizing the report scaffold during multi-round retrieval and generation is needed.
AI.method: ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three discrete operations: Expansion (adding nodes), Contraction (removing nodes), and Revision (modifying nodes). A utility-guided feedback mechanism estimates the downstream value of each outline operation using three signals: retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. This utility signal drives node selection, operation scheduling, and termination decisions during inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym, ScaffoldAgent consistently improved long-form report generation and factual grounding compared to existing deep research agents.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic outline optimization via utility-guided structured decision-making effectively mitigates scaffold drift and enhances both the coherence and factual accuracy of long-form research reports in OEDR settings.

title: OpenRath: Session-Centered Runtime State for Agent Systems
summary: Modern agent systems often suffer from fragmented runtime state: transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately and become difficult to inspect or reproduce. OpenRath addresses this issue with a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent, multi-session systems. The analogy concerns the role of a central first-class runtime abstraction, not tensor computation. Its core abstraction is Session, the runtime value passed between agents and workflows. A Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. It records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence, while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. Since this state is carried by the same value used in program execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations rather than states reconstructed from external traces. OpenRath further defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector, with Selector turning control flow into runtime-routed decisions. This report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Its claims are limited to controlled runtime properties, while broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are left for follow-on evaluation. The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition.

AI.tldr: OpenRath introduces a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent systems centered on the **Session** abstraction — a branchable, inspectable, replayable, and composable first-class runtime value that unifies fragmented runtime state (transcripts, tool effects, memory events, lineage, etc.), enabling explicit fork/merge/replay as native runtime operations rather than post-hoc reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Modern agent systems suffer from **fragmented runtime state**: conversation transcripts, tool outputs, memory events, workspace artifacts, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded in disparate locations and formats. This fragmentation makes inspection, debugging, reproducibility, and auditable composition of multi-agent, multi-session systems difficult. There is a need for a unified runtime abstraction that carries all execution state as a single first-class value.
AI.method: OpenRath proposes a programming model analogous to PyTorch's central tensor abstraction, but applied to **runtime state** rather than tensor computation. The core abstraction is the **Session**, which encapsulates conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence in one value. Sessions are branchable (fork), mergeable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. The model further defines: **Sandbox** (execution environment), **Tool**, **Agent**, **Memory**, **Workflow**, and **Selector** (which turns control flow into runtime-routed decisions). Memory interactions are explicitly recorded into the Session. Fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations on the Session value rather than states reconstructed from external traces.
AI.result: The paper presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and an evidence protocol. No broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality assessments, optional-backend availability results, or memory quality evaluations are included — these are deferred to follow-on work. The claims are scoped to controlled runtime properties enabled by the Session abstraction.
AI.conclusion: The central thesis is that **Session** provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition. By making runtime state explicit, unified, and manipulable through fork/merge/replay operations, OpenRath enables more transparent, reproducible, and composable multi-agent systems.

title: Quantifying Aleatoric Uncertainty of In-Context Learning for Robust Measure of LLM Prediction Confidence
summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) allows LLMs to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations, but its reliability remains a concern: predictions are highly sensitive to both prompt design and the model's ability to understand the context, obscuring whether failures arise from data properties or model limitations. Uncertainty decomposition-separating aleatoric from epistemic sources-is particularly crucial in this setting, yet existing methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL. To address this, we introduce a concept of self-function vectors, built upon Bayesian views and the mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal model representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, thereby enabling a direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework and circumventing the reliance on brittle input or decoding manipulations. Given the lack of established benchmarks and suitable evaluation protocols, we also propose the first and rigorous evaluation protocol, in which data is manipulated in controlled ways so as to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty. With this new evaluation framework, initially grounded in synthetic tasks for conceptual development and subsequently extended to real-world datasets, we show that our proposed methodology can measure uncertainty of LLM predictions made under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods. Moreover, we show it can be used as a practical tool for trustworthy-related applications, such as hallucination detection. Our findings pave a new direction for connecting the quantitative view of uncertainty with the mechanistic understanding of model behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces self-function vectors — internal model representations that capture latent concepts learned during in-context learning — to estimate aleatoric uncertainty in LLM predictions within a Bayesian framework, bypassing brittle prompt manipulations. The authors also propose the first rigorous evaluation protocol with controlled data manipulation to precisely separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty, demonstrating superior reliability over existing methods on both synthetic and real-world tasks, including hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: In-context learning (ICL) reliability is undermined by high sensitivity to prompt design and the model's contextual understanding, making it difficult to diagnose whether failures stem from data properties or model limitations. Existing uncertainty decomposition methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture ICL's unique dynamics. There is a pressing need for methods that can separate aleatoric (data-inherent) from epistemic (model-knowledge) uncertainty in ICL, along with rigorous evaluation protocols to benchmark such methods.
AI.method: The authors propose self-function vectors grounded in Bayesian principles and mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors use internal LLM representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, enabling direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework without relying on input perturbations or decoding manipulations. They further introduce a controlled evaluation protocol where data is systematically manipulated to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty, validated first on synthetic tasks and then on real-world datasets.
AI.result: The proposed self-function vector methodology measures uncertainty of LLM predictions under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods, as validated by the new evaluation framework. The approach also proves effective as a practical tool for trustworthy applications, specifically hallucination detection.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new direction connecting quantitative uncertainty estimation with mechanistic interpretability of model behavior. Self-function vectors offer a principled, representation-based approach to uncertainty decomposition in ICL, addressing both methodological gaps and the lack of rigorous evaluation standards in this domain.

title: Low-Cost Multi-Precision Systolic Arrays for Accelerating FHE NTTs on AI ASICs
summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) ensures robust data privacy but suffers from prohibitive computational overhead. Accelerating FHE on AI hardware like Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) is promising, yet fundamentally limited by a precision mismatch: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit arithmetic, whereas FHE and its critical parts such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), demand high precision. Current approaches bridge this gap using matrix decomposition to execute NTT computations on low-precision matrix engines. However, reconstructing the full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that does not match the dataflow of matrix multiplication. This forces offloading full-precision reconstruction from matrix engines to vector processors that disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow, creating significant performance bottleneck. To resolve this limitation, we propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array in sync with low-precision matrix multiplication under a uniform dataflow. Synthesized at 7nm with OpenRoad, our design incurs negligible hardware overhead. Cycle-accurate simulations using SCALE-Sim demonstrate that natively executing NTTs on the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33x speedup, for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16 on 128x128 matrix engines, successfully enabling standard AI hardware to support high-precision FHE acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the precision mismatch between FHE workloads and AI accelerators (TPUs). The authors propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that natively reconstructs full-precision NTT results within the array, avoiding the bottleneck of offloading reconstruction to vector processors. Synthesized at 7nm, the design achieves ≥1.33× speedup for NTT transform sizes 2^12–2^16 on 128×128 matrix engines with negligible hardware overhead.
AI.motivation: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit low-precision matrix multiplication, but FHE critical kernels like NTT require high precision. Existing matrix-decomposition approaches must shift-and-add accumulate partial results to recover full precision, but this reconstruction does not match the systolic array's matrix multiplication dataflow. Offloading reconstruction to vector processors disrupts the dataflow and creates a severe performance bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array architecture that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array, synchronized with low-precision matrix multiplication under a unified dataflow. The design is synthesized at 7nm using OpenRoad and evaluated via cycle-accurate simulations with SCALE-Sim.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33× speedup over baseline approaches for NTT operations with transform sizes ranging from 2^12 to 2^16 on 128×128 matrix engines, while incurring negligible hardware overhead.
AI.conclusion: By enabling native full-precision reconstruction within the systolic array without disrupting the matrix multiplication dataflow, standard AI hardware can be effectively adapted to support high-precision FHE acceleration, closing the precision gap between FHE and TPU-style architectures.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
summary: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-based method that decomposes LLM agent uncertainty into action confidence and request uncertainty, enabling proactive clarification-seeking when task specifications are ambiguous. Evaluated on two novel clarification-augmented benchmarks, the decomposition consistently outperforms ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory across five LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: Classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty frameworks are inadequate for interactive LLM agents. There is a need for underspecification-aware, decomposable, and communicable uncertainty representations that enable capabilities like proactive clarification. However, deployment constraints (black-box APIs, latency budgets, no labeled trajectories) rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the only viable approach.
AI.method: The authors propose a prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u). When request uncertainty is high (ambiguous task specification), the agent proactively asks for clarification. They introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks — WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification — where 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified. The method is systematically compared against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) baselines across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B), evaluated on the clarification benchmarks plus standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL for fault detection.
AI.result: Averaged across five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM. It leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating generalization beyond a single LLM.
AI.conclusion: The prompt-based uncertainty decomposition effectively enables LLM agents to recognize underspecified tasks and proactively seek clarification, outperforming existing uncertainty estimation methods across diverse LLM backbones. The results suggest that decomposing uncertainty into interpretable, communicable components is a practical and generalizable path toward more interactive and robust LLM agents.

title: Creating Multilingual Mental Health Dialogue Datasets: Limits of Persona-Based Localization via Nationality and Language
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026), co-located with ACL 2026
summary: AI and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools to address global mental health challenges. Despite the global nature of these challenges, there remains a critical shortage of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating such systems. To mitigate this gap, researchers increasingly generate synthetic clinical personas to simulate user data and test digital mental health support systems. However, most validated personas rely on English-centric contexts. This paper investigates whether similar persona-based methods can be used to generate multilingual mental health datasets. We modified nationality and language parameters in personas to generate clinical dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. We then examined how different LLMs perform when evaluating the depression severity of these generated multilingual datasets against the baseline in English. Our findings indicate that just adding nationality and language parameters in personas might not be adequate, as it can introduce clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models often exhibit inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying across different models. This exposes the systemic limitations of applying English-centric personas to multilingual contexts. Ultimately, our work highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether English-centric synthetic clinical personas can be adapted to generate multilingual mental health datasets (Mandarin, Bengali, Hindi). Findings reveal that merely modifying nationality and language parameters introduces clinical inconsistency, and LLM judges perform inaccurately on non-English depression severity assessment, exposing systemic limitations and underscoring the need for culturally responsive data generation.
AI.motivation: Global mental health challenges demand multilingual datasets, yet validated synthetic persona generation methods remain English-centric. There is a critical gap in understanding whether such methods generalize across languages and cultures, which is essential for equitable deployment of AI-driven mental health support systems worldwide.
AI.method: The authors modified nationality and language parameters in existing clinical personas to generate mental health dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. They then benchmarked multiple LLM judge models on depression severity assessment across these languages, comparing performance against an English baseline to evaluate consistency and accuracy.
AI.result: Simply adding nationality and language parameters proved inadequate — it introduced clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judges showed inaccuracies in non-English depression severity assessment, with significant performance variance across different models, revealing systemic limitations of English-centric persona frameworks in multilingual contexts.
AI.conclusion: English-centric clinical personas do not transfer reliably to multilingual settings through superficial parameter changes alone. The work highlights an urgent need for culturally responsive, language-specific data generation methodologies to build equitable global mental health AI systems.

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.
