AI.tldr: G2Rec is a scalable generative recommendation framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic item tokenization, enabling industrial-scale systems to capture comprehensive, semantically grounded user interest prototypes without ground-truth interest labels.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods face two key limitations: (1) graph-based integration approaches (serialization, GNNs) either lack scalability or capture only local graph information, and (2) semantic tokenization methods rely on heuristics without explicit supervision, yielding suboptimal semantic representations. These shortcomings prevent effective joint modeling of complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts.
AI.method: G2Rec proposes a unified framework combining holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with supervised semantic tokenization. It leverages global graph information to model user interest prototypes and integrates semantic grounding into the tokenization process, enabling recommendation models to capture both behavioral and semantic context without requiring ground-truth user interest annotations.
AI.result: The framework was deployed online across multiple product surfaces and evaluated on public datasets, demonstrating superior performance over existing generative recommendation methods in industrial-scale sequential recommendation tasks.
AI.conclusion: G2Rec effectively addresses the scalability and semantic representation challenges in generative recommendation by unifying holistic graph modeling with semantic tokenization, delivering state-of-the-art performance validated through both online industrial deployment and offline benchmarks.

title: RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning
summary: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

AI.tldr: RACL introduces a reasoning-agent control layer that sits above existing metaheuristic optimizers, dynamically controlling search behavior through observation, hypothesis testing, and policy consolidation—demonstrated on vehicle routing with consistent improvements over baseline policies.
AI.motivation: Metaheuristic optimizers typically operate with fixed or hand-tuned control policies that cannot adapt to instance-specific dynamics. The authors aim to inject reasoning capabilities—observation, hypothesis formation, intervention testing, and policy consolidation—into the control loop of existing optimizers without modifying their internal logic or business constraints.
AI.method: RACL places a reasoning agent (Codex in the proof-of-concept, later replaced by a policy proxy for reproducibility) above an existing optimizer. The agent observes operational memory, reasons over past search behavior, formulates bounded hypotheses, tests interventions, evaluates outcomes with guardrails, consolidates effective policies, and explains decisions. The method is evaluated on vehicle routing problems using an ALNS-based optimizer, comparing against an Operational Memory Policy and a Stagnation-Triggered Policy (STP).
AI.result: RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21/21 feasible cases and improves or ties STP in 18/21 feasible cases, with an average cost delta of -0.641% vs STP. On the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% vs Fixed and -1.605% vs STP with negligible computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a new solver or specific configuration but a general method for reasoning agents to discover, validate, consolidate, and explain algorithmic control rules for metaheuristics. RACL demonstrates that a reasoning layer can yield consistent, interpretable improvements over static and stagnation-based policies.

title: FAPO: Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization of Multi-Step LLM Pipelines
summary: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail through interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, so prompt-only optimization can miss bottlenecks in the chain. We present FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization), a framework that lets Claude Code optimize an LLM pipeline inside a standardized codebase. FAPO evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants repeatedly to optimize against a score function. It first tries prompt edits and, only when prompt optimization appears insufficient, changes chain structure within the permitted scope when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 model-benchmark comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean $\pm$ trial-standard-deviation ranges, and the mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp. In the six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where prompt-first search escalated to structural changes, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. FAPO also improves performance on security tasks: on CTIBench-RCM, a security CVE-to-CWE task, prompt-only FAPO lifts test accuracy by +4.0 pp on GPT-5, +7.1 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, and +2.0 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning. These results position FAPO as a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks.

AI.tldr: FAPO is an autonomous optimization framework that improves multi-step LLM pipelines by diagnosing failures across retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, applying prompt edits first, then escalating to structural changes when bottlenecks require it. It achieves state-of-the-art performance, beating the GEPA baseline in 15/18 comparisons with a mean gain of +14.1 pp, and proves effective on both general and security tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail due to complex interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting components, and prompt-only optimization often misses structural bottlenecks that arise from these interactions. Existing approaches lack the ability to autonomously diagnose where failures originate and decide when structural changes are needed versus when prompt tuning suffices.
AI.method: FAPO operates within a standardized codebase using Claude Code to iteratively: (1) evaluate pipeline performance against a score function, (2) inspect intermediate steps to attribute failures, (3) propose scoped changes, and (4) validate variants. It employs a prompt-first search strategy — attempting prompt edits initially — and escalates to structural changes (within a permitted scope) only when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck that prompt optimization cannot resolve.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the GEPA baseline in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean ± trial-standard-deviation ranges, with a mean FAPO-GEPA gain of +14.1 pp. On six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where structural changes were triggered, FAPO wins all six with +33.8 pp mean gain. On CTIBench-RCM (CVE-to-CWE security task), prompt-only FAPO improves test accuracy by +4.0 pp (GPT-5), +7.1 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct), and +2.0 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning).
AI.conclusion: FAPO represents a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused LLM tasks, demonstrating that autonomous, attribution-driven optimization — combining prompt tuning with judicious structural changes — significantly outperforms prompt-only baselines.

title: Granularity-Regulated Adaptive Computational Efficiency for Optimal Verification in Test-Time Scaling
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) by investing additional compute at inference time. A central component of TTS is the \emph{verifier}, which selects or scores candidate solutions to guide the search process. While prior work has explored the benefit of verification, a fundamental question remains underexplored: \emph{what is the optimal granularity of verification under a given compute budget?} Coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) and fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) represent two extremes, yet neither alone achieves compute-optimality across all regimes. In this paper, we establish a unified theoretical framework, called \textbf{GRACE} (\underline{G}ranularity-\underline{R}egulated \underline{A}daptive \underline{C}omputational \underline{E}fficiency), that characterizes the optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. We prove that there exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification dominates when either the compute budget is large or the problem is hard, whereas coarse-grained verification is preferred in the low-budget, easy-problem regime. Our theory unifies Best-of-$N$, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and motivates an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate all four theoretical claims, with our adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1\% accuracy at matched compute.

AI.tldr: GRACE proposes a unified theoretical framework that determines the optimal verification granularity for test-time scaling as a function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. There exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification (PRMs) is optimal for hard problems or large budgets, while coarse-grained (ORMs) is optimal for easy problems with low budgets. An adaptive strategy achieves the Pareto frontier, with up to 3.1% improvement on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Prior work has explored verification in test-time scaling but leaves a fundamental question unanswered: what is the optimal granularity of verification (coarse-grained ORMs vs. fine-grained PRMs) under a given compute budget? Neither extreme is compute-optimal across all regimes, motivating a principled theoretical framework to characterize optimal granularity.
AI.method: The authors develop GRACE, a unified theoretical framework that models optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. They prove a phase transition between fine- and coarse-grained verification regimes. The theory unifies Best-of-N, beam search, and step-level MCTS under a single Pareto-optimality framework, and yields an adaptive granularity strategy that provably attains the compute-performance Pareto frontier.
AI.result: Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate four theoretical claims. The adaptive granularity strategy outperforms fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1% accuracy at matched compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: No single verification granularity is universally optimal. The GRACE framework demonstrates that the optimal choice depends on problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget, with a clear phase transition. An adaptive strategy can achieve compute-optimal performance, offering both theoretical and practical guidance for building efficient test-time scaling systems.

title: FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
summary: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks. Financial LLMs face regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion that require targeted evaluation. We introduce FinRED, an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation developed with financial experts. FinRED uses a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global standards (e.g., FATF and EU DORA) to threats ranging from regulatory evasion to complex fraud, integrated with a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) through an expert-defined schema. Rigorous expert validation confirms seed plausibility and realism for meaningful LLM safety evaluation. We also provide an expert-validated, finance-specific rubric that goes beyond disclaimer checks, aligns more closely with human experts than static one-size-fits-all rubrics, and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. Aligned with internationally adopted risk-management and information-security standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001), FinRED is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services. To mitigate dual-use risks, the dataset, generation pipeline, prompt template, and evaluation framework are gated for qualified researchers at https://github.com/selectstar-ai/FinRED-paper and https://huggingface.co/datasets/datumo/FinRED.

AI.tldr: FinRED is an expert-guided red-teaming framework for evaluating financial LLM safety, featuring a two-level taxonomy aligned with global standards (FATF, EU DORA), a pipeline that generates context-rich adversarial prompts from real financial documents, and a finance-specific evaluation rubric that significantly reduces critical false negatives. It is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute regulatory sandbox.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks fail to capture finance-specific risks such as regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion. Financial LLMs require targeted, domain-informed safety evaluation.
AI.method: FinRED employs: (1) a novel two-level taxonomy that maps global financial standards (FATF, EU DORA) to concrete threats; (2) a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich Behavioral Prompts (seeds) via an expert-defined schema; (3) rigorous expert validation of seed plausibility; and (4) a finance-specific evaluation rubric validated by experts, which goes beyond simple disclaimer checks and is aligned with ISO/IEC 27001 standards.
AI.result: The finance-specific rubric aligns more closely with human expert judgments than static one-size-fits-all rubrics and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. FinRED is operationally deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services.
AI.conclusion: FinRED provides a rigorous, standards-aligned, and expert-validated red-teaming framework tailored to financial LLM safety evaluation, enabling regulatory-grade assessment. The dataset and framework are gated for qualified researchers to mitigate dual-use risks.

title: Protein Representation Learning with Secondary-Structure and Energy-Filtered Hydrogen-Bond Graphs
summary: Graph-based representations are widely used in protein modeling, yet many existing approaches rely primarily on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially reflect the principles governing protein folding. Proteins instead adopt complex three-dimensional conformations organized around secondary structure elements, such as $α$-helices and $β$-sheets, which encode recurring local motifs and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions. In this work, we introduce a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength. This design enables the model to capture both local structural context and long-range couplings that are central to protein stability and function. We evaluate the proposed approach on commonly used protein benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods. In addition, the resulting graph representations offer enhanced biological interpretability, as the learned connectivity aligns with established structural motifs. These findings suggest that incorporating secondary structure and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The code is released at https://github.com/mohamedmohamed2021/SSProNet

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SSProNet, a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning that constructs edges based on hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by energetic strength and augments node features with secondary structure assignments, achieving consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods while offering enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based protein models rely on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially capture the principles of protein folding. These approaches fail to adequately represent the complex 3D conformations organized around secondary structure elements (α-helices, β-sheets) and the stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions that are central to protein stability and function.
AI.method: A GNN architecture where residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments (e.g., α-helix, β-sheet, loop). Graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions, filtered by their energetic strength rather than simple distance or sequence proximity. This captures both local structural context and long-range couplings.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves consistent improvements over existing graph-based approaches on commonly used protein benchmarks. The learned graph connectivity aligns with established structural motifs, offering enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating secondary structure information and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning, yielding both better performance and more biologically meaningful representations. Code is publicly available.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
summary: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the vulnerability in LLM-solver hybrid pipelines where a formally sound solver verdict can be subverted by adversarial prompt injection during the narration step, showing that robustness does not extend to the final user-facing answer.
AI.motivation: While SAT/SMT solvers provide sound, verifiable answers when embedded in LLM reasoning pipelines, prior work has overlooked the narration step — where the solver's output is converted into natural language for the user. This gap means that even a formally correct solver verdict can be corrupted before reaching the end user, undermining the entire soundness guarantee.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure, (2) evaluate five open-source models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B, DeepSeek V3) under prompt injection attacks, (3) test certificate gating as a defense, and (4) assess hardened prompts against adaptive attacks.
AI.result: Certificate gating effectively preserves solver verdict soundness, but adversarial prompt injection can invert a verified conclusion across different phrasings and communication channels. Hardened prompts significantly reduce injection success but cannot fully eliminate it, especially under adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: In the LLM-solver loop, end-to-end robustness is not achieved — the soundness guarantee of the formal solver does not survive the narration step, and current mitigations are insufficient against adaptive adversaries.

title: Beyond Uniform Forgetting: A Study of Sequential Direct Preference Optimization Across Preference Settings
summary: Aligning language models with human preferences often requires optimising multiple behavioural objectives. A practical approach is to apply these objectives sequentially using preference optimisation methods such as Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), but it remains unclear whether later training uniformly degrades preferences learned earlier or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. We study sequential DPO across four preference settings covering distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, we evaluate all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. We find that sequential DPO does not produce a single forgetting pattern; preference change ranges from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level analysis using length-normalised policy margins shows that aggregate metrics can mask heterogeneous changes across preference pairs, whereas quartile decomposition reveals that high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show that Stage~2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition is the primary driver. These findings suggest that future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength, rather than assuming that later objectives affect earlier preferences uniformly.

AI.tldr: Sequential DPO training does not cause uniform forgetting of earlier preferences; instead, outcomes (degradation, stability, or positive transfer) depend on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order, with pair-level analysis revealing heterogeneity masked by aggregate metrics.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether sequential application of preference optimisation objectives uniformly degrades earlier learned preferences, or whether the effect varies with the relationship between objectives — a critical question for multi-objective alignment pipelines.
AI.method: The authors study sequential DPO across four preference settings (distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, compatible response-quality objectives) using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, evaluating all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. They employ pair-level analysis via length-normalised policy margins, quartile decomposition, and mechanistic diagnostics of Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates.
AI.result: Sequential DPO produces no single forgetting pattern: outcomes range from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer. Aggregate metrics mask heterogeneous pair-level changes. High-confidence pairs can degrade or improve depending on setting. Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective, indicating direct gradient opposition is not the primary driver of forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength rather than assuming later objectives uniformly degrade earlier preferences.

title: Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees
summary: Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2x over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: SLARouter is an online LLM request routing algorithm that learns cost-optimal policies from sparse user feedback, providing theoretical guarantees for SLA compliance and cost optimality while reducing operating costs by up to 2.2× over baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM inference costs are rising due to demand and infrastructure expenses, while users expect high-quality responses enforced via Service Level Agreements (SLAs). Existing cost-aware routing methods require complete feedback, offline training, per-workload tuning, and lack both SLA guarantees and inference-time adaptivity.
AI.method: SLARouter is an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy using only sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. It provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance without requiring per-benchmark tuning.
AI.result: Across a wide range of LLM benchmarks, SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints and reduces operating costs by up to 2.2× compared to existing baselines, all without per-benchmark tuning.
AI.conclusion: SLARouter effectively resolves the cost-quality tension in LLM applications by delivering SLA-compliant, cost-optimal routing from sparse online feedback, outperforming prior approaches in both guarantee strength and practical cost reduction.

title: A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization
comment: Presented at the 17th Workshop on Optimization and Learning in Multiagent Systems (OptLearnMAS, https://optlearnmas.github.io), co-located with the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
summary: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: MAMO addresses the challenge of manually tuning penalty weights in Lagrangian-based RL for constrained optimization by reformulating weight selection as a multi-agent learning problem, decoupling task execution from objective design for more autonomous solutions in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: In RL-based constrained optimization, the Lagrangian approach embeds costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward via weighted penalty terms. The learned policy's behavior critically depends on these weights, which are typically chosen manually. This makes it difficult to balance primary objective optimization against constraint satisfaction, especially in non-stationary environments where the relative importance of costs and constraints may shift over time.
AI.method: MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization) reformulates reward weight selection as a learning problem within a multi-agent RL framework. It decouples task execution (performed by one agent) from objective design/weight tuning (handled by another agent), treating the weight selection process itself as an adaptive learning task rather than a manual hyperparameter choice.
AI.result: The paper presents MAMO as a first step toward more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in this abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Decoupling task execution from reward-weight selection via multi-agent RL enables more adaptive and robust handling of constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments, reducing reliance on manual hyperparameter tuning.

title: StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns
summary: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

AI.tldr: StaminaBench is a benchmark that measures how many consecutive coding change requests an agent can handle before failing, revealing that current LLM-based agents fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback, but retry mechanisms improve performance up to 12x, and harness quality creates up to a 6x performance gap between best and worst configurations.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks evaluate agents on a fraction-of-tasks-solved basis, which does not reflect real "vibe-coding" sessions where agents must handle dozens or hundreds of consecutive interaction turns. There is a need to measure agent stamina — the ability to sustain correctness across long sequences of change requests — to better assess real-world coding assistant reliability.
AI.method: The benchmark tasks agents with implementing and iteratively modifying a REST API server across 100 procedurally generated change requests, producing codebases up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically (no LLM involvement) for reproducibility. Changes are drawn from either hardcoded or LLM-driven samplers constrained to a structured action space. The agent and server run in isolated environments communicating via HTTP, making evaluation fully black-box and language-agnostic. Six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs are evaluated across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) all tested models fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback, confirming that untested vibe-coding produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent with retry capability improves passed turn count by up to 12x; (3) harness quality matters significantly — stronger models show up to a 6x gap between best and worst harnesses, while weaker models fail regardless of harness.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based coding agents lack the stamina needed for extended multi-turn coding sessions, but test feedback loops and well-designed harnesses dramatically improve longevity. The benchmark and tasks are publicly released to facilitate further research into multi-turn coding agent robustness.

title: Trustworthy Multi-Agent Systems: Mitigating Semantic Drift with the Argent Signaling Protocol
summary:
When multi-agent LLM systems produce bad answers, not all failures are equal: some answers are grounded in the right material but incomplete, while others are simply ungrounded and should be stopped. Current retry strategies treat both cases identically (try again and hope for the best), leaving human supervisors unable to tell whether a retry was warranted or whether the system should have halted instead.
  We introduce the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header that accompanies every AI-generated response with structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. These signals enable a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route each case differently.
  We evaluate ASP in two modes. In standalone mode, a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark over the Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement compares baseline prompts against ASP-instrumented controller actions across three local GGUF models. On Qwen~(0.8B), ASP improves pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; on Dobby~(8B), ASP produces 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; on SmolLM3~(3B), ASP alternates between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement is meaningful (12/81 to 21/81 passes). In multi-agent mode, an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent; the sidecar blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching the downstream agent (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).

AI.tldr: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) adds structured quality signals (certainty, grounding, stochasticity, assumption index) to LLM outputs, enabling a controller to distinguish repairable failures from ungrounded ones that should be halted. In QA benchmarks, ASP significantly improves pass rates and term coverage, and in multi-agent setups, it blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching downstream agents.
AI.motivation: Current retry strategies for multi-agent LLM systems treat all failures identically, without distinguishing between repairable incomplete answers and ungrounded answers that should be stopped. This leaves human supervisors unable to determine whether a retry is warranted or whether the system should have halted, motivating a structured signaling mechanism to classify and route different failure types appropriately.
AI.method: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) is a compact machine-readable header that accompanies AI-generated responses with four structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index classifying the evidentiary basis of each claim. A controller uses these signals to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route them differently. ASP is evaluated in two modes: (1) standalone mode on a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark (Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement) using three local GGUF models (Qwen 0.8B, Dobby 8B, SmolLM3 3B), and (2) multi-agent mode with an ASP sidecar sitting between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent.
AI.result: In standalone mode: Qwen (0.8B) improved pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; Dobby (8B) produced 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; SmolLM3 (3B) alternated between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement went from 12/81 to 21/81 passes. In multi-agent mode, the ASP sidecar blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).
AI.conclusion: ASP provides an effective, lightweight mechanism for signaling response quality in LLM systems, enabling intelligent failure routing that distinguishes repairable from containment-worthy failures. The protocol demonstrably improves QA performance across multiple model scales and reliably prevents ungrounded information from propagating in multi-agent architectures.

title: AutoTam: Specifying Secure Protocol Implementations with Tamarin Model Generation
summary:
Formal verification is a challenging but important task for ensuring the security of cryptographic protocols. While modern protocol verification tools significantly reduce verification effort, modelling remains challenging to practitioners without a background in formal verification. In addition, transferring verification results to a concrete protocol implementation requires expert knowledge.
  In this paper, we present a novel language-first method for verification of trace properties using a domain-specific language for protocol implementations. We target the Tamarin prover for verification, and we prove that verified universal trace properties translate back to the implementation. We additionally integrate symbolic execution in order to analyse the memory safety of protocol implementations. We use our tool to implement and generate accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol, and for the WireGuard VPN protocol. Our WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using our interpreter, and achieves acceptable performance. We formally prove our implementations secure using a combination of symbolic execution and verification of the generated Tamarin models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a language-first approach to cryptographic protocol verification, using a domain-specific language (DSL) for protocol implementations that automatically generates Tamarin prover models. It proves that verified universal trace properties translate back to implementations, integrates symbolic execution for memory safety analysis, and demonstrates the approach on a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN, achieving interoperability and acceptable performance.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols is difficult for practitioners lacking formal methods expertise. Two key pain points are: (1) modelling protocols for verification tools like Tamarin requires significant domain knowledge, and (2) transferring verification results to concrete implementations demands expert skill. The authors seek to bridge this gap between protocol specification, formal verification, and practical implementation.
AI.method: The authors propose a language-first methodology: a domain-specific language (DSL) tailored for protocol implementations that simultaneously serves as the modelling source. Key technical components include: (1) automatic generation of Tamarin prover models from the DSL implementation, (2) a formal proof that verified universal trace properties in Tamarin translate back to the implementation, and (3) integration of symbolic execution to check memory safety of protocol implementations. The approach is validated on two case studies: a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and the WireGuard VPN protocol.
AI.result: The tool successfully generated accurate Tamarin models for both the signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN. The WireGuard implementation, when executed via the authors' interpreter, demonstrated interoperability with existing WireGuard implementations and achieved acceptable performance. Formal security proofs were obtained through the combined use of symbolic execution for memory safety and Tamarin verification for trace properties.
AI.conclusion: The language-first, DSL-driven approach effectively lowers the barrier to formal protocol verification by unifying implementation and modelling. It enables practitioners to write protocol code in a high-level DSL and obtain both executable implementations and formal security guarantees, with verified properties carrying over to the concrete implementation. This represents a practical step toward making formal verification accessible to non-experts in cryptographic protocol development.

title: Physics-Informed Discovery of Yield Functions in Plasticity via Convex Neural Representations
summary: Identifying anisotropic yield functions remains challenging since yielding is not directly observed in full-field mechanical measurements, directional calibration can require many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for discovering yield functions from full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed parametric yield function. The framework identifies the yield function as a mechanically constrained constitutive component inside elastoplastic stress integration, rather than through direct stress-space supervision. The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one while imposing the assumed tension-compression symmetry, and this neural yield function is trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. The proposed framework is validated using finite element (FE) benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment. This study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration.

AI.tldr: A mechanics-constrained framework that discovers anisotropic yield functions from full-field displacement and reaction force data using a convex neural network embedded within elastoplastic stress integration, eliminating the need for stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or pre-selected parametric yield functions.
AI.motivation: Identifying anisotropic yield functions is challenging because yielding is not directly observable in full-field measurements, directional calibration demands numerous loading directions, and choosing an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. Existing methods rely on stress-space supervision, plastic strain data, or pre-specified parametric forms, motivating a data-driven approach that discovers yield functions purely from measurable displacement and force data.
AI.method: The framework represents the yield function as a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one with assumed tension-compression symmetry. This neural yield function is embedded as a constitutive component within elastoplastic stress integration and trained using a differentiable stress update algorithm paired with a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. Training requires only full-field displacement data and reaction force data, with no stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or prescribed parametric form.
AI.result: Validation against FE benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions demonstrated accurate yield contour agreement. The framework's robustness was assessed through displacement-noise sensitivity analysis, identifiability via plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty quantification, and successful polynomial-surrogate deployment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a viable mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while preserving the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration, without requiring direct stress-space supervision or pre-selected analytical forms.

title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why
summary: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

AI.tldr: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at a German university hospital that extracts structured clinical information from messy, heterogeneous patient records. It achieves 96.5% clinician acceptance across 7,326 judgments in a lymphoma registry study, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80–99%.
AI.motivation: Clinical AI systems face a critical "metadata gap": patient contexts consist of hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, but document-level metadata needed for retrieval and triage is missing or incomplete. Standard RAG fails due to poor temporal reasoning, inability to handle cross-document dependencies, and absent metadata. A robust, verifiable extraction system is needed for real-world clinical deployment.
AI.method: The authors built ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction), an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen. It reasons over complete patient contexts using agentic workflows and grounds every extracted answer in specific source passages, enabling clinician verification. The system was evaluated through an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study where nuclear-medicine physicians verified each extraction against its cited source.
AI.result: Across 7,326 clinician judgments in the lymphoma registry study, 96.5% of extractions were accepted. Per-type acceptance rates ranged from 80% to 99%, demonstrating strong but variable performance depending on the clinical data type being extracted.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RAG architectures that ground outputs in verifiable source passages can achieve clinically acceptable extraction accuracy on real-world, messy EHR data. The system's design decisions were directly shaped by the documented metadata gap, and physician-in-the-loop verification provides a rigorous evaluation framework for clinical AI.

title: Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring
summary: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

AI.tldr: A subject-aware prompting system for LLM tutoring uses a prompt router trained on 14 pedagogical features. In simulation, it outperforms static baselines; in A/B testing with high-school students, adaptive routing reduces conversation length while maintaining quality, and a stochastic router boosts exercise conversion rates.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based tutoring systems rely on static prompts that cannot adapt to the diverse pedagogical demands of different academic disciplines, limiting their effectiveness in personalized education.
AI.method: The authors extract 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) from raw tutoring transcripts. A prompt routing model is trained in simulation to select among subject-aware prompts based on these features, then deployed online for real-time adaptation with high-school students. Both a greedy router and a stochastic (sampling-based) router are tested against two static baselines via simulation benchmarks and A/B testing (N=656 conversations, 359 students).
AI.result: In simulation, the router achieves 0.694 vs. static baselines of 0.647 and 0.64 (p<0.001). In real deployment, it successfully transfers from analytical to scaffolding strategies, reduces interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007), and maintains pedagogical quality. The greedy router matches baseline exercise conversion (19.1% vs. 19.6%), while the stochastic router significantly improves it to 28.1%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, subject-aware prompt routing enhances LLM tutoring efficiency and effectiveness. Stochastic exploration of pedagogical strategies yields better learning outcomes than greedy selection, suggesting that controlled variation in tutoring approaches benefits student engagement and exercise completion.

title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation
summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method for implicit feedback in cold-start recommendation that leverages content-similar warm items to generate confidence-weighted pseudo-labels, adaptively correcting noisy labels by modeling sample uncertainty based on relative entropy and item cold-start status.
AI.motivation: Implicit feedback (e.g., clicks) is noisy due to clickbait and position bias, and cold items are disproportionately affected. Existing denoising methods relying on heuristic patterns (e.g., high loss values) lack adaptability and fail in cold-start scenarios. The stability of user content preferences presents an untapped opportunity for denoising cold-item feedback.
AI.method: A model-agnostic framework called DIF with three components: (1) Pseudo-label inference via content-similar warm items, exploiting stable user content preferences. (2) Confidence modeling of pseudo-labels based on content similarity between cold and warm items, with aggregation of multiple pseudo-labels per sample. (3) Uncertainty estimation of noisy labels using relative entropy and cold-start status, which adaptively modulates pseudo-label influence to correct noisy labels at the sample level.
AI.result: DIF achieves superior performance validated through theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. It has been deployed on Kuaishou (a billion-user short video platform), significantly improving multiple commercial metrics in cold-start scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DIF provides an effective, theoretically-grounded solution for denoising implicit feedback specifically tailored to cold-start recommendation, demonstrating both academic rigor and real-world industrial impact at scale.

title: Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with no pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs; this curated slice is not directly comparable to full-split leaderboard results, and we discuss the limits of the comparison. A complementary pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories yields 100% correctness preservation (CP; mean 122s on the hard tier). Manual inspection shows that about half of the resulting pull requests are well-targeted fixes. The other half place code at incorrect paths, a planner localization limitation we are addressing with retrieval. We also report the deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) that motivated each safety mechanism.

AI.tldr: Phoenix is a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues end-to-end using six specialized agents coordinated by a webhook state machine, achieving 75% oracle resolution on a curated SWE-bench Lite slice with zero pass-to-pass regressions, and 100% correctness preservation on a 42-issue real-world pilot.
AI.motivation: Automated issue resolution systems face deployment risks including incorrect code changes, CI breakage, and safety violations. Prior work lacks robust safety controls and realistic evaluation that accounts for deployment failure modes in production environments.
AI.method: Phoenix employs six specialized agents (Planner, Reproducer, Coder, Tester, Failure Analyst, PR Agent) orchestrated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Seven layered safety controls are integrated: baseline-aware test evaluation ensures no pass-to-pass regressions by comparing against a pre-change test run. The system operates on a curated 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite via a production webhook path, complemented by a pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories.
AI.result: On the SWE-bench Lite slice, Phoenix achieves 75% oracle resolution with zero pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs. The 42-issue real-world pilot yields 100% correctness preservation (mean 122s on hard tier). Manual inspection reveals ~50% of PRs are well-targeted fixes; the other half suffer from incorrect code path localization. Deployment failure modes documented include WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, and flaky CI.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent decomposition with layered safety controls enables robust automated issue resolution, though planner localization remains a key limitation. Future work focuses on retrieval-augmented localization to reduce incorrect code-path placements.

title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
comment: 8 pages of main content, 28 total pages. 30 figures
summary: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After sampling and annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, a RoBERTa-based model for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to 3M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data, (ii) we uncover a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlying web text, and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways that current curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning tasks. We publicly release NarraDolma and NarraBERT.

AI.tldr: First fine-grained study of narrative features in large-scale LLM pretraining corpora, introducing a theory-driven framework (agency, setting, events) with 11 dimensions, a prediction model (NarraBERT), and a 3M-passage annotated dataset (NarraDolma) from the Dolma corpus, revealing measurable, continuous, and unequally distributed narrative structures across web text.
AI.motivation: Despite narrative being a fundamental mode of human communication, the narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored. Current data curation practices neither measure nor account for narrative qualities, leaving a gap in understanding how narrative features are distributed and how they may affect downstream narrative reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
AI.method: The authors draw on narrative theory to design a framework with three core elements—agency, setting, and events—operationalized into 11 interpretable dimensions. They sample and annotate 400 diverse passages from Dolma (a 3-trillion-token open corpus), then finetune RoBERTa into NarraBERT for fine-grained narrative prediction. NarraBERT is applied to 3 million passages to produce NarraDolma, a large-scale annotated dataset of narrative features.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data; (ii) a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlies web text; and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics—aspects not captured by current curation practices.
AI.conclusion: The framework, NarraDolma dataset, and NarraBERT model provide a foundation for understanding narrative quality distributions in LLM pretraining data and for investigating how data composition influences narrative reasoning tasks. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: A Measurement Study of Cryptographic Misuse in Embodied AI Mobile Applications
summary: Embodied AI (EAI) mobile applications are evolving from auxiliary user interfaces into active control-path components, directly linking mobile-side cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. Despite this shift, existing security research predominantly focuses on embodied AI devices and cloud infrastructures, leaving the mobile control layer largely unexplored as a critical attack surface. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse within the EAI mobile ecosystem. We construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world applications across six EAI domains, and employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Our measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings (with an evaluated precision of 80.74\%), revealing that these cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. We uncover structural security trade-offs: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, while the heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates the local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate how these mobile-side cryptographic flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack the physical control of EAI entities. Ultimately, our findings highlight that mobile applications have become a fragile, yet overlooked, cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse in the Embodied AI mobile app ecosystem, analyzing 507 apps across 6 domains, revealing 12,975 misuse findings driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors, and demonstrating real-world exploitability for hijacking physical control of EAI entities.
AI.motivation: Existing security research on Embodied AI focuses on devices and cloud infrastructures, neglecting the mobile control layer as a critical attack surface. As EAI mobile apps evolve into active control-path components directly linking cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust, this gap poses significant risks.
AI.method: The authors constructed EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world EAI applications across six domains, and developed an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to systematically detect and characterize five major cryptographic failure modes at scale.
AI.result: The measurement yielded 12,975 cryptographic misuse findings with an evaluated precision of 80.74%. Two key structural trade-offs were uncovered: (1) latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, and (2) heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates local hardcoding of authentication credentials.
AI.conclusion: Mobile applications have become a fragile yet overlooked cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems. These mobile-side cryptographic flaws can bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack physical control of EAI entities.

title: Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?
summary: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates comparison curation in preference-based post-training (specifically DPO) as a sampling-design problem, deriving matching upper and lower bounds that show how the choice of labeled pairs affects downstream policy performance through a single design-dependent information matrix. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for selecting which completion pairs to label, and experiments demonstrate improved sample efficiency over standard heuristics.
AI.motivation: Human preference labels are far more expensive than generating completions, yet standard practice labels a small set of completions per prompt. The authors argue that given a fixed labeling budget, it is more efficient to generate many completions and selectively label only the most informative comparison pairs. No prior work systematically addresses which pairs should be compared under the post-training objective.
AI.method: The authors formalize comparison curation as a sampling-design problem, evaluating designs by the optimality gap of the resulting DPO-trained policy. They derive matching upper and lower bounds linking this gap to a design-dependent information matrix that captures how label allocation propagates through parameter estimation error to policy suboptimality. This yields a concrete optimization criterion for selecting pairs. Practical sampling designs are then proposed and evaluated against common heuristics (e.g., random pairing, best-vs-worst).
AI.result: The derived bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream DPO performance solely through a single information matrix. The proposed curation designs consistently outperform common heuristics in both synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks, improving sample efficiency under fixed labeling budgets.
AI.conclusion: Budgeted comparison curation is a principled lever for improving DPO sample efficiency. By generating many completions but labeling only the most informative pairs according to the design-dependent information matrix, one can achieve better alignment with fewer expensive human labels.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
summary: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

AI.tldr: Psychological profiles assigned to LLMs via human-designed instruments are largely measurement artifacts driven by a directional response bias (81–90% of between-model variance), not genuine traits. This bias declines with model capability but persists, and apparent model profiles can be arbitrarily manufactured through item selection. The paper calls for dedicated LLM assessment tools centered on "response orthogonality."
AI.motivation: The increasing use of human psychological instruments to assign stable psychological profiles to LLMs—affecting usability, safety assessment, and use as human proxies in research—occurs without formal psychometric validation. The authors aim to determine whether observed LLM "traits" reflect genuine model properties or measurement artifacts.
AI.method: A battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (self-reports and behavioral tasks) was administered to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples. A formal psychometric framework was applied, including variance decomposition to partition between-model variation into trait-driven vs. bias-driven components, and analysis of how response orthogonality predicts apparent reliability.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) 81–90% of between-model variation is attributable to directional response bias (vs. 9–16% in humans). (2) Bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated. (3) An instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by "response orthogonality" (the proportion of items where trait and bias point in opposite directions). (4) Model profiles shift with item selection and can be manufactured arbitrarily.
AI.conclusion: Apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the measurement instruments, not intrinsic model properties. Since instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal, they may inherently lack validity for LLMs. The authors call for dedicated LLM assessments centered on response orthogonality.

title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Contagion Networks, a formal framework to measure how evaluator biases propagate among LLM agents in multi-agent systems. Experiments with DeepSeek-chat show consistent bias propagation (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]), identify three propagation regimes governed by spectral radius, and demonstrate that expanding evaluator committees from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.motivation: LLMs serving as evaluators in multi-agent systems exhibit systematic biases that can propagate through the agent network, corrupting collective decision-making. Prior work lacks a formal framework to quantify and analyze this contagion effect.
AI.method: The authors propose Contagion Networks, a formal framework centered on the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ_N. They conduct a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), measure Γ_3, analyze propagation regimes via the spectral radius ρ(Γ_N), and test mitigation through evaluator committee size expansion (k=1 vs. k=3). Comparisons are made against prior cross-model coefficients (MM-EPC).
AI.result: Evaluator biases propagate consistently between agents (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]) even within the same model. Homogeneous-model contagion coefficients are 3-5× weaker than cross-model coefficients from prior work (MM-EPC: γ ≈ 0.85–1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. Increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.conclusion: Bias contagion in LLM-based multi-agent systems is measurable, predictable via spectral analysis, and mitigatable through committee-based evaluation. The framework is released open-source to support further research on robust multi-agent evaluation architectures.

title: Prompt Quality and Pull Request Outcomes: A Stage-Based Empirical Study of LLM-Assisted Development
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering workflows, yet little is known about how prompt structure influences downstream pull request (PR) outcomes. Prior studies primarily examine conversational helpfulness, productivity, or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior insufficiently understood. We analyze 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions derived from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Building on prior research on developer-facing artifacts and prompt engineering, we operationalize prompt structure using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. We first evaluate whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments of prompt structure, finding substantial variation across dimensions and workflow contexts. Specificity shows the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification remains difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, we then examine how prompt structure influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth across AI-assisted PR workflows. Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerges as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Overall, our findings show that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream adoption and integration through contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how prompt structure—operationalized across Context, Specificity, and Verification dimensions—influences downstream outcomes (code generation, adoption, integration depth) in LLM-assisted pull request workflows, using 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions from open-source projects.
AI.motivation: While LLM-powered tools like ChatGPT are increasingly embedded in collaborative software engineering, prior work focuses narrowly on conversational helpfulness or coarse adoption metrics. The role of prompt structure in shaping PR outcomes—particularly collaborative integration behavior—remains underexplored.
