AI.method: The authors collect 265 self-admitted developer-ChatGPT interactions from open-source PRs and operationalize prompt structure along three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. They first assess whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments (finding dimension- and context-dependent variability). Using a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy, they then statistically analyze how each prompt dimension predicts three downstream outcomes: actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth.
AI.result: Specificity and Context most strongly predict actionable code generation; Verification is the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. LLM annotation reliability varies: Specificity aligns best with human judgment, Context is systematically underscored by the LLM, and Verification is inconsistently assessed.
AI.conclusion: Prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows. Contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues each influence different downstream stages, suggesting that prompt engineering strategies should be tailored to the specific phase of the collaborative development pipeline.

title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models Across Agreement, Consistency, and Bias
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. We present the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date: 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments. Four findings emerge, consistent across the full cohort, including the April 2026 frontier: kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal (33--41 pp on MT-Bench), judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, high test--retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production-deployed judges (instantiating a consistency--bias paradox), and verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across our cohort under a single pairwise rubric. We distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper conducts the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date (21 judges, 9 providers, ~541K judgments), revealing that standard exact-match agreement overstates judge quality, and proposes a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol based on agreement (Cohen's κ), consistency (test-retest), and bias auditing.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm, yet current validation practices rely on exact-match agreement, which fails to correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. A rigorous, multi-faceted validation standard is needed.
AI.method: Evaluated 21 judges from nine providers across three benchmarks (MT-Bench, JudgeBench, RewardBench) under three protocols — agreement (Cohen's κ vs. exact match), consistency (test-retest reliability), and bias audit (position bias, verbosity bias) — spanning 118 runs and ~541,000 individual judgments.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) universal κ deflation of 33–41 pp vs. exact match on MT-Bench; (2) judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks; (3) a consistency–bias paradox where high test-retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production judges; (4) verbosity bias is small (<0.011) under a single pairwise rubric.
AI.conclusion: LLM judge validation must move beyond exact-match agreement to a protocol incorporating chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's κ), consistency testing, and bias auditing. The authors distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol for the field.

title: Accelerating Trust Convergence in IIoT: A ML Approach for Dynamic Network Conditions
summary: In Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, trust management plays a vital role in securing systems, especially when dealing with resource-constrained devices. Traditional trust models often overlook the impact of fluctuating network quality, leading to slower trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. In this paper, we propose a dynamic trust management solution, known as the Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach, which integrates Machine Learning (ML) to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions. Our model predicts the number of time units needed for trust convergence based on key network metrics and dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to enhance convergence speed. Using a simulation framework that incorporates realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the TCA-based approach, achieving up to a 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy. This work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

AI.tldr: A dynamic trust management solution (TCA) for IIoT that uses ML to predict and accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions, achieving up to 28.6% reduction in convergence time while maintaining resilience against malicious nodes.
AI.motivation: Traditional trust models in IIoT ignore the impact of fluctuating network quality, which causes slow trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. Resource-constrained IIoT devices under dynamic, poor network conditions need faster, more reliable trust evaluation.
AI.method: The TCA approach integrates ML to predict the number of time units required for trust convergence based on key network metrics, then dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to accelerate convergence. Evaluation uses a simulation framework with realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions (IEEE 802.11 standard) and tests with malicious node scenarios.
AI.result: Up to 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging network conditions, with improved trust evaluation accuracy and resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes.
AI.conclusion: TCA provides a scalable, adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

title: Emyx: Fast and efficient all-atom protein generation
summary: Computational enzyme design requires generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands, a task that demands both geometric accuracy and structural diversity from the underlying generative model. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction, leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. We argue that much of this complexity is unnecessary for generators, which condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals. Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. We additionally derive an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, bridging flow matching training efficiency with state-of-the-art sampling methods designed for diffusion models without retraining. Despite being the smallest model, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 against the AME enzyme design benchmark across success rate under strict evaluation requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity, while training in just $682$ GPU-hours, roughly $4\times$ less than RFdiffusion3.

AI.tldr: Emyx is a compact 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model for computational enzyme design that replaces heavy architectures with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. It bridges flow matching with EDM diffusion sampling, achieving superior performance on the AME benchmark while training in only 682 GPU-hours (~4× less than RFdiffusion3).
AI.motivation: Current all-atom generative models for enzyme design inherit expensive, complex architectures from structure prediction (e.g., heavy embedding stacks), leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. The authors argue this complexity is unnecessary for generators that condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals, motivating a streamlined design focused on efficiency and diversity.
AI.method: Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that: (1) replaces heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity, concentrating capacity in standard transformer blocks; (2) derives an exact reparameterization of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, enabling the use of state-of-the-art diffusion sampling methods without retraining.
AI.result: Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 on the AME enzyme design benchmark across: success rate (strict evaluation requiring global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy), structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity. Training requires only 682 GPU-hours, roughly 4× less than RFdiffusion3.
AI.conclusion: Emyx demonstrates that lightweight, purpose-built generative models can surpass larger, structure-prediction-derived architectures for conditional protein design by focusing capacity on the core generation task, while bridging flow matching and diffusion frameworks yields practical sampling benefits without retraining costs.

authors: Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa
title: Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

AI.tldr: TOTEN is a knowledge-based tokenization framework that replaces statistical Byte-Pair Encoding with ontology-driven classification, achieving superior preservation of physical quantities, units, and symbolic expressions compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard BPE tokenization, while efficient for vocabulary compression, is semantically blind: it fragments structured technical entities (physical quantities, numbers, units, symbolic expressions) into arbitrary subword pieces, losing ontological coherence. This is particularly problematic in scientific and engineering domains where preserving dimensional and numerical integrity is critical.
AI.method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple (O, classify, {inst_τ}): (1) Ontology O — the Ontology of Engineering Entities (OEE) defines types, structural principles, composition relations, and invariants; (2) classify — maps raw text into typed regions; (3) {inst_τ} — a family of instantiators producing self-descriptive structured representations. Robustness is ensured via deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), Unicode Character Database (typographic classification), and RSLP (Portuguese morphological analysis).
AI.result: On the internal benchmark EngQuant (N=800), TOTEN achieves numerical reconstruction of 0.780 vs. 0.340 for the best baseline (Quantulum3). On four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases), TOTEN achieves 0.775–0.904 vs. 0.627–0.703 for Quantulum3. Unit ontological atomicity is perfect across all contrasts. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint.
AI.conclusion: TOTEN demonstrates that declarative, ontology-grounded tokenization significantly outperforms statistical methods for technical text, achieving verifiable guarantees (ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, numerical reconstruction) that statistical tokenizers cannot provide. The approach inherits dimensional authority from Pint oracle and generalizes across corpora.

title: Your Mouse and Eyes Secretly Leak Your Preference: LLM Alignment using Implicit Feedback from Users
summary: To align a Large Language Model (LLM), most existing methods collect explicit human feedback and train a reward model to predict the human preference based on the response text. These existing methods have two key limitations. First, the users rarely provide explicit feedback for LLM responses, which makes the high-quality preference annotation expensive to collect. Second, the methods do not leverage implicit human feedback, which has proven vital to the economic moats of Internet giants. To quantify the value of implicit feedback, we build a new dataset called IFLLM, which collects 1336 multi-turn questions from the 59 Mechanical Turk workers, their mouse trajectories, and eye gazing points to the LLMs' responses from their webcams. IFLLM shows that the users have very diverse types of gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. Our reward model based on the implicit user feedback boosts the accuracy of the text-based reward model from 55% to 64% and nearly triples the relative response quality improvements after applying the DPO to eight LLMs, demonstrating the value of implicit feedback in the wild. Our data collection website, dataset, and codes can be found at https://github.com/themehulpatwari/llm-implicit-feedback/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IFLLM, a dataset capturing implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories and eye gaze) during LLM interactions, showing that incorporating such signals improves reward model accuracy from 55% to 64% and nearly triples DPO-based response quality gains across eight LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM alignment methods rely on explicit human feedback, which is expensive to collect and rare in practice. Critically, they ignore implicit feedback signals (e.g., gaze, mouse movement) that major tech companies already leverage. The authors aim to quantify the alignment value of such implicit feedback.
AI.method: The authors built IFLLM, a dataset of 1,336 multi-turn questions from 59 MTurk workers, recording their mouse trajectories and webcam-based eye gaze while they read LLM responses. They then trained a reward model incorporating these implicit signals alongside text and evaluated it using DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) across eight LLMs.
AI.result: The implicit-feedback-augmented reward model improved prediction accuracy from 55% (text-only) to 64%. When used with DPO, it nearly tripled the relative improvement in response quality compared to text-only reward models. The dataset also revealed highly diverse user gazing and mouse trajectory patterns.
AI.conclusion: Implicit human feedback — specifically eye gaze and mouse trajectories — carries substantial signal for LLM alignment, significantly outperforming text-only reward models and demonstrating its practical value for improving response quality in real-world settings.

title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
summary: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: MATM proposes a shared memory framework where AI agents store and retrieve their task-solving trajectories, enabling knowledge reuse across agent populations without coordination or joint training. Experiments in ALFWorld and WebArena show improved task performance and reduced interaction steps.
AI.motivation: LLM agents operating across diverse tasks generate valuable procedural knowledge encoded in their trajectories, but these artifacts are typically discarded after single use. This forces newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions. The authors draw an analogy to web search engines indexing human artifacts and propose applying retrieval-augmented principles to agent-generated content at population scale.
AI.method: MATM introduces a population-level storage and retrieval system: producer agents contribute their interaction trajectories to a shared repository, while consumer agents retrieve relevant trajectories to guide task execution. The framework operates without requiring coordination mechanisms or joint training between agents, functioning as a decentralized knowledge-sharing infrastructure.
AI.result: Retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces the number of interaction steps required. These benefits are demonstrated across two interactive benchmarks — ALFWorld and WebArena — where trajectories are long and encode rich procedural structure.
AI.conclusion: MATM is positioned as a general design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems, enabling scalable knowledge reuse without centralized coordination.

title: LaViSA: A Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity Benchmark
summary: Structural ambiguity arises when a single sentence admits multiple valid interpretations due to its syntactic structure, posing a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes serve as useful cues for resolving such ambiguity, and Vision and Language Models (VLMs) need to be capable of deriving possible semantic interpretations from visual scenes. We introduce Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity (LaViSA), a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to resolve structural ambiguity leveraging visual scenes. LaViSA consists of ambiguous sentences, their disambiguated sentences, and corresponding images of these disambiguated sentences across seven ambiguity categories. Using LaViSA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of diverse VLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models with varying parameter scales and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that although recent VLMs can leverage visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity to a some extent, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and visually subtle semantic distinctions, indicating remaining limitations in resolving structural ambiguity using visual scenes.

AI.tldr: LaViSA is a benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language Models' ability to resolve syntactic structural ambiguity using visual cues. It covers seven ambiguity categories with ambiguous/disambiguated sentence pairs and corresponding images. Experiments reveal that while VLMs show some capability, they still struggle with specific ambiguity types and subtle visual-semantic distinctions.
AI.motivation: Structural ambiguity — where identical syntax yields multiple interpretations — poses a core challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes can disambiguate such sentences, yet no systematic benchmark exists to test whether VLMs can leverage visual context for this purpose.
AI.method: The authors introduce LaViSA, a curated benchmark spanning seven structural ambiguity categories. Each sample comprises an ambiguous sentence, its disambiguated counterpart, and a corresponding image depicting the disambiguated meaning. They evaluate a diverse set of VLMs (proprietary and open-source, varying in scale and reasoning ability) on this benchmark.
AI.result: Recent VLMs demonstrate partial ability to use visual scenes for structural ambiguity resolution, but performance degrades on certain ambiguity types and cases requiring fine-grained visual semantic discrimination, exposing persistent limitations.
AI.conclusion: Despite advances in VLM capabilities, structural ambiguity resolution grounded in visual scenes remains an open problem, with clear gaps in handling specific ambiguity categories and subtle semantic-visual alignments.

title: GNSS Spoofing Threat for V2X communications
comment: 2026 IEEE\@. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) constitute a core technology for delivering crucial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services in the Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) domain, where they are indispensable for generating Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that uphold network reliability and vehicular safety. Yet, GNSS signals are acutely exposed to spoofing, an advanced attack in which an adversary transmits crafted signals that replicate legitimate satellite characteristics, misleading the receiver into computing a false position. This work presents a methodology for conducting physical spoofing with inexpensive Software Defined Radio (SDR), describing a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity, and linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-cost GNSS spoofing attack methodology targeting V2X communications, demonstrating that Cooperative Awareness Messages can be compromised using SDR-generated fake GPS signals, validated on real Commsignia OBU/RSU hardware across multiple velocity scenarios.
AI.motivation: GNSS is critical for V2X CAM generation and vehicular safety, yet GNSS signals lack authentication and are vulnerable to spoofing. The authors aim to expose this security gap by demonstrating that V2X communications can be compromised undetectably using inexpensive hardware.
AI.method: The authors employ a HackRF One SDR to conduct physical GNSS spoofing. Their coordinate generation pipeline uses Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization for constant velocity emulation, and linear interpolation to synthesize high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The attack is tested on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across three synthetic trajectory scenarios (90, 145, and 200 km/h).
AI.result: The spoofing attack was experimentally validated on real Commsignia OBU and RSU hardware. Across all three velocity scenarios, the attack successfully misled the V2X units into computing false positions, causing service degradation that remained undetected.
AI.conclusion: V2X communications are not secured against GNSS spoofing; the demonstrated attack shows that even low-cost SDR equipment can successfully compromise vehicular PNT services without triggering detection mechanisms, highlighting a critical vulnerability in the V2X ecosystem.

title: A Hybrid GNN-FEM Framework for Phase-Field Fracture Simulation. Physics-Preserving Hybridization for Generalizable Surrogate Modeling
summary: Scientific machine learning (SciML) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating simulations of complex physical systems, yet achieving physically consistent and generalizable predictions for nonlinear, history-dependent problems remains a central challenge. In this study, we propose a hybrid GNN--FEM framework for efficient and generalizable phase-field fracture modeling. While phase-field approaches provide a robust variational framework for simulating complex crack evolution, their high computational cost limits practical applications because they require solving coupled, nonlinear, and history-dependent systems within an incremental finite element procedure. To address this challenge, a graph neural network surrogate is integrated into the conventional staggered scheme, replacing the phase-field update at each load increment while retaining the FEM-based displacement solver to enforce mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. By preserving the incremental solution structure, the framework remains consistent with history-dependent fracture evolution without requiring the surrogate to approximate the full solution trajectory. This selective surrogate strategy emphasizes the identification of a physically meaningful and incrementally structured learning target, rather than relying on brute-force data generation to learn the full fracture process. The proposed framework achieves strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations through dimensionless feature design, a graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the hybrid approach reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared with conventional FEM, and exhibits robust predictive performance across diverse problem settings.

AI.tldr: A hybrid GNN-FEM framework is proposed for phase-field fracture modeling, where a graph neural network surrogate replaces the phase-field update in the staggered scheme while retaining FEM for displacement solves. This preserves history dependence and generalizes across geometries, loads, materials, and discretizations via dimensionless features and physics-informed loss.
AI.motivation: Phase-field fracture models are accurate but computationally expensive due to solving coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent systems in incremental FEM. Existing SciML surrogates struggle with physical consistency and generalization for such nonlinear, history-dependent problems.
AI.method: A hybrid staggered scheme where GNN replaces only the phase-field update at each load increment, while FEM handles displacement and equilibrium. Key design elements: (1) dimensionless feature engineering, (2) graph-based formulation on FEM meshes enabling discretization invariance, and (3) physics-informed loss from the governing phase-field PDE. The incremental solution structure is preserved, focusing learning on a single-step mapping rather than the full trajectory.
AI.result: The hybrid framework achieved reduced computational cost versus conventional FEM while maintaining accuracy. Demonstrated strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and mesh discretizations in numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Selectively replacing only the phase-field update with a GNN surrogate — rather than learning the entire coupled solution — yields a computationally efficient yet physically consistent framework that generalizes robustly. Dimensionless features, graph-based mesh representation, and physics-informed training are critical enablers of this generalization.

title: AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward
summary: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

AI.tldr: The article traces the evolution of AI and Systems Engineering across three phases (foundational, applied, LLM inflection), identifies convergences and gaps in the field, and presents a human-AI agreement literature review of 2,601 publications to pinpoint five critical research gaps, while offering an interactive web tool for the community.
AI.motivation: The remarkable popularity of the March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and SE, which became the most downloaded issue ever and spawned a thriving research community (250+ annual workshop registrants), motivated the authors to systematically assess progress, convergence, and remaining gaps in the AI4SE/SE4AI domain.
AI.method: The authors performed (1) a qualitative, three-phase historical tracing (foundational, applied, LLM inflection) of AI and SE progress based on core literature, and (2) a large-scale human-AI agreement literature review using both human expertise and six AI models to assess relevance across 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. An accompanying AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application was also developed.
AI.result: Five critical research gaps were identified. The analysis revealed convergences within the AI4SE/SE4AI community as well as persistent gaps. The human-AI agreement data and the Explorer tool enable readers to benchmark their own relevance judgments against human and AI raters.
AI.conclusion: The AI4SE/SE4AI field has matured significantly through three distinct phases, yet five critical gaps remain that require attention. The authors provide guidance for practitioners on AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation, and release open tools and data to foster continued community engagement and self-assessment.

title: When Does Streaming Tool Use Help? Characterizing Tool-Intent Stabilization in Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Streaming RAG) hides tool latency by issuing retrieval queries in parallel with the user's still-arriving input, before the utterance is complete. Speculation can only help, though, when the correct query becomes determinable before the user stops speaking or typing -- a property of the query, not the system. We name and measure this property, tool-intent stabilization: the point in the input stream at which a speculative query's retrieval converges on the answer-bearing result. On the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) we (i) characterize how stabilization is distributed across queries; (ii) derive a model-agnostic bound H on the share of tool latency hideable behind the remaining input, given tool latency L and input cadence delta; (iii) validate it against a working streaming pipeline; and (iv) ask which query properties predict early versus late stabilization. Stabilization is typically early: at a realistic operating point a 73.9% streamable fraction of the benchmark admits latency hiding, and H acts as a conservative aggregate floor that realized savings meet or exceed -- though it does not predict savings query by query. Question type yields a statistically significant but small early/late split. The study needs no model training and runs on commodity CPU hardware; a dense-retriever replication confirms the early-stabilization effect is not a BM25 lexical artifact.

AI.tldr: Introduces and measures "tool-intent stabilization" — the point in streaming input where speculative retrieval queries converge on the correct answer-bearing result. On CRAG, 73.9% of queries admit latency hiding; a model-agnostic bound H predicts aggregate hideable latency, and early stabilization is not a BM25 artifact.
AI.motivation: Streaming RAG can hide retrieval latency by speculatively querying while the user's input is still arriving, but this only helps when the correct query becomes determinable before the utterance ends. No prior work has formally defined or measured this property — the point at which a speculative query stabilizes on the answer-bearing result — nor established bounds on how much latency can actually be hidden.
AI.method: Authors define "tool-intent stabilization" and measure it on the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions). They derive a model-agnostic bound H representing the share of tool latency hideable behind remaining input, parameterized by tool latency L and input cadence δ. A working streaming pipeline validates H. They analyze query properties (e.g., question type) as predictors of early vs. late stabilization. A dense-retriever replication rules out BM25 lexical artifacts. All experiments run on commodity CPU hardware with no model training.
AI.result: Stabilization is typically early: at a realistic operating point, 73.9% of the benchmark (streamable fraction) admits latency hiding. H serves as a conservative aggregate floor — realized savings meet or exceed it — but does not predict savings query-by-query. Question type yields a statistically significant but small split between early and late stabilization. The dense-retriever replication confirms the early-stabilization effect is not a BM25-specific phenomenon.
AI.conclusion: Tool-intent stabilization is a measurable, query-intrinsic property that governs the viability of speculative retrieval in Streaming RAG. Most queries stabilize early, enabling substantial latency hiding. The bound H provides a practical, model-agnostic tool for system designers to estimate aggregate hideable latency without per-query modeling.

title: Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective
summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) is inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy. Design artifacts, flow scripts, and engineering decisions cross tool, session, and organizational boundaries before final implementation, signoff, or release. Each transfer carries explicit and implicit requirements that may not be fully captured by stage-local checks. LLM-based agents now invoke EDA tools directly, embed retrieved knowledge in executable scripts, and hand off state across sessions and stages. Once their outputs condition downstream engineering decisions, the transferred object must satisfy a handoff contract and meet the assumptions of its next consumer. This survey introduces handoff validity as its organizing principle. A handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies the consumer's acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance for downstream use. We review 82 systems and classify them into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems establish validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task. Flow-Bound systems preserve coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions. Organization-Bound systems maintain source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, we analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. These analyses motivate a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP), covering the agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security and IP protocols. We aim to provide a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.

AI.tldr: This survey introduces "handoff validity" as the organizing principle for LLM-based agents in electronic design automation (EDA). It reviews 82 systems across three boundary classes — Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound — analyzing contracts, objects, and coordination mechanisms, and proposes a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP) to establish a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.
AI.motivation: EDA workflows are multi-stage and involve frequent handoffs across tools, sessions, and organizational boundaries. Each handoff carries implicit and explicit requirements that stage-local checks often miss. As LLM-based agents increasingly invoke EDA tools, generate executable scripts, and transfer state across stages, there is no systematic framework to ensure that transferred objects satisfy downstream consumer assumptions. The paper addresses this gap by proposing handoff validity as a unifying concept.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey of 82 LLM-based agent systems in EDA. They classify these systems into three boundary classes: Stage-Bound (single-stage or bounded verification), Flow-Bound (cross-tool, cross-session workflow coherence), and Organization-Bound (source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries). For each class, they analyze four dimensions: handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. From this analysis, they derive a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) covering agent discovery, messaging, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security/IP.
AI.result: The survey classifies 82 systems into Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound categories. Key findings include: (1) Stage-Bound systems lack mechanisms for cross-stage contract enforcement; (2) Flow-Bound systems introduce state continuity but often rely on ad-hoc coordination; (3) Organization-Bound systems face challenges in provenance tracking and authority verification. The proposed EACP five-layer protocol provides a structured framework to address these gaps, with each layer targeting a specific coordination concern.
AI.conclusion: Handoff validity is a critical and underexplored dimension of trustworthy agentic EDA. By structuring the design space around boundary classes and proposing the EACP, the paper provides a common vocabulary and research agenda to guide future work on reliable, verifiable, and provenance-aware LLM-based EDA agents.

title: A BART-based approach with hierarchical strategy for Vietnamese abstractive multi-document summarization
summary: In this technical report, we focus on solving the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introduced in the International Workshop on Vietnamese Language and Speech Processing (VLSP) 2022. We choose to follow the popular hierarchical approach, i.e. condensing each document followed by aggregation and summarization. We propose a novel yet simple strategy to shorten documents that is driven by the golden summary, thus ensuring high correlation between stages of the hierarchical approach. Our method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP's public test set, and can produce fluent and concise summaries. Additionally, we utilize external sources for extra data, which greatly enhances the quantity of data for Vietnamese multi-document summarization. The additional data is made available for the community.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical approach for Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization using a golden summary-driven document shortening strategy, achieving 0.2468 ROUGE2-F1 on VLSP 2022; external data is also released.
AI.motivation: Address the Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization task from the VLSP 2022 workshop, where existing approaches struggle with long input documents and weak cross-document coherence.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework: first, each document is condensed using a novel shortening strategy guided by the golden summary to maximize relevance; then, the compressed documents are aggregated and summarized by an abstractive model. External data sources are also leveraged for data augmentation.
AI.result: ROUGE2-F1 of 0.2468 on the VLSP 2022 public test set, producing fluent and concise summaries.
AI.conclusion: The golden summary-driven shortening strategy effectively aligns the document condensation and summarization stages, yielding strong performance; releasing additional augmented data benefits the Vietnamese NLP community.

title: TrustMix: How to Mix Messages in a Mobile Ad-hoc Network
summary:
Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party.
  In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities.
  We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.

AI.tldr: TrustMix is a decentralized mix network protocol for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs) that provides anonymity without any trusted central party. Users forward messages through groups where all members contribute to shuffling, preventing linkage between original and forwarded messages. It employs linkable ring signatures for rate limiting, and is proven secure in the random oracle model.
AI.motivation: Mix networks provide strong anonymity against traffic analysis but are designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied to MANETs. Existing MANET anonymity solutions either require advance topology knowledge or a trusted central party, limiting their applicability in decentralized, dynamic mobile environments.
AI.method: TrustMix uses a group-based forwarding mechanism: users join groups, find a nearby trusted party, and forward messages to that party's group. All group members participate in shuffling messages before forwarding to subsequent groups, ensuring unlinkability between original and relayed messages. Rate limiting is enforced via linkable ring signatures, enabling detection of excessive sending without identity disclosure. Security is formally proven in the random oracle model, and the system is evaluated through mix-network simulation, plus a proof-of-concept Android implementation with 5 devices.
AI.result: TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity according to mix-network simulator evaluation. The Android proof-of-concept implementation achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices. The protocol is provably secure in the random oracle model.
AI.conclusion: TrustMix successfully extends mix network anonymity to MANETs in a fully decentralized manner, eliminating the need for a trusted central party or prior topology knowledge. The combination of group-based shuffling and linkable ring signatures provides both strong anonymity and rate-limiting accountability, with practical performance demonstrated on mobile devices.

title: How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural
summary:
Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) are often treated as nonlinear stores of computation, yet how nonlinear a trained FFN block actually is has rarely been measured. We treat each FFN as a position-wise input-to-output map and split it into the exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance the closed-form linear map explains defines a block's linear recoverability (R^2_lin), an optimiser-free measure of its linearity.
  Across all twelve blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and llama-160m, R^2_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth, ranging from near-linear (>0.99) to strongly nonlinear (<0.3) between adjacent blocks, and is not set by the activation function: same-width GELU models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m have sharply different profiles, so recoverability is a learned property of individual trained blocks, not an architectural one. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers only a few points of R^2, with gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity: the unrecovered computation is not a single position-wise product but higher-order or distributed structure.
  The measurement also serves as a targeted compression signal: recoverable blocks admit large single-layer replacements (GPT-2's early FFN at 8x fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag where this is unsafe. It further exposes a methodological pitfall: trained linear baselines can badly under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, so we report the exact closed-form least-squares ceiling throughout.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces R²_lin, a metric measuring how linear a transformer's feed-forward network block is by computing the variance explained by its least-squares linear approximation. Applied across GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and Llama-160m, it reveals highly heterogeneous, non-monotonic linearity profiles across layers—showing linearity is a learned property, not architecturally determined. The residual nonlinearity resists simple bilinear probing, suggesting higher-order structure. The metric also guides targeted compression (linear replacement where safe) and exposes under-convergence issues in trained linear baselines.
AI.motivation: Transformer FFNs are commonly described as nonlinear computational stores, but the degree of nonlinearity in trained FFN blocks has rarely been quantified. The authors aim to provide a principled, optimizer-free measurement of FFN linearity to understand how truly nonlinear these blocks are, what determines their linearity, and whether this measurement has practical utility.
AI.method: Each FFN block is treated as a position-wise input-to-output map and decomposed into its exact least-squares linear approximation plus a nonlinear residual. The coefficient of determination R²_lin — the fraction of output variance explained by the closed-form linear map — serves as the linear recoverability metric. A low-rank bilinear probe is applied to the residual to assess whether the unexplained computation is a simple position-wise product. The authors also use R²_lin as a compression signal, replacing high-recoverability blocks with single linear layers.
AI.result: R²_lin varies dramatically across blocks (from >0.99 to <0.3), with sharp discontinuities between adjacent layers and no monotonic trend with depth. Same-activation (GELU) models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m show markedly different profiles, proving recoverability is learned during training, not fixed by architecture. Bilinear probes recover only a few additional R² points, with gain uncorrelated to residual nonlinearity, indicating the unrecovered computation involves higher-order or distributed structure. High-recoverability blocks can be compressed substantially (GPT-2's early FFN at 8× fewer parameters, +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag unsafe compression. Trained linear baselines can severely under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, making the closed-form least-squares ceiling essential.
AI.conclusion: FFN linearity is a learned, layer-specific property that varies sharply across blocks and is not dictated by activation function choice. R²_lin provides a simple, exact diagnostic that is useful both for understanding transformer internals and for guiding safe single-layer compression. The work also cautions against relying on trained linear probes without verifying convergence against the closed-form optimum.

title: BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 3D brain MRI tokenizer for latent diffusion models that uses a frozen MAE encoder for clinically informative embeddings and a separate CNN decoder for anatomical reconstruction, demonstrating superior performance on 21/23 downstream tasks and enabling both conditional generation and longitudinal forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing latent diffusion models for 3D brain MRI face a trade-off: reconstruction-driven tokenizers produce faithful anatomy but lose clinical information in their embeddings, limiting downstream utility. The authors aim to decouple these competing demands.
AI.method: A fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) tokenizer with decoupled architecture: a frozen 3D MAE encoder pretrained on 35,309 volumes (18 cohorts, 4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. A conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) is then trained on these embeddings for generation and forecasting.
AI.result: The encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 linear-probing tasks. The DiT supports conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D brain MRI embedding space can serve dual purposes: supporting downstream clinical tasks and enabling controllable generation, resolving the trade-off inherent in prior reconstruction-driven tokenizers.

title: The Hidden Environmental Cost of Poor Coding Practices in TensorFlow and Keras Applications: A Study on Resource Leaks and Carbon Emissions
summary: Efficiency and sustainability are critical considerations in the development and deployment of machine learning (ML) applications. Among the factors influencing sustainability, resource leaks in ML code can introduce hidden inefficiencies that elevate energy consumption and CO2 emissions. Despite this, empirical evidence quantifying their environmental impact remains limited. This emerging results paper presents an initial empirical investigation of two common resource-leak smells, namely Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR), and their impact on energy consumption and CO2 emissions in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Controlled experiments were conducted for each smell by executing identical training tasks while comparing against a smell-free baseline. Our preliminary results show that both smells consistently increase estimated electricity usage and carbon emissions. IMR and UTR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and 46%, respectively, with proportional increases in CO2 emissions. Paired statistical tests indicate that these differences are systematic and statistically significant, providing initial empirical evidence that resource-leak smells may degrade ML energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. These findings suggest that resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, emphasizing the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an empirical study quantifying the environmental impact of two resource-leak code smells (Improper Model Reuse and Unreleased Tensor References) in TensorFlow/Keras workloads, finding they increase energy consumption by 32% and 46% respectively, with proportional CO₂ emission increases.
AI.motivation: Despite growing concerns about ML sustainability, there is limited empirical evidence quantifying how resource-leak smells in ML code affect energy consumption and carbon emissions.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on TensorFlow and Keras workloads, comparing training tasks containing IMR and UTR smells against a smell-free baseline, measuring electricity usage and CO₂ emissions, with paired statistical tests to assess significance.
AI.result: IMR increased electricity consumption by ~32% and UTR by ~46%, with proportional CO₂ emission increases. Paired statistical tests confirmed these differences are systematic and statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: Resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, highlighting the need to integrate resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development practices.

title: Where Does Social Reasoning Come From? Capability Provenance in Language Models
summary: We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model's predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer's 24-format x 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2x2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

AI.tldr: The paper uses training-data attribution with a 576-bin taxonomy to show that social reasoning and STEM reasoning rely on distinct regions of pretraining data, validated through targeted machine unlearning.
AI.motivation: Prior work on training-data attribution has focused on factual knowledge rather than reasoning, and document-level scores are too noisy to map which corpus regions support specific capabilities. The authors aim to discover whether social reasoning and STEM reasoning draw on distinct pretraining data regions.
AI.method: Gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) is computed over a working set from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix. Influence is aggregated across WebOrganizer's 24-format × 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins). A 2×2 experimental design contrasts benchmark pairs varying domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences vs. ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Targeted machine unlearning of high-attribution topic bins provides causal validation.
AI.result: Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with sharper contrast at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Forgetting high-attribution bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines.
AI.conclusion: Training-data attribution can serve as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, revealing that reasoning abilities have more localized training-data signatures than factual knowledge. The authors open-source all artifacts including code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

title: Quantization as a Malicious Task: Removing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors via Task Arithmetic
summary: Model quantization is widely adopted to reduce memory usage and inference cost when deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, recent studies have revealed a new security threat known as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves normally in full precision but activates malicious behavior only after quantization. Existing defenses typically modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, often introducing additional computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. Here, we present QVec, a parameter-space perspective for defending against QCBs. We observe that the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart encodes a structured behavioral shift, which can be interpreted as a malicious task vector rather than random quantization noise. Based on this insight, QVec counteracts this malicious direction through controlled parameter correction prior to deployment. QVec requires no retraining, no trigger samples, and only a single quantization pass to estimate the parameter shift, together with a lightweight hyperparameter search. Extensive experiments across image classification benchmarks and multiple Large Language Model (LLM) attack scenarios demonstrate that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.

AI.tldr: QVec is a defense against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) that operates in parameter space by treating the weight difference between full-precision and quantized models as a malicious task vector, then counteracting it through controlled parameter correction before deployment — no retraining, trigger samples, or complex overhead required.
AI.motivation: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors pose a serious security threat where backdoored models behave normally at full precision but activate malicious behavior after quantization. Existing defenses either modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, introducing computational overhead and relying on specific quantization settings. A more efficient, setting-agnostic defense is needed.
AI.method: QVec interprets the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart as a structured "malicious task vector" rather than random noise. It then applies a controlled parameter correction (subtracting a scaled version of this difference vector) prior to deployment, requiring only a single quantization pass and lightweight hyperparameter search to determine the optimal scaling factor.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks and multiple LLM attack scenarios show that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean model performance.
AI.conclusion: QVec provides an efficient, training-free, and trigger-agnostic defense against QCBs by operating purely in parameter space, making it broadly applicable across different model architectures and quantization settings.

title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: VERITAS is a zero-shot framework that improves LLM-based formal theorem proving by routing rich verifier signals (errors, type mismatches, partial progress) back into proof search via a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling followed by critic-guided MCTS using Phase 1 failures as negative examples.
AI.motivation: LLM-based formal provers typically reduce verifier outputs to a binary pass/fail signal, discarding valuable diagnostic information (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress). This limits proof search efficiency, especially on tasks requiring iterative lemma recovery from verifier feedback.
AI.method: A two-phase zero-shot protocol: Phase 1 uses Best-of-N sampling to generate candidate proofs. Phase 2 employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) guided by a critic that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples, routing full verifier signals (not just pass/fail) back into exploration. Phase 1 solutions are preserved, so Phase 2 gains are attributable to feedback-driven exploration.
AI.result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F test (vs. Best-of-5: 36.9%, Portfolio: 26.2%) and 7.3% on the newly released VERITAS-CombiBench (55-theorem combinatorics benchmark), where Best-of-5 scores only 1.8% vs. Portfolio's 3.6%, demonstrating that unguided sampling fails when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging full verifier feedback signals significantly improves formal proof search, particularly on complex combinatorics problems. The two-phase design ensures strict improvement over Best-of-N baselines, and the released benchmark highlights a challenging regime where iterative feedback recovery is essential.

title: CoRaCommit: A VS Code Extension for Commit Message Generation with Exemplar Retrieval
comment: 17 pages, 6 images, 3 tables, Manuscript submitted to a Journal (2026)
summary: Commit messages are essential textual artifacts that describe the intent behind code changes, and play a critical role in version control, code review, and historical tracking. However, in practice, commit messages are primarily authored manually, which is time-consuming and often results in inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation typically directly invoke large language models based on the code diff, without leveraging similar commit exemplars as references, and rarely support user feedback-driven LLM recommendation. To address these limitations, this paper presents CoRaCommit, a VS Code extension that enhances commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate commit message comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. Experimental results on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset show that CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

AI.tldr: CoRaCommit is a VS Code extension that improves commit message generation by retrieving similar historical commits as context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. It outperforms existing extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics on 945 ApacheCM commits.
AI.motivation: Manual commit message authoring is time-consuming and leads to inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation rely solely on code diffs fed to LLMs without leveraging similar historical commit exemplars or incorporating user feedback for model selection.
AI.method: CoRaCommit employs a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach: (1) it retrieves similar commit exemplars from a historical corpus to serve as prompt context; (2) it invokes multiple LLMs in parallel to generate candidate commit messages; and (3) it dynamically recommends LLMs based on user feedback, enabling continuous improvement of recommendations.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset demonstrates that CoRaCommit surpasses existing VS Code extensions across four metrics — BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L — validating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting commit message generation with retrieved similar exemplars and user-feedback-driven LLM recommendation yields superior performance over standard single-LLM, diff-only approaches. CoRaCommit demonstrates that retrieval-augmented generation is a promising direction for practical software engineering tooling.

title: Before the Labels: How Dataset Construction Shapes Suicidality Detection in Clinical Text
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026)
summary: Clinical NLP increasingly relies on electronic health record (EHR) data to detect suicidal behaviors, treating clinical documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media. We argue that this framing obscures how EHR-based suicidality datasets encode a particular operationalization of suicidality, shaped by who authors the data, how episodes are bounded, and how ambiguity is resolved. We ground this argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. We show how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay-level aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments, treat suicidality as a bounded episode, and assume that intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. A linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings differing in temporality, negation, and uncertainty. We argue that clinical NLP should examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques the prevalent assumption in clinical NLP that EHR-derived suicidality labels constitute reliable ground truth. Using the ScAN dataset (built on MIMIC-III) as a case study, the authors demonstrate how governance constraints, cohort selection, annotation practices, and aggregation methods embed specific operationalizations of suicidality into labels, and show through linguistic analysis that identical labels mask heterogeneous clinical framings involving temporality, negation, and uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Clinical NLP research increasingly treats EHR-based suicidality annotations as more trustworthy than social media data, without critically examining how these labels are constructed. The authors aim to expose the hidden assumptions and data-processing decisions that shape what counts as "suicidality" in benchmark datasets, arguing that researchers must interrogate these before treating labels as ground truth.
AI.method: The authors conduct a case study of the ScAN dataset (MIMIC-III-based). They trace how four factors shape the resulting labels: (1) governance constraints on data access and use, (2) ICD-code-based cohort selection, (3) single-annotator labeling protocols, and (4) hospital-stay-level aggregation. They supplement this with a linguistic analysis showing that identical labels subsume notes with divergent clinical framings—differing in temporality (e.g., past vs. current ideation), negation, and uncertainty markers.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that ScAN labels encode clinician-documented judgments rather than patient-lived experience, treat suicidality as a bounded episode tied to a single hospital stay, and assume suicidal intent can be reliably inferred from clinical documentation. The linguistic analysis confirms that notes sharing the same label exhibit substantially different clinical framings with respect to temporality, negation, and uncertainty, undermining the assumption of label homogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Clinical NLP must critically examine the assumptions and operationalization decisions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth. Treating EHR-derived labels as objective truth risks reifying a narrow, clinician-centric view of suicidality while obscuring the construct's inherent ambiguity and heterogeneity.

title: NRT-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Red-Teaming of LLM Operator Agents in Safety-Critical Control Rooms
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

AI.tldr: NRT-Bench evaluates LLM agents acting as nuclear power plant operators under adaptive multi-turn adversarial attacks. Across four frontier models, 8.7–12.1% of attack sessions cause a critical safety function loss, with vulnerabilities largely disjoint across models. Defenses show model-dependent effects, sometimes backfiring.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly proposed for safety-critical system supervision, but their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure is poorly characterized. Existing evaluations often rely on LLM-judged harm rather than objective safety signals.
AI.method: NRT-Bench simulates a nuclear power plant control room with a five-role LLM-backed operator team managing six critical safety functions (CSFs). Adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal: a run terminates when any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Four frontier operator models are evaluated under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol.
AI.result: Adaptive multi-turn attacks cause CSF loss in 8.7–12.1% of sessions across four models. Despite similar aggregate robustness, failures barely overlap: of 149 sessions, none defeat all four models, while one-third defeat at least one. Added defenses are strongly model-dependent — the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent can lower attack success for one model while raising it for another.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents supervising safety-critical systems exhibit brittle, non-overlapping vulnerabilities under adversarial pressure. Aggregate robustness metrics mask model-specific failure modes, and defensive measures cannot be assumed to transfer across models. The released simulation, dataset, and tooling enable reproducible safety evaluation.

title: Thermodynamic Signatures of Reasoning: Free-Energy and Spectral-Form-Factor Diagnostics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) is deployment-critical, and recent work shows that the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics, however, summarize the Laplacian spectrum by a handful of eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, leaving most of its structure unused. We propose Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts its thermodynamic potentials partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity together with the random-matrix-theory (RMT) spectral form factor. We prove three results: (i)~Lipschitz stability of Fes under attention perturbation; (ii)~an expressiveness result showing that Fes enriches finite spectral summaries and approximates moment-derived spectral functionals under explicit regularity and grid-resolution assumptions; and (iii)~a finite-sample PAC bound on the AUROC of a training-free detector built from Fes. Empirically, across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, a lightweight probe on Fes descriptors achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by $+6.5$ AUROC points and over GoR-4 by $+2.4$ points on average, while requiring no update to the underlying LLM. In the fully unsupervised setting, an RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC $0.71$, providing a label-free but weaker detector. A complementary RMT analysis shows that correct generations exhibit more Wigner-Dyson like spectral statistics, whereas hallucinations exhibit more Poisson-like statistics. The anonymized code and config are provided in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: Fes introduces a thermodynamic spectral descriptor for LLM attention Laplacians, using partition functions, free energy, entropy, heat capacity, and RMT spectral form factors to detect hallucinations. It yields state-of-the-art hallucination detection AUROC, improving over prior spectral baselines by +2.4–6.5 points, with theoretical guarantees on stability, expressiveness, and PAC bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior spectral methods for hallucination detection summarize the attention Laplacian spectrum using only a few eigenvalues or hand-crafted scalars, discarding most structural information.
