The authors aim to exploit the full spectrum via thermodynamic and random-matrix-theoretic descriptors to improve detection fidelity.
AI.method: Each layer's attention Laplacian is treated as a Hamiltonian. From its spectrum, thermodynamic potentials are computed: partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity, plus the RMT spectral form factor. These form the Fes descriptor. A lightweight probe is trained on Fes for hallucination detection. An unsupervised variant uses an RMT-deviation score. Theoretical contributions include Lipschitz stability under attention perturbation, expressiveness relative to finite spectral summaries, and a PAC bound on detector AUROC.
AI.result: Across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, the Fes-based probe achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, outperforming LapEig by +6.5 and GoR-4 by +2.4 points on average. The unsupervised RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC 0.71. RMT analysis reveals correct generations exhibit Wigner-Dyson statistics while hallucinations follow Poisson statistics.
AI.conclusion: Fes provides a theoretically grounded, computationally lightweight, and highly effective spectral signature for hallucination detection without modifying the underlying LLM. It unifies thermodynamic potentials and RMT descriptors to fully exploit the attention Laplacian spectrum, establishing new state-of-the-art results and offering both supervised and unsupervised detection modes.

title: MiqraBERT: Regression-Based Sentence-BERT Finetuning for Biblical Hebrew Parallel Detection
summary: Textual reuse pervades the Hebrew Bible, yet the computational methods used to detect it still rest largely on lexical overlap, and they falter once a parallel involves paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. This paper introduces MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) for verse-level semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew. The training set comprises 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels drawn from the Chronicles synoptic material and from foundational studies of poetic parallelism, balanced against 825 randomly sampled negatives. Through cosine-similarity regression, the model learns an embedding space in which parallel verses cluster together and unrelated verses move apart. We evaluate separation with distribution-based metrics, Wasserstein distance and the overlap coefficient, across ten random seeds. MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from roughly 24% to about 6%. Narrative synoptic parallels reach a recall@10 of 87.1%; poetic parallels remain difficult, below 9%. This genre-dependent asymmetry confines the model's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. MiqraBERT is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/davidmsmiley/MiqraBERT

AI.tldr: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model finetuned on Biblical Hebrew verse pairs for detecting semantic similarity, achieving strong performance on narrative textual reuse but struggling with poetic parallels.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting textual reuse in the Hebrew Bible rely on lexical overlap and fail when parallels involve paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. A semantic similarity model trained specifically for Biblical Hebrew is needed.
AI.method: MiqraBERT finetunes AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) as a Sentence-BERT for verse-level semantic similarity. The training set contains 1,650 labeled verse/half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels (from Chronicles synoptic material and poetic parallelism studies) and 825 random negatives. The model learns via cosine-similarity regression and is evaluated using Wasserstein distance and overlap coefficient across ten random seeds.
AI.result: MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pretrained baseline, reducing the ambiguous overlap region from ~24% to ~6%. Narrative synoptic parallels achieve 87.1% recall@10, but poetic parallels remain below 9%.
AI.conclusion: The model is reliable for narrative textual reuse detection but exhibits genre-dependent asymmetry that limits its applicability to poetic parallels. MiqraBERT is publicly released on Hugging Face.

title: Multi-View Decompilation for LLM-Based Malware Classification
summary: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Providing LLMs with pseudo-C output from multiple decompilers (Ghidra and RetDec) improves malware classification F1, primarily by boosting recall on malicious samples, as the decompilers make complementary errors.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based malware classification pipelines rely on a single decompiler view, which is fragile because decompilers are lossy heuristic tools. Different decompilers expose different artifacts of the same binary, and this complementary information remains untapped.
AI.method: A curated benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning diverse threat behaviors was compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, producing matched pseudo-C views. Multiple LLMs from major model families were evaluated on classification performance using single-decompiler vs. dual-decompiler prompting. Agreement analysis between Ghidra and RetDec outputs was also conducted.
AI.result: Multi-decompiler prompting improved malicious-class F1 across LLM families, driven largely by increased recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses revealed that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, confirming that dual decompiler views offer complementary evidence.
AI.conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free method that improves LLM-based malware triage in practical settings by leveraging complementary decompiler outputs.

title: FlexLAM: Resolving the Bottleneck Trade-off in Latent Action Learning
summary: Latent actions provide a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making, yet existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. We identify a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes can discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve additional transition variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. FlexLAM replaces this fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout, yielding prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, without new architectures or losses. A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, indicating that FlexLAM is not merely adjustable at inference time but learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets. The same model supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining, and FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction. These results suggest that variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces.

AI.tldr: FlexLAM replaces the fixed-capacity bottleneck in Latent Action Models with variable-length latent actions via nested dropout, creating prefix-valid codes that capture essential transition structure first and add detail as needed, matching or outperforming fixed-capacity LAMs across all token budgets without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Fixed-capacity bottlenecks in existing LAMs create a trade-off: tight codes discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while loose codes preserve excess variation that is hard to resolve with scarce or narrow alignment labels. The authors aim to resolve this by making capacity adaptive rather than fixed.
AI.method: FlexLAM uses nested dropout during training to produce variable-length, prefix-valid latent action codes. This means earlier bits capture the most compact, essential transition structure, while later bits add refinement. No new architectures or loss functions are introduced; nested dropout is the sole mechanism for inducing the variable-length property.
AI.result: A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under scarce-label supervision and a low-return single-task alignment stress test. It also supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining and improves transition reconstruction on Ego4D.
AI.conclusion: Variable-length latent actions represent an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to fixed-capacity bottlenecks in latent action models, world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces. FlexLAM learns a fundamentally better latent-action interface rather than merely offering inference-time flexibility.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

AI.tldr: The paper aggregates 14 parallel implementation studies of an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark and argues that aggregate-score leaderboards fail to capture deployment-relevant evaluation dimensions. It proposes ranking configurations by predictive validity (in-sample vs. out-of-sample rank correlation) rather than in-sample mean, introduces a twelve-tier measurement apparatus, and outlines three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria for next-generation agentic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks, including HELM and its successors, cover only a narrow slice of the dimensions relevant to real-world deployment. Aggregate-score leaderboards produce rankings that are unstable and fail to transfer to out-of-distribution settings, as evidenced by public-to-hidden competition retrospectives. There is a need for evaluation frameworks that better reflect deployment conditions and yield robust, generalizable rankings.
AI.method: The authors conduct fourteen coordinated implementation studies on a single MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark, spanning new asset classes (including multi-modal visual data), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. These are consolidated with findings from seven prior agent benchmarks. They introduce the concept of predictive validity — the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank — as a ranking criterion, and develop a twelve-tier measurement apparatus exposing dimensions overlooked by HELM-style evaluations. Three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds are formulated.
AI.result: Aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; direct empirical evidence from competition retrospectives confirms rank instability. The twelve-tier apparatus reveals deployment-relevant dimensions that HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. Existing evidence partially supports the proposed criteria but is insufficient for confirmation.
AI.conclusion: The field should shift from aggregate-score leaderboards to evaluation frameworks centered on predictive validity and multi-dimensional measurement. The authors provide a pre-registered pilot design and a vision for what next-generation agentic benchmarks should report, emphasizing robust out-of-distribution generalization as the core evaluative standard.

title: Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation with Large Language Models: From Prompting to Fine-Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in general-purpose code generation, but their effectiveness in specialized software domains remains underexplored. Solidity smart contracts represent a high-stakes domain where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics remain insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation, where models must synthesize complete contracts from natural language requirements. To address this gap, we introduce SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts paired with natural language descriptions. We also propose SolidityScore, a Solidity-aware semantic metric that emphasizes domain-critical constructs such as security modifiers, contract declarations, and Solidity-specific keywords. Using this benchmark, we evaluate representative code LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama, across zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning. The results show that general-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, retrieval-augmented generation performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation and shows that high-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts.

AI.tldr: SolidityBench introduces a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts and SolidityScore, a domain-aware semantic metric, to evaluate LLMs on smart contract generation. Among various strategies, supervised fine-tuning with high-quality domain data proves most effective for improving generation reliability.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at general code generation but remain underexplored in specialized, high-stakes domains like Solidity smart contracts, where strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints must be satisfied. Existing benchmarks and metrics are insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation from natural language requirements.
AI.method: The authors construct SolidityBench (5,470 repository-level Solidity contracts with NL descriptions) and SolidityScore (a Solidity-aware semantic metric emphasizing security modifiers, contract declarations, and domain-specific keywords). They evaluate multiple LLMs (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama) under five strategies: zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
AI.result: General-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, RAG performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters.
AI.conclusion: High-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts. The benchmark and metric provide a rigorous foundation for future work in domain-specific code generation.

title: Image Encryption Algorithm Based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Dynamic S-Box Generation
summary: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.

AI.tldr: A dynamic image encryption method that uses CNN-extracted features to generate adaptive S-boxes, enhancing non-linearity and resistance to linear/differential attacks compared to fixed S-box approaches.
AI.motivation: Conventional fixed S-boxes used in image encryption are vulnerable to linear and differential cryptanalysis. The authors aim to address this by introducing adaptivity — generating input-dependent S-boxes that are unique per image, thereby improving the confusion property and overall cryptographic strength.
AI.method: A CNN is trained to extract salient features from the input image. These learned features are then used to dynamically construct a personalized Substitution box (S-box). The encryption algorithm substitutes pixel values using this CNN-generated S-box. Security is evaluated via entropy, histogram analysis, correlation coefficients, NPCR (Number of Pixel Change Rate), and UACI (Unified Average Changing Intensity).
AI.result: The CNN-based dynamic S-boxes exhibit high non-linearity, uniqueness, and strong input-image dependence. Security metrics (entropy, histogram uniformity, low correlation, high NPCR, and favorable UACI) indicate superior resilience against statistical and structural attacks compared to traditional fixed S-box schemes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CNN-driven adaptive S-box encryption scheme offers greater flexibility and robustness than classical fixed S-box methods, effectively resisting linear, differential, and statistical attacks through dynamic, image-dependent confusion.

title: Spectral DPPs via NEPv: A Scalable Continuous Relaxation of Determinantal MAP for Diversity-Aware Data Selection
summary: Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a massive pool of candidates is a recurring primitive in modern machine learning -- data curation and coreset selection for training and fine-tuning large models, active-learning batch acquisition, prompt and exemplar selection for in-context learning, retrieval diversification, and experimental design. Determinantal Point Processes (\DPP s) give a principled, well-calibrated notion of diversity for this task, but their \emph{MAP} objective -- pick a size-$k$ subset $S$ maximizing $\logdet(L_S)$ -- is NP-hard, and the standard greedy and sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in the ground-set size $n$. This cost is prohibitive precisely in the data-centric regime where diversity matters most, where $n$ ranges over millions to billions of candidate examples, features, or embeddings. We recast \DPP-MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, and show that its first-order optimality conditions form a \emph{Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency} (\NEPv) of a previously unstudied form. This \NEPv\ admits a self-consistent field (\SCF) iteration with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, giving a principled iterative solver where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, \OurMethod, requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in time $O\!\big((ndk+nk^2)\,t\big)$ for a small number of iterations $t$, scaling near-linearly in $n$ and integrating directly with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML. This paper focuses on the relaxation, solver, and scaling analysis; full real-data benchmarking is left to a planned empirical study.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates the NP-hard Determinantal Point Process MAP inference (selecting a size-k subset maximizing log-determinant) as a continuous optimization over the Stiefel manifold. This yields a Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv) solved via a self-consistent field (SCF) iteration with local contraction guarantees. The resulting algorithm, requiring only matrix-vector products, scales near-linearly in the ground-set size n, making DPP-based subset selection tractable for million-to-billion-scale data curation tasks.
AI.motivation: DPP-MAP provides principled diversity for subset selection (data curation, active learning, coresets, prompt selection), but existing greedy/sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in n — prohibitive when n reaches millions or billions. A near-linear-time algorithm is needed to make DPP-MAP viable at modern data scales.
AI.method: The authors recast DPP-MAP as continuous optimization on the Stiefel manifold, deriving first-order optimality conditions that form a novel NEPv. They propose an SCF iteration exploiting a spectral-gap-based local contraction property. The algorithm uses only matrix-vector products with the kernel, runs in O((ndk + nk²)·t) time for t iterations, and integrates with low-rank and feature-map kernels.
AI.result: The paper establishes the NEPv formulation, proves local linear convergence of the SCF iteration under a spectral gap condition, and demonstrates O((ndk + nk²)·t) near-linear scaling in n. Full empirical benchmarking is deferred to future work.
AI.conclusion: DPP-MAP can be relaxed to a continuous Stiefel manifold problem whose NEPv structure enables an efficient SCF solver with near-linear scaling in n. This opens the door to principled diversity-based subset selection at web-scale. Empirical validation on real data is planned as a separate study.

title: GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations
summary: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based interactive interface that translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible, accessible exploration of global explanations for black-box image classifiers.
AI.motivation: Global explanations for vision models are critical but remain monolithic and difficult to explore in practice. Users need targeted, question-driven access rather than static explanation artifacts, yet no existing system provides intuitive natural language querying over global explanation data.
AI.method: An LLM serves as a mediator between users and structured local explanation data. It translates natural language questions into SQL queries, enabling flexible aggregation. Responses are delivered as statistics-augmented natural language answers paired with local explanations and intent-aligned visualizations. Evaluation covers intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries/datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors.
AI.result: LLM-mediated querying significantly improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI, with demonstrated robustness across diverse query types, datasets, and linguistic variations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-based query interface effectively bridges the gap between complex global explanation data and user needs, making black-box model interpretability substantially more accessible and practically useful.

title: Beyond Static Endpoints: Tool Programs as an Interface for Flexible Agentic Web Services
summary: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, yet most interfaces remain \emph{static endpoints} that poorly express long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. We present ToolPro, which represents an agent's tool intent as an \emph{executable tool program} that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. ToolPro combines constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. We instantiate ToolPro over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing and evaluate it on diverse workflows of real-world applications. ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4\% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1\%, with larger gains under higher network latency and workflow complexity.

AI.tldr: ToolPro introduces an executable tool program abstraction that encodes multi-step web service interactions with explicit effect types, enabling LLM agents to efficiently execute long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries, achieving up to 53.4% latency reduction and 96.1% traffic reduction.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based agents treat web services as static endpoints, which poorly support long-horizon workflows involving loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. Stepwise API calling incurs high latency and excessive client-side traffic.
AI.method: ToolPro represents an agent's tool intent as an executable tool program that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions. It combines three techniques: (1) constraint-guided program construction, (2) effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and (3) a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. The system is instantiated over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing.
AI.result: On diverse real-world application workflows, ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1%, with larger gains observed under higher network latency and workflow complexity.
AI.conclusion: Encoding tool interactions as executable programs with explicit effect types and intelligent execution policies substantially improves the efficiency of agentic web service orchestration, particularly for complex, long-horizon workflows.

title: From 50K to 8.2 Million in 24 Hours: Vozinha's Algorithmic Consecration and the Multilingual Making of World Cup Visibility
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; v0.1 pilot preprint. Dataset and evidence package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20722235
summary: We present a multilingual computational discourse analysis of how language constructed the algorithmic consecration of Vozinha, the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, after Spain 0-0 Cape Verde at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The study contributes a multilingual corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; and an analysis of cross-lingual narrative diffusion across discourse phases. We treat the platform follower count itself, narrated as "50k to 8M", as a linguistic object: a circulating and narratable proof of visibility rather than a mere measurement. The follower-growth timeline is used only as contextual metadata: we reconstruct a conservative phase structure, not a continuous API-native series, and type every datapoint by value class, confidence, and evidence type. The only exact primary scraper anchor is 8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC; all other figures are reported as estimated ranges or thresholds, including an estimated pre-match baseline of 45k-56k. Findings suggest that distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilization, Spanish crisis, English nation-making, and a shared platform-metric spectacle through which peripheral athletic performance became globally visible. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline, while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned work.

AI.tldr: A multilingual computational discourse analysis of how four languages framed the viral rise of Cape Verdean goalkeeper Vozinha after a 2026 World Cup match, contributing a corpus, a nine-frame narrative taxonomy, an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and findings on cross-lingual frame diffusion, with the follower-count spike treated as a narratable linguistic object rather than mere metric.
AI.motivation: To understand how distinct linguistic communities construct algorithmic consecration—the transformation of a peripheral athletic performance into global visibility through platform metrics—and to track how narratives diffuse across languages during such media events.
AI.method: Construction of a multilingual corpus (Portuguese, Spanish, English, French); development of a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; reconstruction of a conservative phase structure from follower-growth metadata (with only one exact scraper anchor at 8,235,652 followers, all other figures as estimated ranges); and cross-lingual narrative diffusion analysis across discourse phases.
AI.result: Distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese emphasized mobilization, Spanish focused on crisis, English on nation-making, while all shared a platform-metric spectacle frame wherein peripheral athletic performance achieved global visibility. The follower count ("50k to 8M") functioned as a circulating linguistic object—narratable proof of visibility—not merely a measurement.
AI.conclusion: As a v0.1 pilot, the paper demonstrates the viability of the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, and typed timeline while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned future work.

title: Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on language-model components to interpret instructions, process external data, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks more consequential, especially as attackers adopt model-guided automation to scale probing, prompt refinement, and response evaluation. This work analyzes the resulting attack-defense setting through a probabilistic model of a target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Our analysis shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses can allow attacker success rate (ASR) to approach one as the query budget grows, since predictable refusals provide useful feedback to automated search. We then examine detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge. This strategy reduces the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and yields a bounded asymptotic ASR. We evaluate a proof-of-concept realization of this strategy through Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational misdirection method designed to replace predictable refusal text with safe but strategically misleading responses in automated jailbreak settings. On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the security of agentic AI systems against prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks, showing that traditional detect-and-block defenses inadvertently help automated attackers by providing predictable feedback. The authors propose a "detect-and-misdirect" strategy that returns misleading responses to fool the attacker's automated judge, and implement it as Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), which reduces attack success rates by up to two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: As language-model-based agents increasingly handle tool invocation, data processing, and multi-agent coordination, they become more vulnerable to prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks. The rise of automated, model-guided attack frameworks (which iteratively probe, refine prompts, and evaluate responses) exacerbates this threat. Existing detect-and-block defenses are problematic because their predictable refusal signals provide informative feedback that automated attackers can exploit to refine their attacks, driving attack success rates toward 1 given sufficient query budget.
AI.method: The authors first formalize the attack-defense interaction as a probabilistic model involving a target system, a defense mechanism, and an attacker's automated judge. They analyze this model to show that detect-and-block leads to ASR → 1. They then propose detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious inputs receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to mislead the attacker's judge into false-positive errors, thereby reducing the positive predictive value (PPV) of attacker-selected candidates and yielding a bounded asymptotic ASR. The practical realization, Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), replaces predictable refusal text with contextually safe but strategically misleading responses during automated jailbreak attempts.
AI.result: CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude on jailbreak benchmarks and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs. The theoretical analysis shows that detect-and-misdirect bounds the asymptotic ASR, unlike detect-and-block which allows ASR → 1.
AI.conclusion: Predictable refusals in detect-and-block defenses are fundamentally self-defeating against automated attackers. The detect-and-misdirect paradigm, instantiated via CMPE, offers a principled and effective alternative by weaponizing the attacker's reliance on automated judges against them, substantially reducing real-world jailbreak success.

title: Spectral Retrieval-Augmented Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting leverages historical patterns to predict future values, but traditional methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-stationary patterns that are difficult to memorize during training. Retrieval-augmented approaches have emerged as promising solutions by retrieving similar historical patterns to enhance predictions. However, existing retrieval methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: spectral blindness, which overlooks critical frequency-domain characteristics that capture underlying periodic structures, and temporal recency, which treats all historical data equally without emphasizing recent, more relevant patterns. In this paper, we propose SpecReTF, a novel retrieval method that addresses these issues by converting time series into windowed frequency representations, measuring similarity with a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information. To balance recency and historical context, we apply an exponential moving average weighting scheme that emphasizes recent windows. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SpecReTF outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.

AI.tldr: SpecReTF proposes a retrieval-augmented time series forecasting method that converts sequences into windowed frequency-domain representations for similarity matching, addressing spectral blindness and temporal recency bias through combined amplitude-phase metrics and exponential moving average weighting.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods suffer from (1) spectral blindness — they operate solely in the time domain and fail to capture frequency-domain periodic structures critical for non-stationary series, and (2) temporal recency neglect — they treat all historical windows equally rather than prioritizing recent, more relevant patterns.
AI.method: SpecReTF converts time series into windowed frequency representations (e.g., via STFT). Similarity is measured using a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information from the frequency domain. An exponential moving average (EMA) weighting scheme is applied to emphasize recent windows over older ones, balancing recency with historical context.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpecReTF consistently outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval in the frequency domain with recency-aware weighting substantially improves forecasting performance over purely time-domain retrieval approaches, particularly for complex, non-stationary time series.

title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

AI.tldr: EPB introduces the first interpretability framework for Neural Combinatorial Optimization by distilling black-box NCO policies into an evolving portfolio of human-readable programs, using LLM-driven program evolution with hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent.
AI.motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models achieve strong performance but suffer from a black-box nature that hinders deployment and scientific understanding. Existing interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) fail for NCO because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack a defined concept vocabulary.
AI.method: EPB distills black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios via an iterative two-block framework. Block I uses a fixed-capacity program bank with a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme — numerical gradients update a student router, while textual gradients guide LLM-based program revision. Block II dynamically adjusts bank capacity through fault-targeted expansion (adding programs for poorly handled cases) and redundancy pruning (removing overlapping programs).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that distilled program portfolios largely match the original NCO model performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants.
AI.conclusion: EPB advances interpretable NCO and establishes itself as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models, bridging the gap between black-box NCO performance and human-understandable reasoning.

title: SAGE-OPD: Selective Agent-Guided Intervention for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves student models by training them on trajectories induced by their own policy, making it a promising approach for mitigating exposure bias in agent training. However, most OPD studies focus on single-turn settings, while realistic LLM agents interact with environments over multiple turns. In this regime, early errors can alter future observations and compound across the trajectory, and standard dense token-level OPD becomes brittle, as it may over-penalize semantically valid alternatives, reinforce local degeneracies such as repeated actions, and propagate unreliable teacher supervision on off-distribution histories. We propose SAGE-OPD, a verifier-free selective intervention framework specifically designed for multi-turn OPD. Instead of applying teacher supervision uniformly across all turns, SAGE-OPD first observes environment feedback and uses teacher judgment to decide whether each student response should be skipped or intervened on. To further address compounding errors, SAGE-OPD weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, reducing the influence of uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted or ambiguous histories. Finally, SAGE-OPD applies loss normalization to preserve the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting. Experiments on agent tasks show that SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies further demonstrate that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization provide complementary benefits. Our results suggest that effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is necessary and reliable.

AI.tldr: SAGE-OPD is a selective intervention framework for multi-turn on-policy distillation that addresses compounding errors by having a teacher decide which turns to intervene on, weighting distillation by teacher confidence, and normalizing loss — achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement on ALFWorld over standard OPD.
AI.motivation: Standard token-level OPD in multi-turn agent settings suffers from compounding errors: early mistakes corrupt future observations, dense supervision over-penalizes semantically valid alternatives, reinforces local degeneracies (e.g., repeated actions), and propagates unreliable teacher signals on off-distribution histories. Prior OPD work focuses on single-turn settings, motivating a multi-turn-specific approach.
AI.method: SAGE-OPD introduces three complementary mechanisms: (1) turn-level selective intervention using environment feedback and teacher judgment to decide whether to skip or intervene on each student response; (2) teacher confidence weighting for token-level distillation to downweight uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted/ambiguous histories; and (3) loss normalization to preserve overall loss scale while incorporating selective turn-level weighting.
AI.result: SAGE-OPD consistently outperforms baselines on agent tasks, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies confirm that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization each provide complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision must be selectively allocated only to turns where intervention is both necessary and reliable, rather than applied uniformly.

title: A-COMPASS: Formal Foundations for Anonymity Analysis in Microdata
summary: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces A-COMPASS, a modified version of the COMPASS language that operates on standard microdata tables (one record per person) instead of preprocessed grouped tables. A-COMPASS adds anonymization action execution, formal syntax/semantics, and verification of properties like k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy models lack sufficient formal verification, and the original COMPASS language is limited to preprocessed tables in "one record–one group" form, which does not match the standard microdata format of "one record–one person." This gap motivates adapting COMPASS to handle realistic data formats while enabling both verification and enforcement of anonymity.
AI.method: The authors modify the COMPASS language to create A-COMPASS, defining its formal syntax and semantics for operating directly on standard microdata tables. They introduce anonymization actions as a new executable feature, prove key semantic properties (determinism and compositionality), and provide a mechanism for verifying anonymity properties such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.result: A-COMPASS successfully operates on one-record-per-person microdata tables, supports both verification of pre-existing anonymity conditions and execution of anonymization actions, and is proven to exhibit determinism and compositionality. The language can verify standard anonymity properties including k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.conclusion: A-COMPASS extends the formal verification of privacy models to realistic microdata formats, bridging the gap between theoretical privacy models and practical data anonymization. The proven semantic properties provide a solid foundation for reliable privacy-preserving data transformations.

title: Does Text Actually Help? Uncovering and Resolving Text Collapse in Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal time series forecasting, which pairs numerical sequences with domain-relevant textual reports, promises to inject world knowledge into forecasting pipelines. However, we uncover a critical failure mode in existing frameworks that we term text collapse: the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal regardless of the input description. We argue that text collapse is a consequence of a fundamental asymmetry in time series forecasting: the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch, despite carrying complementary and often critical information, is insufficiently utilized, leading to its systematic underexploitation. To address this, we propose \textbf{REST-TS} (\textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{E}xclusive \textbf{S}upervision for \textbf{T}ext in \textbf{T}ime \textbf{S}eries), which turns the asymmetry into a design principle: the numerical backbone produces its own independent numerical forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual, the prediction gap that numbers cannot explain. Because no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch must extract genuine content from the input description. Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that supervising the text branch on the residual compels it to extract genuine content from the input.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "text collapse" in multimodal time series forecasting, where text branches contribute negligible signal. The proposed REST-TS framework addresses this by supervising the text branch exclusively on the residual error that the numerical backbone cannot explain, forcing genuine content extraction and achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Multimodal time series forecasting pairs numerical sequences with textual reports, but suffers from a fundamental asymmetry: numerical inputs are strongly autocorrelated with outputs, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch is systematically underexploited. This leads to "text collapse," where the text branch degenerates into a content-independent transformation, contributing no discriminative signal regardless of input text quality.
AI.method: REST-TS (Residual-Exclusive Supervision for Text in Time Series) converts the asymmetry into a design principle. The numerical backbone independently produces a forecast based solely on numerical inputs. The text branch is then exclusively supervised to predict the structured residual — the components of the prediction gap that the numerical pathway cannot explain. Since no numerical pathway can reduce these residual losses, the text branch is compelled to extract genuine semantic content from textual descriptions.
AI.result: REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures. It consistently demonstrates significantly greater text-branch utilization compared to existing multimodal frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that residual-exclusive supervision compels the text branch to extract genuine content.
AI.conclusion: The identified text collapse phenomenon reveals a critical weakness in current multimodal forecasting. REST-TS demonstrates that forcing the text branch to explain what numbers alone cannot — through residual-exclusive supervision — is an effective remedy, turning the inherent asymmetry from a liability into a design advantage.

title: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to International Journal of Speech Technology
summary: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates fine-tuning Transformer-based self-supervised speech models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) for Quranic ASR, achieving state-of-the-art WER of 0.08–0.11 while dramatically reducing training time compared to the Citrinet baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing Quranic ASR models suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and lack complete coverage of the Quranic corpus. The authors aim to close this gap through systematic domain-specific fine-tuning of modern self-supervised speech representations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive ablation study fine-tuning three pretrained Transformer-based models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on a filtered Quranic dataset of 870+ hours. They systematically vary feature extractors, output label formats (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and clip durations, using self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning on domain-specific data.
AI.result: The best configuration (Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 with non-diacritized Arabic text) achieves WER of 0.08 on EveryAyah and 0.11 on the combined setting, a ~5pp improvement over the Citrinet baseline (WER=0.163), while cutting training time from 140 to 40 hours.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised Transformer models significantly outperform prior approaches for Quranic ASR. Arabic text without diacritics yields best results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest representation. Future work targets improved dataset quality and phoneme-aware models for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

title: The Correctness Illusion in LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, LNCS format. Companion papers to follow on arXiv next week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Benchmarks for LLM-generated GPU kernels (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) score correctness through fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks. The number of inputs varies between benchmarks. The shape, dtype, and tolerance are fixed for each kernel. We test that oracle empirically. We construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls and 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors) and re-evaluate it under op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The seeded oracle flags 9 of 9 buggy kernels and passes 15 of 15 correct controls, at zero precision cost on controls. We extend the corpus to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair) and re-run the same protocol on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). The verdicts are identical across all five GPUs: 10 of 10 illusions caught and 16 of 16 controls clean. The corpus result is about LLM-style transcription bugs that the allclose-on-one-shape oracle certifies as correct, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a controlled corpus of 24 GPU kernels (15 correct, 9 buggy) and demonstrates that standard fixed-shape allclose checks fail to detect LLM-style transcription bugs, while op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with fp64 CPU reference achieves perfect detection (9/9 bugs caught, 15/15 controls passing) across five GPU classes.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU kernel benchmarks (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) evaluate correctness via fixed-shape, small-sample allclose checks with predetermined tolerances. The authors hypothesize that these static, narrow checks systematically miss latent transcription-style bugs introduced by LLMs — bugs that only manifest under different shapes, dtypes, or input distributions. The motivation is to empirically quantify this blind spot and propose a more rigorous, reproducible alternative.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled corpus of 24 kernels: 15 known-correct Triton/CPU stand-ins and 9 deliberately buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors. They design an op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing protocol that (1) generates diverse inputs respecting each op's schema (shape, dtype constraints), (2) compares against a high-precision fp64 CPU reference, and (3) applies per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The corpus is extended to 26 ops (adding flash-attention) and evaluated on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). Every failure is deterministically reproducible via stored seed.
AI.result: The seeded fuzzing oracle achieves perfect classification: 9/9 buggy kernels flagged, 15/15 correct controls cleared, with zero precision cost on controls. The standard allclose-on-one-shape approach would have certified the buggy kernels as correct. Results are identical across all five GPU classes. The extended corpus (26 ops) yields 10/10 illusions caught and 16/16 controls clean. All flagged failures replay byte-for-byte from stored seeds, ensuring full reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-shape, small-sample allclose checks are insufficient for validating LLM-generated GPU kernels; they systematically miss transcription bugs that op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing reliably detects. The proposed protocol — fp64 CPU reference, per-(op, dtype) tolerances, seed-based determinism — provides a strictly stronger correctness oracle with zero false positives on correct kernels. The authors emphasize their finding concerns the evaluation methodology itself, not the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM.

title: CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations, the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20-33 percent relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5 percent of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, indicating that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

AI.tldr: CacheWeaver reorders retrieved evidence chunks before prompting to maximize prefix cache reuse in RAG serving, reducing time-to-first-token by 20–33% without degrading answer quality.
AI.motivation: RAG increases prompt length and prefill cost. Although prefix caching (e.g., vLLM) amortizes this cost, reuse depends on shared token prefixes. In grounded generation, adjacent queries often retrieve overlapping evidence sets but in different orders, so set-level overlap fails to translate into cacheable prefix overlap. The gap between retrieval overlap and prefix cache hit rate motivates a lightweight reordering layer.
AI.method: CacheWeaver maintains a prefix tree (trie) over recently served evidence sequences. For each new request, it performs a greedy walk: starting from the root, it repeatedly selects the child node whose evidence chunk appears earliest in the current retrieved set, thereby concatenating evidence to maximize the shared prefix with prior requests. This reordering operates purely at the prompt-construction layer, leaving the underlying serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged.
AI.result: Across three vLLM configurations, CacheWeaver reduces median TTFT by approximately 20–33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching. QA evaluations confirm no degradation in answer quality. The greedy policy achieves 97.5% of the median TTFT gain attainable under oracle ordering, demonstrating that most reusable prefix locality is recoverable via simple scheduling.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight, cache-aware evidence-ordering layer inserted between retrieval and inference can substantially improve prefix cache utilization in RAG serving, yielding significant TTFT reductions without modifying the serving engine or compromising output quality.

title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software
summary: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CWE-Trace, a benchmark of 834 Linux kernel vulnerability samples with strict temporal splits to test whether LLMs genuinely reason about security or merely exploit data contamination. Findings show contamination provides no measurable advantage; models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes that persist across datasets and resist correction via fine-tuning. Detection peaks at 52.1% (barely above chance), with exact CWE classification below 1.3% Top-1, indicating LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software.
AI.motivation: Resolving the open question of whether LLMs that score well on vulnerability benchmarks actually reason about security or simply pattern-match on training-data contamination. Prior benchmarks fail to control for temporal leakage, making it impossible to distinguish genuine reasoning from memorization.
AI.method: CWE-Trace framework: 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples across 74 CWEs, with strict pre-2025/post-cutoff temporal split, context-aware vulnerable-patched pairs. Two diagnostic metrics introduced: Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). Evaluation of 8 vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification.
AI.result: (1) Data contamination yields no measurable advantage: 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal; ~31% have CWE misclassification. (2) Backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning: DFI ranges from -85.5 to +94.8 pp, failure modes persist across temporal splits and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts thresholds without altering decision policy (calibration without comprehension). DeepSeek-R1 (weakest at binary detection) gains most in CWE classification, showing detection and understanding are decoupled. Best detection: 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE Top-1 below 1.3%.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software. Neither vanilla models nor fine-tuned variants demonstrate genuine vulnerability understanding. The decoupling of detection and classification capabilities, persistent directional failure modes, and ineffectiveness of contamination all point to a fundamental absence of security comprehension, regardless of training strategy.

title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
summary: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 77.1\% exact match accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases accuracy to 80.5\% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

AI.tldr: MortarBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs on mortgage loan origination tasks. Current LLMs perform poorly (max 77.1% accuracy) and exhibit bias against non-English names. The authors propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework that boosts accuracy to 80.5% while reducing bias and improving risk management.
AI.motivation: Loan origination is a critical, high-stakes financial process that firms are beginning to automate with LLM-based agents, yet no public benchmark exists to evaluate their performance, robustness, or fairness. This gap motivates the creation of a standardized evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors introduce (1) MortarBench, a benchmark built using a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline that generates realistic, edge-case-rich examples matching real-world distributions; and (2) CRIT, a confidence calibration framework designed to improve model accuracy, risk steering, and bias mitigation during loan origination decision-making.
AI.result: State-of-the-art closed-source LLMs achieve at most 77.1% exact match accuracy on MortarBench. Systematic biases were discovered against applicants with non-English names (foreignness perception bias). The CRIT framework raises accuracy to 80.5% while simultaneously improving risk management steering and reducing biased outcomes.
AI.conclusion: MortarBench fills a critical evaluation gap in automated loan origination, exposing significant performance and fairness limitations in current LLMs. The proposed CRIT framework demonstrates that confidence calibration can yield improvements across accuracy, risk management, and bias reduction, offering a path toward more reliable and equitable automated lending systems.

title: Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems
summary: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

AI.tldr: Evaluates AI-driven peer review systems (OpenAIReview, coarse, Reviewer3) across six LLMs on real ICLR/NeurIPS papers and an error-injection benchmark. Best system (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) achieves 83% pairwise accuracy in tracking paper quality and 71.6% error recall; multi-model union reaches 83.3% recall. A public deployment shows positive user reception (1.44:1 upvote ratio) with complaints mainly about false positives and nitpicking.
AI.motivation: The rise of AI-assisted research places growing pressure on traditional peer review systems. While agentic AI review systems are emerging as a potential solution, there is no established methodology for evaluating their effectiveness on real academic papers with objective ground truth.
AI.method: Two evaluation frameworks: (1) pairwise accuracy tests measuring whether AI review scores correlate with external quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions) on ICLR/NeurIPS papers; (2) a perturbation benchmark injecting four error categories into papers across eight arXiv subject classes, measuring detection recall. Additionally, a public deployment study of OpenAIReview with real users collecting votes and qualitative feedback.
AI.result: All systems exceed chance in pairwise accuracy; OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 leads at 83.0%. On error detection, OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 achieves 71.6% recall; the union across six models reaches 83.3%, indicating complementary error detection. Public deployment shows 1.44:1 positive vote ratio, with main complaints being false positives and minor nitpicks.
AI.conclusion: AI review systems backed by state-of-the-art models can track human quality judgments, catch important errors, and earn positive user feedback. However, substantial room for improvement remains, particularly in reducing false positives and improving error recall through better multi-model harness design.

title: Learning Critical Testing Literacy Through Puzzles: an Experience Report
summary:
In this paper, we report our experiences and takeaways from workshops using puzzles to learn CTL.
  Background: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. We introduced a BoK of puzzle-based learning activities to teach CTL, based on a model of critical tester's cognition, leading to the pedagogical framework P4TEST. We conducted thirteen workshops with students, testers, teachers, and primary school pupils to assess puzzle-based teaching of critical testing literacy.
  Experience: Across eleven workshops, we used a semi-structured approach, varying puzzles, materials, and timing. In two additional workshops, we introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to gather more data on the learning experience.
  Observations: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting while solving puzzles. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behaviour but hard to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning; written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive reflection. The theme Sensemaking / reflection-in-action captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
  Reflections: Puzzles are not the intervention: the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is. Designing that sequence more deliberately is the work ahead. We also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to customise workshops.

AI.tldr: The paper reports on thirteen workshops using puzzle-based learning to teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL). Findings indicate that the full sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting—not puzzles alone—constitutes the pedagogical intervention. Think-aloud and written reflection elicit different types of cognition, and an open-source web app with analytics was developed to support workshop customization.
AI.motivation: Software testing is important but pedagogically challenging to teach. The authors aim to assess whether puzzle-based learning activities, grounded in a model of critical tester's cognition and the P4TEST pedagogical framework, can effectively teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL) across diverse learner populations.
AI.method: Thirteen workshops were conducted with students, professional testers, teachers, and primary school pupils. Eleven used a semi-structured approach varying puzzles, materials, and timing. Two additional workshops introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions for richer data. Data collection included observation, written reflection, and verbal protocols.
AI.result: Participants consistently framed their activity as experimentation. Students converged on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were behaviorally visible but not well-captured in written reflection. Think-aloud surfaced immediate reasoning; written reflection elicited meta-cognition. The theme "Sensemaking / reflection-in-action" captured problem framing, dead-end navigation, and strategy shifting.
AI.conclusion: Puzzles alone are insufficient; the integrated sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is the true intervention. Future work lies in deliberately designing this sequence. An open-source web application with built-in analytics was developed to enable customized workshop delivery.

title: Code-Switching Reveals Language Anchoring in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to handle Code-Switched (CS) inputs, yet mixing languages frequently degrades performance relative to source- or target-language monolingual counterparts. To understand this degradation, we use grammar-forced CS as a controlled diagnostic setting for locating CS representations relative to their source and target counterparts. We introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric measure that quantifies language anchoring, whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source or target language counterpart. Across diverse MLLMs, Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS stays source-anchored, whereas target-framed CS shifts target-ward and shows larger Question Answering (QA) degradation.
