Motivated by this representational pattern, we propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side canvas from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during prefill. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across MLLMs and CS conditions, showing that internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures.

AI.tldr: Code-switched inputs degrade MLLM performance, especially under target-framed grammar. The authors introduce Anchor Bias to measure whether CS representations align closer to source or target language, then propose CANVAS, a source-anchoring inference intervention that recovers QA performance.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer performance degradation on code-switched inputs compared to monolingual inputs, and the representational mechanisms underlying this degradation are poorly understood. The authors seek to diagnose where CS hidden states fall relative to source and target language representations, and whether this geometric alignment can be leveraged for mitigation.
AI.method: The authors use grammar-forced code-switching (Equivalence Constraint Grammar) as a controlled setting. They introduce Anchor Bias, a cosine-similarity-based geometric measure quantifying whether a CS hidden state is closer to its source-language or target-language monolingual counterpart. They then propose CANVAS, an inference-time intervention that extracts a "source canvas" representation from the input prefix and applies soft steering to pull target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during the prefill phase.
AI.result: Anchor Bias reveals a grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS remains source-anchored, while target-framed CS shifts target-ward and exhibits larger QA degradation. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 scores across multiple MLLMs and CS conditions.
AI.conclusion: Internal anchoring signals provide a geometrically interpretable and actionable target for mitigating code-switching inference failures. The grammar-frame effect demonstrates that syntactic structure governs representational alignment in CS contexts, and CANVAS shows that lightweight inference-time steering can effectively correct these misalignments.

title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
summary: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a runtime monitoring framework for AI agents that enforces security policies with probabilistic predicates. Unlike prior deterministic approaches, it uses distributionally robust optimization to compute sound upper bounds on policy violation probability without requiring independence assumptions. The method outperforms existing approaches on benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime monitoring approaches for AI agent security policies are limited to deterministic Datalog-based policies. In practice, security policies often involve probabilistic components (e.g., PII detectors, declassifiers with failure rates), and independence assumptions required by prior probabilistic Datalog work are typically untenable in these settings. There is a need for a framework that can enforce policies under ambiguity with rigorous probabilistic guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose a verification framework based on distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Rather than relying on independence assumptions, the method computes sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation that hold regardless of possible correlations between probabilistic predicates. This allows enforcement of policies expressed in Datalog extended with probabilistic predicates and state transitions.
AI.result: Evaluated on standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling AI agents, the proposed approach outperforms prior art on the security-utility trade-off while maintaining rigorous (sound) upper bounds on policy violation probability.
AI.conclusion: The distributionally robust optimization framework provides a sound and efficient solution for runtime enforcement of security policies with probabilistic components in AI agent systems, overcoming the limitations of both deterministic prior work and independence-assuming probabilistic inference approaches.

title: 3D-DLP: Self-Supervised 3D Object-Centric Scene Representation Learning
summary: We introduce 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, each particle encodes disentangled attributes, including 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features, and represents a distinct entity in the scene. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective. We demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable: by manipulating particle positions and decoding, we can generate novel scene configurations. Furthermore, we show that leveraging these compact 3D latent particles for downstream robotic manipulation improves performance over baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure. Code and videos are available at https://eubooks3003.github.io/3d-dlp.

AI.tldr: 3D-DLP extends the Deep Latent Particles framework to 3D, learning to decompose RGB-D or voxel scenes into a set of interpretable 3D latent particles — each encoding disentangled keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance — via self-supervised reconstruction, enabling controllable scene generation and improving robotic manipulation over dense or 2D baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing scene representation models either lack explicit 3D object-centric structure — limiting interpretability and controllability — or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without disentangled entity-level representations. The authors aim to fill this gap with a compact, disentangled, object-centric 3D latent representation learned self-supervised from RGB-D or voxel observations, suitable for downstream tasks like robotic manipulation.
AI.method: 3D-DLP builds on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, extending it to 3D. The model takes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations and decomposes them into a set of 3D latent particles. Each particle encodes disentangled attributes: 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features. The model is trained end-to-end with a self-supervised reconstruction objective, during which it learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps without explicit segmentation supervision. Scene manipulation is achieved by directly editing particle positions in latent space and decoding.
AI.result: On both simulated and real-world datasets, the learned latent space is shown to be interpretable and controllable — novel scene configurations can be generated by manipulating particle positions. For downstream robotic manipulation tasks, using these compact 3D latent particles outperforms baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or use memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure.
AI.conclusion: 3D-DLP provides an effective self-supervised approach for learning compact, disentangled, object-centric 3D scene representations that are both interpretable and actionable, with demonstrated benefits for robotic manipulation. The code and videos are publicly released.

title: Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models
summary: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

AI.tldr: Defines four primitives for AI-blended architecture that enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic generative models, and identifies two common anti-patterns, providing a foundational framework for safely integrating AI into traditional computational systems.
AI.motivation: Early adopters have experienced significant failures and costs when integrating generative models into traditional systems without proper architectural guidance. The field lacks foundational frameworks to systematically de-risk AI integration.
AI.method: The paper proposes a design framework based on four architectural primitives that encapsulate probabilistic generative models within deterministic boundaries. It also identifies and formalizes two industry-wide anti-patterns through analysis of real-world integration failures.
AI.result: The framework yields four specific primitives for AI-blended architecture and two overarching anti-patterns that serve as cautionary design warnings for practitioners.
AI.conclusion: The proposed primitives and anti-patterns establish a foundation for successful, de-risked integration of generative AI into traditional systems, and also provide a basis for next-generation generative model interfaces.

title: N-Version Programming with Coding Agents
summary: This paper revisits the classical concept on N-version programming in the setting of contemporary AI coding agents. Revisiting the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment, we study whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages creates diverse failure modes. Using the Knight-Leveson's, Launch Interceptor Program Specification, we evaluate 48 agent-generated implementations on a shared oracle and a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. The results show substantial common-mode failure, along the findings of Knight-Leveson. Further analysis that many of those co-occuring failures can be traced to where is specification is particularly hard or ambiguous. We also demonstrate that diversity from coding agents provides practical benefit: across majority voting three-version units, the mean failure count drops from 387.44 for single versions to 130.99 for triples, and 11,844 N-version units exhibit zero observed failures. Our original results is the strongest evidence to date that N-Version Programming with coding agents is a useful engineering strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits N-version programming using modern AI coding agents, replicating the Knight-Leveson experiment. Testing 48 agent-generated implementations against 1M random inputs reveals substantial common-mode failures, many traceable to ambiguous specification parts. However, diversity across agents, models, and languages provides clear practical benefit: majority-voting triples reduce mean failures from 387.44 (single) to 130.99, with 11,844 three-version units showing zero failures.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the classical Knight-Leveson finding — that N-version programming suffers from common-mode failures due to shared specification ambiguity — holds in the era of contemporary AI coding agents, and whether diversity across agent systems, models, and languages can mitigate such failures.
AI.method: Using the Knight-Leveson Launch Interceptor Program Specification, 48 implementations were generated by varying AI coding agents, models, and programming languages. All were evaluated against a shared oracle using a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. Majority voting was applied across three-version N-version units to assess reliability improvement.
AI.result: Substantial common-mode failures were observed, consistent with the original Knight-Leveson findings, many linked to ambiguous or difficult specification sections. However, diversity yielded practical gains: mean failure count dropped from 387.44 (single version) to 130.99 (three-version majority vote), and 11,844 three-version units exhibited zero observed failures.
AI.conclusion: This study provides the strongest evidence to date that N-version programming with AI coding agents is a useful engineering strategy, despite persistent common-mode failures rooted in specification ambiguity.

title: What sentiment analysis can't see: Measuring whether customers were helped, and what went wrong, across 70,000 support conversations
summary: Most companies read their customer support data at scale using sentiment analysis, which measures how customers sound rather than whether they were satisfied with the result. We tested a richer alternative on 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform: alongside tone, we used GPT-5.4 to estimate each customer's satisfaction and to flag whether they reported a concrete problem, then validated all three readings against the 1-to-5 ratings customers left on the conversations they rated. The satisfaction estimate tracked those ratings far better than sentiment did, correlating at 0.47 against 0.36 and flagging unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. The structured read also sees what sentiment cannot: tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of conversations, a single "Neutral" label hides everything from quietly satisfied customers to ones who quietly gave up, and the largest group of all is "tolerated friction," customers who are satisfied but still reporting a fixable problem, a standing issue that no sentiment-based dashboard can surface. The broader finding is that LLM-based annotation can capture far more than the tonality of a customer's language, offering strong potential for new business metrics grounded instead in the customer's state (whether they were satisfied) and the cause of their problem extracted directly from the raw textual data of interactions and feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper compares traditional sentiment analysis with GPT-5.4-based satisfaction estimation and problem detection on 70,450 customer support conversations. The LLM approach outperforms sentiment analysis (correlation 0.47 vs 0.36 against actual ratings), reveals that tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of cases, and identifies "tolerated friction" — satisfied customers reporting fixable problems — which sentiment-based dashboards miss entirely.
AI.motivation: Traditional sentiment analysis measures how customers sound (tonality) rather than whether they were actually satisfied with their support outcome. This creates blind spots: customers may sound neutral but be dissatisfied, or sound frustrated yet be satisfied with the resolution. The authors argue that richer, LLM-based annotation can capture customer state and problem causality directly from conversational text, enabling more actionable business metrics.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 70,450 customer support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform. They used GPT-5.4 to produce three readings per conversation: (1) a satisfaction estimate, (2) a flag for whether a concrete problem was reported, and (3) sentiment/tone. All three were validated against 1-to-5 customer ratings on the subset of conversations where customers left ratings. They then compared the predictive performance of satisfaction estimates versus sentiment analysis and examined cases of tone-satisfaction disagreement.
AI.result: The satisfaction estimate correlated at 0.47 with actual customer ratings, outperforming sentiment analysis at 0.36, with substantially fewer false alarms for unhappy customers. Tone and satisfaction disagreed in 44% of conversations. The "Neutral" sentiment label collapsed distinct customer states — quietly satisfied versus quietly frustrated. The largest discovered group was "tolerated friction": customers who are satisfied overall but still report a fixable problem, invisible to sentiment-based systems.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based annotation goes beyond tonality to capture the customer's actual state (satisfaction) and the cause of their problem directly from raw interaction text. This opens the door to new business metrics that sentiment analysis cannot provide, such as surfacing fixable problems among satisfied customers and disaggregating the heterogeneous "Neutral" category into actionable segments.

title: Sovereign Execution Broker: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.

AI.tldr: SEB is a runtime enforcement broker that sits between autonomous agents and production infrastructure, consuming certified execution contracts (from SAB) and authorizing mutations only when all validity conditions are met, thereby converting certified authority into short-lived, auditable, revocable capabilities.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents lack deterministic behavior, making it unsafe to grant them direct production mutation authority. Existing solutions either authorize identities (access control) or certify proposed actions (assurance), but neither provides a mandatory enforcement point at the moment of mutation, leaving a gap between certification and execution.
AI.method: SEB acts as a runtime boundary that: (1) consumes certificates from a Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), (2) verifies mutation-request/certificate match, (3) checks validity windows, policy/revocation epochs, and live-state drift, (4) mints scoped execution identity, (5) invokes infrastructure APIs, and (6) records signed decision/outcome records. Deployment patterns enforce bypass prevention by ensuring production APIs reject non-broker identities. A prototype is implemented and evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes.
AI.result: The prototype was evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation speed, drift detection efficacy, and security under fault injection. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: By cleanly separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB provides a mandatory, auditable enforcement point that makes certified authority for agentic infrastructure both practically usable and securely bounded at runtime.

title: Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?
summary: Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or "intrinsic curiosity", remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its "learning progress", which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model's predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner's prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) can replace expensive gradient-based inner loops for computing intrinsic curiosity rewards. The authors prove that for general MDPs, unbiased ICL-based learning progress estimation is impossible, but for non-temporal settings (active learning, Bayesian Experimental Design), ICL-derived rewards converge to true learning progress. Experiments confirm the theory.
AI.motivation: Traditional intrinsic curiosity methods reward agents based on "learning progress" — how much a new observation improves a world model. However, computing this requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent within each trajectory, making it computationally impractical at scale. The authors investigate whether emergent in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models.
AI.method: The authors formally analyze whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress using only prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. They provide theoretical analysis across two settings: (1) general Markov decision processes (negative result — proving unbiased estimation is impossible due to nuisance terms or implementability constraints), and (2) non-temporal settings like active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design (positive result — ICL-derived rewards bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress). Controlled experiments in continuous and symbolic environments validate the framework.
AI.result: In general MDPs, unbiased ICL-based estimation of learning progress is provably impossible: rewards either contain nuisance terms biasing estimation or cannot be implemented via ICL prediction errors. However, for non-temporal settings (active learning, BED), ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Experiments confirm that the ICL-driven framework trains curious policies that explore optimally.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning can serve as an effective, computationally efficient substitute for gradient-based world model updates in non-temporal exploration settings like active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design, but fundamental limitations prevent unbiased application in general MDPs.

title: Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers
summary: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper models a future paid QA forum as a queuing system where expert knowledge workers answer requests across multiple topics, calculates maximum stable system capacity, designs capacity-achieving schedulers, and explores how inter-expert collaboration can further increase throughput.
AI.motivation: Current QA forums are volunteer-based and lack systematic performance guarantees. The authors envision a professionalized system with paid knowledge workers, necessitating formal analysis of how to schedule multi-topic requests among experts with heterogeneous expertise levels to maximize throughput while maintaining system stability.
AI.method: The authors model the QA forum as a multi-class queuing system with experts (servers) possessing varying expertise levels across different topics (classes). They employ queuing-theoretic analysis to characterize the stability region (capacity) and design scheduling policies that achieve it. Collaboration among experts is also incorporated into the model.
AI.result: The paper derives the system's capacity region — the set of request arrival rates for which a stable scheduling policy exists — and presents scheduling algorithms that achieve this capacity. Furthermore, it demonstrates that expert collaboration can expand the achievable capacity beyond what is possible with independent operation.
AI.conclusion: Professional QA systems with appropriately designed schedulers can operate at maximum theoretical capacity while remaining stable. Enabling collaboration among experts further enhances system throughput, providing design principles for future knowledge-worker-based QA platforms.

title: Qiskit Code Migration with LLMs
summary: The rapid evolution of Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) introduces a specific form of technical debt that compromises code maintainability and hinders software reuse. In the specialized domain of Quantum Software Engineering (QSE), this challenge is intensified by the scarcity of high-quality training data and the high volatility of emerging frameworks, which often lead general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce unreliable or hallucinated results. This paper proposes a hybrid approach integrating LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate the migration of Qiskit code across versions. The proposed methodology enhances the precision and reliability of migration suggestions by leveraging an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as the structured, version-specific knowledge source to guide the models. The approach is implemented through an automated, extensible workflow evaluating LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under different retrieval schemes (unconstrained and restrictive). Results demonstrate that the taxonomy-based RAG architecture, particularly under the restrictive scheme, significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality, with Google Gemini Flash-2.5 showing superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios. These findings confirm the potential of this data-centric methodology to foster technological independence and provide robust, intelligent assistants that mitigate API obsolescence, ensuring the long-term availability of quantum algorithms within a rapidly shifting ecosystem and flattening the learning curve within Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).

AI.tldr: A hybrid LLM+RAG approach using a taxonomy of migration scenarios automates Qiskit cross-version code migration, with restrictive retrieval significantly reducing hallucinations and Google Gemini Flash-2.5 excelling at complex refactoring detection.
AI.motivation: Quantum Development Kits evolve rapidly, causing API obsolescence that compromises code maintainability and creates technical debt. General-purpose LLMs produce unreliable results due to scarce QSE training data and volatile frameworks, motivating a reliable, data-centric migration solution.
AI.method: A hybrid LLM + Retrieval-Augmented Generation architecture leveraging an automatically generated taxonomy of Qiskit migration scenarios as structured, version-specific knowledge. Two LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5, OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) are evaluated under unconstrained and restrictive retrieval schemes within an automated, extensible workflow.
AI.result: The taxonomy-based RAG architecture under the restrictive retrieval scheme significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality. Google Gemini Flash-2.5 demonstrates superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios compared to the OpenAI model.
AI.conclusion: The data-centric taxonomy-based RAG methodology effectively mitigates API obsolescence, fosters technological independence, and provides robust intelligent assistants that flatten the QSE learning curve while ensuring long-term availability of quantum algorithms.

title: TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature
summary: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The resulting pipeline generates both types of output and provides a foundation for integrating knowledge from scientific literature into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling for Mars. The output from this pipeline looks promising, but further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

AI.tldr: TerraMARS is an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that uses a domain-adapted Small Language Model (Google Gemma 3 1B fine-tuned with QLoRA on Mars-specific QA and IE datasets) to convert unstructured Mars scientific literature into structured JSON outputs, supporting Mars terraforming research and habitability modeling.
AI.motivation: To enable human habitability of Mars, researchers need comprehensive, machine-readable knowledge about the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation, and spatial features extracted from the scientific literature. The unstructured nature of this literature hinders its use in downstream models such as habitability assessments and terraforming studies.
AI.method: The authors built TerraMARS, a pipeline that (1) collects and processes open-access Mars papers using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework, (2) fine-tunes Google Gemma 3 1B using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets, and (3) outputs structured JSON alongside answering terraforming-related questions.
AI.result: The pipeline produces both question-answering responses and structured JSON extractions from Mars literature. Results are described as promising, though further improvements are needed to enhance extraction accuracy and factual consistency.
AI.conclusion: TerraMARS provides a foundational pipeline for converting unstructured Mars science text into structured, machine-readable knowledge, with potential integration into digital twins and habitability modeling. However, extraction accuracy and factual consistency remain areas requiring further refinement.

title: From Efficiency to Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.

AI.tldr: NeuroImprint is a privacy attack in federated learning where a malicious server injects a backdoor into PEFT adapters, forcing the model to memorize each client training sample in isolated neurons. These per-sample updates can later be analytically inverted to reconstruct the original text, achieving 59–79% reconstruction rates across multiple models and datasets without harming model utility.
AI.motivation: Federated learning with PEFT is widely adopted for privacy-preserving fine-tuning, but the security assumption that the server is trusted may not hold. This work challenges that assumption by demonstrating a server-side attack that covertly exfiltrates client training data through manipulated adapter updates, exposing a critical vulnerability in practical FL deployments.
AI.method: The attack, NeuroImprint, works by (1) assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample, (2) constraining each neuron to be updated at most once during local fine-tuning to avoid cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing from large batches and stateful optimizers like Adam/AdamW, (3) after fine-tuning, analytically inverting the isolated per-sample parameter updates in closed form to recover text embeddings, and (4) deterministically mapping those embeddings back to token sequences.
AI.result: NeuroImprint successfully reconstructs 59% to 79% of all fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity across four diverse datasets and multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, Llama3.2), all without degrading model utility.
AI.conclusion: PEFT-based federated learning is vulnerable to server-side privacy backdoors that can exfiltrate client training data at scale. NeuroImprint demonstrates that current FL protocols lack sufficient protection against a malicious parameter server, highlighting the need for stronger defenses in practical FL systems.

title: Insulin4RL: Real-Time Insulin Management in the Intensive Care Unit for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (ORL) offers the potential to improve the quality of clinical decision-making using historical electronic health record (EHR) data. Current training and evaluative practices in this field rely heavily on EHR datasets that have been temporally discretised into fixed, regular time intervals. Discretisation creates fictional representations of complex clinical scenarios and compromises the generalisability of retrospective model evaluations. In this paper, we introduce Insulin4RL, a healthcare ORL dataset featuring naturally irregular inputs and actions from real clinical trajectories. Derived from MIMIC-IV, Insulin4RL comprises over 375,000 labelled decisions across 12,209 patients requiring insulin infusion titration in the Intensive Care Unit. The dataset can thus be used for research into ORL model performance under realistic clinical sampling assumptions. We provide a description of the dataset's structure and characteristics, baseline performance metrics using model-free offline reinforcement learning, and a standardised evaluation protocol using fitted Q-evaluation. We conclude with suggested areas for future research that could be addressed using this resource.

AI.tldr: Insulin4RL is a healthcare offline RL dataset derived from MIMIC-IV, featuring naturally irregular clinical time series for insulin titration in the ICU, with over 375,000 labeled decisions across 12,209 patients. It addresses the gap caused by temporal discretisation in existing EHR-based RL benchmarks and provides baseline model-free ORL results with fitted Q-evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current offline RL research in clinical decision-making relies on EHR data artificially discretised into fixed, regular intervals, which distorts complex clinical scenarios and undermines the generalisability of retrospective evaluations. There is a need for a realistic, irregularly-sampled dataset to better assess ORL methods under authentic clinical conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct Insulin4RL from the MIMIC-IV database by extracting real clinical trajectories of ICU patients requiring insulin infusion titration, preserving naturally irregular input and action timestamps. They provide baseline performance metrics using model-free offline RL algorithms and establish a standardised evaluation protocol via fitted Q-evaluation (FQE).
AI.result: Insulin4RL contains over 375,000 labeled clinical decisions spanning 12,209 patients. The paper presents baseline results from model-free offline RL methods evaluated under the proposed FQE protocol, establishing initial benchmarks for future comparisons on this irregularly-sampled clinical dataset.
AI.conclusion: Insulin4RL enables more realistic evaluation of offline RL methods in healthcare by preserving natural temporal irregularity. The authors highlight several future research directions that can leverage this resource, including methods robust to irregular sampling, off-policy evaluation under realistic clinical conditions, and clinically grounded policy learning.

title: Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework, which shifts the optimization focus from scalar uncertainty to the distributional properties of token logits. By leveraging the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logits distributions, ICT identifies tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points for guiding effective exploration in LLM reasoning. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, proves that selectively updating on these tokens regulates policy concentration: it reduces the overall distribution uncertainty measured by Shannon entropy, while controlling probability concentration captured by second-order Rényi entropy. This dual effect prevents over-concentrated token generation from weakening exploration and effectively stabilizes the training landscape. Empirical results demonstrate that updating only the top 10% of unique tokens on Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B) models yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58%, with a maximum gain of 14.9%, over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks spanning math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework to address the instability in RLVR for LLM reasoning. ICT shifts optimization from scalar uncertainty to distributional token properties, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to identify critical tokens whose selective updating prevents both entropy collapse and explosion, yielding significant performance gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: RLVR for LLM reasoning suffers from a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates cause entropy collapse (premature convergence to suboptimal strategies), while excessive Shannon entropy maximization causes entropy explosion (blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning). There is a need for a principled method to balance exploration and exploitation during RL training.
AI.method: The ICT framework shifts optimization from scalar uncertainty (e.g., entropy) to distributional properties of token logits. It uses Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logit distributions to identify tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points. These critical tokens are selectively updated (top 10% by uniqueness). The method is theoretically grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, showing that selective updating regulates policy concentration by reducing overall distribution uncertainty (Shannon) while controlling probability concentration (Rényi).
AI.result: On Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B), updating only the top 10% unique tokens achieves an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58% (maximum 14.9%) over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks covering math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.
AI.conclusion: Selectively updating tokens identified by distributional divergence (ICT) effectively stabilizes RLVR training by preventing both entropy collapse and explosion, leading to robust and significant improvements in LLM reasoning performance.

title: SysML Modeling of Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities
comment: Presented at the Workshop on Digital Twin Experiences and Model-Based Testing Methods, 12 June 2026, Västerås, Sweden, co-located with the 30th Ada-Europe International Conference on Reliable Software Technologies (AEiC 2026)
summary: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) are emerging as a key organizational model for local and global sharing of renewable generation, storage, and flexible loads. Engineering Digital Twins of RECs is made difficult by the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data involved. In this paper, we take a first step toward a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for REC's Digital Twins. Starting from an industrially-validated REC domain model, we re-express a representative house subset in SysML using the open-source Modelio tool, yielding two Block Definition Diagrams - a device taxonomy and a community organizational view. We then discuss four semantic gaps that plain SysML leaves open and sketch how the SAREF4ENER ontology could be imported as a reference package to close them. Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins remains largely unexplored, and we position this paper as a first step along that line.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for Renewable Energy Community (REC) Digital Twins using SysML, identifies four semantic gaps in plain SysML, and suggests bridging them with the SAREF4ENER ontology.
AI.motivation: Engineering Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities is challenging due to the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data. Existing approaches lack a structured, model-based methodology that can formally capture both the architectural and semantic dimensions of RECs.
AI.method: The authors take an industrially-validated REC domain model, re-express a representative house subset in SysML v2 using the open-source Modelio tool, and produce two Block Definition Diagrams: one for device taxonomy and one for community organization. They then identify four semantic gaps left open by plain SysML and sketch how importing the SAREF4ENER ontology as a reference package can close them.
AI.result: Two SysML Block Definition Diagrams are produced that capture device taxonomy and community organizational structure. Four specific semantic gaps are identified where plain SysML falls short, and a preliminary mapping to SAREF4ENER concepts is outlined as a remedy.
AI.conclusion: Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins is a largely unexplored direction. This paper serves as an initial step, demonstrating feasibility and outlining future work toward a fully integrated MBSE-ontology workflow for REC Digital Twins.

title: FineREX: Fine-Tuned NER-RE for Human Smuggling Knowledge Graphs
summary: Court proceedings contain valuable evidence about human smuggling networks, but this information is often buried within unstructured, jargon-heavy legal documents. While large language models (LLMs) can support knowledge graph construction through automated information extraction, existing approaches rely on general-purpose models that are not tailored to the entity and relationship definitions required in this domain. We introduce FineREX, a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline built around a fine-tuned LLM for named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). Using a manually annotated dataset of $512$ text chunks, FineREX achieves absolute improvements of 15.50% and 31.46% in entity and relationship F1-score, respectively, compared to a larger general-purpose baseline. These gains translate into higher-quality knowledge graphs, reducing legal noise by nearly half and lowering node duplication on long documents from 17.78% to 11.17%. By eliminating document rewriting and redundant extraction stages, FineREX also reduces end-to-end processing time by 50.0%. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning can substantially outperform larger general-purpose models while improving both the quality and efficiency of knowledge graph construction for illicit network analysis.

AI.tldr: FineREX is a pipeline that fine-tunes an LLM for domain-specific named entity recognition and relation extraction from legal documents about human smuggling. It outperforms larger general-purpose models by 15–31% in F1-score, cuts legal noise by half, reduces node duplication, and halves processing time.
AI.motivation: Court records on human smuggling contain valuable evidence but are buried in unstructured, jargon-dense legal text. General-purpose LLMs used for knowledge graph construction are not adapted to the domain-specific entity and relation definitions needed, motivating a fine-tuned, task-specific approach.
AI.method: FineREX is a streamlined KG construction pipeline centered on a fine-tuned LLM for joint NER and RE. A manually annotated dataset of 512 text chunks is used for training. The pipeline eliminates document rewriting and redundant extraction stages, directly extracting entities and relations in one pass.
AI.result: On the annotated dataset, FineREX achieves absolute F1 improvements of +15.50% for entities and +31.46% for relations over a larger general-purpose baseline. Knowledge graph quality improves: legal noise reduced by ~50%, long-document node duplication drops from 17.78% to 11.17%, and end-to-end processing time is reduced by 50.0%.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning substantially outperforms larger general-purpose LLMs for KG construction in the illicit-network domain, simultaneously improving extraction quality and computational efficiency.

title: Concept Flow Models: Anchoring Concept-Based Reasoning with Hierarchical Bottlenecks
summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance interpretability by projecting learned features into a human-understandable concept space. Recent approaches leverage vision-language models to generate concept embeddings, reducing the need for manual concept annotations. However, these models suffer from a critical limitation: as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, information leakage increases, enabling the model to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations and undermining interpretability. In this work, we propose Concept Flow Models (CFMs), which replace the flat bottleneck with a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree. Each internal node in the hierarchy focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing the prediction scope. Our framework constructs decision hierarchies from visual embeddings, distributes semantic concepts at each hierarchy level, and trains differentiable concept weights through probabilistic tree traversal. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs, while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. Furthermore, CFMs yield stepwise decision flows that enable transparent and auditable model reasoning with hierarchical class structures.

AI.tldr: Concept Flow Models (CFMs) address information leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models by replacing the flat concept bottleneck with a hierarchical decision tree, where each node uses a localized subset of discriminative concepts, preserving predictive performance while enhancing interpretability and reducing spurious concept reliance.
AI.motivation: Flat Concept Bottleneck Models suffer from information leakage: as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, the model can exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations between concepts and classes, thereby undermining the very interpretability CBMs are designed to provide.
AI.method: CFMs construct a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree from visual embeddings. Concepts are distributed across tree levels, with each internal node specializing in a localized subset of discriminative concepts. The model trains differentiable concept weights using probabilistic tree traversal, progressively narrowing the prediction scope from root to leaf.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks show CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs while substantially mitigating information leakage (measured by reduced effective concept usage). CFMs also yield stepwise, auditable decision flows with hierarchical class structures.
AI.conclusion: CFMs offer a compelling alternative to flat CBMs by introducing hierarchical structure that constrains concept usage per decision step, effectively reducing information leakage without sacrificing accuracy, and enabling transparent, step-by-step reasoning.

title: AgentFinVQA: A Deployable Multi-Agent Pipeline for Auditable Financial Chart QA
summary: Financial chart question answering in regulated settings demands more than accuracy: practitioners must know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers. Yet existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, and most assume proprietary API access; to our knowledge, none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise. We present AgentFinVQA, a multi-agent pipeline that decomposes each query into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification, recording every step in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves $+7.68$ pp over a primary-backbone matched zero-shot baseline with a proprietary backbone (Gemini-3 Flash; 71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar $p \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}$), and $+4.84$ pp with open-weights Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served locally. The verifier's verdict also serves as a useful confidence signal (68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers), enabling human-in-the-loop review routing. Error analysis shows that question misunderstanding, legend confusion and extraction error account for nearly two-thirds of failures and are the categories least detected by the verifier, identifying clear directions for future work. Together these results show that auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical and that the open-weights system keeps most of the accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. We release our code to support reproducible evaluation.

AI.tldr: AgentFinVQA is a multi-agent pipeline for financial chart QA that combines auditability via traceable Model Evaluation Packets (MEPs) with on-premise deployability using open-weights models, achieving strong accuracy gains over zero-shot baselines while providing verifier-based confidence signals for human-in-the-loop routing.
AI.motivation: Regulated financial settings require both trustworthy, auditable answers and on-premise deployment (data residency), yet existing chart QA systems are accuracy-focused, opaque, and assume proprietary API access. No existing system combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy loss.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline decomposing each query into five stages: planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification. Every step is recorded in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. The verifier also produces a confidence signal (confirmed vs. revised answer) to enable human-in-the-loop review routing. Evaluated with both a proprietary backbone (Gemini-3 Flash) and an open-weights model (Qwen3.6-27B-FP8) served locally.
AI.result: On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves +7.68 pp over zero-shot baseline with Gemini-3 Flash (71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar p≈1.1×10⁻¹⁶) and +4.84 pp with Qwen3.6-27B-FP8. The verifier's confirmed-vs-revised signal yields 68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy, demonstrating useful confidence calibration. Error analysis reveals question misunderstanding, legend confusion, and extraction error account for ~2/3 of failures and are least detected by the verifier.
AI.conclusion: Auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical. The open-weights system retains most accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. The error analysis identifies clear directions for future work, and code is released for reproducible evaluation.

title: NRITYAM: Language Models Meet Art and Heritage of Dance
summary: Language models have become essential tools in shaping modern workflows. However, their global effectiveness hinges on a nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts. To address this gap, we present NRITYAM, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the cultural comprehension capabilities of language models in the context of global dance traditions. NRITYAM comprises 9,260 carefully curated question-answer pairs spanning 12 languages, making it the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. The dataset has been developed from the ground up through close collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers of the languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant questions specific to their regions. We evaluate a broad set of models, including large language models, small language models, multimodal large language models, and small multimodal language models. As a multilingual and multicultural benchmark, NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating the ability of AI systems to understand and reason about traditional performing arts. Detailed dataset samples are available at~\url{https://github.com/niladrighosh03/NRITYAM}.

AI.tldr: NRITYAM is a multilingual, multicultural benchmark of 9,260 QA pairs across 12 languages for evaluating language models' understanding of global dance traditions, created with native artists and speakers.
AI.motivation: Language models lack nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts, limiting their global effectiveness. Existing benchmarks do not adequately assess cultural comprehension in traditional performing arts.
AI.method: The authors constructed NRITYAM from scratch through collaboration with native dance artists and native language speakers, who authored and validated culturally relevant QA pairs specific to their regions. The benchmark spans 12 languages with 9,260 QA pairs. A broad set of models was evaluated: LLMs, small LMs, multimodal LLMs, and small multimodal LMs.
AI.result: The paper presents NRITYAM as the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. Evaluation results across diverse model types are reported, though specific performance metrics are not detailed in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: NRITYAM establishes a new standard for evaluating AI systems' ability to understand and reason about traditional performing arts across multiple languages and cultures.

title: Algebraic Dead Directions in LayerNorm Transformers: A Forward-Pass-Only Diagnostic at LLM Scale
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Empirical companion to arXiv:2606.05957
summary: Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima of the loss, where the Fisher information metric degenerates along dead directions: directions in parameter space along which the directional Fisher vanishes. Locating such a direction normally needs a forward pass and an eigendecomposition of activations, or a sampling-based complexity estimate; none returns a direction computable from the network's parameters alone. We give one, for LayerNorm transformers. The inverse-scale direction $γ^{-1}/\|γ^{-1}\|$ of the LayerNorm affine is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution, and induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space. It is read from the LN scale parameter alone, with no forward or backward pass and no eigensolve: the cheapest dead-direction read, specific to LayerNorm. We test it on $14$ pretrained transformers ($9$ LayerNorm, $5$ RMSNorm; $160$M-$35$B; language and vision objectives). At random initialisation the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction (one forward pass, direct SVD) to four decimal places on $9/9$ LayerNorm models, and is correctly absent on $5/5$ RMSNorm models, which lack the mean-subtraction projector that creates it. On the trained checkpoint the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ${\sim}10^3\times$ and further dead directions open; the random-init-to-trained gap is a one-forward-pass, per-checkpoint readout of singular structure along the predicted coordinate. Two consequences follow in closed form: the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on $13/14$ transformers measured on their own input distribution, the one exception (Gemma$4$-$31$B) a genuine dead direction the same read pinpoints; and the kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation from the parameters alone.

AI.tldr: LayerNorm transformers possess an analytically identifiable dead direction — the inverse-scale direction of the LayerNorm affine parameter — that is an exact kernel of the post-final-norm activation covariance. This direction is readable from the LN scale parameter alone, requires no forward/backward passes or eigendecomposition, and is validated across 14 pretrained transformers, distinguishing LayerNorm from RMSNorm architectures.
AI.motivation: Prior methods for identifying dead directions (vanishing Fisher information) in neural networks require expensive forward passes, eigendecompositions of activations, or sampling-based estimates. No existing method yields a dead direction computable solely from network parameters. This work aims to provide a closed-form, parameter-only dead direction for LayerNorm transformers, enabling cheap structural diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors derive analytically that the inverse-scale direction γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖ of the LayerNorm affine parameter is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance matrix, for any input distribution. This holds because LayerNorm's mean-subtraction projector creates the degeneracy. The direction is read directly from the LN scale parameter γ with zero computational cost beyond parameter access. Validation uses direct SVD (one forward pass) on 14 pretrained transformers (9 LayerNorm, 5 RMSNorm; 160M–35B parameters; language and vision) at both random initialisation and trained checkpoints.
AI.result: At random initialisation, the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction to four decimal places on all 9 LayerNorm models and is correctly absent on all 5 RMSNorm models. At trained checkpoints, the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ~10³× and additional dead directions emerge. The residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on 13/14 transformers; the one exception (Gemma 4-31B) reveals a genuine dead direction that the same method pinpoints. The kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation type from parameters alone.
AI.conclusion: The inverse-scale direction of LayerNorm affine parameters provides the cheapest possible dead-direction readout for LayerNorm transformers — parameter-only, no forward pass, no eigensolve. This enables instant structural diagnostics, distinguishes LayerNorm from RMSNorm, and offers a per-checkpoint readout of singular structure evolution during training.

title: ORAgentBench: Can LLM Agents Solve Challenging Operations Research Tasks End to End?
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step tasks in executable environments, yet their ability to perform realistic operations research (OR) work remains unclear. Existing OR evaluations often decouple modeling from solving, rely on pre-formalized or text-only instances, and rarely test the full workflow from operational artifacts to validated decisions. In this work, we introduce ORAgentBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on challenging end-to-end operations research tasks. It contains 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each packaged in an isolated environment with a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and run solution code, and their submissions are evaluated by hidden validators for schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Experiments with fourteen frontier agent-model configurations show that current agents remain far from reliable OR practice. The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, and many feasible submissions still fall below the required quality threshold. Failure analysis further shows that errors are dominated by strategic weaknesses, including missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills increase hard-task feasibility, but do not reliably improve solution quality or pass rate. These results suggest that progress in OR agents requires moving beyond plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making.

AI.tldr: ORAgentBench is a benchmark of 107 end-to-end operations research tasks that evaluates autonomous LLM agents on the full workflow—from raw operational artifacts to validated decisions. The best agent configuration passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, revealing that current agents lack the strategic reliability needed for realistic OR practice.
AI.motivation: Existing OR evaluations decouple modeling from solving, use pre-formalized or text-only instances, and fail to test the complete pipeline—from operational artifacts to validated decisions. The authors aim to assess whether LLM agents can realistically perform autonomous OR work in executable, end-to-end settings.
AI.method: The authors construct ORAgentBench: 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each isolated with a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and execute solution code; submissions are evaluated by hidden validators on schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Fourteen frontier agent-model configurations are tested.
AI.result: The best agent achieves only 35.51% pass rate overall and 20.59% on hard tasks. Many feasible submissions fall below the required quality threshold. Failure analysis reveals errors dominated by strategic weaknesses: missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills improve hard-task feasibility but do not reliably boost solution quality or pass rates.
AI.conclusion: Progress in OR agents demands moving beyond generating plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making. Current LLM agents are not yet reliable for realistic OR practice.

title: Token-Operations-Oriented Inference Optimization Techniques for Large Models
summary: Large model inference optimization serves as a key foundation for supporting the scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation of large model services. Centered on token-oriented inference optimization technology, this paper proposes for the first time a four-layer technical architecture consisting of Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion. It systematically reviews the key technologies and current industry status across these four levels and analyzes the application value of related technologies in real-world business scenarios. This paper provides a practical technical path for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, ensuring the stability of token supply, and driving the transition of large model services from being merely callable to being operable.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-layer architecture (Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, Compute-Network-Model Fusion) for token-oriented large model inference optimization, systematically reviewing key technologies and their business value for reducing cost, improving efficiency, and ensuring stable token supply.
AI.motivation: Enable large model services to transition from being merely callable to fully operable by achieving scalable, low-cost, and highly stable inference. The core driver is reducing token production costs while improving token service efficiency and supply stability.
AI.method: Proposes a four-layer technical architecture: (1) Multi-model Fusion — combining multiple models; (2) Model Optimization — optimizing individual models; (3) Compute-Model Fusion — joint optimization of computation and model; (4) Compute-Network-Model Fusion — co-optimization across compute, network, and model layers. The paper systematically reviews key technologies across all four layers and analyzes their industry status.
AI.result: The paper provides a practical technical pathway demonstrating how each layer's technologies contribute to lowering token production costs, boosting token service efficiency, and ensuring token supply stability in real-world business deployments.
AI.conclusion: The four-layer token-oriented inference optimization architecture offers a viable roadmap for transforming large model services from experimental callability to production-grade operability, with direct business value in cost reduction, efficiency improvement, and service stability.

title: Calibrating Generative Models to Feature Distributions with MMD Finetuning
summary: Generative models can produce individually plausible samples while deviating substantially from a target set in the distribution of key features. For example, a model pretrained on broad drug-like chemical space may generate molecules whose molecular features differ from those of a therapeutic class of interest, such as known antibiotics. Correcting such distributional miscalibration is challenging: direct finetuning on the target set can overfit and does not control which features are matched. To fill this gap, we introduce kernel Calibrating Generative Models (kCGM). kCGM minimizes a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, with KL regularization to remain close to the pretrained model. On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrifices chemical validity for feature-distribution matching, whereas kCGM improves target feature matching while increasing validity. We further demonstrate kCGM in protein and DNA generation tasks, showing it can adapt autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models using only feature-level supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/smithhenryd/cgm.

AI.tldr: kCGM is a method for calibrating generative models to match feature distributions of a target set (e.g., a specific therapeutic class) using MMD minimization with KL regularization, avoiding overfitting and validity loss common in direct finetuning.
AI.motivation: Pretrained generative models often exhibit distributional miscalibration — generating samples that are individually plausible but deviate from a target set's feature distribution. Direct finetuning on small target sets leads to overfitting and cannot control which features are matched. Existing methods lack a principled way to align feature distributions while preserving sample validity and staying close to the pretrained model.
AI.method: kCGM (kernel Calibrating Generative Models) minimizes the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator. A KL divergence regularization term keeps the fine-tuned model close to the pretrained model. The method operates using only feature-level supervision without requiring explicit target samples for discrimination, making it applicable across diverse model architectures.
AI.result: On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrificed chemical validity for feature matching, whereas kCGM improved target feature matching while increasing validity. The method was also successfully demonstrated on protein and DNA generation tasks, adapting autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models.
AI.conclusion: kCGM provides a principled, architecture-agnostic framework for distributional calibration of generative models, enabling effective adaptation to target feature distributions with only feature-level supervision while maintaining or improving sample validity.

title: CombEval: A Framework for Evaluating Combinatorial Counting in Large Language Models
summary: We present CombEval, a dynamic benchmark for evaluating combinatorial counting in large language models. CombEval represents each problem as a typed Cofola specification over entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints, enabling controlled generation of natural-language counting problems with exact solver-verified answers. Unlike static collections, CombEval supports systematic variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. We evaluate 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings and find that models remain brittle on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis further identifies failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles. CombEval provides a diagnostic testbed for studying when and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. The code and generated benchmark suites are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/YuxuZhou-CN/combination-problem-generation}.

AI.tldr: CombEval is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating LLMs on combinatorial counting problems, featuring typed specifications, solver-verified answers, and systematic variation of problem parameters. Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals brittleness on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relative positioning, and nested dependencies, with failures rooted in constraint interpretation and counting principles.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for combinatorial reasoning in LLMs are static collections that lack controlled, systematic variation of problem parameters and do not provide exact, verifiable answers. This limits diagnostic insight into specific failure modes of LLMs on counting problems.
AI.method: CombEval represents each combinatorial counting problem as a typed Cofola specification comprising entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints. From these specifications, natural-language problems are generated with exact answers verified by a solver. The framework supports systematic variation along four axes: object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. Eleven LLMs are evaluated under both direct answering and code-augmented (Python) settings.
AI.result: LLMs consistently exhibit brittleness on: (1) ordered objects, (2) indistinguishable elements, (3) relatively positional constraints, and (4) nested object dependencies. Error analysis reveals two primary failure categories: misinterpretation of constraints and misapplication of fundamental counting principles.
AI.conclusion: CombEval serves as an effective diagnostic testbed for understanding when and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. The systematic variability enables fine-grained analysis, and code augmentation alone does not resolve core reasoning deficiencies. The benchmark and code are publicly released.

title: A Model-Driven Approach for Developing Families of Reinforcement Learning Environments
summary: Virtual training environments are software-intensive systems in which reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn, adapt, and demonstrate meaningful behavior. Virtual training environments offer a safe and cost-efficient alternative to training agents in real-world settings. However, to converge, most realistic RL problems require training in multiple, mostly similar but slightly different environments - i.e., families of environment variants. The typical development process of environment families is a labor-intensive and error-prone manual endeavor that does not scale well. To alleviate these issues, in this paper, we propose a model-driven approach for developing families of RL training environments. To obtain the family of environments, we develop an approach and prototype tool. In our approach, a hybrid genetic algorithm - a combination of population-based global search and heuristic local search - generates environment families. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and are operationalized into a search process by a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. We demonstrate the soundness of our approach in a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning - a particular learning paradigm that relies on environment families.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-driven approach using a hybrid genetic algorithm (global + local search) to automatically generate families of RL training environments, addressing the manual, error-prone nature of environment variant creation, demonstrated in wildfire mitigation and curriculum learning.
AI.motivation: Realistic RL problems require training across families of similar-but-different environments. Manual creation of these environment variants is labor-intensive, error-prone, and not scalable, motivating automation.
AI.method: A model-driven approach with a hybrid genetic algorithm combining population-based global search and heuristic local search. Environment family mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations, operationalized by a model transformation engine. A prototype tool implements the approach.
AI.result: The approach is demonstrated and validated in two contexts: a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning (which inherently relies on environment families). Soundness is shown in both cases.
AI.conclusion: The model-driven, search-based approach effectively automates the generation of RL environment families, improving scalability and reducing manual effort compared to traditional development processes.

title: Clusters are All You Need: Pre-Training the Tsetlin Machine with Semantic Clusters from Language Models for Interpretability
