We show that, unlike popular alternatives based on proper scoring rules, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks confirm that QUEST performs favourably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.

AI.tldr: QUEST introduces a new UQ framework based on highest density regions (HDRs) of a distribution, measuring uncertainty via Lebesgue measure concentration at peaks, parameterized by α. It satisfies key axioms (monotonicity under spread, location invariance) and outperforms variance and entropy on selective prediction.
AI.motivation: Standard scalar UQ methods for regression (e.g., proper scoring rules) rely on pointwise predictive risk, which yields counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. There is a need for an axiomatic, geometrically principled alternative.
AI.method: QUEST (Quantifying Uncertainty via highest dEnSiTy regions) defines uncertainty as the volume (Lebesgue measure) of the most probable subset of a distribution's support, computed via highest density regions at one or more robustness levels α. Both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty measures are derived, with theoretical connections to information theory and economics.
AI.result: QUEST measures satisfy axioms including monotonicity under distributional spread and location-shift invariance, unlike proper scoring rule alternatives. In selective prediction benchmarks, QUEST performs favorably against variance and differential entropy.
AI.conclusion: QUEST provides an axiomatically sound, geometrically intuitive UQ framework that decouples uncertainty quantification from conditional expectation, making it broadly applicable in safety-critical probabilistic ML settings.

title: The Tao of Agency: Autotelic AI, Embedded Agency and Dissolution of the Self
summary:
Most artificial intelligence systems are built on the assumption that goals are exogenous and specified by the designer. Exploring what happens when an agent begins generating its own goals opens the field of autotelic AI. Agents are expected not merely to pursue objectives but to discover them. In this article, we trace its consequences through intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness; the last of which is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent at the cost of revealing that the individuation is non-unique, such that the same dynamics admit many valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self.
  The deepest problem with autotelic AI is therefore not how the agent generates goals, but how it generates and relativizes the self to which the goals are assigned. The agent must believe in its own boundary in order to act, and see through that boundary in order to understand. We consolidate these developments into a single framework and extend it along three directions: a quantum formulation in which the agent-environment cut becomes physical, a philosophical reading against non-dual contemplative traditions, and a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

AI.tldr: The paper explores autotelic AI—agents that generate their own goals—arguing that the fundamental challenge is not goal generation itself but how the agent defines, maintains, and relativizes the self-boundary to which those goals are assigned. It consolidates intrinsic motivation, causal learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness into a unified framework, then extends it through quantum formulations, non-dual philosophy, and an LLM-based implementation.
AI.motivation: Conventional AI treats goals as externally specified by designers. The authors argue this is a fundamental limitation and explore the consequences of agents that autonomously discover and generate their own goals. The deeper motivation is to shift focus from goal-generation mechanisms to the more foundational problem of how an agent individuates itself from its environment—the self-boundary problem.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual framework synthesizing five key ideas: intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness. It then extends this framework in three directions: (1) a quantum mechanical formulation where the agent-environment cut becomes physically grounded, (2) a philosophical analysis drawing parallels with non-dual contemplative traditions, and (3) a concrete implementation using LLM-based agents.
AI.result: Embeddedness is identified as necessary but insufficient for autotelic agency. Its critical consequence is that individuation is non-unique—the same underlying dynamics admit multiple valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self. The core tension is that the agent must simultaneously believe in its boundary (to act) and see through it (to understand).
AI.conclusion: The deepest challenge of autotelic AI is the self-relativization problem: how an agent generates and relativizes the self to which goals are assigned. Resolving the tension between reifying and transcending the self-boundary is essential for building agents that both act effectively and maintain coherent self-models.

title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
summary: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit--DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

AI.tldr: A lightweight pronunciation assessment framework using only native speech, combining SSL-based surprisal from a token language model with transcript-guided DTW alignment. Transcript guidance boosts PCC from 0.60 to 0.66 on SpeechOcean762, nearing supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Supervised pronunciation assessment models require costly labeled learner errors or non-native corpora. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency by building a system trained solely on native speech resources, with optional light calibration.
AI.method: Learner speech is discretized via an SSL encoder and K-means codebook into acoustic tokens. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal (higher = greater phonotactic deviation). A Text2DUnit--DTW module predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens via DTW, yielding error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused through simple regression for pronunciation scoring.
AI.result: On SpeechOcean762, Pearson Correlation Coefficient improves from 0.60 (surprisal-only) to 0.66 with transcript guidance, approaching supervised baselines. Consistent improvements are also observed in cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight, native-only framework effectively assesses pronunciation quality without requiring costly labeled learner data. Transcript-guided alignment significantly enhances performance, bringing unsupervised assessment close to supervised methods.

title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
summary: Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the problem of learning high-level causal abstractions directly from low-level data, rather than hypothesis-testing a candidate model. The authors leverage low-rank causal discovery to show that low-rank graph observations induce latents forming a causal abstraction, provide identifiability guarantees, and propose a practical learning objective.
AI.motivation: Existing work on causal abstraction follows a hypothesis-testing paradigm where an expert manually proposes a high-level model and tests whether the low-level system implements it. This paper addresses the complementary, underexplored problem of automatically learning the high-level SCM from low-level measurements, removing the need for expert-supplied candidate models.
AI.method: The approach leverages low-rank causal discovery frameworks. The authors (1) prove that when observations come from a low-rank causal graph, the induced latent variables form a valid causal abstraction of the low-level SCM, (2) derive identifiability results for these latents, and (3) formulate a practical optimization objective to learn the abstracted high-level SCM directly from data.
AI.result: The paper establishes theoretical results: low-rank graph structures induce latent representations that satisfy the formal definition of causal abstraction. It also provides identifiability guarantees, showing that these latents can be uniquely recovered under specified conditions, and demonstrates a tractable learning objective for practical use.
AI.conclusion: Causal abstraction can be framed as a learning problem rather than solely a hypothesis-testing one. Low-rank structure in the observational data provides a principled path to automatically discovering abstracted high-level causal models with identifiability guarantees.

title: PhysDrift: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in Humanoid Co-Speech Motion Generation
summary: Humanoid robots require co-speech motions that are not only expressive and speech-aligned, but also physically executable under embodiment constraints. Existing co-speech generation pipelines are predominantly human-centric: motions are first generated in human-body representations such as SMPL-X and subsequently retargeted to humanoid robots. In this work, we identify a fundamental embodiment gap in this paradigm, where the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency during motion transfer and physical execution. Through extensive analysis, we show that although retargeting can preserve coarse motion semantics, it significantly compresses motion diversity and weakens prosody-motion synchronization, limiting expressive humanoid behaviors. To address this problem, we first propose IK-EER, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting. Building upon the curated robot-native motion dataset, we further introduce PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without relying on intermediate human-body representations. Unlike conventional human-centric pipelines, PhysDrift maintains embodiment consistency throughout both training and inference while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics. Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability.

AI.tldr: Human-centric co-speech motion pipelines suffer from an "embodiment gap" when retargeting to humanoid robots. The authors propose IK-EER for curated robot-native data and PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware framework that directly generates executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech, bypassing human-body representations and improving alignment, plausibility, and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing co-speech motion generation pipelines generate motions in human-body representations (e.g., SMPL-X) and then retarget them to humanoid robots. This introduces an "embodiment gap": a mismatch between the human motion manifold and humanoid embodiment constraints (kinematic limits, dynamics, physical feasibility), which disrupts embodiment consistency, compresses motion diversity, and weakens prosody-motion synchronization during retargeting. The work aims to bypass this gap entirely.
AI.method: Two key contributions: (1) **IK-EER**, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting, producing a robot-native motion dataset. (2) **PhysDrift**, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech input, avoiding intermediate human-body representations. PhysDrift incorporates physical regularization to stabilize motion dynamics and maintains embodiment consistency throughout training and inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that the embodiment-aware, robot-native generation approach substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability compared to conventional human-centric retargeting pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Direct robot-native co-speech motion generation, as realized by PhysDrift, effectively eliminates the embodiment gap inherent in human-centric pipelines. By training and inferring directly in the humanoid joint space with physical regularization, the approach achieves superior embodiment consistency, expressive prosody-aligned gestures, and practical real-time deployment capability on physical humanoid robots.

title: GEMS: Geometric Constraints Enable Multi-Semantic Superposition in LLMs
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code and logs are available at: https://github.com/LuLu663939/gems-multi-semantic-steering
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate hidden states at inference time without retraining. Existing methods handle only single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, the model collapses. We show that this collapse decomposes into two independently acting sources: distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and drive activations outside the training distribution, and directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. These two sources define the design constraints that any training-free multi-directional intervention must address. As one instantiation of these principles, we propose GEMS, a training-free method that maps each source to a corresponding geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization for directional interference. On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%; on Wikitext-2, the same injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation isolates the causal role of each constraint, and layer-level probes confirm that orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B.

AI.tldr: Activation steering with multiple directions causes model collapse due to distributional deviation and directional interference; the proposed GEMS method resolves this via norm-preserving superposition and real-time orthogonalization, achieving near-baseline performance with multi-directional control.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods only support single-direction injection. When multiple semantic directions are applied simultaneously without constraints, model performance catastrophically degrades. The authors aim to decompose and understand this collapse mechanism, then derive principled constraints for training-free multi-directional intervention.
AI.method: First, the authors theoretically decompose multi-direction collapse into two independent sources: (1) distributional deviation — additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers, pushing activations out of distribution; (2) directional interference — non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually attenuate when superposed. GEMS addresses each with geometric constraints: norm-preserving weighted superposition and attention-pathway-targeted injection mitigate distributional deviation, while real-time orthogonalization (e.g., Gram-Schmidt) eliminates directional interference between concurrently injected semantic vectors.
AI.result: On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions with GEMS preserves accuracy at 98% (vs. 92% baseline and 4% for unconstrained addition). On Wikitext-2, the same multi-direction injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Ablation studies isolate the causal contribution of each constraint. Layer-level probes confirm orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with maintained semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Distributional deviation and directional interference are the two fundamental failure modes of multi-directional activation steering. GEMS demonstrates that addressing both with simple geometric constraints enables robust training-free multi-concept control, with strong empirical results and cross-scale transferability.

title: IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows
summary:
Voice agents deployed in structured workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management) must handle frequent user interruptions while maintaining progress through multi-step procedures. Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus on the timing of interruptions: barge-in detection, endpointing, and turn-taking dynamics. They leave unmeasured what happens after the interruption: does the agent resume the workflow at the correct step? Does it address the user's interjection? Does it avoid re-delivering content the user already heard?
  We introduce IHBench (Interruption Handling Benchmark), a benchmark that evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents executing state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance, with per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality.
  We evaluate 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community. Models vary widely, and recovery quality depends strongly on the interruption type. Across our experiments, closed-weight models are consistently more robust to interruptions than open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade roughly 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, whereas the open-weight models lose ground on all three. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge indicates that recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis.

AI.tldr: IHBench evaluates how well voice agents recover after user interruptions in structured workflows across 10 enterprise domains, scoring 27 audio-language models on task fulfillment and recovery quality. Closed-weight models prove significantly more robust than open-weight ones.
AI.motivation: Existing speech benchmarks measure interruption timing (barge-in detection, turn-taking) but ignore post-interruption recovery quality. Real-world voice agents in structured workflows must correctly resume multi-step procedures after interruptions, address user interjections, and avoid repeating content—capabilities that remain unevaluated.
AI.method: IHBench injects six interruption types at controlled mid-utterance points into state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Each interruption is scored on two axes (task fulfillment and recovery quality) using per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and open-weight communities are evaluated. A human study validates the LLM judge, and cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge is performed.
AI.result: Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade ~3.3x more slowly as conversations lengthen, and show no audio-vs-text modality gap. Open-weight models underperform on all three dimensions. Recovery quality depends strongly on interruption type.
AI.conclusion: Post-interruption recovery quality is a distinct capability axis from existing speech benchmarks. Closed-weight models currently hold a substantial advantage in robustness to interruptions, particularly in longer conversations and across modalities.

title: Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation
summary: For embodied agents capable of physical interaction, the capability to create and understand dialog is crucial to ensure both safety and effectiveness. While DialNav~\cite{han2025dialnav} provides a framework for holistic evaluation of the dialog--execution loop in photorealistic indoor navigation, its performance remains limited by a critical scarcity of training data (2K episodes). To address this, we propose an automatic generation pipeline, and construct the \textbf{RAINbow} dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog and creates cost-efficient and high-quality dataset. Then, we introduce two additional complementary advances to unlock the data's full potential: (1) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme to align the navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop, and (2) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge. By combining these complementary solutions, our model substantially outperforms the baseline in success rate on both \textbf{Val Seen} (58.24, \textbf{+89\%}) and \textbf{Val Unseen} (29.05, \textbf{+100\%}) splits, establishing a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: To address the severe training data scarcity in dialog-guided navigation (DialNav), the authors propose an automatic data generation pipeline creating RAINbow, a 238K-episode dataset, complemented by Dual-Strategy Training and a VLN-knowledge-enhanced localization model, achieving dramatic improvements (+89% on Val Seen, +100% on Val Unseen).
AI.motivation: Embodied agents need dialog understanding for safe, effective physical interaction. DialNav offers a photorealistic evaluation framework for the dialog–execution loop, but its performance is critically bottlenecked by only 2K training episodes. The core motivation is to overcome this data scarcity to unlock the full potential of dialog-guided navigation.
AI.method: Three complementary contributions: (1) An automatic generation pipeline that converts existing Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) datasets into large-scale, multi-turn dialog episodes, producing the RAINbow dataset (238K episodes). (2) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme that aligns the learning process with the dynamic dialog–navigation loop. (3) A localization model that leverages pre-existing VLN knowledge to improve spatial reasoning.
AI.result: The combined model sets a new state of the art on DialNav benchmarks: Val Seen success rate of 58.24 (+89% vs. baseline) and Val Unseen success rate of 29.05 (+100% vs. baseline).
AI.conclusion: Automatic data scaling via the RAINbow dataset, together with training and architectural innovations (Dual-Strategy Training, VLN-enhanced localization), dramatically advances dialog-guided navigation performance, establishing a new SOTA and demonstrating that data scarcity was the primary bottleneck in DialNav.

title: Source-Grounded Data Generation for Text-to-JSON Learning
summary: From financial filings to clinical records, legacy industries rely heavily on long, unstructured documents to store high-value information. Reliably extracting this information into structured, machine-readable representations is a key prerequisite to making the contents accessible to automated systems. JSON is a natural target for such structured extraction, yet constructing reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline that constructs reports and JSON schema by using LLMs for scalable synthesis while validating ground-truth values against the underlying spreadsheet. Evaluations on STAGE-Eval, our source-grounded benchmark with an 851-example test set, show that STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches. This improves Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.

AI.tldr: STAGE is a data generation pipeline that uses spreadsheets as ground-truth sources to create text-to-JSON training data with LLMs, achieving substantial improvements in structured extraction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Legacy industries rely on long, unstructured documents (financial filings, clinical records) containing high-value information. Reliably extracting this into structured JSON is critical but hindered by the lack of scalable, reliable training data for text-to-JSON tasks.
AI.method: STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration) uses LLMs to synthesize reports and JSON schemas, while validating ground-truth values against an underlying spreadsheet. This source-grounded approach ensures data fidelity. A benchmark, STAGE-Eval, with 851 test examples was created for evaluation.
AI.result: STAGE-generated training data significantly outperforms existing approaches when fine-tuning Qwen3-4B: exact match improves from 31.37% to 74.27%, and value accuracy improves from 45.46% to 90.69%.
AI.conclusion: Source-grounded data generation using spreadsheets as ground truth is a highly effective strategy for building text-to-JSON extraction systems, yielding dramatic accuracy gains over prior methods.

title: Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity
summary: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe's MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC (R^2 = 0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe and a reference OOD-trained probe linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC. The authors prove this relationship in closed form under Gaussian class-conditional assumptions, showing both metrics are sigmoid functions of the probe's SNR, and empirically validate the theory across models, layers, and concept domains.
AI.motivation: Linear probes are commonly compared via Euclidean cosine similarity, but this metric is task-agnostic. Ying et al. (2026) found that MCS—which reweights by test-data covariance—near-perfectly predicts OOD AUROC. This paper seeks to explain why this linear relationship holds so strongly and to determine its generality and theoretical underpinnings.
AI.method: The authors extend the empirical finding of Ying et al. across multiple models, layers, and concept domains. They then derive a closed-form theoretical proof: assuming balanced classes with Gaussian projections, both OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are shown to be sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test distribution, implying a linear relationship between them. The theory also yields conditions under which the linearity breaks down, which are tested empirically.
AI.result: The linear relationship between MCS and OOD AUROC replicates robustly across diverse settings. The theoretical derivation confirms that both quantities are linked through a common dependence on SNR. Predicted failure modes of the linear relationship are empirically verified.
AI.conclusion: MCS provides a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to standard cosine similarity for comparing linear probes. Its linear relationship with OOD AUROC is explained by their shared sigmoidal dependence on SNR, and the theory delineates precisely when this relationship holds or fails.

title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
summary: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

AI.tldr: ENPIRE is a closed-loop harness framework enabling coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies through a repeatable physical feedback loop (reset, execute, verify, refine), achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks like pin-box organizing, zip-tie fastening, and tool use.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous robotic manipulation currently requires heavy human supervision and algorithm engineering, creating a bottleneck for general physical intelligence. While coding agents can automate algorithm search in digital domains, they lack the physical feedback loop — scene reset, policy execution, outcome verification, and iterative refinement — needed to operate autonomously in the real world.
AI.method: The authors propose ENPIRE, a harness framework with four modules: (1) Environment (EN) for automatic scene reset and outcome verification; (2) Policy Improvement (PI) for launching policy refinement; (3) Rollout (R) for evaluating policies on one or multiple physical robots in parallel; and (4) Evolution (E) where coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, and improve both training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This forms a closed-loop optimization procedure.
AI.result: Using ENPIRE, frontier coding agents autonomously trained policies achieving a 99% success rate on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks (organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, tool use). Performance further accelerated when deploying an agent team across a robot fleet.
AI.conclusion: ENPIRE demonstrates a practical, scalable path toward using coding agents to autonomously advance real-world robotics research, minimizing human effort while enabling fair ablation studies across training recipes and agent variants.

title: IHUBERT: Vector-Based Semantic Deduplication and Domain-Balanced Pretraining for Persian Resources
summary: Persian pretrained language models (PLMs) are still limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and by insufficient evaluation beyond standard classification and NER tasks. We present IHUBERT, a monolingual Persian PLM trained from scratch with the RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) on a 45 GB curated subset of the Sepahr-Danesh collection (about 7-8B tokens). To improve corpus quality and reduce redundancy, we employ a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for distribution balancing control across domains and registers. We additionally train a 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer on the full pretraining corpus to better capture Persian morphology and orthographic variation. IHUBERT is evaluated on seven Persian NLU benchmarks covering NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive question answering, and relation extraction, using task-standard metrics (entity-level F1, Macro-F1, EM/F1). IHUBERT achieves its strongest gains on extractive QA, ranking first on both PQuAD (F1 88.3542) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and attains the best result on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). On NER and topic classification, it remains competitive (e.g., 0.8308 F1 on ParsTwiNER; 0.7953 Macro-F1 on DigiMag), while relation extraction remains the main remaining gap (0.6684 Macro-F1 on PERLEX). A controlled tokenizer ablation on the IHUBERT pretraining corpus shows that BPE yields slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size, supporting our tokenization design. Overall, IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling through semantically curated large-scale pretraining and broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks.

AI.tldr: IHUBERT is a monolingual Persian RoBERTa-base model pretrained on a 45GB semantically deduplicated corpus with a 139k BPE tokenizer, achieving state-of-the-art results on Persian extractive QA and competitive performance across seven NLU benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Persian PLMs suffer from limited high-quality pretraining data and narrow evaluation (mostly classification/NER). There is a need for better corpus curation and broader downstream assessment including comprehension tasks.
AI.method: IHUBERT uses a RoBERTa-base encoder (125M params) trained from scratch on a 45GB (~7-8B tokens) subset of Sepahr-Danesh. Preprocessing includes normalization, exact/near-deduplication, anonymization, and vector-database semantic deduplication for domain/register balance. A 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer is trained on the full corpus. Evaluation spans seven NLU tasks: NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive QA (PQuAD, ParsiNLU-RC), and relation extraction (PERLEX), plus a BPE vs. WordPiece tokenizer ablation.
AI.result: IHUBERT ranks 1st on PQuAD (F1 88.35) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.10), and best on FarsTail NLI (Macro-F1 0.8350). Strong NER (ParsTwiNER F1 0.8308) and topic classification (DigiMag Macro-F1 0.7953). Relation extraction remains the weakest (PERLEX Macro-F1 0.6684). BPE tokenizer shows slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size.
AI.conclusion: Semantically curated large-scale pretraining combined with a morphology-aware BPE tokenizer advances Persian NLU, particularly for comprehension tasks, though relation extraction remains a challenge.

title: Latent Confounded Causal Discovery via Lie Bracket Geometry
summary: Recent work on Kan-Do-Calculus (KDC) has established that the boundary between passive observation and active intervention in causal inference is a category-theoretic bi-adjunction, with interventions modeled by left Kan extensions and conditioning by right Kan extensions. This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms under latent confounding, building on the information-geometric and categorical consequences of KDC. In smooth statistical settings, Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields; failures of these fields to close under Lie brackets become computable Frobenius residuals, which we interpret as witnesses of failed visible integrability and possible latent or unmodeled structure. Our first algorithm, BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), combines an interventional density or Radon-Nikodym-ratio engine with a geometric screen that proposes a high-recall family of admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes the reduced family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery routines. The second algorithmic contribution, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), learns amortized intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally, exposing the direct Lie-space endpoint toward which BRIDGE points. A detailed set of experiments show that both algorithms are capable of discovering causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. This paper introduces a new paradigm in causal discovery, where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two novel causal discovery algorithms (BRIDGE and SKFM) that leverage Kan-Do-Calculus and information geometry to detect latent confounders. BRIDGE uses Lie bracket failures (Frobenius residuals) on causal vector fields to identify candidate latent-obstruction pairs, while SKFM learns amortized intervention fields spectrally. Both dramatically reduce the DAG search space and infer latent structure from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery with latent confounding suffers from a super-exponential DAG search space. The authors aim to exploit the category-theoretic bi-adjunction in KDC — where interventions (left Kan extensions) and conditioning (right Kan extensions) have precise geometric consequences — to develop algorithms that infer latent structure directly from observable geometric obstructions in intervention-induced flows, rather than through exhaustive search.
AI.method: The paper builds on KDC's information-geometric consequences: Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields. When these fields fail to close under Lie brackets, the non-closure yields computable Frobenius residuals — witnesses of latent confounding. BRIDGE screens for high-recall admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and feeds a reduced family to downstream discovery routines. SKFM learns amortized intervention fields and performs spectral factorization of latent curvature.
AI.result: Both BRIDGE and SKFM successfully discover causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. The geometric obstruction signals (Frobenius residuals) reliably indicate where latent structure must exist.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new paradigm: latent causal structure can be inferred directly from the differential geometry of intervention-induced flows, circumventing combinatorial explosion. The category-theoretic foundation linking interventions, conditioning, and integrability conditions provides both theoretical grounding and practical algorithmic payoff.

title: Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models
summary: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that conservative exploration in RL-based world model refinement is unnecessary and that the real bottleneck is unreliable reward verification. It proposes two complementary solutions: (1) Reward as an Agent—an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates behaviors to mitigate reward hacking, and (2) DynDiff-GRPO—a dynamic-aware rollout diversification method that expands action-space exploration. Together, they enable broader, more reliable exploration, yielding significant accuracy gains across open-source world models.
AI.motivation: Current RL approaches for world model refinement rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and discovery of richer dynamics. The authors contend that the fundamental issue is not exploration per se, but the absence of reliable verification strategies. Without such strategies, broader exploration leads to reward hacking—where policies exploit imperfect reward signals rather than achieving genuine improvement.
AI.method: The paper introduces two components: (1) Reward as an Agent—an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals under distribution shift, and (2) Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification via DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors. The two are unified to enable RL on a reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling.
AI.result: The unified approach effectively mitigates reward hacking and yields significant accuracy improvements across multiple open-source embodied world models, demonstrating that broad exploration can scale successfully when anchored in robust verification.
AI.conclusion: Broader exploration in RL-based world model refinement is viable and beneficial, provided it is grounded in reliable verification. The proposed agentic reward framework and dynamic-aware diversification together overcome the limitations of conservative rollouts, enabling richer behavioral discovery and more accurate world models without succumbing to reward hacking.

title: Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision: A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly review and revise text, including their own. A documented self-preference bias (models favoring their own generations when acting as judges) raises the question of whether models also resist valid corrections to their own writing. We test this in a setting where "valid" is decided not by another model but by a deterministic verifier: instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then accepts or rejects that edit either as the genuine in-context author or as a fresh model that sees the draft neutrally. Across four mid-tier model families and 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons, we find no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. The one robust observation is qualitative: when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference, that is, about the character of rejections, not an elevated rate. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit self-preference bias when evaluating corrections to their own writing. Using the deterministic IFEval checker to verify objectively correct edits, the authors compare acceptance rates between "author" models (who wrote the draft) and "fresh" models (neutrally judging the same draft). Across 85 comparisons and four model families, they find no statistically significant self-preference — authors reject verified-good fixes at roughly the same rate as fresh evaluators (gap ≈ -5.1 pp, within noise). The key qualitative finding: when authors do reject corrections, 97% of their justifications are flaw-catching rather than mere preference.
AI.motivation: Prior work has documented a self-preference bias where LLMs favor their own outputs when acting as judges. This raises a practical concern: if models resist valid corrections to their own writing, it would undermine their reliability in iterative revision workflows. The authors aim to test this in a rigorous setting where correctness is determined by a deterministic verifier (IFEval) rather than another fallible model, isolating whether authorship genuinely induces resistance to verified-good edits.
AI.method: The experimental design uses instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model generates a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it. The model then decides whether to accept or reject the verified-good edit. This decision is made under two conditions: (1) as the genuine in-context author of the draft, and (2) as a "fresh" model that sees the same draft neutrally. Four mid-tier model families are tested, yielding 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons. The analysis focuses on rejection rate gaps, confidence intervals, and qualitative coding of stated reasons for rejection.
AI.result: No statistically significant self-preference bias was detected. Authors rejected verified-good fixes at nearly the same rate as fresh models (gap -5.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint observed in a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. Qualitatively, when authors did reject verified-good fixes, 97% of their stated reasons were coded as flaw-catching (identifying issues with the edit) rather than mere preference for their own writing. The sample size leaves open the possibility of effects smaller than approximately 13 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to concerns raised by LLM self-preference bias in judging, models do not appear to resist verified-good corrections to their own drafts at rates detectably higher than neutral evaluators. The dominant behavior when rejecting corrections is substantive critique rather than ego-driven preference. However, the study cannot rule out smaller effects below ~13 pp, and the findings are limited to mid-tier models on IFEval-style constrained generation tasks.

title: SEAGAN: domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a flexible framework for learning from scientific data linked through physical, biological, or functional relationships. One promising domain is plant physiology, where measured responses often arise from multiple interacting processes whose exact separation remains difficult even with manual intervention. In plant physiology, a key example is the A-Ci curve, which relates net CO2 assimilation rate (Anet) to leaf intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci) and is used to estimate photosynthetic parameters in leaf and crop-canopy models. However, reliable estimation requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point, which remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we formulate limitation-state identification along A-Ci curves as a graph-based node classification problem, with curve points as nodes. Domain-specific graph representations are created using distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The framework was evaluated against conventional learning baselines, graph-based architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark. Results on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states show that graph-based models improve classification, particularly near biochemical transition regions. The best-performing configuration, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes), integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882. The results show that representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates biochemical limitation-state identification along photosynthetic A-Ci curves as a graph node classification problem. The proposed SEAGAN model integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and accuracy of 0.882 on synthetic data, outperforming conventional baselines particularly near biochemical transition regions.
AI.motivation: Estimating photosynthetic parameters from A-Ci curves requires correctly identifying which biochemical limitation state (e.g., Rubisco-limited, RuBP-regeneration-limited, TPU-limited) is active at each measurement point. This identification remains a major source of uncertainty in plant physiology, hindering reliable parameter estimation for leaf and crop-canopy models.
AI.method: The authors cast limitation-state identification as a graph-based node classification task, where each A-Ci curve point is a node. They construct graphs using two connectivity strategies: distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG), with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The best model, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network), combines process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention layers with a weighted cross-entropy loss to handle class imbalance. Evaluation is conducted on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth labels, comparing against conventional learning baselines, other graph architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark.
AI.result: Graph-based models consistently improved classification over conventional baselines, with gains most pronounced near biochemical transition regions where limitation states change. SEAGAN with kNN connectivity achieved the top performance (F1: 0.857, accuracy: 0.882). Edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods proved the most effective strategy overall.
AI.conclusion: Representing A-Ci curves as graphs substantially improves biochemical limitation-state analysis. Edge-aware graph attention mechanisms operating over local kNN neighborhoods provide the most effective strategy for this node classification task, suggesting graph-based representations are well-suited to capturing the structured dependencies inherent in photosynthetic response curves.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: Analysis of two multi-agent architectures (DAG Plan & Execute vs. ReAct) across 208 enterprise scenarios at varying scales (Persona, Department, Enterprise) reveals that scale—not task complexity—dominates orchestration performance, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. A Task Manager with priority inference, event merging, and preemption significantly improves latency and correctness at enterprise scale.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring and action across specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems are designed for discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at enterprise scale (200+ agents). This gap motivates systematic benchmarking of orchestration architectures and development of mechanisms for continuous operation.
AI.method: The authors evaluated DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct architectures across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). They introduced a Task Manager component that enables continuous operation through three mechanisms: priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Performance was measured along dimensions of orchestration quality, latency, and correctness.
AI.result: Scale dominates orchestration performance more than task complexity. Both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan & Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales but suffers from overhead at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust via incremental failure handling. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent orchestration at enterprise scale requires architectures resilient to agent discovery noise and mechanisms for continuous operation. ReAct's incremental handling makes it more scalable than DAG-based approaches, and a dedicated Task Manager with priority-aware scheduling and event merging is critical for maintaining SLAs in production enterprise deployments.

title: HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization
summary: The quadratic complexity of attention poses a critical bottleneck for long-context processing, spurring interest in hybrid attention designs. Most open-source hybrid models adopt a layer-wise strategy. Yet, prior work has noted the inherent difficulty of integrating Linear Attention (LA) with Full Attention (FA), suggesting that the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. To probe this space, we conduct interpretability analysis and observe that layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, while individual heads within the same layer display distinct functional specialization despite sharing input features. This head-level heterogeneity suggests that the head dimension provides a natural and principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention signals. Building on this insight, we introduce HydraHead, a novel architecture that hybridizes FA and LA along the head axis. HydraHead features two key innovations: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and preserves FA only for them, and (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. By leveraging a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation, we achieve high-performance hybrid models with minimal training overhead. Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs in long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Crucially, trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5, a leading model of comparable size with a native context length of 256K. This highlights the significant scaling potential of head-level hybridization.

AI.tldr: HydraHead introduces head-level hybridization of Full Attention and Linear Attention, using interpretability-driven head selection and a scale-normalized fusion module. It achieves strong long-context performance with minimal training overhead, significantly outperforming layer-wise hybrids at higher LA-to-FA ratios.
AI.motivation: The quadratic complexity of Full Attention (FA) limits long-context processing. While hybrid models combining Linear Attention (LA) and FA exist, they typically use layer-wise strategies that struggle to integrate heterogeneous attention signals effectively. Prior work suggests the design space for attention hybridization is underexplored, motivating a finer-grained approach.
AI.method: The authors first conduct interpretability analysis, revealing that (1) layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, but (2) individual attention heads within the same layer show distinct functional specialization. This motivates HydraHead, which hybridizes FA and LA at the head dimension. Key components include: (a) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and retains FA only for those heads, (b) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles distributional gaps between FA and LA head outputs, and (c) a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and knowledge distillation to minimize training overhead.
AI.result: Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs on long-context tasks while preserving strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching the performance of Qwen3.5 (a comparable-size model with native 256K context).
AI.conclusion: Head-level hybridization is a principled and effective granularity for fusing FA and LA signals. HydraHead demonstrates significant scaling potential, achieving strong long-context capabilities with minimal training overhead, suggesting that the head dimension is a natural axis for attention hybridization in future long-context models.

title: MassSpecGym in the Wild: Uncovering and Correcting Evaluation Pitfalls in AI-Driven Molecule Discovery
summary: Reliable benchmarking is critical for developing machine learning models for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) based molecule discovery. Subtle issues in experimental design and model evaluation procedures can degrade the trustworthiness of such benchmarks and lead to erroneous conclusions. We conduct a thorough review of model evaluation issues in the recent MS/MS machine learning literature, using the standard MassSpecGym benchmark suite as a case study to illustrate the impact of these issues. We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption. We isolate three classes of failures: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Through extensive experimentation and code replication, we quantify the impact of these issues and show how they corrupt the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce. We distill our findings into recommendations generalizable to MS/MS challenges, benchmarks, and custom evaluation setups. We also release MassSpecGym v1.5, an implementation of our recommendations in the MassSpecGym benchmarking suite which addresses the failure modes identified in this audit. MassSpecGym v1.5 is publicly available at https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym.

AI.tldr: An audit of the MassSpecGym benchmark for MS/MS machine learning reveals evaluation issues in 17 of 26 papers, categorized as data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs/metric divergence. The authors quantify these failures and release MassSpecGym v1.5 with corrected evaluation protocols.
AI.motivation: Reliable benchmarking is essential for progress in MS/MS-based molecule discovery via machine learning, but subtle evaluation flaws can undermine trustworthiness and lead to erroneous conclusions. A systematic audit was needed to identify and quantify such issues in the rapidly adopted MassSpecGym benchmark.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive literature review of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym results within its first year, identifying evaluation issues through code replication, extensive experimentation, and systematic classification into three failure modes: data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs with metric divergence.
AI.result: At least 17 of 26 papers (≈65%) exhibited evaluation issues. The three failure classes were isolated and their impact quantified, demonstrating how they corrupt the benchmark standards. The findings were distilled into generalizable recommendations for MS/MS benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarking integrity in MS/MS ML research is compromised by widespread evaluation flaws. The release of MassSpecGym v1.5 operationalizes the audit's recommendations, addressing identified failure modes and providing a more trustworthy evaluation framework for the community.

title: Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean
summary: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using the Lean proof assistant as a symbolic process oracle that provides both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during RLVR training, rather than relying solely on binary verification signals. By parsing proof attempts into tactic sequences and leveraging Lean's elaboration to identify locally sound steps and the earliest failure, the authors obtain dense, verifier-grounded credit signals. These structured rewards are integrated into a GRPO-style RL objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods, demonstrating that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines on MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The key gap identified is that RLVR traditionally uses a single binary verification signal, while symbolic proof assistants like Lean offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback during formal reasoning. The authors argue that training would benefit from feedback that is both dense (at the tactic/step level) and sound (formally verified by the proof assistant's type-theoretic elaboration), bridging the disconnect between structured proof processes and unstructured rewards.
AI.method: The method treats Lean's elaboration mechanism as a symbolic process oracle: (1) Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences; (2) Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory; (3) These structured rewards are incorporated into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective using first-error propagation and first-token credit assignment methods that balance outcome-level and process-level advantages. Experiments use STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 as base models.
AI.result: Tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on formal reasoning benchmarks including MiniF2F and ProofNet.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that symbolic proof assistants can serve dual roles — as verifiers at evaluation time and as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward RL frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

title: Hard or Just Unreached? Diagnosing the Sampling Blind Spot in Math-Reasoning Difficulty Estimation
comment: 9 pages of main paper, 4 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, with more in the appendix
summary: Math and science reasoning benchmarks rely on pass@k, the fraction of sampled chains that reach gold, as the canonical per-example difficulty signal. The same signal drives RL with verifiable rewards, math data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. We show this proxy has a persistent blind spot on its hardest stratum: on the eight free-form math cells we test (GSM8K and MATH across four open-weight models), 10.3-22.9% of the examples that no sampling seed solves in six tries are instead solved at matched compute by a six-chain deterministic regime. These are greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting, while greedy alone solves at most 6% on these math cells. Recovery scales with the additional budget, across perturbations whose mechanistic distinctness we verify across all twelve cells (cross-kind fix-set Jaccard <= 0.47 in every setup). Activation grafting is used as an intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method; we use it purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool, and our recovered items show that the pass@k= 0 % stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than that the unmodified model reaches them under ordinary inference.

AI.tldr: Pass@k=0% fails to capture solvability: many "unsolvable" math problems are actually solvable via deterministic activation-grafting perturbations across multiple open-weight models on GSM8K and MATH benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Expose a systematic blind spot in the standard pass@k difficulty metric—specifically that examples with zero successful samples under repeated stochastic decoding may still be solvable via cheap deterministic interventions, implying current difficulty signals conflate genuine hardness with sampling inadequacy.
AI.method: Compare stochastic pass@k (six independent sampling chains) against a six-chain deterministic regime combining greedy decoding with five residual-stream perturbations via activation grafting. Measure recovery rates (pass@k=0% examples solved at matched compute), cross-kind fix-set Jaccard to verify mechanistic distinctness across perturbations, and scaling with additional budget.
AI.result: Across GSM8K and MATH on four open-weight models, 10.3–22.9% of pass@k=0% examples are recovered by the deterministic regime. Greedy alone solves ≤6%. Cross-kind fix-set Jaccard ≤0.47 across all twelve model–benchmark cells, confirming perturbation distinctness. Recovery scales with budget.
AI.conclusion: The pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than genuinely unsolvable. Activation grafting serves as a diagnostic revealing that current difficulty proxies systematically underestimate model capability on hardest examples.

title: Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop SPIGM, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-agnostic framework called residual-space evolutionary optimization that combines flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. By operating in the residual space of conditional flow matching (CFM) models, it separates local exploitation (self-pollination) from global exploration (cross-pollination), enabling effective editing with non-differentiable or black-box objectives. Validated on MorphoMNIST and crystal data.
AI.motivation: Existing generative editing methods require differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, which fail in flow-based settings where edits use forward/backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. There is a need for a framework that can perform generative editing in such flow-based contexts without relying on gradient descent through the objective.
AI.method: The framework leverages the property that conditional flow matching (CFM) disentangles condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals. Editing is performed directly in this residual space using evolutionary algorithms decomposed into two regimes: (1) self-pollination — local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement within a single sample, and (2) cross-pollination — broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. This exploration–exploitation decomposition balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity.
AI.result: The framework was validated on MorphoMNIST (benchmark for counterfactual generation) and on crystal data. Results demonstrate that the exploration–exploitation decomposition effectively balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and the approach extends successfully beyond images to real-world scientific domains (crystal structures).
AI.conclusion: Residual-space evolutionary optimization provides a practical and model-agnostic mechanism for flow-based generative editing when objectives are non-differentiable. The self- and cross-pollination decomposition offers a principled way to balance competing desiderata (target alignment, preservation, diversity), and the framework generalizes across modalities, including scientific applications like crystal data.

title: From Texts to Scores: Tracing the Emergence of Essay Quality Representations in Large Language Models
comment: This is a preprint of a manuscript currently under peer review
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have substantially transformed Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet the internal mechanisms underlying LLM-based scoring remain poorly understood. In this work, we systematically analyze the hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English essay datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Using linear probing, cross-prompt generalization, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analyses, we find consistent evidence that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. These representations emerge progressively across layers, remain robust across prompting strategies, and partially transfer across essay prompts despite differences in scoring rubrics. In addition, nonlinear probes provide only marginal and inconsistent improvements over linear probes, suggesting that most essay quality information is already linearly decodable. We further identify individual ``essay scoring neurons'' whose activations strongly correlate with essay scores and whose behavior is sensitive to targeted intervention. Moreover, the layer-wise distribution of these neurons systematically shifts with essay length, with longer essays relying more heavily on deeper layers. Overall, our findings provide evidence that LLMs encode structured representations related to essay quality and offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems.

AI.tldr: Analyzing eight LLMs across three datasets, this work reveals that essay quality information is encoded linearly within model hidden representations, emerges progressively across layers, transfers across prompts, and can be localized to individual "essay scoring neurons" whose layer distribution shifts with essay length.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread adoption of LLMs for Automated Essay Scoring (AES), the internal mechanisms driving their scoring decisions remain opaque. This work seeks to open the black box of LLM-based AES by systematically probing how and where essay quality information is encoded within model representations.
AI.method: The authors apply a suite of interpretability techniques — linear probing, cross-prompt generalization tests, dimensionality reduction (PCA), and neuron-level activation analysis — across eight LLMs on three datasets (ASAP++, CSEE for English; ENEM for Portuguese). They compare linear vs. nonlinear probes, test robustness across prompting strategies, and conduct targeted interventions on identified "essay scoring neurons."
AI.result: Essay quality is encoded in a linearly accessible form that emerges progressively across layers and is robust to prompting variations. Representations partially transfer across prompts despite rubric differences. Nonlinear probes yield only marginal gains over linear ones. Individual neurons strongly correlating with scores are identified and respond to interventions. Layer-wise distribution of these neurons shifts deeper for longer essays.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode structured, linearly decodable representations of essay quality, with functional specialization at the neuron level. These findings advance interpretability of LLM-based AES and suggest that scoring-relevant information is not merely superficial but embedded in the models' internal representations.

title: Convex training of Lipschitz-regularized shallow neural networks
summary: In this work, we introduce a training procedure for shallow neural networks that promotes robustness against adversarial attacks. We solve a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program by introducing a convex restriction that can be efficiently solved to global optimality.
