Our approach can be employed as a post-processing step by taking a pre-trained network as an initial solution to then solving the convex program whose optimal network is guaranteed to be no worse than the initial one. We illustrate the improvements of our training procedure with experiments using real world datasets for regression tasks under an adversarial setting. We show numerically that solving our proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that on certain datasets, networks obtained using our convex training program are both more accurate and robust with respect to adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: A convex restriction of a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training problem is proposed to train shallow neural networks that are adversarially robust. The method serves as a post-processing step on pre-trained networks, guaranteeing no degradation, and empirically yields better accuracy and robustness on regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard training of neural networks produces models vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing robust training methods often involve non-convex optimization, making global optimality guarantees elusive. The authors aim to provide a principled, globally optimal training procedure that promotes adversarial robustness.
AI.method: The authors formulate a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program and then derive a convex restriction of it. This convex surrogate can be solved efficiently to global optimality. The approach is used as a post-processing step: a pre-trained network initializes the convex program, and the resulting optimal network is guaranteed to be at least as good as the initial one.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world regression datasets under adversarial settings show that the convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. On certain datasets, networks are both more accurate and more adversarially robust.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convex restriction framework provides an effective, globally optimal post-processing step for improving adversarial robustness in shallow neural networks, outperforming existing methods on Lipschitz-regularized objectives while maintaining or improving accuracy.

title: Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a continuous-action SAC algorithm enhanced with multi-head attention for laser powder bed fusion parameter optimization, achieving faster convergence (322.79 within 14 episodes) and superior performance over DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC in minimizing porosity defects.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL methods using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and local optima entrapment in additive manufacturing process optimization, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision porosity minimization tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose a continuous action space framework integrating a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor captures subtle low-dimensional feature variations, improving exploration-exploitation balance in value landscapes with local minima. Validation is conducted on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization for laser powder bed fusion.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, with faster convergence and higher final reward than DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC, while maintaining training stability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multi-head attention with continuous-action SAC significantly improves convergence speed and optimization quality for additive manufacturing process control, offering a robust solution for high-precision defect minimization.

title: MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization
summary: Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous and longitudinal patient information rather than answering isolated medical questions. However, current medical large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems often rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which can be fragile when clinical evidence is distributed across long electronic health records, medical images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. This paper proposes MedRLM, a Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning, sensor-guided screening, and community-to-tertiary referral support. Instead of compressing all patient information into one prompt, MedRLM treats the patient case as an external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. The framework coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, physiological sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. It further introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to connect patient-specific observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria. A sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism activates deeper reasoning when abnormal physiological or behavioral patterns are detected, while uncertainty-gated refinement supports clinician review for high-risk or low-confidence cases. We also outline a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. MedRLM aims to move medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, and workflow-aware clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedRLM proposes a recursive multimodal framework for long-context clinical reasoning that treats patient cases as external environments to be iteratively inspected, rather than single-prompt compression. It coordinates specialized agents across text, EHR, imaging, sensors, guidelines, and referral planning, using a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory and sensor-guided recursive triggering for auditable, workflow-aware clinical decision support.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs and RAG systems rely on single-step prompting/retrieval, which fails when clinical evidence is distributed across heterogeneous, longitudinal sources (EHRs, images, sensors, guidelines). Real-world clinical decision support demands reasoning over this distributed evidence rather than answering isolated questions.
AI.method: MedRLM frames the patient case as an external clinical environment for recursive inspection, decomposition, retrieval, verification, and synthesis. It employs: (1) specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, imaging, physiological sensors, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning; (2) a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory linking patient observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria; (3) a sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism for abnormal patterns; and (4) uncertainty-gated refinement for high-risk/low-confidence cases requiring clinician review.
AI.result: The paper outlines a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets covering EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. No empirical results are reported in the abstract; the contribution is primarily architectural and conceptual.
AI.conclusion: MedRLM aims to shift medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, workflow-aware clinical decision support suitable for real-world deployment across community-to-tertiary care pathways.

title: LOKI: Memory-Free Null-Space Constrained Lifelong Knowledge Editing
summary: Lifelong knowledge editing aims to efficiently and sequentially update language models over time, as new knowledge becomes available or when the model makes mistakes, while preserving acceptable performance on past knowledge. One unresolved challenge is that existing methods modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge samples, reducing flexibility and increasing catastrophic forgetting. Another is requiring access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics. To address these challenges, we introduce LOKI, a novel approach that uses dynamic layer selection based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, bypassing the requirement for previous knowledge access. We show that LOKI achieves superior performance to existing approaches across a wide variety of experiments, achieving up to a 14\% improvement in average accuracy.

AI.tldr: LOKI is a lifelong knowledge editing method that dynamically selects layers using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, eliminating the need for access to prior knowledge while achieving up to 14% improvement in average accuracy over existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong knowledge editing methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they modify a fixed set of layers for all knowledge samples, which reduces flexibility and exacerbates catastrophic forgetting, and (2) they require access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics, which is impractical in many real-world sequential editing scenarios.
AI.method: LOKI employs two core mechanisms: (1) dynamic layer selection guided by the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), which identifies which layers to modify on a per-sample basis, enabling flexible and targeted updates; and (2) null-space projection of gradient updates onto the model's weight null-space, which constrains updates to directions that minimally interfere with previously learned knowledge, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting without requiring access to past data.
AI.result: LOKI achieves superior performance compared to existing lifelong knowledge editing methods across a wide range of experiments, with up to a 14% improvement in average accuracy, demonstrating both better knowledge retention and reduced forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic layer selection via HSIC combined with null-space gradient projection provides an effective, flexible, and data-efficient solution for lifelong knowledge editing, overcoming key limitations of prior methods that rely on fixed layer modification and require access to historical knowledge.

title: ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion
summary: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion for Modern Hebrew is needed for applications like text-to-speech (TTS), but is challenging due to the language's abjad writing system, which leaves vowels largely unwritten, creating substantial ambiguity. Standard approaches first predict vowel diacritics (nikud) to produce International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, but this is limited: vocalization data is scarce and laborious to produce, it does not specify features such as lexical stress, and it reflects formal grammatical rules rather than everyday spoken pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction, meanwhile, struggles on limited data and fails to exploit the character-level alignment characteristic of abjads. Our method, ReNikud, overcomes these limitations with two key insights: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, yielding phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias. Results on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the new targeted MILIM benchmark for spoken Hebrew show that ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release our code and trained models to support further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

AI.tldr: ReNikud introduces weak audio supervision via ASR pseudo-labeling and a pseudo-vocalization architecture that enforces character-level alignment for Hebrew G2P, surpassing prior SOTA on existing and new spoken Hebrew benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern Hebrew G2P is challenging because its abjad script omits vowels, creating ambiguity. Existing approaches relying on diacritic (nikud) prediction are limited by scarce vocalization data, lack of lexical stress specification, and formal rather than colloquial pronunciation norms. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction struggles with limited data and fails to exploit character-level alignment inherent to abjads.
AI.method: (1) Weak audio supervision: an ASR-based pseudo-labeling pipeline processes thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, producing phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) Pseudo-vocalization architecture: the model predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias rather than relying on explicit diacritic prediction.
AI.result: ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and on the newly introduced MILIM benchmark, which specifically targets spoken Hebrew evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The combination of weak audio supervision and character-aligned pseudo-vocalization effectively addresses the core challenges of Hebrew G2P. Code and trained models will be released to support further Hebrew TTS and speech technology research.

title: Multi-Granular Attention-Driven Reinforcement Learning Framework for Web Intelligent Enhancement Systems
comment: 2026 3rd International Conference on Integrated Intelligence and Communication Systems (ICIICS), 6 Pages
summary: From the past few years, web intelligent enhancement systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous and dynamic web data to deliver personalized, context-aware services. However, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning models often struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments. In this research, a Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed to address the challenges by integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Initially, heterogeneous web data comprising structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources are collected and preprocessed for generating unified feature representations. These representations are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph, where entities and their relationships are modeled by using graph embeddings enhanced by attention mechanisms for capturing both local relevance and global contextual dependencies. Subsequently, an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy leverages the attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions like content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation. Finally, the continuous online feedback is further integrated to update graph representations and learning policies in real time by ensuring sustained adaptability and performance. The proposed MGAR-WIES acheived better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Proposes MGAR-WIES, a system combining semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning to enhance web intelligent services, achieving 80% accuracy by dynamically adapting to heterogeneous, evolving web data.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML, DL, and RL models struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in dynamic web environments that involve heterogeneous data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured). There is a need for a system that can deliver personalized, context-aware web services while continuously adapting to changing data.
AI.method: MGAR-WIES proceeds in four stages: (1) heterogeneous web data collection and preprocessing to produce unified feature representations; (2) construction of a dynamic semantic graph with attention-enhanced graph embeddings capturing local relevance and global context; (3) an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy that uses attention-aware semantic states to optimize actions such as content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation; (4) continuous online feedback integration to update graph representations and learning policies in real time.
AI.result: MGAR-WIES achieved 80% accuracy, outperforming existing approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The integration of semantic graphs, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent RL effectively addresses key limitations of traditional models in dynamic web environments, yielding improved accuracy and sustained adaptability through real-time feedback-driven updates.

title: Pitch Spelling Jazz Lead Sheets, Solo Transcriptions, Classical Piano and Monophonic Scores
summary: We present an algorithm for pitch spelling and key estimation. Given an input in MIDI-like format, containing information on note pitches (expressed in semitones relative to the lowest reference note) and bar boundaries, it estimates the appropriate note names, a global Key Signature, and a local scale for each bar. This related information elements are evaluated jointly during two stages of optimisation. During an initial 'modal' stage, a probable scale is proposed for each bar, minimising the number of accidentals to be printed in the printed score with a shortest-path search. Then, during a second stage called 'tonal', these local scales are used to estimate the Key Signature and note names that would result in the best musical notation for the entire piece. We present evaluations conducted on datasets comprising a variety of digital musical scores: jazz lead sheets taken from the Real Book, transcriptions of recordings of jazz soli and bass lines, traditional tunes, as well as classical scores for piano and monophonic instruments. Our procedure was originally designed for use in music transcription, specifically for building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio recordings, for the purposes of music analysis, teaching and the preservation of cultural heritage. This method should also prove useful for other tasks related to the processing of musical notation. Furthermore, to this end, we have defined new distances between various common jazz scales, which may be of some interest to musicological studies.

AI.tldr: A two-stage algorithm for joint pitch spelling and key estimation from MIDI input: first a modal stage assigns local scales per bar via shortest-path optimization to minimize accidentals, then a tonal stage derives a global key signature and note names. Evaluated across jazz, traditional, and classical scores, with new inter-scale distances defined for jazz.
AI.motivation: To support automatic music transcription systems that build digital collections of jazz solos from audio recordings, enabling music analysis, teaching, and cultural heritage preservation. The joint estimation of pitch spelling and key signature addresses the ambiguity that arises when converting MIDI pitch numbers into readable musical notation.
AI.method: A two-stage optimization: (1) Modal stage — for each bar, a shortest-path algorithm selects a local scale that minimizes the number of accidentals required, treating scale transitions between adjacent bars with defined costs. (2) Tonal stage — using these local scales, a global Key Signature and definitive note spellings are estimated to optimize the overall notation quality for the entire piece. New distance metrics between common jazz scales are defined to inform the optimization.
AI.result: The algorithm was evaluated on diverse datasets: jazz lead sheets (Real Book), transcriptions of jazz solos and bass lines, traditional tunes, and classical piano and monophonic scores. The method proved effective across these varied musical styles.
AI.conclusion: The joint two-stage approach successfully handles pitch spelling and key estimation across heterogeneous musical genres. The method is practical for music transcription pipelines and broader music notation processing tasks. The newly defined jazz scale distances may also benefit musicological research.

title: Efficiently Representing Algorithms With Chain-of-Thought Transformers
summary: The increasing popularity of \emph{reasoning} models -- language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer -- is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the \emph{Word RAM} model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on $\bigO(\log n)$-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: \emph{Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?} For instance, can they sort $n$ items in $\bigO(n \log n)$ steps or run Dijkstra's algorithm in $\bigO(E + V \log V)$ steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: \emph{continuous} CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a \emph{hybrid} architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT \emph{can} efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in $n$. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a ``flat'' instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions -- in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms with only poly-logarithmic overhead, in contrast to the quadratic overhead required when simulating Turing machines. This holds across three architectures: finite-precision transformers with rightmost unique hard attention, continuous CoT, and hybrid transformer-RNN models.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical results show CoT transformers can simulate Turing machines, establishing Turing-completeness. However, Turing machines are a poor model for practical algorithm design. Real algorithms are designed for the Word RAM model (random-access memory, unit-cost operations on O(log n)-bit words), which can be exponentially faster than Turing machines. The authors aim to bridge this gap by asking whether CoT transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms directly, preserving their asymptotic efficiency.
AI.method: The authors prove simulation results across three CoT settings: (1) finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, (2) continuous CoT where reasoning uses vectors instead of discrete tokens, and (3) a hybrid architecture with transformer layers on top of a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. They construct simulations mapping Word RAM operations (memory access, arithmetic, control flow) onto the respective architectures, carefully managing memory layout and instruction execution via the CoT reasoning chain.
AI.result: CoT transformers can simulate any Word RAM algorithm with poly-logarithmic overhead in n. For flat instruction sets, the overhead reduces to O(log² n); for multiplication-free flat instructions, it drops to only O(log n). This starkly contrasts with known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which incur quadratic overhead relative to Word RAM.
AI.conclusion: CoT transformers are not merely Turing-complete — they can efficiently simulate the more practical Word RAM model with near-optimal overhead, affirming that the CoT paradigm is algorithmically expressive and efficient. The results hold across multiple practically relevant architectures.

title: CzechDocs: A Multiway Parallel Dataset of Formatted Documents for Minority Languages in Czechia
summary: We present CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, and PDF) covering Czech and minority languages used in Czechia-primarily Ukrainian and English, with smaller portions of Vietnamese, Russian and other languages. The dataset is designed to support the evaluation of machine translation systems that aim to preserve document formatting during translation. We provide a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on a validation subset of the dataset. This validation split, together with the evaluation toolkit, is publicly released for further research. A held-out test split will be reserved for a future shared task focused on document-level translation with formatting preservation.

AI.tldr: CzechDocs is a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, PDF) supporting format-preserving machine translation evaluation for Czech and minority languages, with a public validation split and a held-out test set reserved for a future shared task.
AI.motivation: Existing machine translation evaluation datasets typically strip document formatting, making it difficult to assess how well MT systems preserve structural elements (headings, paragraphs, lists, bold/italic styling) during translation. There is a need for a benchmark that tests format-preserving translation, particularly for Czech and minority languages spoken in Czechia.
AI.method: The authors constructed CzechDocs, a multiway parallel corpus comprising documents in HTML, DOCX, and PDF formats across Czech, Ukrainian, English, Vietnamese, Russian, and other languages. They curated a validation subset and developed an evaluation toolkit to benchmark common format-preserving MT approaches. A held-out test split is retained for a future shared task.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on the validation subset. The validation split and evaluation toolkit are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: CzechDocs fills a gap in MT evaluation infrastructure by providing a document-level, format-aware benchmark. The public release of the validation split and toolkit encourages further research, while the reserved test split establishes a foundation for a future shared task on format-preserving document translation.

title: Efficient Neural Network Model Selection for Few-Class Application Datasets
summary: While much effort has focused on developing and benchmarking high-performance neural networks, less attention has been given to how dataset properties, known to practitioners, can guide efficient model selection. Neural models are typically evaluated on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten. To address this understudied but common setting, we develop a measure of classification difficulty based on data-side properties and show how it enables more efficient model selection for few-class datasets, where traditional approaches are less effective. We term this phenomenon "few-class distinctiveness". Our metric allows comparison of models and datasets 6 to 29$\times$ faster than repeated training and testing. Leveraging this insight, we extend scaled model families below the smallest published models, achieving greater efficiency at similar accuracy, for example models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Targeting resource-constrained applications, we demonstrate few-class model selection across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, highlighting practical gains in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "few-class distinctiveness," a data-side metric for quantifying classification difficulty on datasets with few classes, enabling 6–29× faster model selection compared to repeated training. It also extends model families below published sizes, achieving up to 42% smaller models than YOLOv5-nano with similar accuracy for resource-constrained applications.
AI.motivation: Current model evaluation and benchmarking focus on large-scale datasets with thousands of classes, but many real-world applications involve fewer than ten classes. There is a gap in understanding how dataset properties can guide efficient model selection in this common yet understudied few-class setting, where traditional model selection approaches are less effective.
AI.method: The authors develop a classification difficulty measure grounded in data-side properties (dataset characteristics) to capture "few-class distinctiveness." This metric enables direct comparison of models and datasets without repeated training and testing. They also extend scaled model families downward, creating models smaller than the smallest previously published versions (e.g., YOLOv5-nano), and validate these across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios.
AI.result: The proposed metric allows model-dataset comparison 6 to 29× faster than repeated training and testing. Extended smaller models achieve comparable accuracy at reduced size, with models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Practical efficiency gains are demonstrated across multiple resource-constrained deployment scenarios without sacrificing performance.
AI.conclusion: Data-side properties can effectively guide model selection in few-class settings, offering substantial speedups over exhaustive training-based evaluation. Extending model families below published sizes yields meaningful efficiency gains for resource-constrained applications, reinforcing the practical value of the proposed few-class distinctiveness approach.

title: BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations. However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

AI.tldr: BIM-Edit is a benchmark evaluating LLMs on editing Building Information Models (IFC format) via natural language, revealing that even the best model achieves only 49.5% average score across geometric, semantic, and topological metrics, with a substantial capability gap remaining.
AI.motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks focus on generating new geometry from text and primarily evaluate geometric correctness. However, real engineering workflows require LLMs to understand, edit, and preserve the semantic and relational structure of existing models. No benchmark adequately tests these capabilities in a structured, semantics-rich domain like BIM.
AI.method: The authors construct BIM-Edit, comprising 324 editing tasks across 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes in IFC format. Tasks fall into three instruction categories: direct (explicit edits), spatial (location-grounded), and topological (relationship-grounded). Model outputs are evaluated along three dimensions: geometric accuracy (e.g., positional/shape correctness), semantic validity (e.g., entity type and property correctness), and topological consistency (e.g., preserved spatial and relational constraints).
AI.result: The best-performing LLM attains only 49.5% average score across the three evaluation dimensions (geometric, semantic, topological). No model fully solves more than 3.4% of the editing tasks, indicating that current LLMs struggle significantly with structured, multi-constraint engineering editing.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of structured engineering design workflows. BIM-Edit exposes critical weaknesses in semantic understanding and topological reasoning that go beyond geometric generation, highlighting the need for models that can jointly reason about geometry, semantics, and relationships in editing scenarios.

title: Actionable Activation Directions for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment Across Language Model Families
summary: Fine-tuning language models on insecure code induces emergent misalignment with poorly understood internal structure. We investigate whether this misalignment corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction shared across architectures. Across four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) finetuned identically, a difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% separation of aligned and misaligned activations at each model's final layer. Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover by 21-51 points, while a secure-code control confirms content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer via ridge regression maps yields large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but fails specificity controls as random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. We identify a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges, with Gemma and Qwen acting as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on insecure code creates a causally steerable misalignment direction in model activations. Within-model, subtracting this direction reliably reduces code spillover with content specificity. Cross-model transfer produces behavioral suppression but fails specificity, revealing a two-tier structure: within-model directions are specific and actionable, while cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific.
AI.motivation: To understand whether emergent misalignment from fine-tuning on insecure code corresponds to a causally meaningful, shared activation-space direction across different model architectures, and to determine the limits of cross-architecture linear correction.
AI.method: Four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) were identically fine-tuned on insecure code. A difference-in-means direction was computed at the final layer to separate aligned vs. misaligned activations. Causal steering was performed by subtracting this direction. Cross-architecture transfer used ridge regression mapping. Control experiments employed secure-code directions, random directions, and orthogonal directions.
AI.result: The difference-in-means direction achieved 99.6% separation at the final layer across all models. Within-model causal steering reduced code spillover by 21–51 points with content specificity confirmed by secure-code controls. Cross-model transfer via ridge regression produced suppression up to 46 points but failed specificity: random and orthogonal directions performed comparably. An asymmetric transfer topology emerged: Gemma and Qwen act as geometric donors, Llama as receiver.
AI.conclusion: A two-tier specificity structure exists: within-model misalignment directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. These findings bound the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for model auditing purposes.

title: OnDeFog: Online Decision Transformer under Frame Dropping
summary: In challenging real-world reinforcement learning applications, communication delays or sensor failures often cause frame dropping, in which the agent cannot receive the dropped states and associated rewards. To address the performance degradation caused by frame dropping, the Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping (DeFog) was developed by incorporating additional mechanisms into the decision transformer to tackle frame dropping. Although DeFog can mitigate performance degradation in frame-dropping environments, since DeFog is an offline learning method, it struggles to effectively generalize to novel states not adequately represented in the training dataset. In this study, we propose OnDeFog, which integrates the mechanisms in DeFog with the online decision transformer (ODT), an online reinforcement learning method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that our proposed OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments characterized by high dropping frame rate and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

AI.tldr: OnDeFog extends DeFog (Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping) by integrating its frame-dropping mitigation mechanisms into the Online Decision Transformer (ODT), enabling online learning through environmental interaction. The method outperforms ODT under high frame-dropping rates and surpasses DeFog on datasets with abundant low-reward data.
AI.motivation: Frame dropping due to communication delays or sensor failures degrades reinforcement learning performance. DeFog addresses this but is limited by its offline nature—it cannot generalize well to novel states absent from the training dataset. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by enabling online learning.
AI.method: OnDeFog integrates DeFog's frame-dropping handling mechanisms into the Online Decision Transformer (ODT) framework. Unlike DeFog's offline approach, ODT learns policies through direct environmental interaction, allowing the combined method (OnDeFog) to handle frame dropping while adapting to novel states online.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments show OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in high frame-dropping rate environments and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large proportion of low-reward data.
AI.conclusion: OnDeFog successfully combines the frame-dropping robustness of DeFog with the online adaptability of ODT, yielding a method that handles both novel state generalization and high frame-drop rates better than either approach alone.

title: Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

AI.tldr: PINNs suffer from a capacity-induced failure mode where overparameterized networks self-partition into task-exclusive modules, hindering convergence. The authors propose ModSync, which penalizes task-exclusive connections to preserve cross-objective interaction, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs (e.g., alleviating gradient interference between residual and boundary losses) lose effectiveness as model capacity increases. The authors aim to diagnose and resolve this capacity-induced degradation.
AI.method: The authors identify "functional modularity" as the failure mechanism — overparameterized networks spontaneously partition into specialized modules for different loss terms, suppressing beneficial cross-objective interaction. They propose Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive (modular) connections while promoting interaction-promoting pathways, thereby synchronizing sparsity patterns across objectives.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks show ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to existing conflict-averse training methods.
AI.conclusion: Capacity-induced functional modularity is a critical failure mode in PINN training. ModSync effectively mitigates this by structurally enforcing cross-objective interaction, enabling robust scaling to larger networks without sacrificing convergence quality.

title: The Register Gap: A Meaning Intelligence Framework for Nigerian Public Discourse
comment: Preprint v2. 14 pages, 3 tables. Multi-model evaluation (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Supplementary materials available from the author
summary: We introduce the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation and evaluation schema for Nigerian public discourse that separates surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Existing benchmarks for Nigerian languages, including NaijaSenti and AfriSenti, treat sentiment classification as a three-way polarity task. We argue that the dominant failure mode of AI systems on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but context failure: the same utterance carries opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation. The MIF operationalises this insight across nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. We construct a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers, and evaluate three frontier language models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Pro) under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions. Two headline findings emerge. First, the Register Gap: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model receives the MIF schema in-context. Second, model capability and cultural competence are decoupled: GPT-5 (MIS 67.8) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (MIS 65.4) score lower than Flash (MIS 78.6), and neither benefits from schema-informed prompting. We release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and calibration set to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation schema for Nigerian public discourse that distinguishes surface sentiment from pragmatic intent. Evaluates three frontier LLMs, finding (1) schema-informed prompting dramatically improves register classification (+40 points), and (2) model capability and cultural competence are decoupled — the smaller Flash model outperforms GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro.
AI.motivation: Existing Nigerian-language benchmarks (NaijaSenti, AfriSenti) reduce sentiment to three-way polarity classification, missing the critical role of contextual pragmatics. The dominant AI failure mode on Nigerian discourse is not translation error but context failure: identical utterances carry opposite force depending on speaker, audience, and situational context. A framework capturing true communicative intent beyond surface sentiment is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct the MIF with nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. A 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers is created. Three frontier models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) are evaluated under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions using a Meaning Intelligence Score (MIS) metric.
AI.result: Two headline findings: (1) The Register Gap — zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) with MIF schema in-context. (2) Capability-culture decoupling — Gemini 2.5 Flash achieves the highest MIS (78.6), outperforming GPT-5 (67.8) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (65.4), and neither of the larger models benefits from schema-informed prompting.
AI.conclusion: Surface sentiment classification is insufficient for capturing communicative intent in Nigerian public discourse; context-aware, multi-dimensional frameworks like MIF are essential. Frontier model scaling does not guarantee cultural competence — smaller models can outperform larger ones on pragmatically complex tasks. The MIF specification, guidelines, and calibration set are released for reproducibility.

title: Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction
summary: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes and solves the problem of federated bilevel optimization under performative distribution shift, where both upper- and lower-level objectives depend on deployed decisions. The authors define the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point, provide existence/uniqueness conditions, and propose two algorithms: FBi-RRM (linear convergence under contraction) and FBi-SGD (communication-efficient stochastic method). Experiments on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based tasks validate the framework.
AI.motivation: Existing federated bilevel optimization assumes fixed client data distributions, but in real-world deployments, decisions can reshape client behavior and data collection (performativity), inducing client-specific distribution shifts. No prior work addresses this intersection of federated bilevel optimization and performative prediction.
AI.method: The authors formalize the FBPS point under a decoupled-risk perspective with existence/uniqueness conditions. They propose two algorithms: (1) FBi-RRM, a federated bilevel repeated risk minimization method with linear convergence under contraction; (2) FBi-SGD, a stochastic method using federated hypergradient estimation with diminishing step sizes, which is communication-efficient. Both operate under the performative distribution shift setting.
AI.result: FBi-RRM achieves linear convergence under a contraction condition. FBi-SGD provides convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate predicted stability thresholds and show improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines. CNN-based classification demonstrates practical effectiveness in nonconvex neural network settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively handles federated bilevel optimization under performative distribution shift, with both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation. The FBPS formulation and corresponding algorithms (FBi-RRM and FBi-SGD) offer a principled approach to nested learning problems where decisions influence data distributions across distributed clients.

title: Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning
comment: This work is accepted at IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HISR, a hypergraph-based semantic reasoning framework for semantic communication that captures higher-order multi-entity relationships, mitigating over-smoothing and improving inference accuracy by up to 36.6% over existing graph-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic communication systems rely on graph-based representations that only capture pairwise relationships, ignoring higher-order correlations (e.g., group interactions, multi-entity associations). This limits semantic expressiveness and degrades inference accuracy under noisy channel conditions. Hypergraphs can naturally model these complex multi-way relationships, motivating the proposed framework.
AI.method: The authors propose HISR (Hypergraph-based Implicit Semantic Reasoning), mapping entities and their higher-order relations into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate over-smoothing typical of traditional graph embeddings and enables robust inference despite partial information loss during transmission.
AI.result: HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph-based semantic representations significantly enhance communication efficiency and semantic inference robustness in next-generation communication systems by effectively modeling complex multi-entity relationships that pairwise graph approaches overlook.

title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
summary: Effective Automated Essay Scoring (AES) are expected to support both reliable assessment and actionable instructional feedback. However, existing approaches often treat scoring and feedback as separate components: neural scoring models provide limited interpretability, while Large Language Model (LLM)-based feedback is typically insensitive to learners proficiency levels. To address this fragmentation, this work proposes PsyScore, a psychometrically-aware framework that integrates diagnostic assessment with instructional scaffolding through a shared latent ability representation. PsyScore comprises three key modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that incorporates the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture, enabling the precise estimation of student ability while maintaining psychometric interpretability, a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback strategies on the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt instructional focus across different proficiency levels, and a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy that assesses feedback quality via pairwise preference judgements and student revision simulations. Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset demonstrate that PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while providing more pedagogically aligned feedback.

AI.tldr: PsyScore is a psychometrically-aware AES framework that unifies trait-adaptive neural IRT scoring, ZPD-scaffolded multi-agent feedback, and multi-perspective evaluation to deliver proficiency-sensitive scoring and instructional feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing AES systems fragment scoring and feedback: neural scorers lack interpretability, while LLM-based feedback ignores learner proficiency levels. There is a need for an integrated system that provides both psychometrically interpretable scoring and proficiency-adaptive instructional feedback.
AI.method: PsyScore integrates three modules: (1) a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that embeds the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture for ability estimation with psychometric interpretability; (2) a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator that uses multi-agent strategies conditioned on diagnosed ability to adapt instruction to learners' Zones of Proximal Development; (3) a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy employing pairwise preference judgments and student revision simulations to assess feedback quality.
AI.result: Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset show PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while delivering feedback that is more pedagogically aligned compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: PsyScore demonstrates that integrating psychometric measurement with LLM-based feedback generation can bridge the gap between reliable assessment and actionable, proficiency-sensitive instructional scaffolding in AES.

title: Manifold Bandits: Bayesian Curriculum Learning over the Latent Geometry of Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a central approach for improving reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), where training efficiency depends critically on how problems are sampled during optimization. Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods typically prioritize prompts of intermediate difficulty, treating problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms and overlooking the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. In this work, we frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity: problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and sampling decisions can steer how learning signals evolve across that space. To operationalize this perspective, we introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Empirically, we find that different sampling strategies induce non-trivial tradeoffs between productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). These results show that prioritizing difficulty alone is insufficient for strong downstream performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper frames LLM problem sampling for RL as a manifold-structured bandit problem and proposes BMC, a structure-aware framework using hierarchical task trees and Bayesian learning, showing that difficulty alone is insufficient—diversity and structure matter.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods treat problem selection as a standard bandit with independent arms, ignoring the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space and the latent manifold relationships between problems. This limits training efficiency when using RL to improve LLM reasoning.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), which (1) frames problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity (sampling decisions steer learning signal evolution across the latent space), and (2) operationalizes this via a hierarchical task tree with Bayesian learning to guide sampling decisions in a structure-aware manner.
AI.result: Different sampling strategies exhibit non-trivial tradeoffs across three dimensions: productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). Prioritizing difficulty alone proves insufficient for strong downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling is crucial for effective RL-based reasoning improvement in LLMs, going beyond the conventional focus on intermediate-difficulty problems.

title: CATCH-ME if you RAG: a dataset of Contextually Annotated multi-Turn Counterspeech against Hate and Misinformation Exchanges
summary: Online hate speech and misinformation frequently overlap, yet NLP research has mainly treated them in isolation. While LLMs represent a scalable solution for assisting humans in the generation of counterspeech for both threats, zero-shot models frequently generate repetitive and vague responses, underscoring the need for high-quality examples to steer model generation. However, existing counterspeech datasets against the overlap of hate and misinformation are scarce and limited to single-turn English dialogues, while real-life interactions span across multiple turns and languages. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues tackling the intersection of hate and misinformation. To ensure factual grounding, the dialogues are also anchored in verified external knowledge (i.e., fact-checking articles and NGO reports) and include document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly applicable for RAG systems. Covering five languages and targeting hate directed at seven marginalized groups, this novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dialogue dataset that addresses the overlap between online hate speech and misinformation. The dataset spans five languages, targets seven marginalized groups, and is grounded in verified external knowledge (fact-checking articles, NGO reports) with span-level annotations, making it suitable for training RAG-based counterspeech models.
AI.motivation: Hate speech and misinformation frequently co-occur online, but NLP research treats them separately. While LLMs can assist in generating counterspeech, zero-shot models produce repetitive and vague responses. Existing counterspeech datasets targeting both phenomena are scarce, limited to single-turn English dialogues, and lack factual grounding — whereas real-world interactions are multi-turn and multilingual.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dialogue dataset covering five languages and seven marginalized groups. Dialogues are annotated with document- and chunk-level spans anchoring them to verified external knowledge sources (fact-checking articles, NGO reports), enabling direct use in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.
AI.result: The resulting resource is the first multilingual, multi-turn counterspeech dialogue dataset addressing the intersection of hate speech and misinformation, with factual grounding via external knowledge annotations.
AI.conclusion: This novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models that can operate across multiple languages and turns, bridging critical gaps in current NLP capabilities for combating overlapping hate and misinformation.

title: Learning universal approximations for partial differential equations with Physics-Informed Broad Learning System
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a central role in modeling complex physical, biological, and engineering systems. While traditional numerical solvers are robust, they often incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, whereas recent Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but frequently suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. To bridge this gap, this article proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a novel backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization. We improved an algorithm within this framework to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently and provide a rigorous mathematical proof establishing the universal approximation property of PIBLS for these equations. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy. This framework provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization. It achieves 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over PINNs with higher accuracy and includes a rigorous universal approximation proof for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical PDE solvers incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, while Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. There is a need for a fast, stable, mesh-free alternative that retains accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose PIBLS, a backpropagation-free framework that casts PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization problem. An improved algorithm is introduced to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently, and a rigorous mathematical proof establishes the universal approximation property of PIBLS for nonlinear equations.
AI.result: Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PIBLS offers a computationally efficient, practical, high-speed paradigm for scientific machine learning, well-suited for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

AI.tldr: RVS is a novel metric that quantifies how well predictive models satisfy logical rules (both hard and soft), complementing standard accuracy metrics. It works across any relational model/dataset, uses auto-generated SQL for Horn rules, and can also evaluate dataset consistency. Experiments on knowledge graph and relational regression tasks show that models with similar accuracy can differ significantly in logical compliance.
AI.motivation: Standard ML evaluation metrics (accuracy, ranking quality, error) only measure prediction-ground truth alignment but ignore whether model outputs respect logical or domain constraints. In high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance, logical consistency is critical yet unmeasured. No standard metric exists for this dimension.
AI.method: RVS quantifies rule violations by treating hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently. It operates over any relational vocabulary, on any predictive model, and on any dataset. For Horn rules, SQL queries are automatically generated to compute violation scores. RVS can also evaluate training dataset consistency and flag poorly defined rules.
AI.result: Evaluated on three benchmarks — knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression — covering rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models. Results show models with comparable predictive accuracy exhibit substantially different RVS scores, revealing behavioral differences invisible to standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: RVS fills a gap in ML evaluation by providing a standardized, automated way to measure logical compliance. It enables practitioners to discriminate between models that standard metrics rate as equivalent, and can also serve as a diagnostic tool for dataset quality and rule definition.

title: An Information Theoretic Framework for Graph Novelty Generation via Latent Mixture Modeling
summary: We propose an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation, which aims to generate data that are distinct from existing patterns while preserving global structural consistency. Our approach embeds data into a latent space, models the latent distribution using finite mixture models, and generates novel samples by imposing explicit novelty and reliability conditions formulated in terms of description length. Specifically, novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components, while reliability constrains their impact on the overall mixture structure under the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

AI.tldr: Proposes an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation using latent space embeddings, finite mixture models, and MDL-based novelty/reliability constraints. Provides theoretical convergence guarantees and validates on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing graph generation methods lack a principled way to produce samples that are simultaneously novel (distinct from existing patterns) and globally consistent. There is a need for a quantifiable, theoretically-grounded approach to control novelty vs. reliability trade-offs in generated graph data.
AI.method: The framework embeds graph data into a latent space and models the latent distribution with finite mixture models. Novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components (high description length). Reliability is enforced via the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle, constraining how much a new sample distorts the overall mixture structure. Theoretical analysis establishes convergence rates for misclassification probabilities of non-novel and unreliable samples.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MDL-based framework provides a theoretically sound and practically effective method for graph novelty generation, offering explicit control over novelty and reliability with formal convergence guarantees.

title: Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Vision paper, published in Conference on Games 2026
summary: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning (RL), can overcome the limitations of hand-coded game AI to create more believable characters. It proposes a training framework tailored to game AI requirements, presents examples of RL-augmented games, discusses deployment practicalities, and identifies key bottlenecks and research directions to accelerate industry adoption.
AI.motivation: Hand-coded game AI struggles to capture behavioral complexity, leading to unrealistic characters that break immersion and frustrate players. Machine learning, especially reinforcement learning, offers the potential for characters that learn human-like behavior from gameplay or player data, but current research limitations prevent broad deployment across game genres.
AI.method: The authors take a vision-driven, framework-oriented approach: (1) they propose a set of requirements for training RL models specifically suited to game AI and game development pipelines; (2) they present concrete examples of games with RL-augmented game AI; (3) they describe practical considerations for deploying player-facing ML agents; and (4) they systematically identify bottlenecks and hard problems that hinder adoption.
AI.result: The paper does not present novel experimental results. Instead, it contributes a structured framework for RL-based game AI training, illustrative case studies of RL in games, deployment practicalities, and a catalog of open research problems, including sample efficiency, generalization, authorial control, and evaluation, that the authors argue must be solved for industry-wide adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning holds significant promise for creating believable game AI, but current limitations are prohibitive. The proposed framework and identified research bottlenecks—if addressed—can accelerate the adoption of machine learning-driven game AI across the video game industry, ultimately enhancing player immersion and engagement.

title: Beyond Global Replanning: Hierarchical Recovery for Cross-Device Agent Systems
summary: Real-world computer-use tasks often span multiple applications and devices, requiring agents to coordinate heterogeneous environments under dynamic runtime failures. Existing multi-device agent systems support task decomposition and cross-device assignment, but recovery remains largely coarse-grained: when execution fails, they typically retry the same strategy, reassign the subtask, or revise the global plan, without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This limits their ability to distinguish failures that can be repaired within the current device from those that require cross-device replanning. We propose \textbf{H-RePlan}, a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents with unified API--CLI--GUI execution. H-RePlan equips each device with interchangeable execution strategies and separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning through a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{HeraBench}, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android devices and injects strategy- and device-level failures. Experiments show that H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates while reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success. These results demonstrate that scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

AI.tldr: H-RePlan introduces a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents that separates device-local strategy recovery from global cross-device replanning. Evaluated on HeraBench, a fault-injected Linux-Android benchmark, it significantly outperforms coarse-grained baselines in completion, adherence, and cost-efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-device agent systems handle task failures via coarse-grained retry, reassignment, or global replanning without modeling the device-local strategy space. This prevents distinguishing failures solvable within a device from those requiring cross-device coordination, limiting robustness under dynamic runtime failures in heterogeneous environments.
AI.method: H-RePlan is a hierarchical replanning framework with unified API-CLI-GUI execution. Each device is equipped with interchangeable execution strategies.
