A compact cross-layer failure abstraction enables device-local strategy recovery to operate independently from orchestrator-level global replanning, creating a scope-aware recovery hierarchy.
AI.result: On HeraBench (cross-device Linux-Android workflows with injected strategy- and device-level failures), H-RePlan achieves substantially higher task completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates compared to single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, while reducing token cost for reliable end-to-end success.
AI.conclusion: Scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution. By explicitly separating device-local from cross-device recovery decisions, H-RePlan enables more precise, efficient, and reliable fault handling in heterogeneous agent environments.

title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
summary: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.

AI.tldr: Flow map models with a lookahead parameter t continuously span the distortion-perception (DP) frontier, enabling controllable tradeoffs between fidelity and perceptual quality in image restoration without requiring retraining or auxiliary models.
AI.motivation: Existing image restoration methods face a rigid distortion-perception tradeoff: they are locked to a single operating point on the DP frontier. Accessing different tradeoff points requires paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or sampler hyperparameter tuning. The authors aim to provide a unified, continuous, and training-free mechanism to traverse the entire DP frontier.
AI.method: The authors leverage flow map models—a few-step sampling extension of flow matching that learns an average vector field. They show that the lookahead parameter t in these models defines a one-parameter family of denoisers. By varying t, the model continuously spans from MMSE (minimum mean squared error) to perceptual-quality regimes. This mechanism is analyzed theoretically for Gaussian targets (proving exact optimal DP frontier recovery) and extended to general inverse problems via a Plug-and-Play solver framework, where t controls the perceptual alignment vs. data consistency tradeoff.
AI.result: For Gaussian targets, varying t provably recovers the optimal DP frontier. For natural images on CelebA (128×128) and AFHQ (256×256) across multiple linear/nonlinear inverse tasks, a single trained flow map matches or exceeds specialized baselines at both MMSE and perceptual extremes, spanning the entire DP tradeoff continuum.
AI.conclusion: Flow map models provide an elegant, unified solution to the distortion-perception tradeoff: a single model with a tunable lookahead parameter t traverses the DP frontier without retraining, auxiliary networks, or paired data, offering a practical and principled approach for controllable image restoration.

title: StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the non-archival workshops AI4Good and Culture x AI at ICML 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and create about 50 single-attribute variations per face, producing about 25K images. This design keeps identity fixed and changes one visual attribute at a time. It lets us measure how specific cues shift model judgments. We evaluate six MLLMs across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. We find that age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. We further find that about 15 attributes account for nearly 80\% of the total variation, showing that bias is concentrated in a small set of visual cues. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments that are semantically aligned with appearance, especially socioeconomic and style-related judgments. We release StylisticBias as a benchmark for fine-grained bias evaluation in multimodal models. Code and dataset: https://github.com/timo-cavelius/StylisticBias and https://hf.co/datasets/shaghayegh/stylistic-bias-dataset.

AI.tldr: StylisticBias is a controlled benchmark that isolates single-attribute visual variations on fixed-identity photorealistic faces to measure how specific cues (age, body type, fashion, etc.) shift social judgments in multimodal LLMs. Analysis across 6 MLLMs reveals bias is concentrated in ~15 visual attributes driving ~80% of judgment variation, with strongest effects in semantically aligned socioeconomic/style judgments.
AI.motivation: MLLMs are widely deployed in high-stakes settings, but the specific visual cues driving social bias remain poorly understood. Prior work confounds identity differences with appearance effects by comparing different individuals. A controlled method is needed to isolate single-attribute visual effects on model judgments while holding identity constant.
AI.method: The authors create StylisticBias: 500 photorealistic base faces with ~50 single-attribute variations each (~25K images total). Each variation changes exactly one visual attribute (e.g., adding glasses, aging, changing body type) while keeping the face identity fixed. Six MLLMs are evaluated across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. Variance decomposition identifies which attributes contribute most to judgment shifts.
AI.result: Age and body type dominate identity-level effects; fashion style and other visual cues produce the largest attribute-level shifts. Approximately 15 attributes account for nearly 80% of total variation in judgments. Sensitivity is strongest for socioeconomic and style-related judgments that are semantically aligned with the manipulated visual attribute.
AI.conclusion: Social bias in MLLMs is concentrated in a small number of specific visual cues rather than uniformly distributed. The StylisticBias benchmark enables fine-grained, attribute-level bias auditing and is publicly released along with code and dataset.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models by training reward models on preference data and optimizing policies to maximize predicted rewards. However, this pipeline faces two fundamental challenges: (1) reward models cannot signal when their predictions are unreliable, since they usually act as deterministic point estimators; and (2) modern group-based policy optimization can amplify unreliable reward signals, as exemplified by GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards during advantage computation. As policies explore increasingly diverse responses, these two limitations create a critical vulnerability: unreliable reward estimates may be granted disproportionate influence, triggering severe reward hacking. We propose Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM), which equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. Experiments across HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF demonstrate that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

AI.tldr: UARM combines quantile-based conformal prediction for reward model uncertainty calibration with heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight GRPO advantages, mitigating reward hacking and improving alignment quality.
AI.motivation: RLHF faces two key limitations: (1) reward models act as deterministic point estimators without signaling prediction unreliability, and (2) group-based policy optimization (e.g., GRPO) treats all rewards uniformly during advantage computation, amplifying unreliable signals. As policy exploration diversifies, these flaws enable severe reward hacking.
AI.method: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM) uses quantile-based conformal prediction to equip reward models with calibrated uncertainty estimates and performs heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight advantages in GRPO, down-weighting unreliable reward signals during policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF show that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality over standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Integrating calibrated uncertainty into both reward modeling and policy optimization effectively addresses reward hacking in RLHF, yielding more reliable and better-aligned language models.

title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
summary: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence as "lawful amplification of rare but valid futures" and proves that recursive self-simulation is necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high intelligence under this framework, making intelligence measurable across all systems.
AI.motivation: To establish a universal, measurable definition of intelligence grounded in physics (thermodynamics), moving beyond ad-hoc or domain-specific metrics, and to rigorously connect the architectural property of recursive self-simulation to quantifiable intelligent behavior.
AI.method: Formalizes intelligence as "rare-valid lift" — the amplification of low-probability but admissible futures relative to passive dynamics. Uses a thermodynamic framework where an intelligent system models the world including itself, leading to recursive self-simulation. Derives necessity and conditional near-sufficiency theorems linking fidelity of internal simulation to achievable lift, with bounds set by actuation limits.
AI.result: (1) Necessity: high rare-valid lift is impossible without the internal simulation identifying rare-valid futures with high fidelity. (2) Conditional near-sufficiency: when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum.
AI.conclusion: Recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible architectural feature of intelligence but, under stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The framework enables universal intelligence measurement from passive matter to LLMs to Maxwell-demon-like systems.

title: Gender Bias in LLM Hiring Decisions: Evidence from a Japanese Context and Evaluation of Mitigation Strategies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in hiring workflows, yet most research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has focused on English-language, Western-format resumes. This study examines whether pro-female gender bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and evaluates two practical mitigation strategies. Using a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes, 12 name pairs selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria, and five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B), we conducted 43,200 API calls across baseline, prompt instruction, and privacy filter conditions. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model confirms a significant pro-female bias across all five models, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. A prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produces no meaningful reduction in bias. A name-reliance analysis formally identifies the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name from the prompt reduces the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate, highlights a practical deployment challenge for name anonymization in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

AI.tldr: This study investigates gender bias in LLM hiring evaluations using Japanese rirekisho-format resumes. Across five state-of-the-art LLMs (43,200 API calls), a significant pro-female bias is found, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. Gender-neutrality prompts fail to mitigate bias, while name removal nearly eliminates it. A critical incompatibility between name anonymization and GPT-4o's safety filter caused a 42% refusal rate, revealing practical deployment challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions is largely limited to English-language, Western-format resumes. The authors seek to determine whether previously documented pro-female bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and to evaluate whether practical mitigation strategies—prompt-based gender-neutrality instructions and name anonymization (privacy filters)—are effective in this non-Western setting.
AI.method: A counterfactual resume design was employed using 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes paired with 12 linguistically grounded gender-signaling name pairs. Five LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B) were tested across three conditions—baseline, prompt instruction (gender-neutrality directive), and privacy filter (name removal)—yielding 43,200 API calls. Analysis was conducted via a crossed random-effects linear mixed model, supplemented by a name-reliance analysis to isolate the primary gender-signaling channel.
AI.result: A statistically significant pro-female bias was confirmed across all five models. The prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produced no meaningful reduction. Name-reliance analysis identified the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing names reduced the female effect nearly to its full magnitude. A critical deployment issue emerged with GPT-4o's content safety filter, which rejected 42% of anonymized prompts, revealing incompatibility between privacy filtering and safety mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring evaluations is robust across linguistic and cultural contexts, extending from Western to Japanese settings. Simple prompt-based debiasing is ineffective; name removal is effective but introduces operational risks such as safety-filter interference. The findings caution against naive deployment of LLMs in automated recruitment without rigorous context-specific validation and highlight the need for more robust, culturally informed mitigation approaches.

title: Enhancing Graph Neural Networks Using Proximity Graphs for Dust Source Emission Forecasting
summary:
Accurate prediction of dust source emissions is critical for mitigating the significant environmental and health hazards posed by dust storms. Traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of these phenomena.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that proximity graphs enable Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively model the intricate spatial and temporal relationships between data points. Specifically, we use proximity graphs--such as Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph--as the input for GNNs (including GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Graph Attention Networks) to perform message passing.
  Our approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating proximity graphs with GNNs for robust and accurate dust source forecasting. To emphasize the importance of proximity graph representations, we compare our method against GNNs using random graphs for message passing. The results show that GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform those with random graphs and are also far superior to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model in dust source emission forecasting.

AI.tldr: Proximity graphs (Delaunay, Gabriel, k-NN, Yao) combined with GNNs (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) significantly outperform random-graph GNNs and LSTM in forecasting dust source emissions by capturing complex spatiotemporal dynamics.
AI.motivation: Dust storms pose significant environmental and health hazards, yet traditional forecasting methods fail to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of dust source emissions. Accurate prediction requires modeling intricate spatial and temporal relationships that conventional approaches cannot adequately represent.
AI.method: The authors propose using proximity graphs—Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph—as input structures for GNNs. These graphs serve as the message-passing topology for three GNN architectures: GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), and Graph Attention Networks (GAT). The method is benchmarked against GNNs using random graphs and standard LSTM models.
AI.result: GNNs employing proximity graphs significantly outperform both GNNs with random graphs and LSTM models in dust source emission forecasting. The proximity-graph-based representations yield robust and accurate predictions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating proximity graphs with GNNs is a highly effective strategy for dust source emission forecasting. The choice of graph representation is critical—proximity graphs capture meaningful spatiotemporal relationships that random graphs fail to encode, leading to substantially superior predictive performance.

title: When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form. Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Binning introduces a self-supervised learning pretext for medical tabular data that uses a feature-wise, coarse-to-fine discretization curriculum. The method progressively refines bins based on representation learning progress, combining categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision, and establishes a standardized benchmark for tabular SSL in medicine.
AI.motivation: Medical tabular data are abundant but labeling is expensive, leaving deep learning for tables underexplored. Existing binning-based self-supervised objectives rely on a single fixed global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision, failing to adapt to the learning dynamics of neural networks or the heterogeneous nature of clinical features.
AI.method: Adaptive Binning couples discretization to representation learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Leveraging the spectral bias of neural networks (which learn low-frequency patterns early), the method starts with coarse bins, detects learning plateaus via training dynamics, and then refines discretization per feature. It selects representation-aware splits to balance value-space concentration with representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction for discrete features with ordinal supervision for numerical features.
AI.result: Experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols demonstrate consistent gains over baselines in both linear probing and fine-tuning, without requiring dataset-specific discretization tuning.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive Binning advances tabular SSL by making discretization training-adaptive and feature-aware, and the proposed standardized benchmark facilitates reproducible research in medical tabular deep learning.

title: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

AI.tldr: MACR is a multi-agent framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in LLMs. It uses semantic entropy to assess when external knowledge is needed, then deploys three specialized agents to induce rules, analyze conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across internal and external knowledge sources.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to LLM knowledge conflict resolution assume either the model or external context is reliable, adopting a binary choice paradigm that privileges one source over another. This overlooks scenarios where both internal and external knowledge may contain errors or where multiple external contexts conflict with each other. The authors identify the need for active conflict resolution rather than mere source selection.
AI.method: MACR operates in two stages: (1) Adaptive Knowledge Assessment and Retrieval — uses a modified semantic entropy measure to estimate the LLM's confidence in its answer. If confidence is high, internal knowledge is externalized as textual representations; if low, relevant external knowledge is retrieved, forming basic contexts. (2) Inductive Multi-Agent Reasoning — deploys three specialized agents: one induces explicit rules from contexts, one analyzes potential conflicts among these rules and contexts, and one resolves inconsistencies to produce the final answer with interpretable conflict resolution.
AI.result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks and provides interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent reasoning framework with adaptive knowledge assessment can effectively handle complex knowledge conflicts — including internal-external and external-external conflicts — moving beyond binary source selection to active, interpretable conflict resolution.

title: Neural Additive and Basis Models with Feature Selection and Interactions
comment: Accepted at PAKDD 2024. Code is available at https://github.com/shiralab/NAM-FS
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit attractive performance in various fields but often suffer from low interpretability. The neural additive model (NAM) and its variant called the neural basis model (NBM) use neural networks (NNs) as nonlinear shape functions in generalized additive models (GAMs). Both models are highly interpretable and exhibit good performance and flexibility for NN training. NAM and NBM can provide and visualize the contribution of each feature to the prediction owing to GAM-based architectures. However, when using two-input NNs to consider feature interactions or when applying them to high-dimensional datasets, training NAM and NBM becomes intractable due to the increase in the computational resources required. This paper proposes incorporating the feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM to resolve computational bottlenecks. We introduce the feature selection layer in both models and update the selection weights during training. Our method is simple and can reduce computational costs and model sizes compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. In addition, it enables us to use two-input NNs even in high-dimensional datasets and capture feature interactions. We demonstrate that the proposed models are computationally efficient compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, and they exhibit better or comparable performance with state-of-the-art GAMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a feature selection layer into Neural Additive Models (NAM) and Neural Basis Models (NBM) to overcome computational bottlenecks when handling feature interactions or high-dimensional data, achieving reduced costs and competitive performance.
AI.motivation: NAM and NBM offer high interpretability via GAM-based architectures but become computationally intractable when using two-input neural networks for feature interactions or when applied to high-dimensional datasets. The authors aim to resolve these computational bottlenecks.
AI.method: The authors incorporate a feature selection layer into both NAM and NBM architectures. The selection weights are updated during training, enabling the models to dynamically prune irrelevant features. This simple mechanism reduces computational cost and model size while still allowing the use of two-input NNs for capturing feature interactions, even in high-dimensional settings.
AI.result: The proposed models demonstrate superior computational efficiency compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, while achieving better or comparable predictive performance relative to state-of-the-art GAMs.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM effectively resolves their computational bottlenecks, making them scalable to high-dimensional data and capable of modeling feature interactions without sacrificing interpretability or performance.

title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
summary: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

AI.tldr: A Vision Transformer with parameter-efficient adaptation and a confidence-aware framework enables selective automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings, deferring low-confidence cases for human review to balance coverage and scoring reliability.
AI.motivation: Scoring student-generated drawings for NGSS modeling-based tasks requires expert human judgment, making large-scale assessment costly and unsustainable. Automated methods are needed but must be trustworthy enough for educational contexts.
AI.method: A Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation is trained for automated scoring. A confidence-aware scoring framework derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions, enabling selective automation: high-confidence responses are scored automatically, while low-confidence cases are deferred for human review.
AI.result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items demonstrate improved scoring reliability and a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-aware methods are valuable for trustworthy educational assessment, enabling a viable balance between automation efficiency and the accuracy demands of high-stakes scoring.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Squeeze-Excitation-like Attention
summary: We introduce SEA-PINN, a novel architecture that incorporates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks to dynamically recalibrate the importance of neurons across layers. A key feature of SEA-PINN is its highly stable initialization. On 17 out of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibit nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, establishing a quasi-deterministic and favorable starting point for optimization. Notably, without employing Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions, SEA-PINN attained competitive accuracy (83\% vs. 90\% improvement relative to FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7) as compared with TSA-PINN-a model specifically engineered for high-frequency problems via learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations. Furthermore, integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN boosted performance by 42.49\%. These results underscore SEA-PINN as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes more robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the overall reliability of physics-informed learning.

AI.tldr: SEA-PINN introduces a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks, achieving highly stable initialization with near-zero variance on 17/20 benchmarks, competitive accuracy on high-frequency problems without specialized Fourier features, and serving as an effective lightweight plug-in module that boosts performance when integrated with existing architectures like TSA-PINN.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from poor initialization, training instability, and limited capacity to represent high-frequency and nonlinear functions, typically requiring specialized architectures like Fourier feature embeddings or sinusoidal activations. The authors aim to develop a general-purpose, lightweight attention mechanism that improves representation power, convergence robustness, and initialization stability without relying on problem-specific architectural modifications.
AI.method: SEA-PINN incorporates a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention mechanism that dynamically recalibrates channel-wise (neuron-wise) feature responses across network layers. The SE block performs global average pooling (squeeze), followed by a learned gating mechanism (excitation) that produces per-neuron scaling weights. This is integrated into standard fully-connected PINN architectures and also into TSA-PINN (which uses learnable-frequency sinusoidal activations). The method is evaluated on 20 benchmark PDE problems, including high-frequency cases.
AI.result: On 17 of 20 benchmarks, SEA-PINN achieved nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, yielding a quasi-deterministic starting point. Without Fourier features or periodic activations, SEA-PINN attained 83% improvement over FNN-PINN on high-frequency case 7, compared to TSA-PINN's 90% improvement. When SEA-PINN was integrated into TSA-PINN, performance improved by an additional 42.49%. The module demonstrates strong plug-and-play compatibility.
AI.conclusion: SEA-PINN is a lightweight, plug-in attention module that enhances nonlinear representation power in PINNs, promotes robust and efficient convergence, stabilizes initialization, and strengthens overall reliability of physics-informed learning. It can be effectively combined with specialized architectures like TSA-PINN for further gains.

title: Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving
summary: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

AI.tldr: Lagrange proposes an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse autonomous driving framework that uses Masked Latent Fields (MLF) to bridge dense geometric representations and sparse query-based planners. It encodes VLM-derived semantic tokens into a continuous energy field and frames planning as Lagrangian action minimization, achieving robust, kinematically feasible driving in both standard and long-tail scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving paradigms face a dichotomy: dense models (occupancy networks) are geometrically robust but computationally heavy and semantically limited; sparse query-based planners are efficient but brittle under out-of-distribution events. VLA models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their discrete autoregressive token generation conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency demands of vehicle control. A framework that unifies open-vocabulary semantic understanding with kinematically valid, computationally efficient planning is thus needed.
AI.method: Lagrange introduces Masked Latent Fields (MLF): (1) VLMs encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens; (2) an intent-driven masked cross-attention module temporally filters irrelevant entities; (3) attended tokens are decoded into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates; (4) decision-making is cast as a Lagrangian action minimization problem over this energy field, enforcing vehicle kinematic constraints during collision avoidance.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations on nuScenes (standard benchmark) and CODA (long-tail/OOD benchmark) demonstrate that Lagrange achieves robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy, establishing a promising new framework.
AI.conclusion: Lagrange successfully bridges the gap between open-vocabulary semantic reasoning and kinematically feasible planning through Masked Latent Fields and Lagrangian optimization. It offers a computationally sparse, generalizable alternative to both dense occupancy-based and closed-set query-based paradigms, showing strong performance on both standard and anomalous driving scenarios.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures via Reverse Fisher Divergence
summary: The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a $\widetildeΩ(1)$-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes gradient descent optimization under the reverse Fisher divergence for fitting Gaussian mixture models, proving global convergence guarantees from arbitrary or random initializations, in contrast to the problematic initialization-dependent behavior of the standard forward Fisher divergence.
AI.motivation: The standard forward Fisher divergence (score matching) can exhibit undesirable, initialization-dependent convergence behavior even in simple Gaussian mixture settings. The authors investigate whether using reverse Fisher divergence—where expectation is taken over the student distribution instead of the teacher—offers improved optimization properties.
AI.method: The authors analyze gradient descent (GD) dynamics under the reverse Fisher divergence objective for Gaussian mixture models. They employ a Lyapunov-based analysis to prove global convergence. Two settings are studied: (1) a single Gaussian teacher with a Gaussian mixture student (fixed weights, identity covariances), and (2) a Gaussian mixture teacher with the student under a global random initialization scheme and a Ω̃(1)-separation assumption on target means.
AI.result: First, for a single Gaussian teacher and Gaussian mixture student, global convergence of GD is proven from arbitrary initializations. Second, for a Gaussian mixture teacher, global convergence is guaranteed under random initialization and mean separation, with each student component converging near its closest teacher component with high probability. Conditions for convergence in total variation distance are also provided.
AI.conclusion: The reverse Fisher divergence yields a significantly more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence, enabling global convergence guarantees that avoid the initialization sensitivity plaguing standard score matching.

title: Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems
summary: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel vibration-based Intelligent Fault Diagnosis System (IFDS) using Deep Transfer Learning under severe data scarcity. It introduces a periodic multi-excitation procedure exploiting system nonlinearities to generate images for pre-trained CNNs, along with a new data visualization and augmentation method. The approach is validated on a railway pantograph structure.
AI.motivation: Deep Transfer Learning for fault diagnosis still requires large amounts of labeled data, which is difficult and expensive to obtain for real-world machinery and structures. There is a pressing need for IFDS that can function effectively under conditions of strong data scarcity.
AI.method: A periodic multi-excitation level procedure is employed to exploit intrinsic nonlinearities of real-world systems, converting vibration signals into images. These images are then analyzed using pre-trained CNNs via transfer learning. A novel data visualization method and a corresponding augmentation technique are introduced to address the typical lack of training data in IFDS design.
AI.result: Experimental validation conducted on a railway pantograph structure demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method for fault diagnosis under strong data scarcity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis using deep transfer learning even when labeled data is extremely scarce, leveraging system nonlinearities, novel image-based data representation, and augmentation techniques. The railway pantograph case study confirms its practical viability.

title: On the Oracle Complexity of Interpolation-Based Gradient Descent
summary: Recent work on first-order optimizers for empirical risk minimization (ERM) has suggested that smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data, rather than in the optimization parameters, can be leveraged to improve the oracle complexity of gradient descent (GD) methods. In this paper, we propose an inexact gradient method, piecewise polynomial interpolation-based gradient descent (PPI-GD), which approximates the full gradient in each iteration by querying the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain to construct polynomial interpolants of the resulting gradient samples over appropriately sized patches of the data domain. We analyze the oracle complexity of PPI-GD for strongly convex and non-convex loss functions when the data space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples, and find it to outperform several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Furthermore, our analysis extends several techniques from the error analysis of bicubic spline interpolants to the setting of $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants which may be of independent interest in interpolation analysis.

AI.tldr: Proposes PPI-GD, an inexact gradient method that uses piecewise polynomial interpolation over data patches to approximate full gradients, achieving improved oracle complexity over standard GD variants when loss functions are sufficiently smooth and data dimension is polylogarithmic in sample size.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows that smoothness of ERM loss with respect to training data (rather than model parameters) can be exploited to improve gradient descent oracle complexity. The authors aim to leverage this data-domain smoothness via polynomial interpolation to construct cheaper, approximate gradients that reduce total first-order oracle queries.
AI.method: PPI-GD queries the first-order oracle at equidistant grid points across the data domain, then constructs piecewise polynomial interpolants (tensor product form) over patches to approximate the full gradient. The analysis extends bicubic spline error analysis to d-variate tensor product polynomial interpolation and bounds oracle complexity for both strongly convex and non-convex losses.
AI.result: PPI-GD outperforms several gradient descent variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth, with the data dimension bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples. The interpolation error analysis for d-variate tensor product polynomials is also a standalone contribution.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting data-domain smoothness via piecewise polynomial interpolation is a viable strategy for reducing gradient computation cost in ERM, with PPI-GD demonstrating provable oracle complexity improvements over existing methods under appropriate smoothness and dimensionality conditions.

title: SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation
summary: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

AI.tldr: SoftSkill replaces long natural-language Markdown skill descriptions with compact, trainable continuous prefixes (virtual tokens) that act as latent behavioral priors for frozen LLMs, achieving substantial accuracy gains over both no-skill prompting and prior skill-tuning methods while using far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Current agent skills are encoded as verbose natural-language Markdown files that must be reinterpreted by a frozen language model at each inference. This is token-inefficient and fails to leverage the model's capacity for compact internal representations. The authors ask whether skills can instead be represented as compact continuous latents that directly steer frozen model behavior.
AI.method: SoftSkill initializes a continuous prefix from a natural-language skill description, then tunes a soft delta on that prefix using next-token prediction while keeping the base LLM completely frozen. At inference, the resulting length-32 prefix (virtual tokens) serves as a latent behavioral prior. The method is evaluated in single-round settings (SearchQA, LiveMath, DocVQA) and on harder multi-step agentic execution with sparse trajectory imitation.
AI.result: A length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 on LiveMath, and 1.3 on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while compressing hundreds to thousands of Markdown tokens into just a few virtual tokens. For long-horizon agentic execution, sparse trajectory imitation provides signal but does not yet robustly compress procedural behavior.
AI.conclusion: Some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown for inference-time reinterpretation, but as compact latent controls that steer how a frozen model enters a task. SoftSkill demonstrates that compact continuous skill representations can outperform lengthy text-based skill descriptions in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Matching Markets meet Cumulative Prospect Theory: Towards Optimal and Adversarially Robust Learning
summary: We study a multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem in the competitive setup with two-sided matching markets under a human centric decision making model. To capture human preferences, we use cumulative prospect theory (CPT) that weighs the actions of the agent in a nonlinear fashion using a ($α$-Hölder continuous) weight function. CPT has been widely used in behavioral economics and risk sensitive machine learning to emulate human preferences. We analyze the state-of-the-art learning algorithm with CPT weight distorted rewards and obtain a player optimal regret of $\mathcal{O}(K\log T \left(\frac{1}Δ\right)^{2/α})$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms, $T$ is the learning horizon, and $Δ$ represents (suitably defined) players' minimum preference gap. Noticing the dependence on $Δ$ to be sub-optimal, we further improve this regret by judiciously selecting the active set of arms during exploration, which removes the dependence on $K$ in the dominant term and achieves an improved (optimal) regret guarantees in the setting where the number of arms $K$ is significantly larger than the number of players $N$. In addition, we consider adversarial markets where the observed rewards of the agents may be corrupted. We propose and analyze algorithms for robust markets with CPT as risk sensitive measure in both settings where the total corruption budget is known and where it is unknown, and establish logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees in both cases.

AI.tldr: This paper studies multi-agent multi-armed bandits in competitive two-sided matching markets under Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT), achieving improved and optimal regret bounds, and extends to adversarial/corrupted reward settings with robust algorithms.
AI.motivation: Traditional multi-armed bandit models fail to capture realistic human decision-making, where preferences are nonlinear and risk-sensitive. By incorporating CPT—a well-established behavioral economics framework—the authors aim to model human-centric learning in matching markets, addressing the sub-optimal dependence on the minimum preference gap Δ in existing regret bounds and extending to adversarial reward corruptions.
AI.method: The authors analyze a state-of-the-art learning algorithm under CPT-weighted (α-Hölder continuous) distorted rewards. They improve regret by judiciously selecting an active set of arms during exploration, removing dependence on K (number of arms) in the dominant term. They further propose and analyze robust algorithms for markets with corrupted rewards, covering both known and unknown total corruption budgets, while maintaining logarithmic player-optimal regret.
AI.result: The baseline analysis yields player-optimal regret of O(K log T (1/Δ)^(2/α)). The improved active-set exploration strategy removes the K dependence in the dominant term, achieving optimal regret when K ≫ N. For adversarial markets with corruption, both known-budget and unknown-budget robust algorithms achieve logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating CPT into multi-agent bandit matching markets yields tractable, near-optimal regret bounds. The active-set exploration method significantly improves regret in large-arm regimes, and robust algorithm variants successfully handle adversarial reward corruptions while preserving logarithmic regret, broadening the practical applicability of human-centric bandit models.

title: Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
summary: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

AI.tldr: Mining GUI interaction trajectories yields readable skill clusters, but these clusters fail to meaningfully improve downstream policies when transferred across domains.
AI.motivation: Determine whether skill libraries can be automatically mined from interaction data in a way that produces inspectable skills and improves downstream agent policies.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment GUI trajectories using a boundary detector, (2) cluster segments into candidate skills with an orderless segment representation, (3) train a skill-aware policy (via GRPO) from the resulting annotations. Evaluation uses InteraSkill Workflows labels for purity analysis and cross-domain benchmarks (BrowseComp+) for transfer.
AI.result: Five of eight mined clusters achieved ≥0.95 purity against ground-truth labels. However, GRPO-based skill-aware training improved InteraSkill Workflows skill-step accuracy only marginally (18.5% → 20.5%), left BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperformed trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement. The work is framed as a diagnostic study.

title: SL-S4Wave: Self-Supervised Learning of Physiological Waveforms with Structured State Space Models
summary: Modeling long-sequence medical time series data, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), poses significant challenges due to high sampling rates, multichannel signal complexity, inherent noise, and limited labeled data. While recent self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, based on various encoder architectures such as convolutional neural networks, have been proposed to learn representations from unlabeled data, they often fall short in capturing long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling, but existing S4 architectures fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. In this work, we propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models. The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels, enabling the capture of both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines in a challenging arrhythmia detection task, (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples, showcasing strong label efficiency, and (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, highlighting its capacity to model complex temporal dynamics in long sequences that most existing approaches fail to efficiently model, and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, underscoring its robust cross-domain generalization. We additionally evaluate SL-S4Wave on multiple EEG tasks, achieving superior performance over strong baselines, demonstrating generalizability of our approach beyond cardiac waveforms.

AI.tldr: SL-S4Wave is a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a structured state space model (S4) encoder enhanced by multi-scale global convolution, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ECG arrhythmia detection and EEG tasks while demonstrating strong label efficiency, long-sequence modeling capability, and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised methods for medical time series (e.g., ECG) struggle to capture long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. While S4 models excel at long-sequence modeling, they fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. There is a need for an SSL framework that addresses both challenges simultaneously.
AI.method: SL-S4Wave combines contrastive self-supervised learning with a custom S4-based encoder. The encoder integrates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels to simultaneously capture fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms.
AI.result: The framework (1) consistently outperforms both supervised and self-supervised baselines on arrhythmia detection; (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples (strong label efficiency); (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments; and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types. Superior performance also extends to multiple EEG tasks.
AI.conclusion: SL-S4Wave effectively addresses the limitations of prior work by marrying contrastive SSL with an S4 architecture tailored for multichannel physiological signals, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance, label efficiency, long-sequence robustness, and strong cross-domain generalization across both ECG and EEG modalities.

title: Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe
summary: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that E2M1 FP4 formats suffer from Shrinkage Bias—a systematic negative rounding error from geometric bin asymmetry—causing training instability in FP4 LLM pretraining. The authors propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe using E1M2/INT4 formats with RHT applied to all three GEMMs and stochastic rounding restricted to dY, achieving lower BF16-relative loss degradation than E2M1 baselines across models up to 124B parameters.
AI.motivation: Current FP4 hardware (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) centers on E2M1 formats, but FP4 LLM pretraining recipes using E2M1 exhibit training instability. The authors seek to diagnose the root cause of this instability and propose a remedy, arguing that the format choice itself—not just quantization techniques—is the fundamental bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors first analytically identify "Shrinkage Bias": a systematic negative rounding error inherent to non-uniform formats like E2M1, arising from geometric asymmetry of representable bins. They demonstrate this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT). They then propose UFP4: a uniform 4-bit training recipe employing E1M2/INT4 grids, applying RHT to all three training GEMMs (forward, backward, and update), and restricting stochastic rounding solely to the dY gradient computation. Validation includes Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining with scaling-law analysis and ablation studies.
AI.result: UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines across all tested model scales (Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, MoE 124B). The uniform grid better converts improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Scaling-law analysis and ablation studies support these findings. The results suggest E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids should be first-class training primitives in future accelerators.
AI.conclusion: Non-uniform FP4 formats (E2M1) are fundamentally limited by Shrinkage Bias for LLM pretraining. Uniform 4-bit grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error. Future hardware should natively support uniform 4-bit training formats alongside E2M1 to enable stable, high-quality FP4 pretraining at scale.

title: Adversarial Bandit Optimization with Globally Bounded Perturbations to Convex Losses
summary:
We study adversarial bandit optimization in which the loss functions may be non-convex and non-smooth. In each round, the learner selects an action and observes only the loss incurred at that action. The loss consists of an underlying convex and $β$-smooth component and an adversarial perturbation that may be chosen after observing the learner's action. The perturbations are subject to a global budget controlling their cumulative magnitude over time.
  This framework extends the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from underlying linear losses to general convex and $β$-smooth losses. For this broader class, we establish expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget.
  To establish these guarantees, we modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that controls the additional regret caused by the perturbations. In the absence of perturbations, our results reduce to regret guarantees for the standard bandit convex optimization setting with $β$-smooth losses.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adversarial bandit optimization with non-convex, non-smooth loss functions. Each round's loss has a convex β-smooth component plus an adversarial perturbation applied after observing the learner's action, subject to a cumulative perturbation budget. The authors extend prior work (which only handled linear losses) to general convex β-smooth losses, derive expected regret bounds that explicitly capture the perturbation budget's impact, and modify a standard bandit algorithm to control the extra regret from perturbations.
AI.motivation: Existing work on bandit optimization with post-action adversarial perturbations was limited to underlying linear loss functions. The authors aim to generalize this framework to the broader and more practical class of convex β-smooth losses, while still providing rigorous regret guarantees that explicitly quantify how the perturbation budget affects performance.
AI.method: The authors modify a standard bandit convex optimization algorithm to handle the composite loss structure (convex β-smooth base + adversarial perturbation). Their analysis decomposes the regret into a standard bandit convex optimization component and an additional perturbation-induced component, then bounds each. The perturbation budget constraint is leveraged to control the cumulative adversarial effect. In the zero-perturbation limit, the analysis recovers standard bandit convex optimization regret guarantees.
AI.result: The paper establishes expected regret bounds that explicitly characterize the effect of the global perturbation budget for the class of convex β-smooth losses. The bounds show how regret degrades as the adversary's cumulative perturbation magnitude increases. When perturbations are absent, the results reduce to standard regret guarantees for bandit convex optimization with β-smooth losses.
AI.conclusion: The framework of globally budgeted post-action perturbations is successfully extended from linear losses to general convex β-smooth losses. The modified algorithm and accompanying analysis provide tight regret characterizations, demonstrating that meaningful learning remains possible even under adversarial perturbations, so long as the cumulative perturbation magnitude is bounded.

title: Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning
summary: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

AI.tldr: An attention-enhanced EfficientNet-B0 with CBAM achieves high accuracy (90.2%–93.9%) and interpretability via Grad-CAM++ for sperm morphology classification, outperforming baseline models on two public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models for automated sperm morphology analysis lack interpretability, hindering clinical adoption. There is a need for accurate yet transparent models that clinicians can trust.
AI.method: A pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone is combined with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to attend to key sperm head regions. Grad-CAM++ is employed for post-hoc interpretability, visualizing discriminative features. Evaluation is conducted on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets.
AI.result: The proposed model attains 90.2% accuracy (macro F1: 0.913) on SMIDS and 93.9% accuracy (macro F1: 0.948) on HuSHem, outperforming both SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0 baselines.
AI.conclusion: The attention-guided framework provides both high classification performance and visual interpretability, making it a practical, transparent tool suitable for deployment in fertility clinics.

title: Score Approximation for Diffusion Models on Arbitrary Low-Dimensional Structures
summary: The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension $d$. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with $d$, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a universal score approximation theorem for diffusion models that works for any distribution on compact sets with finite upper Minkowski dimension, showing that ReLU networks can approximate the score function with complexity exponential only in intrinsic dimension rather than ambient dimension, even for non-smooth, irregular data.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical complexity bounds for score-based diffusion models rely on restrictive assumptions — Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports — that are routinely violated by real data exhibiting singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters. The authors aim to bridge this gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel discrete-mixture formulation and prove that for any distribution supported on a compact set with upper Minkowski dimension d, the score function can be approximated by a ReLU network whose complexity scales exponentially with d (the intrinsic dimension) rather than the ambient dimension, thereby avoiding the exponential curse of dimensionality.
AI.result: The work establishes that diffusion models can provably adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures. Combined with existing theories on backward diffusion SDE solvers, this demonstrates that score approximation is tractable under realistic data assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models' empirical success on real-world generative tasks is theoretically justified: they do not require smooth densities or manifold structure, and their complexity depends on intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.

title: Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions
summary: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

AI.tldr: Engineering 55 context-aware temporal features from incubator microenvironment data reduces IVF prediction error to 1.27% (vs. 3-5% for raw averages). A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model with partial pooling across clinics achieves R²=0.86 and 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group, demonstrating transferable clinical signal in structured environmental monitoring.
AI.motivation: Current IVF pregnancy rate prediction models rely heavily on patient-level variables while neglecting high-resolution laboratory environmental data. The authors identify this as a missed opportunity and aim to demonstrate that structured, context-aware temporal features derived from incubator microenvironments contain clinically meaningful, transferable predictive signal that generalizes across clinics.
AI.method: The authors engineered 55 context-aware temporal features from incubator sensor data (e.g., rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, post-stress recovery speed) instead of raw sensor averages. They used 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic for feature validation via cross-validation. A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model was then trained with partial pooling to share environmental effects between an Asian and a Northern European clinic while preserving site-specific baselines. Performance was evaluated on held-out Northern European clinic data.
AI.result: The 55 engineered features reduced cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% using raw sensor averages. The hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model achieved R² = 0.86 on held-out Northern European clinic data, with a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating transferable signal across clinics.
AI.conclusion: Structured, context-aware environmental monitoring of incubator microenvironments captures clinically meaningful and transferable signal for IVF pregnancy rate prediction. The combination of engineered temporal features and hierarchical Bayesian modeling with partial pooling enables cross-clinic generalization, substantially outperforming naive approaches that rely on raw sensor averages.

title: ADaPT: Token-Level Decoupling for Efficient Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought to achieve strong performance, but applying such reasoning uniformly incurs high computational cost. Existing efficiency-oriented methods attempt to shorten or mix reasoning strategies, yet often degrade reasoning capability. We identify the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency incentives and correctness optimization, which implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Dual-Process Thinking (ADaPT), a token-level dual-process framework that explicitly decouples efficiency and correctness signals during training.
