ADaPT introduces a mode-selection token to control fast and slow reasoning, applying efficiency-related rewards exclusively to this token to avoid penalizing correct long reasoning while encouraging efficiency when appropriate. Moreover, ADaPT enables precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off at inference time: by adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token, a single trained model can smoothly move along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ADaPT decouples efficiency and correctness signals at the token level during training via a mode-selection token, enabling smooth inference-time control over the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier without degrading reasoning capability.
AI.motivation: Existing efficiency methods for large reasoning models (e.g., shortening or mixing reasoning) degrade reasoning performance because efficiency incentives and correctness optimization are coupled at the sequence level, implicitly penalizing long but correct reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: ADaPT is a token-level dual-process framework that introduces a mode-selection token to control fast vs. slow reasoning. Efficiency-related rewards are applied exclusively to this token during training, preventing penalty on correct long reasoning. At inference, adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token enables continuous traversal of the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier using a single model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks, with smooth and precise controllability over the efficiency-performance trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Token-level decoupling of efficiency and correctness via a mode-selection token effectively resolves the core tension in efficient reasoning, offering a practical and flexible solution for deploying large reasoning models under varying resource constraints.

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
summary: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how in-context compliance demonstrations jailbreak language models, examining the interplay between benign and harmful demonstrations, model training stages, demonstration ordering, and refusal behavior. Key findings show benign demonstrations can either mitigate or amplify harmful compliance depending on the model, preference optimization is critical for safety, and models exhibit strong recency bias and divergent refusal strategies.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak LMs, but the mechanisms by which models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations remain poorly understood. The authors aim to move beyond merely showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing *how* it works.
AI.method: The authors mix benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request + helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request + helpful response) and test three hypotheses about demonstration composition. Experiments span four models, analyzing the effects of demonstration type, ordering (recency bias), training stage (particularly preference optimization), and refusal behavior patterns.
AI.result: Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demos can either reduce or increase harmful compliance model-dependently. Preference optimization is the critical training stage preventing benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance. Demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias. Models diverge in refusal behavior: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal.
AI.conclusion: What models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology. The work provides mechanistic insight into demonstration-based jailbreaking rather than merely documenting its existence.

title: Compositionality Emerges in a Narrow Depth-Connectivity Regime: Architecture Constraints and Solution Manifolds
summary: Compositionality is believed to be the foundation for generalization, enabling models to reuse meaningful primitives in novel combinations. Yet, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely, and often only weakly, exhibit compositional internal structure, and it remains unclear how or why such compositionality forms. In this work, we show that compositionality emerges in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality only appears in some specifically sparse networks, heavily depends on which connections remain rather than on weights' sparsity alone. Along the depth axis, compositionality emerges within a narrow, target-dependent regime, peaking at specific depths, while both shallower and deeper networks fail. When either the depth or connectivity condition is violated, gradient descent silently converges to fractured solutions rather than compositional ones. To discover and exploit this emergence, we introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate where compositionality is most likely to appear. Finally, we support these empirical findings with a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds, explaining why compositional solutions are reachable only in a narrow depth-connectivity regime.

AI.tldr: Compositionality—the ability to reuse primitives in novel combinations—emerges only within a narrow sweet spot of network connectivity and depth. Sparse, specifically structured connectivity and a target-dependent optimal depth are both required; otherwise, gradient descent converges to fractured solutions. The authors introduce similarity-based pruning and a depth predictor to discover this regime, supported by a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity and feature-interference bounds.
AI.motivation: Despite compositionality being considered foundational for generalization, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely exhibit compositional internal structure. It remains unclear how or why compositionality forms, motivating the authors to investigate the conditions under which it emerges.
AI.method: The authors systematically explore the connectivity-depth space to identify where compositionality emerges. They introduce (1) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity from trained networks, and (2) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate the depth at which compositionality is most likely. They also develop a theoretical framework using compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds to explain the narrow emergence regime.
AI.result: Compositionality emerges exclusively in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot: along the connectivity axis, only specific sparse subnetworks exhibit it, depending on which connections remain rather than mere weight sparsity; along the depth axis, it peaks at specific target-dependent depths, with both shallower and deeper networks failing. Violating either condition causes gradient descent to silently converge to fractured (non-compositional) solutions.
AI.conclusion: Compositional structure in neural networks is not an automatic consequence of gradient-based training but requires precise architectural conditions—specifically, a narrow regime of sparse, structured connectivity and target-dependent depth. The proposed SP pruning and depth predictor offer practical tools to discover and exploit this emergent compositionality.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
summary:
LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: Multi-LCB extends the Python-only LiveCodeBench to 12 programming languages, preserving contamination controls and evaluation protocols. Evaluation of 24 LLMs reveals Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and significant cross-language performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LiveCodeBench is a leading contamination-aware code benchmark but is restricted to Python, leaving unaddressed whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
AI.method: Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks across 11 additional languages (12 total, including Python), fully preserving LCB's contamination controls, evaluation protocol, and format. It is designed for compatibility with future LCB updates for ongoing systematic assessment.
AI.result: Evaluation of 24 instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs on Multi-LCB uncovered evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual code generation performance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LCB provides a rigorous, multi-language benchmark that directly addresses LCB's primary limitation, exposing critical gaps in current LLMs' cross-language code generation capabilities.

title: Towards Graph-Based Deep Learning for Map Generalization: Insights from Building Footprints Simplification and Aggregation
summary: Map generalization remains one of the fundamental tasks in cartography, especially for the simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints. This study presents the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to both tasks, reformulating simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. We evaluate representative graph neural network architectures (GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE) on multi-scale building datasets, showing that GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy, while also revealing persistent challenges in precise node movement prediction. Beyond quantitative performance, the results highlight that aggregation poses greater complexity and challenges than simplification, underscoring the difficulty of capturing higher-level spatial relationships in map generalization with current deep learning approaches. Although limitations such as data imbalance and the need for post-processing remain, the study provides valuable insights and methodological directions for advancing automated map generalization with deep learning approaches.

AI.tldr: First exploration of graph neural networks for map generalization, reformulating building simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction. GraphSAGE performed best on link prediction; node movement remains challenging. Aggregation proved harder than simplification overall.
AI.motivation: Automated map generalization — particularly simplification and aggregation of building footprints — remains a fundamental yet unsolved cartographic challenge. Existing approaches struggle with higher-level spatial relationships, motivating the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to unify these two tasks.
AI.method: The authors reformulate building simplification as a node movement prediction task and building aggregation as a link prediction task within a unified graph learning framework. Building footprints are represented as graphs, and three representative graph neural network architectures — GCN (Graph Convolutional Network), GAT (Graph Attention Network), and GraphSAGE — are evaluated on multi-scale building datasets for both tasks.
AI.result: GraphSAGE demonstrated relative strengths in link prediction accuracy for the aggregation task. However, all architectures struggled with precise node movement prediction for simplification. Quantitatively and qualitatively, aggregation posed greater complexity and challenges than simplification, revealing limitations in current deep learning methods for capturing higher-level spatial relationships.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based deep learning shows promise for automated map generalization but faces significant hurdles: precise node movement prediction is difficult, aggregation is more complex than simplification, and issues like data imbalance and post-processing needs persist. The study offers methodological directions for future research rather than a production-ready solution.

title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
summary: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit enables frozen flow-matching TTS models to learn pronunciation corrections for out-of-vocabulary proper nouns via latent embedding edits stored in a Modern Hopfield Network, achieving 92.7% relative Phoneme Error Rate reduction with no degradation to general-speech quality.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems excel at zero-shot synthesis but are static post-deployment — pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns cannot be fixed without costly retraining. The authors seek a life-long, sample-efficient adaptation method that corrects specific pronunciations while preserving the frozen model's general capabilities.
AI.method: FlowEdit operates in three stages: (1) Upon corrective feedback, it optimizes a token-level perturbation vector in the text-embedding space to correct pronunciation, keeping all model weights frozen. (2) The learned perturbation is stored in a Modern Hopfield Network acting as content-addressable episodic memory. (3) At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching so that related word forms (e.g., plurals, case variants) also benefit from the correction.
AI.result: On a curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns spanning 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Each correction completes in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit provides an effective, efficient framework for life-long pronunciation adaptation in frozen flow-matching TTS systems, combining latent-space editing with associative memory to correct proper-noun errors without sacrificing general synthesis quality or requiring retraining.

title: Low-Energy Reduced RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor for Tsetlin Machine Inference at the Edge
comment: 6 pages, 6 Figures, Accepted in IEEE ISVLSI Conference 2026
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning approach that relies on simple bitwise operations and finite-state automata, which makes it attractive for edge AI deployments. Recent work has focused on co-processor and accelerator designs based on Tsetlin Machines (TMs). Although these designs achieve high performance, they typically depend on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and ease of programming. In this work, we present a domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor architecture and design flow tailored for TM inference. Leveraging the modular structure of RISC-V, we design a reduced instruction subset processor that retains programmability while targeting improved performance and lower energy consumption for TM workloads. Instruction profiling is employed to guide instruction reduction, followed by datapath and control path simplifications tailored to TM inference. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and compared with Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), which serve as a hardware-efficient baseline due to their reliance on bitwise operations during inference. Results show that TM achieves comparable or higher accuracy (e.g., up to 88.18% on CIFAR-2 compared to 60.0% for BNN) while reducing execution time by up to 98% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves an average $29.7\times$ reduction in energy consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness for programmable and efficient edge AI systems.

AI.tldr: A domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor is proposed for Tsetlin Machine inference, achieving up to 98% execution time reduction and 29.7× energy savings versus a baseline RV32IM core, while outperforming Binarized Neural Networks in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing TM accelerator designs rely on rigid microcode-style interfaces and external host processors, limiting programmability and flexibility. There is a need for a programmable, energy-efficient processor architecture tailored to TM inference workloads for edge AI.
AI.method: A reduced instruction-set RISC-V core is designed by profiling TM workloads to identify and eliminate unnecessary instructions, followed by datapath and control path simplification. The design is evaluated against a baseline RV32IM core and Binarized Neural Networks across multiple datasets.
AI.result: TM achieves up to 88.18% accuracy on CIFAR-2 (vs. 60.0% for BNN), reduces execution time by up to 98%, and yields an average 29.7× reduction in energy consumption compared to the baseline RV32IM processor.
AI.conclusion: The proposed domain-specific RISC-V core effectively combines programmability with substantial performance and energy gains, making it well-suited for programmable, efficient edge AI inference using Tsetlin Machines.

title: DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs
summary: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

AI.tldr: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog that reduces neural predicates to probabilistic choices, enabling exact counterfactual inference via weighted model counting on a single transformed program. It identifies sources of instability in standard ProbLog conditionals and demonstrates correctness and speedups over DeepTwin baselines, while also analyzing calibration bias in neural models.
AI.motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is associational and cannot support counterfactual reasoning. Counterfactuals require a causal semantics with interventions and evidence, which existing neurosymbolic frameworks lack. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a principled causal-probabilistic semantics for neural predicates.
AI.method: The paper proposes DeepSWIP, which extends Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) to DeepProbLog. Neural predicates are materialized into ordinary ProbLog choices under a fixed context. Counterfactuals are then computed by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program, under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions. The quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals is analyzed to explain intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments use MPI3D for transformation validation against DeepTwin and SUMO HOV for bias analysis with an AIPW estimator.
AI.result: On MPI3D, DeepSWIP matches DeepTwin predictions across 12,000 queries and achieves a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. The SUMO HOV experiment reveals that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, but a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWIP provides the first exact single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog, enabling efficient counterfactual inference in neurosymbolic systems. It clarifies the behavior of ProbLog conditionals under interventions and highlights the importance of proper calibration and doubly robust estimation in neural-causal pipelines.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing
summary: Reservoir computing offers a lightweight framework for forecasting dynamical systems but may struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional reservoir computing recurrently uses trainable reservoirs with hyperparameter sensitivity, while the next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence at the cost of rapidly growing feature dimensions. Here, we develop Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. We rigorously show that KARC is a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving the potential expressive capacity of KANs while admitting efficient closed-form training of reservoir computing. At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It can also be integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation. This work thus establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient and high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting.

AI.tldr: KARC replaces reservoir computing's recurrent reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, creating a lightweight KAN variant that retains expressive capacity while enabling efficient closed-form training, outperforming existing methods on dynamical systems and PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional reservoir computing suffers from limited representational capacity for long-range dependencies and hyperparameter sensitivity, while next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC) removes recurrence but suffers from rapidly growing feature dimensions. There is a need for a method that balances representational power with computational efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces the reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions derived from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. KARC is formulated as a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that preserves KAN expressive capacity while admitting the efficient closed-form training characteristic of reservoir computing. The method bridges RC and KAN frameworks.
AI.result: At comparable computational cost, KARC outperforms both conventional reservoir computing and next-generation reservoir computing on challenging benchmarks, including partial differential equations. The method also demonstrates versatility by integrating with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: KARC establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, enabling efficient, high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting without the representational bottlenecks of prior RC methods or the feature explosion of NGRC.

title: LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

AI.tldr: LedgerAgent introduces a separate, explicit state ledger for tool-calling agents that maintains task states across turns and checks policy constraints before executing environment-changing tool calls, reducing failures caused by stale or incorrect state grounding and policy violations.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling agents store all observations, tool returns, and policy instructions directly in the prompt, forcing the agent to reconstruct task state implicitly each turn. This leads to two failure modes: (1) grounding decisions in stale, missing, or incorrect information despite having retrieved correct facts earlier, and (2) syntactically valid tool calls that violate state-dependent domain policies.
AI.method: LedgerAgent is an inference-time method that maintains observed task states in a separate, explicit ledger data structure. The ledger contents are rendered into the prompt for decision-making. Critically, before executing any environment-changing tool call, the ledger is used to check state-dependent policy constraints, blocking calls that would violate domain policies.
AI.result: Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains observed under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state management via a separate ledger, combined with policy-constraint checking, significantly improves the reliability and policy adherence of tool-calling agents, particularly when evaluated under rigorous consistency requirements.

title: Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR): Function-Preserving SVD Compression for LLMs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM), Seoul, South Korea (non-archival)
summary: We present Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR), an SVD-based LLM compression framework that guides each weight matrix's low-rank approximation with a backward-signal influence metric. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W), AIR runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise under a monotone-descent guarantee. AIR is layer-local and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods: alone it exceeds ACIP, and AIR+LoRA outperforms it further. AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at <=60% parameter retention, matches its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and turns parameter savings into FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

AI.tldr: AIR introduces an influence-aware metric into SVD-based LLM compression, using a single ALS sweep to improve low-rank approximation quality beyond activation-aware methods like SVD-LLM(W), with significant perplexity gains, data efficiency, and downstream speed/memory benefits.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LLM compression methods (e.g., SVD-LLM) optimize low-rank approximations using only activation-awareness (forward-pass statistics). They neglect the backward signal — how each weight element influences the final loss. AIR addresses this gap by incorporating an influence metric that captures each parameter's importance to the training objective, yielding better compression with less calibration data.
AI.method: AIR starts from the activation-aware SVD-LLM(W) optimum and performs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep. This sweep integrates the backward-signal influence metric element-wise into the low-rank factorization. Crucially, the procedure guarantees monotonic descent of the objective. The method is layer-local (no end-to-end backpropagation needed) and composes orthogonally with methods like LoRA for further gains.
AI.result: AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at ≤60% parameter retention. It matches SVD-LLM(W)'s quality with ~90% less calibration data. Alone, AIR exceeds ACIP; combined with LoRA (AIR+LoRA), performance improves further. Parameter savings translate into concrete gains in FLOPs, peak memory, and per-token latency.
AI.conclusion: AIR demonstrates that incorporating backward-signal influence into SVD-based LLM compression yields substantial improvements in both compression quality and data efficiency. Its layer-local nature and orthogonality to end-to-end methods make it a practical, plug-and-play component for LLM deployment optimization.

title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
summary: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

AI.tldr: First application of cross-attention attribution (adapted DAAM) to speech diffusion TTS, analyzing 3,600 combinations to reveal how style caption tokens condition acoustic output — showing global temporal influence, correlation with F0/energy, peak conditioning in early ODE steps and deep layers, and maximal selectivity at layer 17.
AI.motivation: Style-captioned TTS systems lack interpretability: how individual words in natural language style descriptions influence acoustic output is unknown. This opacity hinders failure diagnosis and limits controllability improvements in expressive TTS.
AI.method: The authors adapt the DAAM (Diffusion Attentive Attribution Maps) framework from vision to speech, applying cross-attention attribution to CapSpeech-TTS. They extract per-token heatmaps across 25 transformer layers and 24 ODE (probability flow) steps. Analysis covers 3,600 combinations: 120 distinct style captions × 30 text transcripts each. Metrics include temporal variance of attention, correlation with F0 and energy, attention dynamics across layers and diffusion steps, and attention entropy.
AI.result: (1) Style tokens exhibit lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning behavior. (2) Style attention significantly correlates with fundamental frequency (F0) and energy. (3) Style conditioning peaks in early ODE steps and deeper network layers. (4) Attention entropy reaches minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with peak style importance, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical processing stage.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first empirical characterization of how natural language style descriptions modulate cross-attention in speech diffusion models, revealing layer- and timestep-specific dynamics that inform both interpretability and future controllable TTS design.

title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Work in progress; we will continuously update the codebase and arXiv version
summary: This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents: as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context. Major components of the CoD framework include: (1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation. We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework, including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL). Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting, and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization -- within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings -- of the elicited meta-capability. Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works, and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents. To facilitate further research and applications, we release our implementations at \url{https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod}.

AI.tldr: A framework for training LLMs to self-improve over long action sequences by alternating between solving tasks and updating their environmental context via end-to-end RL, demonstrating out-of-distribution generalization of this meta-capability.
AI.motivation: Long-lifecycle AI agents need to continuously learn from experience and adapt their understanding of the environment across extended task sequences, yet standard LLM training paradigms lack mechanisms for cultivating this "Connect the Dots" meta-capability of iterative context updating for progressive self-improvement.
AI.method: The CoD framework comprises: (1) an end-to-end RL training pipeline using a GRPO-style algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment over long rollouts that interleave solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) specially designed tasks and environments that incentivize and measure the targeted meta-capability rather than domain-specific skills.
AI.result: Proof-of-concept experiments show that end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting is effective. The elicited meta-capability exhibits out-of-distribution generalization: within training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings.
AI.conclusion: CoD bridges multiple prior research threads and enables LLMs to acquire a foundational meta-capability for autonomous, long-horizon adaptation. The authors open-source their implementation to spur further work.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
summary: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that expert-level calibration guarantees overall MoE calibration under distribution shift only for hard-routed models, not soft-routed ones. The authors propose an adversarial reweighting method to penalize calibration errors in the routed aggregate, improving the accuracy-calibration tradeoff across tasks and shifts.
AI.motivation: Calibration at the individual predictor level has been shown to improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with MoE models benefiting particularly. However, the theoretical conditions under which calibration aids MoE models—especially under distribution shift—remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze how routing mechanisms (hard vs. soft) interact with expert-level calibration under distribution shift. They prove sufficiency of expert calibration for hard-routed MoE but demonstrate its insufficiency for soft-routed models. To remedy this, they introduce an adversarial reweighting procedure that directly penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift.
AI.result: Expert calibration is sufficient for overall model calibration in hard-routed MoE under a broad class of distribution shifts. For soft-routed models, this does not hold. The proposed adversarial reweighting method improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult data subsets across multiple model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: The interaction between routing mechanisms and expert calibration critically determines MoE calibration under distribution shift. Hard routing preserves calibration guarantees, while soft routing breaks them. Adversarial reweighting effectively bridges this gap, offering a practical solution for calibrating soft-routed MoE models.

title: StreamKL: Fast and Memory-Efficient KL Divergence for Boosting Attention Distillation
summary: Attention distillation, which trains one attention distribution to match another by minimizing their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, is widely used in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training. However, existing approaches materialize both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring $O(N_QN_K)$ memory and IO costs that become prohibitive at long context lengths. We present StreamKL, the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates this quadratic materialization. StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for the coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, StreamKL recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. We further design and implement efficient GPU kernels with dedicated optimizations. Experiments show StreamKL delivers up to $43\times$ and $14\times$ speedups over baseline methods in the forward and backward passes, respectively. Most importantly, StreamKL reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from $O(N_QN_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: StreamKL is a fused GPU primitive that computes the KL divergence between two attention distributions in a single streaming pass, eliminating the O(N²) memory materialization required by prior methods, thereby enabling attention distillation at long context lengths on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Attention distillation (minimizing KL divergence between two attention distributions) is widely used but requires materializing both O(N_Q × N_K) attention matrices before computing the KL reduction, incurring prohibitive memory and IO costs at long context lengths. Existing approaches cannot scale attention distillation to long sequences on memory-constrained GPUs.
AI.method: StreamKL reformulates the coupled two-distribution KL reduction into an online computation that processes query-key tiles in a single forward pass through on-chip SRAM, avoiding quadratic materialization. The backward pass recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile rather than storing intermediate results. Custom GPU kernels are designed with dedicated optimizations for both passes.
AI.result: StreamKL achieves up to 43× speedup in forward pass and 14× in backward pass over baselines. Critically, it reduces the extra HBM footprint from O(N_Q × N_K) to O(1), enabling long-context attention distillation on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: StreamKL is the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates quadratic materialization, making attention distillation practical for long-context scenarios and unlocking new capabilities in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training.

title: VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a central tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but current methods face a trade-off between simplicity and credit assignment. Group-relative methods such as GRPO avoid training a critic, but typically assign a trajectory-level advantage to every token. Actor-critic methods provide denser learning signals, but require a learned value function with its own training instability. We introduce VIMPO, a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized reinforcement learning. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence can be written in terms of policy-reference log-ratios and anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at the end of a trajectory. This gives a simple value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without training a critic. The same derivation also yields a critic-free actor advantage, allowing VIMPO to separate reward incorporation through the value loss from policy improvement through a PPO-style actor update. On mathematical RLVR benchmarks, VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with especially larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO, suggesting that policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment while preserving the practical simplicity of critic-free training.

AI.tldr: VIMPO is a critic-free RL method for LLMs that derives a policy-implied value function from KL-regularized RL optimality conditions, enabling token-level credit assignment without training a critic. It outperforms GRPO on math reasoning benchmarks and is more robust under noisy rewards.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods for improving LLM reasoning face a trade-off: GRPO is simple but assigns only trajectory-level advantage to every token (poor credit assignment), while actor-critic methods provide denser signals but suffer from critic training instability. The authors aim to achieve fine-grained credit assignment while preserving critic-free simplicity.
AI.method: VIMPO derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL. For autoregressive generation, this yields a value recurrence expressed in policy-reference log-ratios, anchored by a terminal condition (zero future reward at trajectory end). This produces a simple value loss using outcome-level verifiable rewards, with no critic needed. The same derivation yields a critic-free actor advantage, enabling separation of reward incorporation (via value loss) from policy improvement (via a PPO-style actor update).
AI.result: VIMPO outperforms GRPO on MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with particularly large gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO consistently outperforms GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Policy-implied value optimization (VIMPO) provides finer credit assignment than group-relative methods while retaining critic-free simplicity, offering a practical and effective middle ground for RL-based LLM reasoning improvement.

title: Self-Adaptive Scale Handling for Forecasting Time Series with Scale Heterogeneity
comment: This is the full version of the paper accepted by the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF
summary: Current time series forecasting (TSF) research predominantly focuses on scale-homogeneous data, where different time series share similar numerical magnitude ranges. However, in real-world industrial scenarios such as financial product sales, different time series often differ by orders of magnitude (scale heterogeneity). Since these series share similar temporal patterns, joint modeling is desirable for better data utilization, yet existing scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module that learns adaptive scale factors tailored to each input, preserving semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. AS consists of Scale Calibrating (SC), which calibrates prior mean scaling factors through neural networks, and Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply calibration or retain the original factor, avoiding over-calibration. Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay show that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their performance. The code and dataset are available at the link https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF.

AI.tldr: Proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module for time series forecasting with scale-heterogeneous data, using learned adaptive scaling factors to preserve semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors, validated on real-world fund sales data.
AI.motivation: Existing TSF methods assume scale homogeneity, but real-world data (e.g., financial sales) exhibits scale heterogeneity where series differ by orders of magnitude. Global normalization compresses low-scale signals, while window-based scaling destroys semantic discriminability and amplifies inverse-scaling errors. Joint modeling is desirable due to shared temporal patterns, but current scaling approaches are inadequate.
AI.method: The AS module comprises two components: (1) Scale Calibrating (SC), which uses neural networks to calibrate prior mean scaling factors, and (2) Scaling Selection (SS), which adaptively decides whether to apply the calibrated factor or retain the original, preventing over-calibration. The module integrates as a plug-and-play component into existing TSF models.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay demonstrate that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their forecasting performance.
AI.conclusion: The AS module effectively addresses scale heterogeneity in TSF by learning input-adaptive scale factors, enabling better joint modeling of heterogeneous time series without the drawbacks of conventional scaling methods. Code and dataset are publicly released.

title: Hierarchical Control in Multi-Agent Games: LLM-based Planning and RL Execution
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong performance in sequential decision-making, yet scaling to complex multi-agent environments remains challenging due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. We propose a hierarchical architecture where a pretrained large language model (LLM) acts as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. We evaluate this hybrid system in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and \emph{``Flat''} RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition) baselines. The LLM+RL system achieves task performance statistically equivalent to hand-crafted BT (46.4\% vs 51.5\% win rate, $p=0.103$) while both significantly outperform Flat RL trained without skill decomposition. A user study ($n=15$) reveals that 60\% of participants perceive LLM+RL agents as the most human-like ($p=0.027$), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability. These results demonstrate that pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills, achieving competitive multi-agent coordination and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical architecture combining a pretrained LLM as a strategic controller with specialized RL skill policies outperforms end-to-end RL and matches hand-crafted behavior trees in a 2v2 competitive game, while being perceived as the most human-like.
AI.motivation: Scaling RL to complex multi-agent environments is hindered by sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. The authors aim to leverage LLM reasoning for high-level strategic coordination while retaining RL for reactive low-level control.
AI.method: A hierarchical architecture where a pretrained LLM serves as a centralized strategic controller, selecting among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents. RL policies handle low-level reactive execution. Evaluated in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and Flat RL (end-to-end without skill decomposition) baselines. A user study (n=15) assessed perceived human-likeness.
AI.result: The LLM+RL system achieved a 46.4% win rate vs. the BT baseline's 51.5% (statistically equivalent, p=0.103), both significantly outperforming Flat RL. In the user study, 60% of participants rated LLM+RL agents as most human-like (p=0.027), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive performance against hand-crafted BTs and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

title: Adaptive Distance-Aware Trunk Deep Operator Learning for Long-Span Roadway Bridges
summary: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally expensive for applications such as influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML approaches struggle to accurately capture these localized responses. To address this challenge, this study proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet for localized structural response prediction in large-scale bridge systems. The framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy, allowing the network to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is further enhanced using distance-aware features that encode the geometric relationship between the load and structural nodes. A physics-based full-field reconstruction is incorporated through a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation, enabling predictions at adaptive nodes to be extended to the entire structural domain. To enable scalable training, response data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that preserves the dominant global behavior while significantly reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is validated on both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge. Results show that the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%, while reducing the total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) by approximately 60x; excluding the post-processing reconstruction step, the AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM. In addition, the framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading configurations, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

AI.tldr: An adaptive-trunk DeepONet framework combining KNN-based dynamic domain construction, distance-aware features, and stiffness-informed Schur complement reconstruction is proposed for localized structural response prediction in long-span bridges, achieving FEM-level accuracy with ~60x speedup and enabling rapid influence surface generation for digital twins.
AI.motivation: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally prohibitive for influence surface generation and digital twin applications. Existing SciML methods fail to accurately capture these localized responses.
AI.method: The proposed adaptive-trunk DeepONet (AD-DeepONet) employs: (1) a KNN strategy to dynamically construct load-dependent learning domains focusing on structural influence zones; (2) distance-aware features in the trunk network encoding geometric relationships between loads and structural nodes; (3) a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation for physics-based full-field reconstruction from adaptive node predictions; and (4) a reduced-order equivalent shell model for scalable training data generation that preserves dominant global behavior.
AI.result: On both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge, the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%. Total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) is reduced by approximately 60x compared to FEM. Excluding post-processing, AD-DeepONet inference speed is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM.
AI.conclusion: The AD-DeepONet framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

title: What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT}{this repository}.

AI.tldr: Latent Chain-of-Thought suffers from gradient attenuation and representational drift—collectively termed dual collapse. The authors propose decomposing process supervision into Trajectory and Space Supervision, finding that generative reconstruction outperforms rigid geometric compression. They introduce the Unified Latent Probe to measure mutual information between latent and explicit reasoning, establishing an Information-Performance Binding principle.
AI.motivation: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is appealing because it avoids verbose discrete reasoning traces, but outcome supervision alone provides weak learning signals. This causes latent trajectories to suffer from semantic drift, making robust latent reasoning difficult. The work aims to diagnose why this failure occurs and provide principled remedies.
AI.method: The authors analyze Latent CoT through an information-theoretic lens, identifying the failure mode as a dual collapse: (1) gradient attenuation along the optimization path, and (2) representational drift in the latent space. They decompose process supervision into Trajectory Supervision (dense stepwise reasoning signals) and Space Supervision (preserving semantic structure of the latent manifold). They introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to quantify mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments compare rigid geometric compression against generative reconstruction as supervision strategies.
AI.result: Rigid geometric compression collapses the reasoning space, while generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. The ULP reveals a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy is directly tied to the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision, recommending a shift from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. The work suggests that preserving information fidelity in latent chains is critical for robust latent reasoning.

title: Exploring the potential of AlphaEarth and TESSERA embeddings for Fine-scale Local Climate Zone Mapping: A case study across five cities in Switzerland
summary: Understanding urban spatial morphology is critical for climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable urban design, and Local Climate Zone (LCZ) mapping provides the basic framework for this. However, many cities still use coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ records, which are unsuitable for fine-scale urban research. In this study, precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared to traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites in five Swiss cities to see if they can upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net. Three experiments assess multi-city transferability, the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. We find that all datasets achieve strong performance with test data Intersection-over-Union (IoU) ranging from 0.59-0.69 and 0.77-0.82 in the first two experiments. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings As expected, we find that the transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Overall, however, our results demonstrate the promising potential of embeddings derived from EO foundation models to reduce time consuming preprocessing, respectively, manual feature engineering tasks and to guide a universal deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow. When combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net architecture, the embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive and reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications Improving reference data quality remains the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: This study compares precomputed embeddings from two EO foundation models (TESSERA and AlphaEarth) against traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites for upscaling coarse ~100-m LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net in five Swiss cities. TESSERA consistently outperforms alternatives (IoU: 0.59–0.82 across experiments), demonstrating that foundation model embeddings can reduce preprocessing overhead and enable transferable, fine-scale LCZ mapping, though temporal robustness across years remains an open challenge.
AI.motivation: Many cities rely on coarse ~100-m resolution Local Climate Zone maps, which are inadequate for fine-scale urban climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable design. There is a need for scalable, automated workflows that can upscale these maps to finer resolutions (10-m) while reducing the manual feature engineering and preprocessing burden inherent in traditional remote sensing approaches.
AI.method: The authors compare three input data sources — traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites and precomputed embeddings from two Earth Observation foundation models (TESSERA, AlphaEarth) — across five Swiss cities. An attention-based U-Net architecture is used to upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution. Three experiments are conducted: (1) multi-city transferability, (2) impact of higher-resolution reference data, and (3) temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. Performance is evaluated using Intersection-over-Union (IoU).
AI.result: All datasets achieve strong performance: test IoU ranges from 0.59–0.69 in the first experiment and 0.77–0.82 in the second. TESSERA embeddings consistently outperform both S1S2 composites and AlphaEarth across both settings. Temporal transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Higher-quality reference data proves to be the strongest lever for further accuracy improvements.
AI.conclusion: Foundation model embeddings, particularly from TESSERA, show promising potential to streamline LCZ mapping workflows by reducing preprocessing and manual feature engineering. Combined with a location-aware attention U-Net, they enhance regional transferability and scalability toward comprehensive, reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps. Improving reference data quality is identified as the most impactful direction for future accuracy gains.

title: Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using a Multimodal Approach with 3D MRI and PET
comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of death worldwide. Early diagnosis plays an important part especially at the Mild Cognitive Impairment stage, where timely intervention can help slow its progression before it advances to AD. Neuroimaging data, like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, can help detect brain changes early by providing structural and functional brain changes related to the disease. Yet, many multimodal models still fuse MRI and PET with static concatenation and apply identical computation to all subjects, which limits robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and can waste computation. To address these limitations, we present the first study of combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies - concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention - and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most informative experts per case. Finally, we utilize Grad-CAM to visualize disease-related regions, ensuring model interpretability. Experiments are performed across three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD). Results show that GMU achieves accuracies of 80.46 % (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47 % (NC vs. AD), while gated self-attention attains 82.08 % on MCI vs. AD. Ablations show that removing the MoE consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks. These findings underscore the value of input-adaptive, multimodal modeling for AD diagnosis by leveraging the complementary nature of MRI and PET.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an input-adaptive multimodal framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis that combines 3D CNN feature extractors with gated fusion mechanisms (GMU, gated self-attention) and a sparse Mixture-of-Experts classifier, achieving strong accuracy across NC/MCI/AD classification tasks while using Grad-CAM for interpretability.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal models for AD diagnosis suffer from two key limitations: (1) they fuse MRI and PET data using static concatenation, failing to leverage complementary modality information adaptively; and (2) they apply identical computation to all subjects, ignoring patient/site heterogeneity and wasting computational resources. Early diagnosis at the MCI stage is critical for timely intervention.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework integrating: (1) 3D convolutional feature extractors for processing MRI and PET volumes; (2) three fusion strategies compared head-to-head — simple concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention; (3) a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that routes each input sample to only the most relevant experts, enabling input-adaptive computation; and (4) Grad-CAM visualizations for model interpretability. Evaluation covers three binary classification tasks: NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD.
AI.result: GMU fusion achieved 80.46% accuracy on NC vs. MCI and 95.47% on NC vs. AD. Gated self-attention reached 82.08% on the more challenging MCI vs. AD task. Ablation studies demonstrated that removing the MoE classifier consistently degraded performance across all tasks, confirming the contribution of input-adaptive routing.
AI.conclusion: Input-adaptive multimodal modeling that pairs gated fusion with sparse MoE routing effectively leverages the complementary nature of MRI and PET for AD diagnosis. The approach improves robustness to patient heterogeneity, enhances computational efficiency, and maintains interpretability through attention-based visualizations.

title: Comparative Study of Neural Surrogate Architectures for Autoregressive Prediction of Internal Battery States
summary: The Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model resolves internal electrochemical states in lithium-ion batteries with high fidelity. However, the numerical solution of its governing equations is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, limiting scalability from individual cells to pack and fleet-scale applications. While machine learning surrogates can substantially reduce inference latency through GPU acceleration, most existing approaches learn solution approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics. This work presents a systematic comparison of four neural network architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states across a wide range of operating conditions. To ensure a controlled architectural comparison, all models are trained under a unified framework using multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning, isolating the impact of spatial inductive bias. Results demonstrate that the U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, while providing a 5.38x speed-up over the numerical solver. These findings highlight spatial inductive bias as a critical determinant of surrogate performance, advancing the development of surrogates for internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

AI.tldr: Four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) are systematically compared as autoregressive state-transition operators for accelerating DFN battery model simulations. U-Net achieves 3% nRMSE after 300-step rollouts with 5.38× speedup, demonstrating that spatial inductive bias is critical for surrogate performance.
AI.motivation: The DFN model offers high-fidelity electrochemical state resolution for Li-ion batteries but is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment at pack/fleet scales. Existing ML surrogates learn fixed operating-condition approximations rather than generalizable dynamics, motivating a systematic study of architecture choice for learning state-evolution operators across diverse conditions.
AI.method: Four architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, Fourier Neural Operator) are formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states. All models are trained under a unified framework with multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning to isolate the effect of spatial inductive bias. Evaluation uses 300-step autoregressive rollouts across wide operating ranges.
AI.result: U-Net achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, with a 5.38× speed-up over the numerical solver, outperforming all other architectures tested.
AI.conclusion: Spatial inductive bias, particularly U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy, is a critical determinant of surrogate performance for DFN state dynamics. These findings advance neural surrogates for internal state observability in next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

title: PaAno+: Multiscale Encoding and Cross-Variable Attention for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time-series anomaly detection has significant practical value for industrial and medical monitoring, as well as other critical domains. Current Transformer- and large-model-based detection approaches incur excessive computational overhead, while existing lightweight alternatives are constrained by insufficient feature extraction and inadequate modeling of dependencies across multivariate variables. To mitigate the above drawbacks, this study develops a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection model, dubbed PaAno, within the patch-oriented representation learning paradigm. In the encoder module, a multiscale feature-extraction backbone is constructed using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal characteristics; subsequent cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation, combined with residual connection optimization, further stabilizes feature representation learning. A cross-variable fusion attention module is embedded to explicitly characterize inter-variable correlations, empowering the model to identify anomalous patterns amid intricate operational conditions. Moreover, a novel pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting is customized to uncover intrinsic structural properties of time series, and triplet loss is leveraged to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that the proposed PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, yielding significant performance gains across evaluation metrics, including VUS-PR, relative to the original PaAno. Leveraging a compact network design, the presented model achieves favorable computational efficiency, enabling deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference.

AI.tldr: PaAno is a lightweight, patch-based anomaly detection model that uses multiscale convolutional encoders, cross-scale adaptive attention, cross-variable fusion, and a temporal patch-window sorting pretext task with triplet loss to achieve SOTA accuracy on TSB-AD while maintaining computational efficiency for edge deployment.
AI.motivation: Transformer- and large-model-based anomaly detectors are computationally expensive, while existing lightweight methods suffer from insufficient temporal feature extraction and weak modeling of inter-variable dependencies in multivariate time series. There is a need for an accurate yet resource-efficient solution deployable on resource-constrained terminals.
AI.method: PaAno employs a patch-oriented representation learning framework. The encoder uses multiscale convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields for hierarchical temporal feature extraction, followed by cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation with residual connections. A cross-variable fusion attention module explicitly models inter-variable correlations. A novel pretext task — temporal patch-window sorting — uncovers structural properties of the series, while triplet loss optimizes the patch embedding space for enhanced discrimination.
AI.result: On the TSB-AD benchmark, PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy for both univariate and multivariate tasks, with significant improvements in VUS-PR and other evaluation metrics compared to the baseline. The compact design yields strong computational efficiency suitable for real-time inference on resource-limited terminals.
AI.conclusion: PaAno successfully balances detection accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that patch-oriented representation learning combined with multiscale convolution, cross-variable attention, and a sorting-based pretext task can outperform both heavy Transformer-based and prior lightweight methods, making real-time industrial and medical anomaly monitoring feasible on edge devices.

title: Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics
summary: Perception for action suggests that representations of the world should be shaped not by visual fidelity alone, but by their relevance for actions. At the same time, latent JEPA-style world models advocate learning compact predictive states from high-dimensional observations to facilitate the prediction of future states, but end-to-end training of these models is nontrivial because representations may collapse if our only goal is to construct a latent state that is easy to predict. We introduce a sensorimotor world model (SMWM): a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization.
