This single regularizer addresses both issues: it prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations. By forcing latent states to preserve information about the action underlying a transition, it biases the model toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment while discarding uncontrollable distractors. This yields stable latent world models trained from offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers. Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and enables competitive planning performance across simple 2D and 3D control tasks.

AI.tldr: SMWM is a sensorimotor world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization, which simultaneously prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned latent states for planning in control tasks.
AI.motivation: Two problems are addressed: (1) perception-for-action requires representations aligned with action relevance, not just visual fidelity; (2) JEPA-style world models suffer from representation collapse when trained end-to-end, since easy-to-predict latent states tend to collapse to trivial solutions. Existing remedies (frozen encoders, EMA, complex regularizers) are cumbersome.
AI.method: The authors propose SMWM, a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization — a single regularizer that forces latent states to preserve information about the action that caused a transition. This biases the model toward controllable degrees of freedom while discarding uncontrollable distractors, without needing frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers.
AI.result: SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and achieves competitive planning performance on simple 2D and 3D control tasks, trained from offline, reward-free trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Inverse dynamics regularization is a simple yet effective single mechanism that jointly solves representation collapse and action-alignment in end-to-end latent world model training, enabling stable learning and effective planning.

title: Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning
summary: Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds without requiring count-based uncertainty estimates, thereby providing the first theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration in reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Optimal RL algorithms rely on count-based uncertainty estimates that are theoretically sound but computationally hard in practice. Ensemble methods work well empirically but lack theoretical grounding. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a theoretically justified ensemble approach.
AI.method: The authors extend a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits to finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes. They propose a quantile-based ensemble method that is entirely count-free, using the empirical quantiles of an ensemble of value function estimates to drive exploration.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, matching the theoretical performance of count-based approaches while using a purely ensemble-driven exploration strategy.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based exploration can be theoretically justified in RL. The quantile-based ensemble method provides a practical, count-free alternative to traditional uncertainty estimation while retaining optimal regret guarantees.

title: When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees on segmentation quality by calibrating a prediction-set threshold on held-out data. In federated deployments, the standard approach pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold. We provide the first quantification, on real multi-institutional brain tumor data (FeTS-2022, 1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), showing that this naive pooled CRC protects the average hospital but violates coverage at 40% of individual institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. The naive alternative, per-site local CRC, largely restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, rendering them clinically useless. We propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 smoothly trades worst-case coverage for prediction-set efficiency; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis identifies n0=19, achieving 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. We further show that direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals, and that the finite-sample correction term is essential: removing it triples violations. The marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction under the stated site-mixture assumption; per-site coverage is validated across four targets with three seeds. No patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that standard pooled conformal risk control (CRC) in federated medical image segmentation fails to provide per-institution coverage guarantees, with 40% of hospitals experiencing violations. The authors propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol that transmits only empirical risk curves (G scalars) to a central server, achieving a tunable trade-off between worst-case coverage and prediction-set size via a single hyperparameter n₀, all without sharing patient data.
AI.motivation: Federated medical image segmentation requires distribution-free quality guarantees, but naive pooled CRC — the standard approach — only protects the average institution while leaving individual hospitals vulnerable to coverage violations. Per-site local CRC restores coverage but yields clinically useless, massively inflated prediction sets (83×). There is no existing method that simultaneously provides per-site coverage guarantees, maintains clinically useful prediction-set sizes, and preserves data privacy in a federated setting.
AI.method: The proposed shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol works as follows: (1) each site computes its empirical risk curve (G scalar values representing risk as a function of threshold) locally and transmits only these scalars to a central server; (2) the server applies shrinkage regularization, shrinking each site's threshold toward a pooled estimate using a hyperparameter n₀ that controls the degree of shrinkage; (3) a finite-sample correction term is incorporated to maintain marginal coverage guarantees; (4) the server returns a site-specific calibrated threshold. A leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis is used to select n₀. The method is validated on the FeTS-2022 dataset (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions) with brain tumor segmentation, testing four coverage targets across three random seeds.
AI.result: Naive pooled CRC violated coverage at 40% of institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. Per-site local CRC inflated prediction sets by 83×. The proposed shrinkage protocol with n₀=19 achieved only 2.7/20 violations at a modest 2.0× stretch relative to pooled CRC. Direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets failed by concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals. Removing the finite-sample correction term tripled violations. The marginal CRC guarantee was preserved by construction under the site-mixture assumption.
AI.conclusion: Shrinkage-based federated CRC provides a practical solution for distribution-free segmentation quality guarantees in multi-institutional settings, balancing per-site coverage with prediction-set efficiency. The method transmits only aggregate risk curves (G scalars), ensuring no patient-level data leaves any site. The finite-sample correction term is essential for validity, and the single hyperparameter n₀ offers interpretable control over the coverage-efficiency trade-off.

title: Multi-Modal Contrastive Learning for Implicit Earth Embeddings via Location Tying
summary: Spatial prediction tasks are often limited by a lack of high-quality labelled ground-truth observations. To overcome this challenge, self-supervised pre-training is a possible solution, with contrastive learning dominant for location encoders. Those approaches usually align geographic coordinates with just one additional modality. We propose two multimodal contrastive learning architectures: Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying (MELT) and Sequential Alternating Location Training (SALT). These architectures expand this framework beyond two modalities by utilising unpaired geospatial data. Both methods are technically viable and match the performance of the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting that the chosen location encoder is the main limitation - the contrastive objective reaches its peak early, regardless of modality diversity or pre-training volume. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and presents a stronger foundation for future scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MELT and SALT, two multimodal contrastive learning architectures for geospatial self-supervised pre-training that align location encoders with multiple unpaired data modalities. While both match the best two-modality baseline (SATCLIP), adding more modalities does not consistently boost performance—the location encoder, not modality diversity, is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Spatial prediction tasks suffer from scarce high-quality labelled ground-truth data. Self-supervised contrastive pre-training offers a remedy, but existing methods align location with only one other modality. The authors aim to scale contrastive location encoding to multiple modalities using unpaired geospatial data to improve representation quality.
AI.method: Two architectures are introduced: (1) MELT (Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying), which ties all modality embeddings through a shared location encoder in a single joint objective; and (2) SALT (Sequential Alternating Location Training), which alternately trains the location encoder against different modalities in sequence. Both leverage unpaired geospatial data and are evaluated against the SATCLIP baseline across four downstream tasks.
AI.result: Both MELT and SALT match SATCLIP's performance across all four downstream tasks. However, increasing modality count does not consistently improve outcomes. The contrastive objective saturates early regardless of modality diversity or pre-training data volume, indicating the location encoder architecture is the primary limiting factor. MELT exhibits more stable training than SALT.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal contrastive pre-training with unpaired data is viable and can match two-modality baselines, but naively adding modalities yields diminishing returns. Future work should focus on improving the location encoder itself rather than merely scaling modalities. MELT is recommended as the more stable foundation for such scaling efforts.

title: Predicting gestational age at birth in the context of preterm birth from multi-modal fetal MRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA) https://melba-journal.org/2026:013
summary: Preterm birth is associated with significant mortality and a risk for lifelong morbidity. The complex multifactorial aetiology hampers accurate prediction and thus optimal care. A pipeline consisting of bespoke machine learning methods for data imputation, feature selection, and regression models to predict gestational age (GA) at birth was developed and evaluated from comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI data from 333 control cases and 93 preterm birth cases. The GA at birth predictions were classified into term and preterm categories and their accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were reported. An ablation study was performed to further validate the design of the pipeline. Performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The pipeline achieves an R2 score of 0.13 and a mean absolute error of 2.74 weeks. It also achieves a 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity across folds. The predominant features selected by the pipeline include cervical length and statistics derived from placental T2* values. The confluence of fast, motion-robust and multi-modal fetal MRI techniques and machine learning prediction allowed the prediction of the gestation at birth. This information is essential for any pregnancy. To the best of our knowledge, preterm birth had only been addressed as a classification problem in the literature. Therefore, this work provides a proof of concept. Future work will increase the cohort size to allow for finer stratification within the preterm birth cohort. Our code is available at https://github.com/dfajardorojas/ml-for-preterm-birth-.

AI.tldr: A machine learning pipeline using multi-modal fetal MRI data (333 controls, 93 preterm cases) predicts gestational age at birth with moderate accuracy (R²=0.13, MAE=2.74 weeks) and classifies preterm vs. term birth (0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, 0.82 specificity). Cervical length and placental T2* features were most predictive.
AI.motivation: Preterm birth carries high mortality and lifelong morbidity risks, yet its complex multifactorial etiology hampers accurate prediction, limiting optimal clinical care. There is a need for data-driven predictive tools leveraging comprehensive fetal imaging.
AI.method: A bespoke pipeline integrating data imputation, feature selection, and regression models was developed using multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI from 426 cases (333 controls, 93 preterm). Performance was assessed via stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with an ablation study for pipeline validation. The task was framed as both regression (predicting GA at birth) and classification (term vs. preterm).
AI.result: The pipeline achieved R²=0.13 and MAE=2.74 weeks for GA regression, with classification metrics of 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity. Dominant predictive features were cervical length and placental T2* statistics.
AI.conclusion: Combining fast, motion-robust multi-modal fetal MRI with machine learning enables prediction of gestation at birth, establishing proof of concept. Prior work treated preterm birth only as classification; this study introduces a regression approach. Larger cohorts are needed for finer preterm stratification.

title: Computational Methods and Challenges in Cell-Free DNA Analysis for Multi-Cancer Early Detection
summary: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a promising avenue for non-invasive multicancer early detection (MCED), in that, it can enable multiple cancer detection simultaneously from a single blood draw, with particular sensitivity to cancers that currently lack established screening programs. Here we review the computational methods developed between 2022 and 2025 for cfDNA-based MCED. We focus on how fragmentomics and epigenetic features are extracted and analyzed to detect cancer at early stages. We first briefly outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then review classical statistical and machine learning approaches alongside deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. For each method we discuss biological interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical integration. Furthermore, we categorize the current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological while outlining open problems in the field. This review shows that multimodal ensemble approaches have the strongest promise for clinical integration and the highest readiness. However, for better assessment of future work and side-by-side comparison, standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results will be crucial.

AI.tldr: This review surveys computational methods (2022–2025) for cell-free DNA-based multicancer early detection, focusing on fragmentomic and epigenetic feature extraction. It covers classical statistical methods, machine learning, and deep learning (autoencoder-based models), assessing each for interpretability, validation, and clinical readiness. The review concludes that multimodal ensemble approaches are most promising for clinical integration, but standardization of evaluation protocols is urgently needed.
AI.motivation: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) enables non-invasive, simultaneous detection of multiple cancers from a single blood draw, especially for cancers lacking established screening programs. However, the field lacks a systematic survey of recent computational methods (2022–2025) for cfDNA-based MCED, particularly regarding how fragmentomic and epigenetic features are leveraged, and there is no consensus on evaluation standards or clinical readiness assessment.
AI.method: This is a narrative review. The authors first outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then systematically survey computational methods published between 2022 and 2025. They categorize approaches into (1) classical statistical and machine learning methods and (2) deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. Each method is analyzed along three axes: biological interpretability, validation strategy, and clinical integration readiness. The review also identifies and categorizes current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological domains.
AI.result: Multimodal ensemble approaches demonstrate the strongest promise and highest readiness for clinical integration. Across the surveyed methods, key challenges span technical (e.g., low tumor fraction in early-stage disease), computational (e.g., feature extraction robustness), and methodological (e.g., lack of standardized benchmarks) domains. The review identifies standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting as critical for enabling fair comparison and advancing the field.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal ensemble methods combining fragmentomic and epigenetic features represent the most clinically viable direction for cfDNA-based MCED. However, progress is hindered by the absence of unified evaluation standards. Future work must prioritize benchmark standardization and transparent reporting to enable rigorous, side-by-side comparisons and accelerate clinical translation.

title: cAPM: Continual AI-Assisted Pace-Mapping with Active Learning
summary: Ventricular tachycardia is a life-threatening rhythm disorder and a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Pace-mapping is a clinical procedure for identifying the intervention target during catheter ablation of VT. It requires clinicians to pace different sites in the ventricles and rapidly interpret the resulting electrocardiograms to determine where to pace next or whether a target site has been identified. Active learning AI models have been proposed to guide clinicians to the next pacing site, showing promise in reducing the number of pacing sites and improving the efficiency of pace-mapping. Existing methods require retraining each target without the ability to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. We introduce cAPM for continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping to capture and transfer knowledge accumulated from past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pace-mapping data needed for future target VTs. This is made possible by a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, an active-learning strategy that refines this surrogate model by selecting the most informative pacing site for each target, and a continual learning strategy to do so sequentially while retaining knowledge from prior targets. Evaluated on an in-silico testbed consisting of sequentially-presented localization tasks across different physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM with and without replay of past data samples achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (5 mm accuracy) using 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% probability using 13.7 pacing sites. These results provide a strong basis for preparing cAPM towards in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies where it can be used to guide pace-mapping.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces cAPM, a continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping framework that leverages continual and active learning to transfer knowledge across sequential ventricular tachycardia (VT) localization tasks, dramatically reducing the number of pacing sites needed (4.5 vs 13.7) while achieving substantially higher localization accuracy (81% vs 38% within 5 mm) compared to existing active-learning methods.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-assisted pace-mapping methods for VT localization require retraining from scratch for each new target, failing to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. This inefficiency demands excessive pacing — a burdensome clinical procedure. A method that accumulates and transfers knowledge across tasks would reduce pacing burden and improve clinical workflow.
AI.method: cAPM combines three components: (1) a task-agnostic surrogate neural network mapping pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, (2) an active-learning strategy selecting the most informative next pacing site for each VT target, and (3) a continual learning strategy enabling sequential learning across targets without catastrophic forgetting, optionally augmented with replay of past data samples. Evaluation used an in-silico testbed with sequentially-presented localization tasks spanning varied physiological conditions and ventricular geometries.
AI.result: cAPM achieved 81% probability of localizing within 5 mm clinical tolerance using only 4.5 pacing sites on average, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving only 38% probability with 13.7 pacing sites. The replay variant helped retain prior task knowledge while maintaining strong forward-transfer performance.
AI.conclusion: cAPM demonstrates that continual and active learning can be combined to transfer knowledge across VT pace-mapping tasks, significantly reducing data requirements and improving localization accuracy. These results provide a strong basis for advancing toward in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies.

title: Effective Dimension Governs Generalization in Quantum Kernel Vision Models
summary: Recent quantum vision models-quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks-report two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena: (i) ansatze with more, or more uniformly distributed, entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy rather than degrade it. These observations are currently treated as curiosities, discovered by grid search and explained, if at all, by hand. We show that both are manifestations of a single, measurable quantity: the \emph{effective dimension} $d_{\rm eff}$ of the (noise-shaped) quantum feature kernel. Working primarily with quantum-kernel vision models-a quantum feature map read out by a kernel classifier-we give a spectral account in which entanglement structure and quantum noise are two knobs that move $d_{\rm eff}$; in an overfitting regime, contracting $d_{\rm eff}$ acts as ridge-like regularization. We analyze the mechanism: an \emph{exact} decomposition of the depolarized kernel $K_p=(1-p)^2K+\tfrac{p(2-p)}{D}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ with $d_{\rm eff}(K_p)\to1$, a contraction result (and its boundary) for amplitude damping, a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition; the monotone contraction operative in our entangled experiments is verified empirically, not proven in general. Along the one-parameter depolarizing family the collapse is instead exact by construction; we use it only to confirm the kernel decomposition to machine precision and at up to $12$ qubits, not as evidence for $d_{\rm eff}$. Amplitude damping contracts $d_{\rm eff}$ and lifts test accuracy by up to $+13\%$ along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between the over- and under-fitting regimes; noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. Our results organize two reported anecdotes into a single measurable principle for designing quantum-vision models.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that two unexplained empirical phenomena in quantum vision models—better generalization with more entanglement and improved accuracy from noise injection—are both manifestations of a single measurable quantity: the effective dimension of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel. In overfitting regimes, reducing effective dimension via entanglement structure or quantum noise acts as ridge-like regularization.
AI.motivation: Two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena have been observed in quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks: (i) ansätze with more uniformly distributed entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy. These observations lack a unifying theoretical framework and are currently explained only by hand or grid search.
AI.method: The authors work primarily with quantum-kernel vision models (quantum feature map + kernel classifier). They provide a spectral analysis centered on the effective dimension d_eff of the quantum feature kernel. Key technical contributions include: (1) an exact decomposition of the depolarized kernel K_p = (1-p)²K + [p(2-p)/D]·11ᵀ with d_eff(K_p)→1; (2) a contraction result for amplitude damping; (3) a kernel-machine capacity bound; (4) a capacity/alignment risk decomposition. Empirical verification is performed at up to 12 qubits, confirming the kernel decomposition to machine precision.
AI.result: Both entanglement structure and quantum noise are shown to be two knobs controlling d_eff. In overfitting regimes, contracting d_eff acts as ridge-like regularization. Amplitude damping contracts d_eff and lifts test accuracy by up to +13% along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between overfitting and underfitting regimes. Noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier.
AI.conclusion: The paper organizes two previously reported empirical anecdotes into a single measurable principle—effective kernel dimension—for designing quantum vision models. Entanglement and noise are unified as mechanisms that modulate spectral properties of the quantum feature kernel, with regularization-like benefits in overfitting scenarios.

title: Learner-based Concept Drift Detection: Analysis and Evaluation
summary: Machine learning algorithms deployed for evolving streaming environments must handle the non-stationary data distributions, commonly referred to as concept drift. The presence of concept drift poses a major challenge for many real-world applications because it can severely degrade their predictive performance, hindering their ability to support robust decision-making. Consequently, the timely and efficient detection of drift events is critical for sustaining high accuracy over time. This study examines theoretically the concept drift characteristics and numerous drift detection algorithms across several categories. Furthermore, we evaluate their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, such as abrupt and gradual changes. This study aims to enhance understanding of the complex notion of concept drift characteristics and behavior of drift detectors, along with their applicability to diverse contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a theoretical examination of concept drift characteristics and a comparative evaluation of numerous drift detection algorithms across different categories, tested on both synthetic and real-world streaming datasets with abrupt and gradual drift patterns.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models in streaming environments suffer performance degradation due to concept drift (non-stationary data distributions), making timely and efficient drift detection essential for maintaining high predictive accuracy and robust decision-making in real-world applications.
AI.method: The authors conduct a two-part study: (1) a theoretical analysis of concept drift characteristics, and (2) an empirical evaluation of multiple drift detection algorithms from various categories on both synthetic and real-world datasets featuring diverse streaming scenarios and drift types (abrupt, gradual).
AI.result: The paper presents comparative performance results of various drift detectors under different drift characteristics and streaming scenarios, though specific quantitative outcomes are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The study enhances understanding of concept drift characteristics and the behavior of drift detectors, providing insights into their applicability across diverse contexts, thereby aiding practitioners in selecting appropriate detection methods for specific streaming environments.

title: Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities. In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.

AI.tldr: Graph neural networks suffer from spurious correlations from irrelevant neighbors, especially near class boundaries. The authors propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning plug-in that selectively suppresses structural noise at decision boundaries, achieving consistent improvements in node classification and link prediction.
AI.motivation: GNN performance is degraded by graph structural entanglement — semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings via spurious correlations. This problem is most severe for nodes near class boundaries, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries. Existing robust GNN methods treat all nodes uniformly, overlooking these boundary-specific vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The paper proposes Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning plug-in module for GNNs. BES identifies boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal perturbation to model parameters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms leading methods. BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.
AI.conclusion: Graph structural disentanglement, particularly targeting boundary-region vulnerabilities, is an effective strategy for improving GNN robustness. BES demonstrates that selective, boundary-aware noise suppression yields significant gains with minimal parameter overhead.

title: Integrating national forest inventory, airborne lidar, and satellite imagery for wall-to-wall mapping of forest structure with computer vision
summary: Remote sensing is increasingly relied upon to deliver actionable science for forest and wildfire risk management across large landscapes. Wall-to-wall, annually updated maps are a persistent need for effective forest management. Many planning systems and data collections combine disparate data sources with different purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, which leads to confounding behavior in operational planning systems. We introduce the VibrantForests framework, developed and applied to map forest attributes and provide a coherent foundation for effective forest and wildfire planning. VibrantForests includes a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples and applied across the contiguous United States to concurrently generate estimates of canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter at 10-meter resolution. We demonstrate predictive capability spanning the full spectrum of forest conditions ranging from sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass. Results show that our model extends the range at which saturation is commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models, and reduces regression-to-mean behavior that commonly produces overestimation of forest attributes in small/sparse conditions and underestimation in large/dense conditions. The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at annual cadence and 10m resolution.

AI.tldr: VibrantForests is a satellite-based framework that produces wall-to-wall, 10m-resolution, annually updated maps of forest attributes (canopy cover, height, biomass, basal area, quadratic mean diameter) across the contiguous US, trained on lidar-derived samples. It reduces saturation and regression-to-mean biases common in passive-sensor models, providing a coherent foundation for forest and wildfire risk management.
AI.motivation: Current forest and wildfire planning systems combine disparate data sources with varying purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, causing confounding behavior in operational planning. There is a persistent need for coherent, annually updated, wall-to-wall forest attribute maps at management-relevant scales.
AI.method: The VibrantForests framework uses a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived reference samples. The model concurrently estimates five forest attributes — canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter — at 10-meter spatial resolution across the contiguous United States.
AI.result: The model demonstrates predictive capability across the full spectrum of forest conditions (sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass). It extends the saturation range typical of comparable passive-sensor models and reduces regression-to-mean behavior, mitigating overestimation in sparse conditions and underestimation in dense conditions.
AI.conclusion: VibrantForests addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent, wall-to-wall, annually updated estimates of management-relevant forest attributes at 10m resolution, enabling more effective operational decision-making.

title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
summary: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: SLiR is a broadly applicable method for generating linear relaxations of neural network activation functions for formal verification, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or critical points. It parameterizes relaxations by slope and computes offsets via a shifting procedure, achieving up to 7.8x more verified properties than existing hand-crafted approaches.
AI.motivation: Neural network verification methods rely on linear relaxations of activation functions to provide formal guarantees, but existing techniques require labor-intensive, hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. This manual effort limits extensibility to new and complex activation functions used in state-of-the-art models.
AI.method: SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) uses slope-parameterized linear bounds and computes offsets via a shifting procedure that guarantees sound upper and lower bounds across the entire input domain. The method requires only minimal function-specific information: a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that SLiR produces tight relaxations for a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: SLiR provides a general, automated, and efficient approach for generating linear relaxations, significantly reducing the manual effort needed for NN verification across diverse activation functions while improving verification performance.

title: Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions
summary: Classical approximation theorems ask for a new neural network whenever the target accuracy is improved. This paper studies the opposite possibility: can the network be chosen once and for all, and can accuracy be bought only by letting it run longer? We prove that this is possible for every continuous function on [-1,1]. More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The mechanism behind the construction is a new intermediate model, the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). This model retains the algorithmic freedom needed to implement polynomial approximation schemes, while remaining rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. The resulting convergence rates reflect the underlying polynomial approximation rates. We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension can uniformly approximate any continuous function on [-1,1] by simply running longer, eliminating the need to redesign the network for improved accuracy. The key enabler is the Turing Machine with Neural Units (TMNU), an intermediate abstraction that balances algorithmic flexibility with structural rigidity.
AI.motivation: Classical approximation theory requires constructing a new neural network each time target accuracy increases. The authors challenge this paradigm by asking whether a single fixed network can instead achieve arbitrary accuracy merely through extended runtime, thereby decoupling approximation quality from architectural redesign.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Turing Machine with Neural Units (TMNU), an intermediate model that retains sufficient algorithmic freedom to implement polynomial approximation schemes while being restrictive enough to be simulated by ReLU RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitudes. Using TMNU as a bridge, they construct a single fixed-weight RNN whose time evolution uniformly approximates any continuous function on [-1,1] to arbitrary precision as runtime increases. Convergence rates are tied to underlying polynomial approximation rates. Minimax lower bounds complement the construction.
AI.result: Every continuous function on [-1,1] can be uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU RNN with fixed architecture. The convergence rates are governed by polynomial approximation rates. Minimax lower bounds demonstrate that runtime is an essential and unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The fixed-network, runtime-driven approximation paradigm is viable for continuous functions on compact intervals. The TMNU abstraction provides a principled bridge between algorithmic expressiveness and neural realizability. Runtime is not a mere proof artifact but a fundamental resource in this setting.

title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs
summary: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

AI.tldr: QCPIKAN is a hybrid quantum-classical framework combining Chebyshev-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold networks with parameterized quantum circuits to solve PDEs. It embeds physical constraints via a physics-informed loss, achieves exponential high-frequency error convergence, and outperforms existing quantum-classical PINNs on seepage problems in porous media.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks face limitations in accuracy, error control, and numerical dispersion when solving complex PDEs. The authors aim to leverage the approximation power of Kolmogorov-Arnold representations with Chebyshev polynomials and quantum circuits to overcome these shortcomings.
AI.method: The framework, QCPIKAN, integrates Chebyshev-polynomial-based Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) layers with parameterized quantum circuits. Physical laws are embedded as constraints in the training loss function. Approximation theory is used to prove exponential convergence rates for high-frequency error components and effective mitigation of numerical dispersion.
AI.result: Validated on three seepage scenarios — single-phase flow, component transport, and two-phase flow in porous media — QCPIKAN outperforms existing quantum-classical PINNs in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking, and displacement front localization.
AI.conclusion: QCPIKAN offers a robust, efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative for solving complex PDEs, with demonstrated superiority in physics-constrained learning tasks involving porous media flows.

title: Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems
summary: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

AI.tldr: A hybrid modeling framework that uses neural networks to predict biokinetic parameters of a soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits, constrained by ecological theory, demonstrating improved performance over baselines even with small datasets.
AI.motivation: Soil microorganisms govern organic matter cycling and climate feedbacks, but representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is data-limited. Integrating genomic (metagenomic) data offers promise, yet the relationship between genomes and microbial process rates is complex and unknown — an unsolved modeling challenge.
AI.method: The authors develop a hybrid modeling framework combining: (1) a process-based soil organic matter turnover model, (2) a neural network that maps metagenome-inferred functional traits (from DNA sequencing) to biokinetic parameters of that model, and (3) constraints from ecological theory and literature to enforce realistic behavior, including for unobserved state variables. Evaluation is performed on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data.
AI.result: The hybrid approach outperforms multiple baselines in predicting soil carbon dynamics. It effectively learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model and maintains strong performance even with small training datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating genomic data into process-based soil models via hybrid neural-network-constrained modeling is feasible and effective, offering a path toward more predictive soil carbon cycling models that leverage metagenomic information without requiring direct measurement of all microbial parameters.

title: Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a family of synthetic datasets built on critical mean-field percolation clusters, featuring hierarchical, multi-scale structure with sparsity, fractal geometry, and power-law size distributions. It proposes an almost linear-time sampling algorithm and demonstrates that ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations, positioning critical percolation as a principled testbed for interpretability research.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic datasets for evaluating interpretability methods lack the hierarchical, multi-scale structure characteristic of natural data, limiting their realism as toy models. The authors aim to create analytically tractable synthetic data that better reflects these structural properties.
AI.method: The authors construct hierarchical functions on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional space. These clusters are sparse, low-dimensional fractals with power-law size distributions. Latent variables following a taxonomic hierarchy generate target values. They establish a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to develop an almost linear-time algorithm for jointly sampling trees and their hierarchical latent decompositions at arbitrary scale. Probing experiments are used to assess whether latent variables are linearly decodable from neural network activations.
AI.result: The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without hyperparameter tuning. Probing experiments confirm that ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations.
AI.conclusion: The combination of sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability makes critical percolation a principled and realistic testbed for interpretability research, bridging the gap between simplistic synthetic datasets and natural data structure.

title: On the Variance of Temporal Difference Learning and its Reduction Using Control Variates
summary: We analyze the variance of temporal difference (TD) learning using the phased setting with tabular representation, and show that one of the mechanisms behind its ability to reduce variance is by effectively aggregating over a larger number of independent trajectories. Based on this insight, we demonstrate that (1) the variance of TD is asymptotically bounded from above by Monte Carlo (MC) estimators, and (2) shorter horizon updates incurs less variance for a fixed number of samples. Beyond TD, we show that Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE), a method for estimating the advantage function, can be seen as a type of regression-adjusted control variate, which achieves a tighter bound on the variance compared to TD in the large-sample limit. Finally, we numerically illustrate the behaviors of these estimators with carefully designed environments.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes TD learning variance in the tabular phased setting, showing it reduces variance by aggregating over more independent trajectories. It proves TD variance is asymptotically bounded above by MC estimators, shorter horizons reduce variance, and DAE achieves tighter variance bounds via regression-adjusted control variates.
AI.motivation: To understand why temporal difference (TD) learning exhibits lower variance than Monte Carlo methods, and to formally characterize the variance properties of TD learning and related advantage estimation methods in reinforcement learning.
AI.method: The authors use the phased setting with tabular representation to analyze variance. They decompose TD learning's variance reduction mechanism as effective aggregation over independent trajectories, derive asymptotic variance bounds comparing TD to MC, analyze horizon length effects, and recast Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) as a regression-adjusted control variate for tighter variance analysis.
AI.result: Key results: (1) TD variance is asymptotically upper-bounded by MC estimator variance; (2) shorter horizon updates yield lower variance for a fixed sample budget; (3) DAE, viewed as a regression-adjusted control variate, achieves a tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit. Numerical experiments in controlled environments corroborate the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: TD learning's variance advantage over MC stems from effectively leveraging more independent trajectories through shorter-horizon updates. DAE further improves upon TD by functioning as a regression-adjusted control variate, offering tighter variance guarantees asymptotically.

title: Train, Retrieve, or Both? A Four-Arm Head-to-Head for Correct Statutory Citation on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act
summary: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need to be pointed at the provision of law that actually governs a question, with a correct statutory citation. We study this task on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) and its core regulation, asking the operator's question empirically: is fine-tuning enough, or is hybrid retrieval needed? We run a four-arm head-to-head on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (base zero-shot, LoRA SFT-only, RAG-only, and an SFT+RAG hybrid), scored on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The base model cannot cite the RTA and SFT-only mis-recalls sections; retrieval is essential and drives hallucination to zero by construction; and the SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. Its edge comes from SFT making provision selection more robust to the higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. Notably, this cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats a pipeline built on bigger, specialized retrieval models (a larger embedder and a cross-encoder reranker), and a larger/improved training set does not help either: strong statutory-citation performance here does not require specialized retrieval models or more data. The artifact zeroes hallucination and clears the lift-over-base bar but does not reach the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set and are reported as preliminary.

AI.tldr: Evaluates whether fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or a hybrid approach best enables statutory citation of the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act. Fine-tuning alone mis-recalls sections; retrieval eliminates hallucination; the SFT+RAG hybrid achieves the highest exact-match (0.481) with zero hallucinated citations, matching or exceeding pipelines using larger specialized retrieval models.
AI.motivation: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need accurate statutory citations to the governing law. The authors empirically investigate whether fine-tuning alone suffices for this legally sensitive task or whether hybrid retrieval is necessary to achieve reliable, hallucination-free citations.
AI.method: Four-arm comparison using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: (1) base zero-shot, (2) LoRA SFT-only, (3) RAG-only, and (4) SFT+RAG hybrid. Evaluated on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, real-world, human-verification-pending eval set. Also compares bge-small hybrid against pipelines with larger embedders and cross-encoder rerankers, and tests effect of larger training sets.
AI.result: Base model fails entirely. SFT-only mis-recalls sections. RAG eliminates hallucination by construction. SFT+RAG hybrid achieves 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. SFT improves robustness to higher-recall candidate sets that degrade zero-shot RAG. The cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats larger specialized retrieval pipelines. Larger training data provides no benefit.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval is essential; SFT+RAG hybrid is the strongest approach, zeroing hallucination. Strong statutory-citation performance does not require specialized retrieval models or large training data. Results fall short of the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target and are preliminary, pending human verification.

title: Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation
summary: A companion study established a de-biased, cross-model VLM-as-3D-judge that reliably ranks single-image-to-3D mesh quality where cheap geometry and CLIP proxies fall short. This paper asks: can that judge's preferences specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on one asset class (furniture), cheaply and without human labels? Taking the judge from ranking to optimization is where the work lives. Pushing a VLM judge into the training and evaluation loop exposes failure modes ranking never triggered, so our contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the judge: a training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) held distinct from an evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; position-bias correction; and fixes for three failure modes (image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs), with calibration evidence (clear-gap win-rate 0.83-1.0; base-vs-base ~0.5). Using this protocol as an independent evaluator, and working only from public models and data with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation, we find our methods match the strong base rather than exceed it. Independent base samples carry essentially no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), so signal must be engineered by quality-contrastive construction. Across six adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, the most targeted - conditioner repair under severe degradation - reaches parity (0.50) with the base, while no method clears the >=65% win-rate target. The result is mechanistic: clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DIT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects. Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it needs more than lightweight PEFT on public data, and the judge protocol is reusable.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a VLM-as-3D-judge can be used to cheaply specialize a strong open 3D generator (TRELLIS) on furniture assets without human labels. The core contribution is hardening the judge for optimization loops, then testing six lightweight adaptation methods — finding none exceed the base model, with only conditioner repair under severe degradation reaching parity.
AI.motivation: Prior work established VLMs as reliable 3D quality judges for ranking, but using such judges for optimization/training introduces failure modes that ranking never surfaces. The authors aim to bridge this gap: can a VLM judge's preferences effectively drive cheap, label-free specialization of a strong generator, and what engineering is needed to make the judge robust enough for this purpose?
AI.method: The authors harden the VLM judge for optimization-grade use via: (1) separating training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) from evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to prevent circularity; (2) position-bias correction; (3) fixing three failure modes — image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs. Using this protocol, they test six parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods across two input regimes and a degradation severity sweep, applying quality-contrastive construction since independent base samples lack learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate). All work uses public models and data only.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Independent base samples carry almost no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), necessitating engineered quality-contrastive signal. (2) Across six adaptation methods, only conditioner repair under severe degradation reaches parity with the base (0.50 win-rate); no method achieves the ≥65% win-rate target. (3) Clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DiT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the only locus that meaningfully moves geometry. (4) Calibration evidence shows clear-gap win-rates of 0.83–1.0 and base-vs-base near 0.5, validating the evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: Matching a strong public-data base model via cheap, label-free adaptation is informative in itself: exceeding it requires more than lightweight PEFT on public data. The hardened judge protocol is reusable for future work. The mechanistic insight is that conditioning repair is the most effective intervention point for geometry improvement, while other adaptation approaches wash out or saturate.

title: CRAX: Fast Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmarking
summary: Safety is a core concern for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving. While benchmarks have been central to progress in RL, existing safety benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics remain computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. To address this gap, we propose CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX). Built on top of the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine with realistic 3D dynamics, CRAX leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration, yielding up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. The benchmark features six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Evaluating six popular safe RL methods shows that no single approach dominates across all tasks, and reveals the trade-offs between performance and safety. We find that curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer can improve performance over direct training in harder settings.

AI.tldr: CRAX is a hardware-accelerated safety benchmark for constrained RL built on MuJoCo XLA, achieving ~100x speedups over CPU-based alternatives, featuring six environment suites with three difficulty levels, and revealing that curriculum learning and safety transfer improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks for RL with high-fidelity 3D physics are computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. There is a need for a fast, scalable benchmark that enables systematic evaluation of safe RL methods.
AI.method: CRAX is built on the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine using JAX. It leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration (GPUs/TPUs) to achieve massive parallelism. The benchmark includes six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each with three difficulty levels (easy, medium, hard). Six popular safe RL methods (CPO, PPO-Lagrangian, TRPO-Lagrangian, SAC-Lagrangian, safety-layer-based approaches, etc.) are evaluated across all configurations.
AI.result: CRAX achieves up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. No single safe RL method dominates across all tasks — performance-safety trade-offs are task-dependent. Curriculum learning (training on easier difficulties before harder ones) and safety transfer improve performance compared to direct training on harder settings.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-accelerated benchmarks like CRAX enable rapid, large-scale experimentation in safe RL. The findings highlight the need for adaptive safe RL approaches, as no universal method excels universally. Curriculum learning and safety transfer are effective strategies for scaling to harder tasks.

title: Towards Modality-imbalanced Federated Graph Learning: A Data Synthesis-based Approach
summary: MultiModal Federated Graph Learning (MM-FGL) offers a natural collaborative training paradigm, but its practical deployment is challenged by two granularities of modality imbalance. Client-level imbalance occurs when certain clients lack entire modalities, while node-level imbalance occurs when individual nodes exhibit missing visual or textual attributes. While several relevant studies exist, our investigation reveals that they predominantly target graph-agnostic or centralized scenarios, rendering them difficult to adapt directly. To address these challenges, we formalize modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as an implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis problem. This paradigm recovers missing modal semantics directly within the representation space, thereby maximizing alignment with the original data's semantic distribution and mitigating the high variance induced by missing modalities. To this end, we propose FedMGS (Federated Modality-aware Graph Synthesis), which integrates three core components. The availability-aware graph encoder prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation. The prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities. The reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism regulates the impact of recovered latent representations prior to predictive readout. Extensive experiments on four tasks show that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41% with best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

AI.tldr: FedMGS addresses modality-imbalanced MultiModal Federated Graph Learning by synthesizing missing modal semantics in latent representation space via a prototype-guided approach, outperforming baselines by up to 17.41%.
AI.motivation: Practical deployment of MM-FGL suffers from two granularities of modality imbalance — client-level (entire modalities missing) and node-level (individual nodes missing visual/textual attributes). Existing solutions target graph-agnostic or centralized settings and cannot be directly adapted.
AI.method: FedMGS formulates modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis with three components: (1) an availability-aware graph encoder that prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation; (2) a prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer that establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities; (3) a reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism that regulates the impact of recovered latent representations before predictive readout.
AI.result: FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines across four tasks with gains up to 17.41% while maintaining the best efficiency-performance tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FedMGS effectively addresses both client-level and node-level modality imbalance in federated graph learning by synthesizing missing semantics in latent space, offering a practical and superior solution for real-world MM-FGL deployment.

title: The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. Also, we propose two novel post-hoc stylization models called Univ and Exam to transform synthetic LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like linguistic styles. To enhance data quality, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge filtering process. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Crucially, the findings reveal that style diversity is more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating style attributes during the generation process is more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.

AI.tldr: A framework for generating synthetic dialogue data for intent classification without any human-annotated seed data, using only intent definitions. It employs topic/style attributes for diversity, two post-hoc stylization models (Univ and Exam), and LLM-as-a-judge filtering. Style diversity proves more critical than topic diversity for downstream utility.
AI.motivation: Human-annotated seed data for intent classification is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings, creating a need for fully automated synthetic data generation that relies solely on intent definitions.
AI.method: The framework generates synthetic dialogues using only intent definitions, incorporating topic and style attributes during generation. Two post-hoc stylization models (Univ and Exam) transform LLM-generated utterances into varied linguistic styles. An LLM-as-a-judge filtering process is applied to enhance data quality.
AI.result: The approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained with human-annotated training data on both industrial and public datasets. Style diversity is more critical than topic diversity, and incorporating style attributes during generation outperforms post-hoc style adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Style diversity prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations and is the dominant factor for synthetic data utility. Attribute-controlled generation is preferable to post-hoc stylization. The framework offers a viable path for intent classification without human annotation in industrial contexts.

title: Direct Advantage Estimation for Scalable and Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) has been shown to improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its reliance on full environment observability limits its applicability in realistic settings, and its requirement to model transition probabilities incurs substantial computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. In the present work, we address both limitations. First, we extend the theoretical framework of DAE to partially observable domains with minimal modifications. Second, we reduce its computational complexity by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities. We evaluate our approach on the Arcade Learning Environment and find that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

AI.tldr: DAE is extended to partially observable domains and made computationally efficient via discrete latent dynamics models, demonstrating scalability and sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.
AI.motivation: DAE improves sample efficiency in deep RL but is limited by its requirement for full observability and high computational cost from modeling transition probabilities in high-dimensional observation spaces.
AI.method: The theoretical framework of DAE is extended to partially observable settings with minimal modifications. Computational complexity is reduced by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities.
AI.result: The approach scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.
AI.conclusion: DAE can be successfully adapted to partially observable domains with discrete latent dynamics, overcoming its two key limitations while preserving sample efficiency.

title: Pseudo-Feature Padding: A Lightweight Defense Against False Data Injection in Power Grids
summary: Deep Neural Networks DNNs have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks including their application in CyberPhysical Systems CPS for detecting False Data Injection Attacks FDIA during critical operations However the unique infrastructure of CPS makes DNNs vulnerable to exploitation by attackers aiming to evade detection Additionally the distinct nature of CPS presents challenges for conventional defense mechanisms against FDIA This paper proposes an innovative defense framework that strengthens DNNs against such attacks by introducing an additional input layer that performs padding in the input samples using pseudofeature values derived from the inputs statistical distribution This padding increases the input dimensionality in a randomized and dataaware manner making adversarial attacks computationally infeasible due to the nontransferable nature of crafted perturbations and the unpredictability of the padded structure Our method is lightweight modelagnostic and requires no modifications to the core architecture making it highly deployable in realworld CPS settings We evaluated our framework on critical power grid applications such as state estimation using the IEEE 14bus 30bus 118bus and 300bus systems Experiments under adversarial settings demonstrate that our padding strategy significantly improves model robustness with negligible impact on performance and effectively mitigates attacks that would otherwise bypass conventional defenses

AI.tldr: A lightweight, model-agnostic defense framework for DNNs in CPS against FDIA evasion attacks, using randomized, data-aware pseudo-feature padding to increase input dimensionality, making adversarial perturbations non-transferable and computationally infeasible.
AI.motivation: DNNs deployed in CPS for FDIA detection are vulnerable to adversarial evasion attacks due to CPS-specific infrastructure constraints. Conventional defense mechanisms are ill-suited to the distinct nature of CPS environments, creating a need for a tailored, deployable defense.
AI.method: An additional input layer performs padding on input samples using pseudo-feature values drawn from the input's statistical distribution. This increases input dimensionality in a randomized, data-aware manner, making adversarial perturbations non-transferable and the padded structure unpredictable. The approach requires no core architecture modifications.
AI.result: Evaluated on IEEE 14-bus, 30-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus power grid state estimation systems. The padding strategy significantly improved model robustness under adversarial settings with negligible performance impact, effectively mitigating attacks that bypass conventional defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pseudo-feature padding framework is a lightweight, model-agnostic, and highly deployable defense that strengthens DNN-based FDIA detectors in CPS against adversarial evasion, validated across multiple power grid benchmarks.

title: On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the necessity of explicit timestep embeddings in diffusion models, demonstrating both theoretically and empirically that time-agnostic architectures can achieve comparable or superior performance to conditioned counterparts on CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models universally rely on explicit timestep embeddings to guide denoising across noise levels. The authors question whether this architectural convention is truly necessary, aiming to simplify generative models by eliminating temporal conditioning.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical framework proving that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion objective can be reached without timestep conditioning. They conduct extensive ablation studies removing timestep embeddings from both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures, evaluating on CelebA and CIFAR-10 using metrics such as FID, precision, and recall.
AI.result: Time-agnostic models maintain high structural fidelity and can surpass conditioned models on FID, precision, and recall. The architectures appear capable of implicitly inferring noise scales from corrupted inputs, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant under specific assumptions.
AI.conclusion: This work challenges the long-standing paradigm of temporal conditioning in diffusion models and opens the door to more efficient, structurally focused generative architectures that forgo explicit timestep embeddings.

title: Neural network surrogates with uncertainty quantification for inverse problems in partial differential equations
summary: Inverse problems for differential equations arise throughout science and engineering, where one seeks to infer unknown model parameters from noisy or incomplete observations. Traditional numerical methods for these problems are often computationally expensive, particularly in Bayesian settings where evaluating the likelihood becomes costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces.
