To address this challenge, we introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions, reducing overconfident inference when training data are limited. To evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations in practice, we show that a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo can serve as an effective diagnostic. Across a range of numerical experiments, DeepGaLA delivers forward-model approximations with accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates, while better maintaining efficiency as parameter dimension grows. Moreover, it can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings. Overall, these results indicate that uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems.

AI.tldr: DeepGaLA is a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions for Bayesian inverse problems. It matches Gaussian-process surrogate accuracy while scaling better with parameter dimension, supports nonlinear differential-equation constraints, and uses delayed-acceptance MCMC as a diagnostic for surrogate fidelity.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical methods for inverse problems in differential equations are computationally expensive, especially in Bayesian settings where likelihood evaluation is costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. Existing surrogates (e.g., Gaussian processes) can struggle with scaling. There is a need for uncertainty-aware surrogates that avoid overconfident inference under limited training data.
AI.method: The authors propose DeepGaLA, a neural-network-based surrogate for differential equation solvers that quantifies predictive uncertainty. They employ delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo (DA-MCMC) as a diagnostic tool to assess the fidelity of surrogate-induced posterior approximations. The method can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including nonlinear ones.
AI.result: DeepGaLA achieves forward-model approximation accuracy comparable to Gaussian-process surrogates while maintaining better computational efficiency as parameter dimension increases. It successfully handles nonlinear differential-equation constraints. The DA-MCMC diagnostic effectively evaluates surrogate fidelity in practice.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates like DeepGaLA can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems, offering a practical alternative to traditional methods and Gaussian-process surrogates.

title: Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning
summary: Continual learning (CL) systems often forget previously acquired knowledge, yet the mechanisms driving forgetting remain hard to isolate in practice because real datasets entangle many factors. We present a controlled, toy-world framework that makes these mechanisms observable and testable. Using a synthetic generator-separator pipeline, we define ground-truth latent features, build tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional overlap among features). We then study retention dynamics-the temporal change of representation strength by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis based on effective rank characterizes how representational capacity is allocated across tasks. Our controlled experiments yield three takeaways. (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, suggesting boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet does not inevitably cause forgetting; when representations remain strong, forgetting can be reduced despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes. Together, these results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting by showing that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. Our toy analysis provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for CL.

AI.tldr: A controlled synthetic framework reveals that superposition (feature overlap) in continual learning does not inevitably cause forgetting; rather, forgetting depends on the interaction between overlap, representation strength, and capacity allocation, with superposition increasing transiently at task boundaries rather than through steady drift.
AI.motivation: Isolating the mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is difficult with real datasets because many confounding factors are entangled. The authors aim to create a controlled, observable, and testable framework to disentangle these mechanisms.
AI.method: A synthetic generator-separator pipeline defines ground-truth latent features with tunable sparsity and overlap. The authors introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition, then apply SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) to fit sparse dynamical relations among retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary effective-rank analysis characterizes capacity allocation across tasks.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Superposition increases over time with transient dips at task boundaries, indicating boundary-specific interference. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition but does not necessarily cause forgetting when representations remain strong. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, showing broader capacity usage under sparse regimes.
AI.conclusion: The results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting, showing instead that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. The framework provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for continual learning research.

title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: Equal advising: Daria Pugacheva and Fedor Ratnikov. Accepted to the ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and PDEs
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage evolutionary algorithm approach for hyperparameter optimization in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), using low-fidelity screening followed by full training of promising candidates, achieving better accuracy under fixed computational budgets.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and high sensitivity to hyperparameters due to the non-convex, multi-term physics-informed loss. Traditional hyperparameter search strategies (local/gradient-based) are easily trapped in suboptimal regions, motivating the need for robust, population-based exploration methods.
AI.method: A two-stage evolutionary algorithm approach: Stage 1 performs low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate hyperparameter configurations as a black-box outer-loop problem. Stage 2 fully trains only the most promising candidates using standard gradient-based optimizers to refine solutions.
AI.result: Evaluated on Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations, the proposed method consistently outperforms standard PINN training, achieving significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary algorithm-based two-stage hyperparameter search effectively improves PINN accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets by separating exploration (low-fidelity screening) from exploitation (full training of selected configurations).

title: Data Bias Mitigation under Coverage Constraints & The Price of Fairness
summary: Machine learning models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes, such as race and gender. This stems in part from two interrelated challenges: the lack of principled measures for quantifying bias (potentially intersectional), and insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. We extend a recent bias mitigation framework to incorporate coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. Since achieving exactly zero bias for all groups may not be data efficient (meaning it may require large amounts of data), our solution trades small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints. We also formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, and characterize the price of fairness, the minimum data modification cost, as a function of fairness tolerance. This is essential both for legal compliance, where regulations may mandate specific fairness thresholds, and for data governance, enabling practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly, data purchasing) costs. We evaluate our techniques on publicly available datasets, demonstrating that bias mitigation via our framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints, while motivated by statistical considerations, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bias mitigation framework with coverage constraints that ensures sufficient representation of intersectional subgroups while trading off small bias approximation errors for data efficiency. It formulates bias mitigation as an integer linear program, characterizes the "price of fairness," and demonstrates that coverage constraints preserve downstream ML accuracy.
AI.motivation: ML models exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes (e.g., race and gender). Two key challenges drive this: (1) lack of principled intersectional bias quantification measures, and (2) insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. Existing approaches struggle with the data efficiency vs. zero-bias trade-off and lack formal tools for compliance with fairness regulations.
AI.method: The authors extend a prior bias mitigation framework by incorporating coverage constraints that enforce minimum representation across all groups, including intersectional subgroups. They allow small approximation errors in bias to achieve greater data efficiency. Bias mitigation is formulated as an integer linear program (ILP) that optimizes over all possible mitigation strategies. The "price of fairness" is characterized as the minimum data modification cost as a function of fairness tolerance, enabling cost-fairness trade-off analysis.
AI.result: Evaluation on publicly available datasets shows that the proposed framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers. Coverage constraints are shown to be essential for maintaining downstream ML performance, validating their statistical motivation.
AI.conclusion: Coverage-constrained bias mitigation enables practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly data purchasing) costs. The ILP formulation provides a principled way to navigate legal compliance with mandated fairness thresholds while optimizing resource expenditure.

title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
summary: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

AI.tldr: ASYS is a framework that combines agent-guided symbolic search with gradient-based optimization to automatically discover interpretable analytical forms for PDE solutions, recovering known solutions and finding new approximations where none previously existed.
AI.motivation: Traditional PDE analysis relies on manual mathematical insight to uncover solution structures, while numerical methods and neural networks produce opaque results. There is a need for automated methods that can produce interpretable, analytical representations of PDE solutions.
AI.method: ASYS uses an LLM-based agent to translate PDE theory, problem constraints, and search history into differentiable symbolic programs. These programs undergo evolutionary search over their discrete symbolic forms while continuous parameters are optimized via gradient descent, effectively automating inductive-bias injection rather than performing blind symbolic regression.
AI.result: Across five PDE problems (bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, free-boundary focusing), ASYS recovered known analytical forms and discovered new interpretable approximations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up.
AI.conclusion: ASYS demonstrates a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions that goes beyond handcrafted analysis, mesh-based numerics, and neural network surrogates, suggesting automated symbolic discovery can both recover known theory and guide future mathematical analysis.

title: Fisher-Geometric Sharpness and the Implicit Bias of SGD toward Flat Minima
summary: A widely held intuition in deep learning is that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better, but standard Euclidean measures of flatness such as the trace or maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, which undermines the theoretical foundations of this narrative. In this study we resolve this issue by grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We define Riemannian sharpness mathematically and prove that it is invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations, which directly addresses the critique of Dinh et al. in the paper ``Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets''.We note that this invariance is a property of the true FIM; the diagonal empirical estimator used in practice (and in all experiments below) inherits invariance only approximately, and exact invariance under arbitrary reparametrizations would require structured estimators such as K-FAC. We formalize the gradient noise of mini-batch SGD as having a covariance structure proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting stochastic differential equation, and then show that the probability mass is exponentially concentrated at Riemannian-flat minima. A PAC-Bayes generalization bound controlled explicitly by SR formally links this geometric bias to test performance. Our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that SR reliably tracks generalization in ways that Euclidean sharpness does not, and that its scaling with $η/B$ matches the theoretical predictions. Together these results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the reparametrization-invariance problem of flatness measures by defining a Riemannian sharpness based on the Fisher Information Matrix geometry. It proves this measure is invariant under function-preserving reparametrizations, derives how SGD noise concentrates probability at Riemannian-flat minima, and provides a PAC-Bayes generalization bound. Experiments confirm Riemannian sharpness tracks generalization better than Euclidean measures.
AI.motivation: The conventional wisdom that SGD favors flat minima (which generalize well) relies on Euclidean sharpness measures like the Hessian trace or max eigenvalue. Dinh et al. (2017) showed these measures are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, undermining the theoretical basis. The authors aim to resolve this by grounding flatness in a geometrically principled, reparametrization-invariant framework using the Fisher Information Matrix.
AI.method: The authors (1) define "Riemannian sharpness" (S_R) as the product of the loss Hessian and inverse FIM trace, grounded in the statistical manifold's Riemannian geometry; (2) prove S_R is invariant under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations; (3) model mini-batch SGD gradient noise as having covariance proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting SDE, and show probability mass concentrates exponentially at low-S_R minima; (4) derive a PAC-Bayes generalization bound explicitly controlled by S_R; (5) validate on MNIST and CIFAR-10 that S_R tracks generalization and its scaling with η/B matches theory.
AI.result: Riemannian sharpness S_R is provably invariant under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations (exact for true FIM, approximate for diagonal empirical FIM). The stationary distribution analysis shows p(θ) ∝ exp(−S_R(θ)), confirming exponential concentration at flat minima. The PAC-Bayes bound links S_R directly to test error. Experiments show S_R reliably predicts generalization gap while Euclidean sharpness does not, and S_R scales linearly with η/B as predicted, unlike Euclidean measures.
AI.conclusion: The Riemannian sharpness framework provides a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize well, directly addressing Dinh et al.'s critique. The geometric bias of SGD toward low-S_R minima, combined with the PAC-Bayes generalization bound, establishes a theoretically sound link between the implicit regularization of SGD, flatness, and generalization.

title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
summary: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates 4-bit KV-cache compression for multi-round agentic workloads, proposing UltraQuant — an FP4 approximation path leveraging AMD GPU hardware. On long-context, multi-turn agent tasks, UltraQuant achieves 3.47x faster time-to-first-token in cache-pressured late rounds and 1.63x higher output throughput compared to FP8 KV caching.
AI.motivation: Context-heavy LLM agents produce workloads with long, reused prefixes across many short turns, placing extreme pressure on the KV cache. Existing approaches either sacrifice quality (aggressive quantization) or throughput (FP8). The authors aim to push KV-cache compression to 4 bits while jointly optimizing task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput — particularly targeting AMD GPU deployment where native FP4 hardware support exists.
AI.method: The authors build on TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality baseline and vLLM FP8 KV caching as a deployment baseline. Key design choices include: (1) asymmetric treatment of K and V tensors (different quantization strategies per tensor type), (2) Walsh-Hadamard rotation for incoherence processing, (3) QJL (Quasi-Johnson-Lindenstrauss) removal to reduce overhead, and (4) block-scale quantization variants. The final system, UltraQuant, uses FP8 queries with FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and leverages native scaled-MFMA (Matrix Fused Multiply-Add) instructions on AMD CDNA4 architecture, along with optimized decode-attention kernels.
AI.result: On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant reduces P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47× in the cache-pressured late rounds and by 2.3× averaged across all rounds. Output throughput improves by 1.63× over the FP8 KV baseline.
AI.conclusion: 4-bit KV-cache compression is viable for production agent workloads when quality, residency, and throughput are jointly optimized. The UltraQuant approach, combining asymmetric K/V quantization, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, and AMD CDNA4 native FP4 hardware support, delivers substantial latency and throughput gains over FP8 KV caching, particularly in cache-pressure scenarios typical of multi-turn agent serving.

title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution
summary: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

AI.tldr: Batch-style trace distillation suffers from contradictory feedback across batches. The authors formalize two structural conditions (alignability and comparability) and propose Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA), which uses EMA-based signed evidence accumulation with semantic identity merging to distinguish stable operations from accidental hits. MAA achieves best results in 14/16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 models, matching or surpassing online methods while reducing token consumption by ~75%.
AI.motivation: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation can receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing approaches lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to reliably distinguish genuinely effective operations from those that succeed only by chance (accidental hits). This fundamentally limits the quality of distilled traces.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the problem via two structural conditions — **alignability** (ensuring feedback signals can be meaningfully compared across batches) and **comparability** (ensuring the relative advantage of operations is measurable). The proposed **Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA)** method operates as a post-processing architecture with three key components: (1) constructing differential signals to achieve cross-batch comparability, (2) accumulating signed evidence per operation using exponential moving average (EMA), and (3) ensuring cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging, which maps semantically equivalent operations across batches to the same identity.
AI.result: MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 experimental settings spanning 4 benchmarks and 4 target models. It consistently outperforms existing batch-level distillation baselines and matches or surpasses online alternatives in most settings. Additionally, MAA reduces optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75% compared to online methods.
AI.conclusion: MAA demonstrates that a principled cross-batch evidence accumulation mechanism can effectively resolve contradictory feedback in batch-style trace distillation. The strong empirical performance, combined with significant efficiency gains (~75% fewer tokens), positions MAA as a compelling post-processing alternative to online distillation methods.

title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving
summary: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.

AI.tldr: FlashRT introduces execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint/restore mechanism for low-latency, on-device LLM serving. Unlike paged/radix KV caches that reuse token-level KV fragments, capsules snapshot and restore the complete execution state (KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata) at committed boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore achieves byte-exact state recovery and token-identical greedy decode, with sub-millisecond GPU-resident snapshot/restore and TTFT speedups of 3.9x–27x over cold prefill.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving systems optimize for high-throughput, high-concurrency scenarios using paged or radix KV caches, but these manage only one positional fragment of execution state (the KV cache). This is insufficient for low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive agents, speech systems, and robot policies frequently branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. The authors identify a complementary regime requiring complete, restorable execution-state reuse rather than token-addressed KV fragments.
AI.method: FlashRT provides a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime with an NVIDIA CUDA backend. It runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers without block-table indirection. The core innovation is the execution-state capsule: a graph-bound checkpoint that treats the live state as a closed set of named buffers, enabling snapshot, restore, fork, and rollback of the entire execution boundary. A KV-only ablation study isolates the contribution of non-KV state (recurrent, convolution, MTP, metadata). The system is evaluated on RTX 5090, Jetson AGX Thor, and DGX Spark.
AI.result: On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. The KV-only ablation diverges, confirming that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore complete in under one millisecond. TTFT speedup over cold prefill ranges from 3.9× at 2k tokens to 27× at 16k tokens. The same correctness and structural properties hold on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: Execution-state capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; rather, they define a complementary, latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse in low-latency, on-device physical-AI contexts. The approach shifts reuse granularity from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries.

title: Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning
summary: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/martianmartina/multi-task-bayesian-icl/.

AI.tldr: A multi-task in-context learning framework that amortizes hierarchical Bayesian inference by prefixing prior information into context, enabling transformer-based adaptation across diverse priors. It matches oracle Bayesian predictors at a fraction of the cost and generalizes to out-of-distribution priors.
AI.motivation: Exact Bayesian inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations either remain computationally expensive or impose restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context methods offer amortized alternatives but are tightly coupled to the training prior, lacking mechanisms to adapt to new priors at test time, which limits robustness under distribution shift.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference. Prior information is explicitly represented as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer is trained on sequences comprising both prior tasks and target tasks, enabling it to learn to adapt predictions across families of priors.
AI.result: Across evaluations of increasing difficulty — including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures — the method matches the performance of oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. It also demonstrates practical utility on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively decouples amortized inference from the training prior, achieving robust generalization under distribution shift while retaining computational efficiency. This advances the practical applicability of amortized Bayesian methods to real-world settings where prior knowledge varies.

title: Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy
summary: Differential privacy (DP) ensures rigorous individual-level privacy guarantees against even the most knowledgeable attackers, but its worst-case nature can impose a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. We introduce privacy via predictability, a fine-grained framework that explicitly incorporates the attacker's core knowledge, a compromised portion of the dataset generated by a stochastic process, and a specified family of queries. Predictability measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information about unknown individuals after observing the algorithm's output, beyond what can already be inferred from the compromised data. We show that predictability and DP are generally incomparable: each can be small while the other is large. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised, and all binary queries are considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. More generally, predictability provides a finer-grained privacy metric tailored to specific sensitive information and specific attacker models. We introduce a general framework, using the generalized method of moments (GMM), to analyze asymptotic predictability when the compromised data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing process. Using this analysis, we derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM. Our approach is complementary to DP and can be used alongside DP to provide fine-grained privacy control.

AI.tldr: Introduces "privacy via predictability," a fine-grained privacy framework measuring leakage as an attacker's improved ability to predict sensitive information from algorithm outputs beyond what compromised data already reveals. Shows incomparability with DP, derives asymptotic analysis via GMM for stationary ergodic mixing processes, and proposes a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for empirical risk minimization (ERM).
AI.motivation: Differential privacy's worst-case nature imposes a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. The authors seek a finer-grained framework that incorporates attacker knowledge (compromised data from a stochastic process) and specific query families, providing tailored privacy control without the one-size-fits-all burden of DP.
AI.method: The paper formalizes predictability as the incremental gain in an attacker's predictive capability for sensitive attributes given algorithm outputs, over and above what compromised data already leaks. It employs the generalized method of moments (GMM) to analyze asymptotic predictability under stationary, ergodic, mixing data processes, and derives a predictability-calibrated output perturbation mechanism for ERM.
AI.result: Predictability and DP are generally incomparable — each can be small while the other is large. In the worst-case regime (all but one individual compromised, all binary queries sensitive), predictability implies mutual-information DP. The GMM-based asymptotic analysis yields a practical perturbation scheme for ERM calibrated to predictability rather than DP.
AI.conclusion: Predictability offers a complementary, fine-grained privacy metric tailored to specific attacker models and sensitive queries. It can be used alongside DP to achieve nuanced privacy control, bridging the gap between worst-case guarantees and practical attacker-aware privacy.

title: The Token Is a Group Element: On Lie-Algebra Attention over Matrix Lie Groups
summary: We place the attention token on the group: a token is an element $g_i$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ -- a bare transformation, with no feature payload and no external action $ρ(g)$ carrying it. To our knowledge this is the first attention construction whose tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements: their score is the closed-form algebra norm of the relative pose rather than a learned kernel, and it reaches the affine full-frame groups that every irrep- or surjective-exp-based method must exclude. We call it Lie-Algebra Attention. Once tokens are group elements, the rest follows with none of the usual representation-theoretic machinery. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical, $g_i^{-1} g_j$, so the pairwise invariant $w_{ij} = \log(g_i^{-1} g_j)$ is intrinsic rather than designed; equivariance under the diagonal $G$-action is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm, $s_{ij} = -\|\log(g_i^{-1} g_j)\|_λ^2/τ$: the canonical proximity kernel under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product, with no irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernel. The construction applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses, including the non-compact non-abelian affine groups with scale and shear that no vector-token attention method reaches: neither the irrep tradition nor surjective-exp methods. Three sequence-completion experiments, on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2), bear this out: the closed-form score matches a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50 to 80x fewer score parameters, while a vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: Lie-Algebra Attention places tokens as bare matrix Lie group elements, using the closed-form negative squared algebra norm of the relative pose as the attention score, achieving a canonical, intrinsic, and parameter-efficient attention mechanism that extends to non-compact affine groups previously inaccessible to vector-token methods.
AI.motivation: Existing attention mechanisms treat tokens as feature vectors acted upon by group representations, requiring irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernels. These methods cannot reach non-compact non-abelian affine groups (with scale and shear). The authors aim to construct an attention mechanism where tokens are bare group elements, making invariance and equivariance tautological and eliminating representation-theoretic machinery.
AI.method: Tokens are elements g_i of a matrix Lie group G. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical: g_i^{-1} g_j. The pairwise invariant is w_{ij} = log(g_i^{-1} g_j). The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm: s_{ij} = -||log(g_i^{-1} g_j)||_λ^2 / τ, using a block-weighted Frobenius inner product. This applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses. No irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernels are needed.
AI.result: Three sequence-completion experiments on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2) demonstrate that the closed-form score matches or outperforms a learned MLP kernel (on SE(2)) while using 50–80× fewer score parameters. A vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Lie-Algebra Attention provides a canonical, parameter-efficient attention mechanism that is fully intrinsic to the group structure, extends to affine full-frame groups previously unreachable by vector-token methods, and maintains exact equivariance without learned or representation-theoretic components.

title: Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction
summary:
A model is multicalibrated on a collection of group weights $G$ if it is calibrated -- i.e. unbiased even conditional on its prediction -- not just overall, but also after reweighting contexts by each $g \in G$. It is a useful property for many downstream applications and is a basic desideratum of trustworthy machine learning. Before this work, all predictors known to attain the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors were known only with substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration was explicitly asked by [CLNR26] and implicitly in several prior works.
  We resolve this open problem by giving a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor. We then generalize the algorithm to produce optimal deterministic predictors that satisfy outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. As an application, this also gives deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors with optimal sample complexity, resolving open problems posed by [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the open problem of whether randomization is necessary for minimax-optimal sample complexity in multicalibration by presenting a deterministic algorithm achieving the $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate, and extends this to outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.
AI.motivation: Prior to this work, all known predictors achieving the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized; deterministic predictors had substantially worse sample complexity. This raised an explicit open question (posed by [CLNR26] and implicitly in earlier works) about whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration.
AI.method: The authors construct a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor, achieving the $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate. They then generalize this approach to produce deterministic predictors satisfying outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests, and further apply it to obtain deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors.
AI.result: The paper gives a deterministic multicalibration algorithm with minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity, matching the previously best known randomized upper bound. The generalization yields optimal deterministic predictors for outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors, resolving open problems from [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].
AI.conclusion: Randomization is not necessary for achieving optimal sample complexity in multicalibration. The deterministic construction unifies and strengthens results across multicalibration, outcome indistinguishability, omniprediction, and panprediction, settling several open problems simultaneously.

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
comment: 20 main text pages and 6 pages of references and appendices
summary: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmic transparency, whether we can use these snapshots to reconstruct the process by which the model arrived at its outputs. Naively, DiffusionGemma has poor variable transparency: its opaque serial depth, the amount of serial computation that occurs in between interpretable model states, seems at first 28.6X higher than the corresponding autoregressive Gemma 4 model. However, we show that we can map the information flowing between denoising steps through an interpretable token bottleneck with no decrease in downstream performance. Treating these intermediate states as interpretable reduces the opaque serial depth to just 1.1X that of Gemma 4. Algorithmic transparency is harder for diffusion models than for autoregressive models because all token predictions in the canvas can change at every denoising step, giving the model the power to implement complicated distributed algorithms during the denoising process. To begin bridging this gap, we conduct a suite of interpretability case studies, uncovering initial evidence of novel diffusion-specific phenomena such as non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Finally, we test monitorability, a key application of transparency that measures whether model outputs are useful for downstream tasks. We find that DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether diffusion language models (specifically DiffusionGemma) are less transparent than autoregressive models (Gemma 4) due to computation in continuous latent space. It decomposes transparency into variable transparency and algorithmic transparency, shows that token-bottleneck mapping reduces the opaque serial depth gap from 28.6X to 1.1X, identifies novel diffusion-specific reasoning phenomena, and finds comparable monitorability between the two architectures.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning transparency is critical for understanding decisions, mitigating misuse, and debugging. DiffusionGemma performs much of its computation in continuous latent space, raising the question of whether this fundamentally compromises transparency compared to autoregressive models like Gemma 4.
AI.method: The authors decompose transparency into: (1) variable transparency — whether intermediate computational states are interpretable; and (2) algorithmic transparency — whether these states allow reconstruction of the reasoning process. They measure opaque serial depth (serial computation between interpretable states), propose mapping information flow through an interpretable token bottleneck without performance loss, and conduct interpretability case studies to uncover diffusion-specific phenomena (non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing, intermediate-context reasoning). They also test monitorability as a downstream transparency application.
AI.result: Naively, DiffusionGemma's opaque serial depth is 28.6X higher than Gemma 4. After introducing the token-bottleneck mapping, this gap reduces to 1.1X with no downstream performance degradation. Case studies reveal novel diffusion-specific behaviors: non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Monitorability is found to be similar between DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion language models are not inherently less transparent than autoregressive models. With appropriate interpretability techniques (token-bottleneck mapping), variable transparency can approach parity. However, algorithmic transparency remains more challenging due to diffusion models' ability to revise all tokens at each step, enabling distributed algorithms. The novel phenomena uncovered warrant further interpretability research tailored to diffusion architectures.

title: Editorial Alignment: A Participatory Approach to Engaging Editorial Expertise in LLM-mediated Knowledge Dissemination
summary: The emergence of LLM-driven information services is reshaping the conditions under which public knowledge institutions operate, threatening to absorb the editorial function these institutions exist to exercise. While LLMs offer powerful new affordances for knowledge dissemination, editorial authority is challenged by pretrained LLMs that arrive already aligned with the values and dissemination strategies of their commercial developers. This paper investigates editor participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces to editorial standards through design workshops, in a case study where we design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic public knowledge institution. We introduce editorial alignment as a design practice within Participatory AI, framing AI alignment as a design process and positioning the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation. Last, we discuss how editorial alignment can create space for ongoing participation and give editors agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how public knowledge institutions can reclaim editorial authority in LLM-driven information services through "editorial alignment"—a participatory design practice that translates editorial standards into AI alignment objectives, demonstrated via a case study building an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic institution.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven information services threaten to absorb the editorial function of public knowledge institutions by imposing commercially-aligned values and dissemination strategies, undermining the institutional authority these organizations exist to exercise over public knowledge curation.
AI.method: The authors conducted design workshops with editors from a Nordic public knowledge institution, collaboratively designing and implementing an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface. They frame this process through Participatory AI, introducing "editorial alignment" as a design practice wherein editorial standards are treated as design artefacts that translate editorial values into concrete alignment objectives for technical implementation.
AI.result: The case study demonstrates that editor participation can re-align LLM interfaces to institutional editorial standards, producing a functioning encyclopedia interface that reflects the institution's values rather than those of the commercial LLM developer.
AI.conclusion: Editorial alignment creates space for ongoing participation, giving editors meaningful agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination. It positions AI alignment as a design process and editorial standards as design artefacts, enabling public knowledge institutions to maintain their editorial function within emerging LLM-driven information ecosystems.
